docs.title: Zeit — Change detection and time series for satellite imagery
docs.text:
1990 2000 2010 2024 Year of loss One pixel, 40 years of Landsat NDVI 0.2 0.5 0.8 1990 2000 2010 2020 cleared in 2003 observedLandTrendr fit

The stack: 40 years of Landsat NDVI over Rondônia, Brazil, one image per year. Zeit reads each pixel through the stack as a time series and finds when it changed; the map on top is LandTrendr's year of the largest loss, for 2.8 million pixels in about 5 seconds on a desktop CPU. Data: annual Landsat NDVI composites exported from LT-GEE.

docs.title: Find when and where the landscape changed.
docs.text:
Zeit is an ultra-fast Python library for analysing satellite image time series. Reference algorithms such as LandTrendr, CCDC and BFAST are re-engineered in parallel Rust and validated against their original implementations. Use them to detect deforestation, fires, regrowth, crop cycles and long-term trends. Full scenes run on a laptop using every core, and the same code scales out in parallel to your own cluster or the cloud with Dask.

Get started See what it can do GitHub

pip install zeit-cdts

docs.title: What is Zeit?
docs.text:
Every satellite pixel has a history. Stack images of the same place over time and each pixel becomes a time series: a line that stays flat while a forest stands, drops when it is cleared, and climbs back as it regrows. Most land-change questions come down to reading those lines. Did something change? When? How much? Was it sudden or gradual?

The circled pixel was forest until 2002, then was cleared. Seen as a time series, the event is obvious. Zeit finds events like this in every pixel of an image. Data: annual Landsat NDVI composites exported from LT-GEE on Google Earth Engine.

Zeit gives you the standard scientific methods for reading these time series, plus the plumbing around them. It can pull imagery from cloud catalogs, mask clouds, fill gaps, run the analysis in parallel, and write maps back out as GeoTIFF or Zarr.

Gallery

docs.title: What you can do with Zeit
docs.text:
Every image below was produced by Zeit itself. Click one to open its tutorial.

Change detectionMap forest loss and regrowthLandTrendr turns yearly images into maps of when, how much and how fast change happened.

Change detectionMeasure how land recoversYears to recovery, R80P and the relative recovery after each disturbance, from LandTrendr or any annual series.

Change detectionDetect change in dense time seriesCCDC models each pixel's seasonal cycle and flags the moment it breaks.

Change detectionWeigh every possible changeBEAST averages thousands of models of the trend and the season, and says how probable each changepoint is.

MonitoringWatch every new imageS-CCD carries CCDC's models forward with a Kalman filter and flags changes still in progress.

MonitoringRaise near-real-time alertsBFAST Monitor tests each new image against a stable history.

MonitoringMonitor irregular, cloudy seriesEWMACD follows every observation with control charts and dates disturbances, gains and recoveries.

TrendsMap greening and browningMann-Kendall and Theil-Sen give a robust, significance-tested trend per pixel.

TrendsTest a region's trendPARTS asks whether a region, or each land-cover class, is really trending, accounting for correlated pixels.

Space-time patternsFind emerging hot spotsWhere values cluster high or low, and how that changed: new, intensifying, persistent or sporadic hot spots.

PhenologyExtract crop and vegetation calendarsStart, peak and end of season, plus 16 more metrics, for every year.

ClassificationClassify by temporal signatureTWDTW matches each pixel to reference patterns, even when seasons shift.

Spectral mixturesUnmix pixels into materialsThe fraction of vegetation, soil, water or any endmember in every pixel and date, fully constrained.

SegmentationGroup pixels into objectsSNIC superpixels group pixels whose whole trajectories are similar.

ClusteringDiscover patterns without labelsSelf-organizing maps (a bit-exact, much faster port of minisom) cluster millions of trajectories into a few prototypes.

Deep learningTrain land-cover classifiersPyTorch models (TempCNN, LightTAE, U-TAE) written from the papers and the authors' code.

After classifyingClean maps and know where they holdBayesian smoothing, a minimum mapping unit, and the area of applicability: where the model's samples say nothing.

From FORCE

docs.title: From a Sentinel-2 scene to a ready series
docs.text:
Several of FORCE's steps (Frantz 2019, Remote Sensing 11:1124; FORCE 3.11.00, David Frantz, GPL-3.0-or-later) are Zeit functions that take and return the same arrays as the rest of the library, with Zeit's own Fmask 4.7 (Qiu, Zhu and Woodcock 2019) inside the atmospheric correction.

  • Level 1C to surface reflectance

    level2 corrects a Sentinel-2 Level 1C scene, on disk or downloaded by name (find_l1c, download_l1c, download_dem): water vapour, aerosols from the scene's dark targets, adjacency, topography, BRDF, and a cloud, shadow, snow and water mask. Given FORCE's cloud flags, sun, geography and BRDF factor it equals force-l2ps in every pixel; with Zeit's own, its Fmask agrees with FORCE's in 98.1 % of the pixels in cloud or shadow. Sentinel-2 only, on the scene's 10 m grid.

    Tutorial · API

  • Prepare the images

    Co-register dates to a reference (coregister, coregister_local), normalise the view angles (nbar, sentinel2_angles), take Landsat and MODIS to Sentinel-2's bands (spectral_adjust), compute the Tasseled Cap, bring the 20 m bands to 10 m (sentinel2_resmerge), sharpen coarse data (improphe) and pansharpen (pansharpen).

    Tutorial · API

  • FORCE's time series chain

    Interpolate a cloudy series, summarise it by year or season with temporal_metrics, and read the dates, values and rates of each growing season with polar_metrics.

    Tutorial · API

Workflow

docs.title: How a Zeit analysis fits together
docs.text:
Get the data

Stream a cube from a STAC catalog, Earth Engine or local GeoTIFFs.

build_time_series · download_gee_timeseries

Clean it

Correct a Sentinel-2 scene, align the dates, mask clouds, composite to a regular time step, smooth noise.

level2 · coregister · tmask · regularize_time_series · smooth

Analyse every pixel

Run change detection, trends, phenology or a classifier.

landtrendr · ccdc

Map the result

Turn per-pixel output into maps, look at them, and write GeoTIFF or Zarr.

extract_events · plot · save_raster

The same analysis in three styles. Pick the one that fits your data:

Raster fileXarray / Dask cubeCommand line 
import zeit

ndvi = zeit.load_raster("ndvi_1985_2024.tif", start_year=1985)   # (time, y, x), georeferenced

lt = zeit.landtrendr(ndvi)                            # looks for NDVI drops (direction="loss")
loss = zeit.extract_events(lt, min_magnitude=2000)    # greatest loss per pixel

zeit.plot(ndvi, fit=lt)                               # page through the years, click a pixel to see its fit
zeit.save_raster(loss, "lt_results")                  # one GeoTIFF per map: yod.tif, magnitude.tif, ...

import zeit  # registers the .zeit accessor on xarray objects

cube = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="earth_search", collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
    bbox=[-63.2, -10.2, -63.0, -10.0],
    start_date="2019-01-01", end_date="2024-12-31",
    bands=["red", "nir"], apply_cloud_mask=True,
)
ndvi = (cube.sel(band="nir") - cube.sel(band="red")) / (cube.sel(band="nir") + cube.sel(band="red"))
ndvi_16d = zeit.regularize_time_series(ndvi, freq="16D", method="median")

trend = ndvi_16d.zeit.mann_kendall(method="seasonal", period=23)
trend.to_zarr("ndvi_trend.zarr", consolidated=True)   # computed chunk by chunk, in parallel

# No Python needed: every core algorithm is also a CLI subcommand.
zeit landtrendr ndvi_1985_2024.tif results/ --start-year 1985 --event-type loss --min-mag 2000
zeit mmu-filter results/lt_event_yod.tif results/lt_event_yod_clean.tif --mmu-pixels 11

Why Zeit

docs.title: Built for trustworthy results at scale
docs.text:
100%vertex-for-vertex agreement with the original LandTrendr IDL code, and segment-for-segment (dates, categories, observation counts) with CCDC MATLAB 232×faster than the reference LandTrendr on one core, with more from its threads 19×higher throughput than Google Earth Engine on a full Landsat tile, with no queue 0compilers needed. Pre-built wheels for Windows, macOS and Linux

  • Faithful to the originals

    Each algorithm is ported from its reference implementation (IDL, MATLAB, R) and tested against it, for its results and for its speed. You get the published method, not an approximation.

    Fidelity reports · Against the originals

  • Fast by default

    The per-pixel work runs in Rust, on every core and outside the Python GIL. A laptop can process scenes that used to need a cloud platform.

    Performance

  • Scales without rewrites

    The .zeit xarray accessor maps every algorithm over Dask chunks, so the same script runs on one machine or a cluster.

    Scaling up

  • One toolbox, end to end

    Data access, Sentinel-2 atmospheric correction, cloud masking, smoothing, unmixing, change detection, monitoring, recovery, trends, hot spots, phenology, segmentation, deep learning, post-processing and plotting all use the same array conventions.

    API reference

docs.title: Command Line Interface
docs.text: Run the core algorithms on GeoTIFF stacks straight from the terminal, with no Python code. Useful for shell scripts, cron jobs and HPC schedulers. Each command reads and writes files block by block, so inputs can be larger than memory.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
The CLI is structured around subcommands for each algorithm. You can invoke the CLI using the zeit command (if installed via pip) or by executing the python module directly:

zeit <algorithm> [OPTIONS] <input_file> <output_directory>
(Alternatively: python -m zeit.cli <algorithm> ...)

To run a command on a whole folder of tiles, on this computer and on others of the local network, see Many tiles, on this and other computers.

To get general help or see the list of available commands: 

zeit --help

docs.title: 1. LandTrendr (landtrendr)
docs.text: The landtrendr command processes a multi-band GeoTIFF representing a time series of a single spectral index (e.g., NBR, NDVI) and extracts spatial change events.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: zeit landtrendr <input> <output_dir> [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Positional Arguments
docs.text: Argument Type Description input filepath Path to the input multi-band GeoTIFF. Each band must represent a single year, in chronological order. output_dir dirpath Directory where the resulting event maps (Year of Detection, Magnitude, Duration) will be saved.

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --start-year int read from the file The calendar year of the first band. By default the years are read from the band descriptions (e.g. yr1985), as zeit.load_raster does; pass it for stacks whose bands are not named by year. --max-segments int 6 The maximum number of line segments the algorithm can fit per pixel. --jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, a share of them on a machine several users are logged in to, or every core of a cluster job (see zeit doctor). --chunk-size int 512 Size of the image chunks (in pixels) processed simultaneously to manage RAM. --save-vertices flag False If provided, saves the raw multi-band GeoTIFF containing all fitted vertices. --no-data-value float the raster's NoData, or 0 Value marking a missing year. By default the raster's NoData value, or 0 for integer stacks without one (how Earth Engine exports masked pixels). NaN is always missing.

docs.title: Event Extraction Options
docs.text:
These options control how specific change events are extracted from the temporal trajectory:

Option Type Default Description --event-type str loss Type of event to segment for and map. Choices: loss (value decreases) or gain (value increases). It sets both LandTrendr's direction and the events extracted. --sort-by str greatest How to select the event if multiple occur. Choices: greatest, newest, fastest, longest, dsnr. --min-mag float 0.0 Filter out events with a magnitude lower than this threshold. --min-dur int 1 Filter out events shorter than this duration in years. --pre-val-thresh float 0.0 Filter out events if the starting value was already below this threshold. --output-scale float 1.0 Scale factor applied to the output. Useful for converting scaled integers back to floats (e.g., 0.0001). --prefix str lt_event Prefix added to all output file names.

docs.title: End-to-End Example
docs.text:
Run LandTrendr on a 30-year NBR stack, extracting the greatest vegetation loss, using every core but one, and converting the output back to floating point (assuming NBR was scaled by 10000): 

zeit landtrendr ./data/nbr_stack_1990_2020.tif ./results \
    --start-year 1990 \
    --max-segments 6 \
    --event-type loss \
    --sort-by greatest \
    --output-scale 0.0001 \
    --jobs -1

docs.title: 2. Continuous Change Detection (ccdc)
docs.text: The ccdc command runs zeit.ccdc on a dense, multi-band, multi-date GeoTIFF, reading it block by block, and writes each pixel's segments as GeoTIFFs. Values must be surface reflectance × 10,000, bands ordered Blue, Green, Red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2 [, thermal].

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: zeit ccdc <input> <output_dir> [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Positional Arguments
docs.text: Argument Type Description input filepath Path to the input GeoTIFF. Either its bands are named date_band (2020-01-15_blue, 2020-01-15_green, …, as zeit.save_raster writes a (time, band, y, x) cube), and the dates are read from them; or it is interleaved by date (Date1-Band1, Date1-Band2, …, Date2-Band1, …) without such names, with --dates-file and --num-bands. output_dir dirpath Directory where the segment rasters will be saved.

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --dates-file str None Text file with one date per line, an ISO date (2020-01-15) or a Python ordinal day (737439), for a stack without dates in its band names. --num-bands int 6 With --dates-file: the number of bands per date in a stack interleaved by date, including the QA band. --qa-band int -1 The zero-based index, among the bands of each date, of a band of Fmask codes (0 clear, 1 water, 2 shadow, 3 snow, 4 cloud, 255 no observation). It is not used as a spectral band. -1: no QA band, every observation is clear. --max-segments int 6 The maximum number of segments to retain per pixel. --conse int 6 Consecutive anomalous observations that confirm a break (conseq_anom), as in the original CCDC. --chunk-size int 512 Size of the image blocks (in pixels) processed at once. --jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, a share of them on a machine several users are logged in to, or every core of a cluster job (see zeit doctor). --cold flag False Deprecated: the same as --conse 6, now the default. --prefix str ccdc Prefix added to all output GeoTIFF files.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
File Bands Content <prefix>_t_start.tif, <prefix>_t_end.tif one per segment First and last date of each segment, as decimal years (NaN past the last segment). <prefix>_t_break.tif one per segment Date of the break that ended each segment, as a decimal year (NaN: no break). <prefix>_n_segments.tif 1 Number of segments per pixel. <prefix>_rmse.tif one per segment and band (1_blue, …) RMSE of each band's fit. <prefix>_coefs.tif one per segment, band and coefficient (1_blue_a0, 1_blue_c1, …) The harmonic coefficients a0, c1, a1, b1, a2, b2, a3, b3 (see zeit.ccdc).

In a stack interleaved by date, the bands are named b1, b2, … (1_b1_a0, …).

docs.title: End-to-End Example
docs.text:
Run CCDC on a stack written by zeit.save_raster, whose 7th band of each date (index 6) holds the Fmask codes: 

zeit ccdc ./data/landsat_sr.tif ./results \
    --qa-band 6 \
    --max-segments 8 \
    --jobs -1

The same on a stack interleaved by date, with 6 spectral bands and 1 QA band per date, and the dates in a text file: 

zeit ccdc ./data/dense_stack.tif ./results \
    --dates-file ./data/dates.txt \
    --num-bands 7 \
    --qa-band 6

docs.title: 3. BFAST Monitor (bfast-monitor)
docs.text:
The bfast-monitor command runs zeit.bfast_monitor on a multi-band GeoTIFF where every band is one equally-spaced observation (e.g. a 16-day composite), reading it block by block. Time is regular, as in R's ts: observation i is at start_time + i / frequency. Both are read from the band dates (descriptions such as 2020-01-15, as zeit.save_raster writes them); give --start-time and --frequency for a stack without dates. See the BFAST Monitor tutorial for the full method background.

The four time-series commands (bfast-monitor, bfast-lite, bfast, mann-kendall) write one GeoTIFF, <output_dir>/<prefix>.tif, with one float32 band per metric, named after it.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: zeit bfast-monitor <input> <output_dir> --monitor-start-time <year or date> [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Positional Arguments
docs.text: Argument Type Description input filepath Path to the input multi-band GeoTIFF. Each band is one equally-spaced time step. output_dir dirpath Directory where the single output GeoTIFF (7 bands, see below) will be saved.

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description --monitor-start-time float or date (required) When monitoring begins, as a decimal year (2019.0) or a date (2019-01-01): the boundary between the stable "history" and "monitoring" periods. --start-time float from the band dates The series' start time (e.g. 2015.0). --frequency int from the band dates Observations per year (e.g. 23 for 16-day composites). --order int 3 Harmonic order for the seasonal regressors. --h float 0.25 MOSUM window size, as a fraction of history length. Must be one of 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. --period int 10 Monitoring period parameter. Must be one of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. --alpha float 0.05 Significance level for the monitoring boundary. --min-valid int 10 Minimum valid (non-NaN) history observations per pixel. --chunk-size int 512 Size of the image chunks to process simultaneously. --jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, a share of them on a machine several users are logged in to, or every core of a cluster job (see zeit doctor). --prefix str bfast_monitor Filename (without extension) for the output GeoTIFF.

Output bands (in order): breakpoint, breakpoint_idx, magnitude, sigma, n_history, has_break, valid (see zeit.bfast_monitor).

docs.title: End-to-End Example
docs.text:
zeit bfast-monitor ./data/ndvi_16day_stack.tif ./results \
    --monitor-start-time 2019-01-01 \
    --jobs -1

# A stack without dates in its band names: give the time axis
zeit bfast-monitor ./data/ndvi_16day_stack.tif ./results \
    --start-time 2015.0 --frequency 23 --monitor-start-time 2019.0

docs.title: 4. BFAST Lite (bfast-lite)
docs.text: The bfast-lite command runs zeit.bfast_lite: it retrospectively segments the whole series into an optimal number of pieces in a single pass - the modern, non-iterative alternative to classic bfast. Input and time axis as for bfast-monitor. See the BFAST Lite tutorial.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: zeit bfast-lite <input> <output_dir> [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description --start-time float from the band dates The series' start time (e.g. 2010.0). --frequency int from the band dates Observations per year. --order int 3 Harmonic order. --h float 0.15 Minimum segment size, as a fraction of the series length. --max-breaks-output int 5 Maximum number of breakpoints to report per pixel (max_breaks in Python). --min-valid int 20 Minimum valid observations per pixel. --chunk-size int 512 Size of the image chunks to process simultaneously. --jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, a share of them on a machine several users are logged in to, or every core of a cluster job (see zeit doctor). --prefix str bfast_lite Filename (without extension) for the output GeoTIFF.

Output bands: n_breaks, rss, lwz, n_valid, valid, breakpoint_idx_1..N (see zeit.bfast_lite).

docs.title: End-to-End Example
docs.text: zeit bfast-lite ./data/ndvi_16day_stack.tif ./results --max-breaks-output 5

docs.title: 5. Classic BFAST (bfast)
docs.text: The bfast command runs zeit.bfast, the original iterative bfast() algorithm: an STL seasonal seed followed by alternating trend/season segmented regressions, distinguishing trend breaks from seasonal (phenological) breaks. Input and time axis as for bfast-monitor. See the BFAST tutorial for the full method background, scope notes, and R cross-validation results.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: zeit bfast <input> <output_dir> [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description --start-time float from the band dates The series' start time (e.g. 2000.0). --frequency int from the band dates Observations per year. Requires more than 2 * frequency total observations. --order int 3 Harmonic order for the season sub-model. --h float 0.15 Minimum segment size (both trend and season), as a fraction of valid observations. --max-breaks-trend int 5 Maximum number of trend breakpoints to report per pixel. --max-breaks-season int 5 Maximum number of season breakpoints to report per pixel. --max-iter int 10 Maximum trend/season re-estimation iterations. --level float 0.05 Significance threshold for the preliminary structural-stability pre-check. --min-valid int 20 Minimum valid observations per pixel. --chunk-size int 512 Size of the image chunks to process simultaneously. --jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, a share of them on a machine several users are logged in to, or every core of a cluster job (see zeit doctor). --prefix str bfast Filename (without extension) for the output GeoTIFF.

Output bands: n_trend_breaks, n_season_breaks, magnitude, break_time, n_iter, n_valid, valid, trend_breakpoint_idx_1..N, season_breakpoint_idx_1..N (see zeit.bfast).

docs.title: End-to-End Example
docs.text: zeit bfast ./data/ndvi_16day_stack.tif ./results

docs.title: 6. Mann-Kendall Trend Test (mann-kendall)
docs.text: The mann-kendall command runs zeit.mann_kendall, the pixel-wise Mann-Kendall trend test and Theil-Sen slope estimator, across a multi-band GeoTIFF (one band per observation - typically one annual composite per band). No dates are needed. See the Mann-Kendall tutorial.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: zeit mann-kendall <input> <output_dir> [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description --method str hamed_rao Trend test variant. Choices: original, hamed_rao (autocorrelation-corrected, recommended), yue_wang, seasonal. --alpha float 0.05 Significance level. --lag int None First significant lags for the autocorrelation correction (hamed_rao/yue_wang only). Defaults to the full series length. --period int 1 Season slots for --method seasonal (e.g. 23 for MODIS 16-day cycles), letting a raw sub-annual series be tested directly. --min-valid int 4 Minimum valid observations per pixel. --chunk-size int 512 Size of the image chunks to process simultaneously. --jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, a share of them on a machine several users are logged in to, or every core of a cluster job (see zeit doctor). --prefix str mann_kendall Filename (without extension) for the output GeoTIFF.

Output bands: trend, h, p, z, tau, s, var_s, slope, intercept. slope/intercept are per time step (per band), so one observation per year gives a directly interpretable per-year trend.

docs.title: End-to-End Example
docs.text: zeit mann-kendall ./data/annual_ndvi_stack.tif ./results --method hamed_rao --jobs -1

docs.title: 7. Minimum Mapping Unit Filter (mmu-filter)
docs.text: The mmu-filter command applies a spatial Minimum Mapping Unit (MMU) filter to a single-band raster - typically a disturbance-year map from landtrendr - removing isolated pixel groups smaller than a given size to reduce "salt and pepper" noise.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: zeit mmu-filter <input> <output> [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Positional Arguments
docs.text: Argument Type Description input filepath Path to the input single-band GeoTIFF (e.g. a landtrendr year-of-detection map). output filepath Path to save the filtered GeoTIFF.

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Description --mmu-pixels int 11 Minimum connected-patch size, in pixels. Smaller patches are zeroed out (treated as the raster's nodata/background value).

docs.title: End-to-End Example
docs.text: zeit mmu-filter ./results/lt_event_yod.tif ./results/lt_event_yod_mmu.tif --mmu-pixels 9

docs.title: The other cube functions
docs.text:
phenology, smooth, tmask, twdtw, snic, classify, som, coded and bandpass-adjust run the Python function of the same name on any raster load_raster reads, with the dates in the band names (as save_raster writes them, yr1985, 2020-01-15 or 2020-01-15_red for a time × band stack). They share the same syntax and options, and write <output_dir>/<prefix>.tif, one band per map (or per date), computed block by block in one pass:

zeit <command> <input> <output_dir> [OPTIONS]
Option Type Default Description --chunk-size int 512 Size of the image chunks to process at once. --jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, a share of them on a machine several users are logged in to, or every core of a cluster job (see zeit doctor). --prefix str the command Name of the output file, without extension.

docs.title: 8. Phenology (phenology)
docs.text:
zeit.phenology: one band per metric (and year). See the phenology tutorial.

Option Type Default Description --curve str beck beck, elmore, gu, klos, zhang, ag or dl. --method str threshold threshold, derivative, gu or klosterman. --weights filepath None A raster of observation weights in [0, 1] on the input's grid and dates (e.g. written from zeit.qc_sentinel2_scl). --not-annual flag Metrics per season instead of per calendar year. --max-seasons int years Seasons to report. --whittaker-lambda float 10 Whittaker smoothing before the fit. 
zeit phenology ./data/s2_ndvi_2019_2023.tif ./results --curve elmore --weights ./data/s2_weights.tif

docs.title: 9. Smoothing (smooth)
docs.text:
zeit.smooth: the smoothed series, same dates and type.

Option Type Default Description --method str whittaker whittaker (uneven dates, gaps filled) or savgol. --lmbda float 10 Whittaker: smoothness. --weights filepath None Whittaker: a raster of observation weights in [0, 1]. --window, --polyorder int 5, 2 Savitzky-Golay: window length and polynomial order. 
zeit smooth ./data/ndvi_16d.tif ./results --lmbda 20

docs.title: 10. Cloud and shadow screening (tmask)
docs.text:
zeit.tmask on a (time, band) stack (bands named date_band): one band per date, 1 clear, 0 cloud, shadow or no data.

Option Type Default Description --green, --swir str green, swir1 Names of the green and SWIR-1 bands. --scale float 10000 Reflectance scale of the stack (1 for 0-1 floats). 
zeit tmask ./data/landsat_sr_stack.tif ./results

docs.title: 11. TWDTW classification (twdtw)
docs.text:
zeit.twdtw: bands label, distance and one distance per pattern. The patterns come from a CSV with the columns pattern, date and one value column (or one column per band, named as the input's bands):

pattern,date,ndvi
soy,2022-10-01,0.25
soy,2022-11-01,0.48
...
pasture,2022-10-01,0.55
Option Type Default Description --patterns filepath required The CSV of patterns. --band str None A multi-band input with one-band patterns: the band to classify. --steepness, --midpoint float 0.1, 50 The logistic time weight (midpoint in days). --max-elapsed float None Never match observations farther apart than this many days. --no-cycle flag Measure elapsed time between the dates, not between days of the year. 
zeit twdtw ./data/ndvi_2022.tif ./results --patterns ./data/patterns.csv

docs.title: 12. SNIC segmentation (snic)
docs.text:
zeit.snic: the segment labels (the input is read into memory). --polygons also writes <prefix>.gpkg, the segments as polygons with their means.

Option Type Default Description --spacing float 10 Pixels between seeds. --compactness float 0.5 Larger: more regular segments (in data units). --grid str rectangular rectangular, diamond, hexagonal or random. --polygons flag Also write the polygons. 
zeit snic ./data/s2_ndvi_2022.tif ./results --spacing 8 --polygons

docs.title: 13. Classification (classify)
docs.text:
zeit.train_classifier and zeit.classify in one call: a random forest trained on sample points (each band, or date and band, a feature) classifies every pixel. Bands label (and each class's probability with --probability).

Option Type Default Description --samples filepath None Vector file of points with their class. --label str class Column of the samples holding the class. --model filepath None With --samples: where to save the trained model (joblib). Without: a saved model to classify with. --probability flag Also write each class's probability. 
zeit classify ./data/s2_2022.tif ./results --samples ./data/samples.gpkg --model ./results/rf.joblib
zeit classify ./data/s2_2023.tif ./results_2023 --model ./results/rf.joblib      # the same model, next year

docs.title: 14. SOM clustering (som)
docs.text:
zeit.som: bands label and distance, and <prefix>_prototypes.csv with one row per neuron (neuron, its grid position i/j, n_pixels, then the prototype, one column per date or date and band).

Option Type Default Description --x, --y int 3, 3 Neurons of the grid. --sample int 50000 Pixels to train on, at random (0 for all). --algorithm str online online or batch. --sigma, --learning-rate float 1.0, 0.5 Initial neighbourhood radius and learning rate. --seed int 42 Random seed. 
zeit som ./data/LT_Stack_NDVI_Rondonia.tif ./results --x 2 --y 2 --sample 30000

docs.title: 15. Bandpass adjustment (bandpass-adjust)
docs.text:
zeit.bandpass_adjust: the reflectance series with its Sentinel-2 dates on Landsat 8's OLI bands (HLS's bandpass step only), as <output_dir>/<prefix>.tif with the input's bands and type. A GeoTIFF does not say which sensor took each date, so --sensor does.

Option Type Default Description --sensor str ... required The sensor of every date (sentinel-2a, S2B, landsat-8...), or one per date. --etm str None rma or ols: also take Landsat 5/7 dates to OLI (Roy et al. 2016). --scale float auto Reflectance scale of the stack: 10000 for integers or values above 2, else 1. 
zeit bandpass-adjust ./data/s2_2023.tif ./results --sensor sentinel-2b --prefix s2_2023_oli

docs.title: 16. Embeddings (embeddings)
docs.text:
zeit.load_embeddings: download the yearly embeddings of a foundation model over a region into one GeoTIFF, <output_dir>/<prefix>.tif, one band per year and dimension (2024_A00, 2024_A01...), which zeit.load_raster reads back as a (time, band, y, x) cube that remembers which embeddings it holds. Unlike the other commands it takes no input raster: the region is given by --bbox or --region.

Option Type Default Description --source str required tessera or alphaearth. --bbox 4 float None West, south, east, north in longitude and latitude. --region filepath None Vector file of the region; cells outside its polygons are NoData. --years str all Years, e.g. 2018 2020 or 2018-2024. --crs, --res str, float the region's UTM zone, 10 Output CRS and cell size. --version, --variant, --depth v1.1 TESSERA: dataset version and variant; the first DEPTH dimensions of a v2 store. --backend str source.coop AlphaEarth: the open COGs or gee (Earth Engine). --store filepath None A local copy of the product to read instead of the public one. --cache-dir filepath ~/.cache/zeit/embeddings Where downloads are kept. --prefix str the source Name of the output file. 
zeit embeddings ./results --source tessera --bbox -63.0 -10.0 -62.9 -9.9 --years 2018-2024
zeit classify ./results/tessera.tif ./results --samples ./data/samples.gpkg   # every year and dimension a feature

docs.title: Many tiles, on this and other computers
17. Many tiles, here and on other computers
docs.text:
Every command that reads one raster (landtrendr, ccdc, bfast-monitor, bfast-lite, bfast, mann-kendall, phenology, smooth, tmask, twdtw, snic, classify, som, coded, bandpass-adjust) also runs on a whole folder of tiles, with the same options, writing <output_dir>/<tile name>/ per tile. Add --helpers and the computers of the local network running zeit worker process tiles too. The Python form is zeit.run_tiles; the tutorial, with what limits the speed, is Many tiles on several computers.

zeit landtrendr nbr_tiles/ lt_out/ --tiles                    # every tile, on this computer
zeit landtrendr nbr_tiles/ lt_out/ --helpers                  # here and on the helpers
zeit landtrendr nbr_tiles/ lt_out/ --helpers --no-local       # only on the helpers; this computer stays free
zeit landtrendr nbr_tiles/ lt_out/ --helpers --local-cores 4  # here with 4 cores, and on the helpers
zeit landtrendr "nbr_tiles/LT_2*.tif" lt_out/ --tiles         # a quoted glob instead of a folder
zeit landtrendr urls.txt lt_out/ --helpers                    # URLs, one per line: each computer downloads its tiles
Option Type Default Description --tiles flag False The input is a folder of tiles (its .tif files) or a quoted glob: run every tile. --helpers flag False Also send tiles to the helpers of this computer's group (implies --tiles). --no-local flag False With --helpers: process nothing here, only hand out the tiles and collect the results. --local-cores int --jobs Cores for the tiles processed here (as --jobs -1 by default: all but one, all of a cluster job's). Each helper uses the cores it lends. --port int 47801 TCP port the helpers connect to. --shard I/N Process part I (from 0) of N of the tiles, tile k being part k mod N's (implies --tiles). In a Slurm job array the part is the task's without it. --requeue flag False In a Slurm job: when stopped by SIGTERM before the time limit (#SBATCH --signal=B:TERM@120), requeue the job to continue with the tiles left, if it finished at least one.
  • Resumable. Finished tiles are kept: running the same command again processes only the others. Running it with other options into the same output folder is refused rather than mixing results.
  • Where the helpers read the tiles. From shared storage (a NAS) when they see the same file, otherwise this computer sends it (a file stored without compression goes as a lossless ZSTD copy); a helper keeps the tiles it received (20 GB by default), so another run does not send them again. Given a .txt file of URLs, each computer downloads the tiles it processes. Tiles built from STAC or Earth Engine on each computer: zeit.stac_tiles, zeit.gee_tiles (Python).
  • Where the results go. A helper that sees the output folder too (a NAS) writes into it; otherwise it sends them back.
  • Progress. One line with the tiles done, the computers at work, the network rate and the time left; the helpers that join or leave; a tile that fails (tried again elsewhere, given up after two failures and listed at the end, with exit code 1).
  • Files used by every tile (--patterns of twdtw, --dates-file of ccdc, --model of classify, --training of coded) are sent to the helpers. Options naming a file of one raster (--weights, --samples) cannot be used with many tiles.

docs.title: 18. Lending a computer (zeit worker)
docs.text:
Run on each computer that helps. It waits for a computer of its group that runs tiles, processes the tiles it gets with all the cores it lends, and waits again, until Ctrl+C. The first time, it joins the group with the code shown by zeit helpers invite.

zeit worker --join K7QM-2XDP     # the first time
zeit worker                      # from then on
zeit worker --cores 6            # lend only 6 cores
zeit worker --map "Z:\=/mnt/nas" # the NAS the coordinator sees as Z:\ is /mnt/nas here
Option Type Default Description --join str None The invitation code, the first time only. --cores int as --jobs -1 Cores to lend. --connect HOST[:PORT] None The coordinator's address, when broadcasts do not reach it (another subnet, a VPN). --map SRC=DST None A shared folder mounted elsewhere here (repeatable). Mapped Windows drives are sent as UNC paths (\\nas\tiles), which Windows helpers read without a map. --cache-dir dirpath the user's cache folder Where received tiles are kept. --cache-gb float 20 Space the kept tiles may take.

A helper only opens outgoing connections (no firewall rule on it) and only runs zeit's own commands. Both computers need the same zeit version; a helper with another one is told which to install. It keeps the computer from sleeping while it works.

docs.title: 19. The group (zeit helpers)
docs.text: Command What it does zeit helpers invite [--minutes 10] Shows a code (such as K7QM-2XDP) with which other computers join this computer's group, while it runs. Any computer of the group can then run tiles with the others' help. zeit helpers list [--seconds 5] The helpers waiting for work on the local network: name, address, cores, zeit version. Busy helpers do not show. zeit helpers firewall On Windows, creates the inbound rules (TCP 47801 and UDP 47800, from the local subnet only), asking for administrator rights once. Needed on the computer that runs tiles, not on the helpers. zeit helpers leave Takes this computer out of its group (forgets the group's secret).

docs.title: 20. Checking a computer (zeit doctor)
docs.text:
zeit doctor                 # threads, job, caches, network, versions
zeit doctor --no-network    # without checking the services

Prints what zeit finds where it runs: the threads --jobs -1 uses and where that number comes from (on a machine several users are logged in to, how many it counted), the job of Slurm, PBS or LSF and its array task, the caches and whether they can be written, whether the services zeit downloads from answer, and the versions. Run it in a job (srun zeit doctor) to see what a job of yours gets:

zeit 2.3.0 (Python 3.12.8, Linux x86_64, glibc 2.28)
Threads (n_jobs=-1): 16 threads (16 of 128 processors available to this process; Slurm job 123456)
  SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK=16
...

See Threads for how the count is made.

docs.title: 21. A job array for the tiles (zeit slurm)
docs.text:
zeit slurm landtrendr tiles/ out/ --cpus 16 --time 2:00:00 --max-segments 8   # writes the script
zeit slurm landtrendr tiles/ out/ --cpus 16 --time 2:00:00 --submit          # and submits it

Writes the Slurm job script that splits a folder of tiles among the tasks of a job array (one task per tile, up to 1000), prints it and saves it as out/.zeit-tiles/<command>.sbatch; --submit hands it to sbatch. Every task runs zeit <command> tiles/ out/ --tiles --requeue with the options given after the output folder (any of the command's, except --jobs: each task uses every processor it is given). The script sets the job's log per task (out/.zeit-tiles/logs/slurm-<job>_<task>.out), --signal=B:TERM@120 and --requeue, so that a task stopped at its time limit drops the tile at work and requeues itself.

Option Type Default Description --cpus int 16 Processors of each task (--cpus-per-task). --mem str suggested Memory of each task (32G). By default, from the command and the widest tile: a task holds one row of blocks of --chunk-size at a time, at most one block per processor (measured for LandTrendr and CCDC; the script says how it was reckoned). --time str the partition's Time limit of each task (2:00:00, 1-00:00:00). --partition, --account str Where the job runs, and who pays. --tasks int one per tile Tasks of the array; with fewer than tiles, each task processes several. --max-running int Tasks running at once (--array=0-49%N). --sbatch str Another #SBATCH line, e.g. --sbatch=--qos=long (repeatable). --setup str A line run before zeit, e.g. --setup "module load gdal" (repeatable). The script runs zeit with the Python it was written from, so an activated virtual environment needs no setup. --script path out/.zeit-tiles/<command>.sbatch Where to write the script. --submit flag False Submit it with sbatch.

docs.title: 22. The tiles of an output folder (zeit tiles status)
docs.text:
zeit tiles status out/

landtrendr in out: 120 tiles, 115 done, 2 failed, 3 not done
  failed: tile_031 (run 4242_31): MemoryError
          log: out/.zeit-tiles/logs/tile_031.log
  not started: tile_088, tile_101, tile_117
To process the 5 left: sbatch --array=31,40,88,101,117 out/.zeit-tiles/landtrendr.sbatch

What the runs that wrote into an output folder did, across the tasks of a job array: the tiles done, failed (with the error and the tile's log), not done (and those in runs that have not ended: still running, or killed), and the --array that submits again only the tasks with tiles left. Outside an array, run the same command again. Exit code 0 when every tile is done, 3 while some are left.

docs.title: 23. Downloading beforehand (zeit fetch)
docs.text:
zeit fetch weights                    # lists the published weights
zeit fetch weights prithvi-300m-tl    # or presto, ..., all
zeit fetch tiles urls.txt             # the tiles of a list of URLs
zeit fetch embeddings out/ --source tessera --bbox -63.2 -10.1 -62.8 -9.7 --years 2020-2024

The compute nodes of many clusters have no internet access. On the login node, which has it, zeit fetch downloads what zeit would download while running, into the cache: with ZEIT_CACHE_DIR set to a folder the compute nodes also see (the scratch space), they find it there.

  • weights: the pretrained weights of zeit.ai, checked by SHA-256. It does not need torch.
  • tiles: the tiles of a .txt file of URLs (one per line), into the tile cache, where zeit <command> urls.txt out/ --tiles looks first. --threads (default 4) downloads several at once, and --cache-dir names another cache. A tile that cannot be downloaded is reported, and the others are kept: run it again for the rest.
  • embeddings: the same as zeit embeddings (one GeoTIFF of the region, which zeit.load_raster reads), with the same options.

Without network access, zeit says so and names the zeit fetch command that downloads what is missing, instead of a connection error.

docs.title: 24. This user's settings (zeit config)
docs.text:
zeit config                   # every setting, and the file
zeit config threads 12        # the threads of --jobs -1 / n_jobs=-1, for this user
zeit config threads           # the current value
zeit config threads auto      # back to what zeit decides

Keeps settings for the user in config.toml of the config folder (ZEIT_CONFIG_DIR, or %APPDATA%\zeit on Windows, ~/.config/zeit elsewhere), for those who would rather not set an environment variable: on a shared Windows server, a variable for the whole system needs an administrator. threads comes after ZEIT_NUM_THREADS and before OMP_NUM_THREADS, and is not used in a batch job, whose processors are the job's (see Threads). Processes already running see a change within 30 seconds.

docs.title: Note on AI Tools (Deep Learning)
docs.text:
Currently, the AI tools (zeit.ai) are not exposed via the CLI.

Why? Deep learning architectures (like UTAE, TempCNN, or Siamese Networks) require highly specific initializations based on your dataset (e.g., number of input bands, number of target classes, path to pre-trained .pth weights, and GPU allocation strategies). These configurations are too complex and dynamic to be safely passed as simple terminal arguments.

To use the AI tools, use the Python API: zeit.ai.samples, train and predict go from a cube and labelled samples to a map in three calls, and the models can be trained with a loop of your own.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
Every public function and class, with its signature, parameters and an example. Signatures on these pages are generated from the code, so they always match the installed version.

How to import

import zeit gives you the most used functions at the top level (zeit.landtrendr, zeit.save_raster, …) and registers the .zeit xarray accessor. Everything else lives in submodules (zeit.twdtw, zeit.segmentation, zeit.ai, …), shown in each signature.

  • Data & I/O

    STAC and Earth Engine cubes, local files, compositing, GeoTIFF I/O, QA weights.

  • Embeddings

    TESSERA and AlphaEarth yearly embeddings as cubes; similarity search; change from year to year.

  • Pre-processing

    Tmask cloud masking, Whittaker and Savitzky-Golay smoothing, spike removal.

  • Change Detection

    LandTrendr, CCDC, BFAST, BFAST Monitor, BFAST Lite, CODED, event extraction and agreement.

  • Time-Series Analysis

    Mann-Kendall trends, phenology, TWDTW, SNIC segmentation, SOM clustering.

  • Post-processing

    Spatial filters, CCDC classification, water masks.

  • Validation

    Stratified samples, labelling points by eye, accuracies and error-adjusted areas with confidence intervals.

  • Visualisation

    zeit.plot: a fast time-series viewer, pixel inspector, basemaps and static figures.

  • Deep Learning

    TempCNN, LightTAE, Presto, U-TAE, Siamese and foundation models; datasets and losses.

  • Xarray Accessor

    DataArray.zeit.*: every algorithm on lazy Dask cubes, and Zarr output.

  • Many Tiles & Helpers

    A folder of tiles on this computer and on others of the local network, resumable.

  • Command Line

    The core algorithms as zeit subcommands, for scripts and HPC jobs.

docs.title: Deep Learning
docs.text:
PyTorch models in zeit.ai, and the functions that take them from a cube to a map: samples, train and predict. The models are ordinary nn.Modules, which can also be trained with a loop of your own. Tutorials: Deep Learning.

Install

zeit.ai needs PyTorch, which comes with the ai extra: pip install "zeit-cdts[ai]" (since zeit 2.3; for a GPU, see GPU Acceleration).

docs.title: From a cube to a map
docs.text:
The same path as train_classifier and classify, with the deep learning models: labelled points or polygons and a cube give the samples, train fits a model with a ready-made loop, and predict classifies every pixel into a georeferenced map. What prediction has to check (bands, dates, classes, normalization, patch size) travels with the model.

from zeit import ai

samples = ai.samples(cube, "samples.gpkg", label="class")      # pixels; patch=64 for the patch models
model = ai.train(ai.TempCNN, samples, epochs=50)
classes = ai.predict(model, cube)                               # label (y, x), georeferenced
classes.zeit.save("classes")
ai.save(model, "tempcnn.pt")                                    # ai.load("tempcnn.pt") later
Model Samples Dates when predicting TempCNN, LightTAE, Presto pixels (patch=None) as many as in training (e.g. the same composites in another year) UTAE patches, a multiple of 2 ** (stages - 1) pixels (8 by default) any: the positions come from the cube's dates SiameseChangeDetector patches of a pair of images (before, after), 16 or more a pair Prithvi patches of the six HLS bands, a multiple of 16 pixels (224 as pretrained) as in training

docs.title: samples
docs.text:
zeit.ai.samples(
    data, samples, *, label="class", patch=None, split=0.2,
    split_by="block", block_size=64, seed=42, nodata="auto",
)

Labelled samples of a cube, for train.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, path or pair required A (time, y, x) or (time, band, y, x) cube (in memory or dask), anything load_raster reads, or a pair of images (before, after) for the Siamese detector. samples GeoDataFrame or path required Points or polygons with their class, reprojected when in another CRS. label str "class" The column holding the class. patch int None None: one sample per pixel, (time, band), for TempCNN and LightTAE; points on the same pixel count once, a polygon gives every pixel it covers. A size: a (time, band, patch, patch) window around each point or small polygon (larger polygons are tiled by windows), with every labelled pixel in it and -1 elsewhere, for the patch models. split float 0.2 Share of the samples kept for validation (0: none). split_by str "block" "block": whole blocks of block_size pixels go to validation, so that it measures how the model does away from what it was trained on (neighbouring pixels are alike: random pixels on both sides would measure that); "random": samples at random. block_size int 64 Side of the validation blocks, in pixels. seed int 42 Seed of the split. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation.

Returns a SampleSet. The bands are normalized by their 2% and 98% quantiles in the training samples, as sits does, and missing values become 0 after it (gaps can be filled first with zeit.smooth). Patch models learn best from dense labels (polygons): a patch around a point has a single labelled pixel.

docs.title: SampleSet
docs.text:
class zeit.ai.SampleSet(X, y, is_val, meta, indices=None)

The samples, as a PyTorch Dataset, made by samples. Each item is a dict with x (normalized: (time, band) or (time, band, patch, patch)), y (the class index, or a (patch, patch) mask with -1 where unlabelled) and positions (days since the first date). train and val are the two parts of the split, classes the class names, meta what train records in the model. For a loop of your own: DataLoader(samples.train, batch_size=64, shuffle=True).

Parameter Type Default Description X, y ndarray required The raw values and the labels. is_val ndarray required Which samples are for validation. meta dict required Bands, dates, positions, classes, normalization, patch. indices ndarray None The samples this view holds (train, val).

docs.title: train
docs.text:
zeit.ai.train(
    model, samples, *, epochs=50, batch_size=None, lr=0.001,
    weight_decay=0.0, loss="ce", patience=10, device="auto", seed=42,
    verbose=False, **model_kwargs,
)

Trains a model on a SampleSet with Adam, keeping the weights of the epoch with the lowest validation loss.

Parameter Type Default Description model class or nn.Module required TempCNN, LightTAE, Presto, UTAE, SiameseChangeDetector or Prithvi: a class is built with the samples' bands, dates and classes (and model_kwargs); an instance is trained as it is. samples SampleSet required From samples: pixels or patches, as the model takes. epochs int 50 At most this many passes over the training samples. batch_size int None Samples per step: 64 pixels or 8 patches (a patch holds many labelled pixels, and smaller batches leave more steps per epoch). lr, weight_decay float 0.001, 0.0 Adam's learning rate and weight decay. loss str or function "ce" "ce" (cross-entropy), "focal" (for imbalanced classes) or (logits, target) -> loss, with target -1 where unlabelled. patience int 10 Stop after this many epochs without a lower validation loss, once the model has taken 50 steps (validation runs with batch normalization's running statistics, which need them to settle), and keep the best epoch (None: every epoch, the last one kept). device str "auto" "auto" (the GPU if there is one), "cpu", "cuda"... seed int 42 Seed of the initial weights and the order of the samples. verbose bool False Print each epoch's losses and validation accuracy. **model_kwargs For a class: its own arguments (e.g. dropout_rate, UTAE's encoder_widths).

Returns the trained model in evaluation mode, with zeit_meta_ (bands, dates, classes, normalization, patch, the model's class and arguments) and zeit_history_ (per epoch: train_loss, val_loss, val_accuracy).

docs.title: predict
docs.text:
zeit.ai.predict(
    model, data, *, batch_size=256, overlap=0.25, probability=False,
    device="auto", nodata="auto", chunks=None,
)

Classifies every pixel of a cube with a model trained by train (or loaded by load). zeit.classify(cube, model) does the same for such a model.

Parameter Type Default Description model nn.Module required A model with zeit_meta_. data as in samples required The cube; its bands are taken by name and normalized as the training samples were. A lazy cube stays lazy, computed block by block. batch_size int 256 Pixels or windows through the model at a time. overlap float 0.25 Patch models: the image is covered by windows of the training patch size, overlapping by this share; each pixel's probabilities are the average of the windows over it, weighted down towards their edges, so there are no seams. The windows are laid on the whole image, so a lazy cube gives the map in memory. probability bool False Also return each class's probability. device str "auto" As in train. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation. chunks "auto", dict None A raster path: read lazily.

Returns an xarray.Dataset like zeit.classify's: label (y, x) (1 for the first class, 0 where the pixel has no data at any date; the names in flag_meanings) and, with probability=True, probability (class, y, x). Georeferenced as the input.

docs.title: save
docs.text:
zeit.ai.save(model, path)

Saves a trained model: its weights, zeit_meta_ and history.

Parameter Type Default Description model nn.Module required A model trained by train. path path required The file to write.

docs.title: load
docs.text:
zeit.ai.load(path, model=None, device="cpu")

Loads a model saved by save, ready for predict. A model train built from its class is built again; for one trained as an instance, pass one like it.

Parameter Type Default Description path path required The file save wrote. model nn.Module None An instance to put the weights in (a model trained from an instance). device str "cpu" Where to load the weights.

docs.title: STACCubeDataset
docs.text:
class zeit.ai.STACCubeDataset(cube, patch_size=256, stride=256)

A PyTorch Dataset of the windows of a (time, band, y, x) cube, lazy or not, for a loop of your own. The windows start every stride pixels and the last one of each row and column lies against the far edge, so they cover the whole cube (a cube smaller than a window gives one, padded with NaN). Only the window asked for is computed, so it works on cubes larger than memory.

Parameter Type Default Description cube xr.DataArray required (time, band, y, x) cube, e.g. from build_time_series. patch_size int 256 Window side in pixels. stride int 256 Step between windows. Smaller than patch_size gives overlapping windows.

Each item is a dict: x, a float32 tensor (time, band, patch_size, patch_size) with missing values left as NaN; valid, (time, patch_size, patch_size), True where every band has a value; positions, the days since the cube's first date (for UTAE's batch_positions; the day of the year would make dates a year apart collide); and row, col, the window's top-left pixel. dataset.positions holds the same positions.

from zeit.ai import STACCubeDataset

dataset = STACCubeDataset(cube, patch_size=64, stride=64)
item = dataset[0]
x = torch.nan_to_num(item["x"])      # or fill the gaps as your model needs

docs.title: TempCNN
docs.text:
class zeit.ai.TempCNN(
    in_channels, n_times, num_classes=5, filters=64, kernel_size=5,
    n_conv=3, dense_units=256, dropout_rate=0.5,
)

Temporal convolutional network, written from Pelletier et al. (2019) and the authors' code (temporalCNN). Weights trained by other implementations (R sits included) do not load into it. Input (batch, bands, time), output class logits (batch, num_classes). Tutorial: TempCNN.

Parameter Type Default Description in_channels int required Bands per observation. n_times int required Series length. Fixed for the life of the model (the flatten layer depends on it). num_classes int 5 Output classes. filters int 64 Filters of each convolution. kernel_size int 5 Kernel size (odd). n_conv int 3 Convolution blocks. dense_units int 256 Width of the dense layer. dropout_rate float 0.5 Dropout of every block. 
from zeit.ai import TempCNN

model = TempCNN(in_channels=6, n_times=23, num_classes=4)
logits = model(torch.randn(32, 6, 23))   # (32, 4)

docs.title: LightTAE
docs.text:
class zeit.ai.LightTAE(
    n_bands, day_offsets, n_labels,
    encoder_mlp=(32, 64, 128), decoder_mlp=(64, 32), **ltae,
)

Lightweight temporal attention classifier: per-observation MLP encoder, L-TAE temporal attention, MLP decoder. Written from Sainte Fare Garnot & Landrieu (2020) and the authors' code (lightweight-temporal-attention-pytorch); weights trained by other implementations (R sits included) do not load into it. The **ltae arguments go to LTAE (n_head, d_k, n_neurons, dropout, d_model, T, init). Input (batch, time, bands), output logits (batch, n_labels). Tutorial: LTAE & LightTAE.

Parameter Type Default Description n_bands int required Bands per observation. day_offsets list[float] required Day of each observation, counted from the first. Fixes the series length. n_labels int required Output classes. encoder_mlp tuple (32, 64, 128) Widths of the per-observation encoder. decoder_mlp tuple (64, 32) Decoder hidden widths. n_head int 16 Attention heads (an LTAE argument). d_k int 8 Key size per head. n_neurons tuple (256, 128) L-TAE widths; n_neurons[0] is the model width, d_model. dropout float 0.2 Dropout after the L-TAE's MLP. d_model int 256 Width the encoder's output is projected to. 
from zeit.ai import LightTAE

model = LightTAE(n_bands=6, day_offsets=list(range(0, 36 * 16, 16)), n_labels=5)
logits = model(torch.randn(8, 36, 6))    # (8, 5)

docs.title: LTAE
docs.text:
class zeit.ai.LTAE(
    in_channels, day_offsets, n_head=16, d_k=8, n_neurons=(256, 128),
    dropout=0.2, d_model=256, T=1000, init="authors",
)

The L-TAE temporal attention block on its own, to build custom models (Sainte Fare Garnot & Landrieu, 2020, and the authors' code). Input (batch, time, in_channels), output (batch, n_neurons[-1]).

Parameter Type Default Description in_channels int required Features per time step. day_offsets list[float] required Day of each observation, counted from the first. n_head int 16 Attention heads. d_k int 8 Key size per head. n_neurons tuple (256, 128) Widths of the MLP after the heads; the first must be d_model. dropout float 0.2 Dropout after that MLP (the attention weights have 0.1). d_model int or None 256 Width the channels are projected to; None: no projection. T float 1000 Temperature of the positional encoding. init str "authors" The authors' initialization, or "default" (PyTorch's).

docs.title: Presto
docs.text:
class zeit.ai.Presto(
    bands, months, num_classes=2, latlon=None, band_map=None,
    reflectance_scale=1.0, s1_linear=False, pretrained=True,
)

Presto (Tseng et al., 2023), a transformer pretrained on single pixels' series of Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, ERA5 and SRTM, ported from the authors' code; with their weights it gives their encodings. Takes the series (batch, dates, bands) in the cube's units, NaN where missing, and normalizes them as Presto does; forward gives class logits (batch, num_classes), embed the 128-dimension encodings. zeit.ai.train fills in the bands, months, units and position from the samples. Tutorial: Presto.

Parameter Type Default Description bands list of str required The cube's bands, in order, matched to Presto's inputs by name (blue, nir, B8A, swir1, VV, t2m, dem...). months list of int required Calendar month (1-12) of each date; up to 24 dates. num_classes int 2 Classes of the classifier. latlon tuple None Latitude and longitude (degrees) given to the pixels when forward/embed get none of their own. band_map dict None {Presto input: band} for bands whose names are not recognized. reflectance_scale float 1.0 Factor bringing Sentinel-2 to Presto's 0-10000 (1e4 for reflectance from 0 to 1). s1_linear bool False The Sentinel-1 bands hold linear backscatter (converted to dB). pretrained bool True Start from the authors' weights, downloaded once (3 MB, checked by SHA-256; ZEIT_WEIGHTS names a folder with a local copy). 
from zeit.ai import Presto

model = Presto(["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir1", "swir2"], months=range(1, 13), num_classes=4,
               latlon=(-10.5, -55.2), reflectance_scale=1e4)
logits = model(x)            # x: (batch, 12, 6), NaN where missing -> (batch, 4)
encodings = model.embed(x)   # (batch, 128)

docs.title: presto_embeddings
docs.text:
zeit.ai.presto_embeddings(
    data, *, model=None, band_map=None, batch_size=8192,
    device="auto", nodata="auto", chunks=None,
)

Presto's encoding of every pixel of a cube, as an embedding cube (1, 128, y, x) (bands A00-A127, tagged embedding_source="presto"), for similarity, som, train_classifier, zeit.plot and the rest of zeit's embedding tools. Each pixel gets its own latitude and longitude. Tutorial: Presto.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray or path required A (time, band, y, x) cube of up to 24 dates with Sentinel-2 and/or Sentinel-1, ERA5, SRTM bands, with its dates and CRS. model Presto None A (fine-tuned) Presto whose encoder to use; by default the pretrained one, set for the cube's bands, dates and units. band_map dict None {Presto input: band} for bands whose names are not recognized. batch_size int 8192 Pixels per step. device str "auto" "auto" (the GPU if there is one), "cpu", "cuda"... nodata any "auto" Value marking a missing observation. chunks any None A raster path: read lazily with these chunks. A lazy cube stays lazy. 
emb = zeit.ai.presto_embeddings(cube)            # cube: 12 monthly composites
zeit.similarity(emb, "reference_fields.gpkg")

docs.title: UTAE
docs.text:
class zeit.ai.UTAE(
    input_dim, encoder_widths=(64, 64, 64, 128),
    decoder_widths=(32, 32, 64, 128), out_conv=(32, 20), str_conv_k=4,
    str_conv_s=2, str_conv_p=1, agg_mode="att_group",
    encoder_norm="group", n_head=16, d_model=256, d_k=4,
    encoder=False, return_maps=False, pad_value=0,
    padding_mode="reflect",
)

U-Net with temporal attention (Garnot & Landrieu, 2021), ported from the official utae-paps code and bit-exact with it. Input (batch, time, bands, H, W) plus batch_positions (batch, time) (day of each observation); output class scores (batch, classes, H, W). Tutorial: UTAE.

Parameter Type Default Description input_dim int required Bands. encoder_widths list[int] (64, 64, 64, 128) Encoder widths, finest level first. decoder_widths list[int] (32, 32, 64, 128) Decoder widths. Same length as the encoder; last value equal to the encoder's. out_conv list[int] (32, 20) Output convolution widths; the last is the number of classes. str_conv_k, str_conv_s, str_conv_p int 4, 2, 1 Kernel, stride and padding of the strided convolutions. agg_mode str "att_group" Temporal aggregation of skip connections: "att_group", "att_mean" or "mean". encoder_norm str "group" "group", "batch" or "instance". n_head int 16 Attention heads. d_model int 256 Attention width (divisible by n_head). d_k int 4 Key size per head. encoder bool False Return features instead of class scores. return_maps bool False Also return the decoder feature maps. pad_value float 0 Value marking padded time steps (for variable-length batches). padding_mode str "reflect" Spatial padding of the convolutions. 
from zeit.ai import UTAE

model = UTAE(input_dim=6, out_conv=[32, 10]).eval()
x = torch.randn(2, 12, 6, 128, 128)
days = torch.arange(12.0).expand(2, -1) * 16
scores = model(x, batch_positions=days)   # (2, 10, 128, 128)

docs.title: SiameseChangeDetector
docs.text:
class zeit.ai.SiameseChangeDetector(
    in_channels, num_classes=2, dropout=0.2,
)

Two-date change detection: FC-Siam-diff of Daudt et al. (2018), a U-Net whose encoder, shared by both images, passes the absolute difference of their features at every scale to the decoder. Written from the paper, it gives the outputs of the authors' SiamUnet_diff with the same weights. Images of 16 pixels or more (it halves them four times). Tutorial: Siamese Change Detector.

Parameter Type Default Description in_channels int required Bands per image. num_classes int 2 Output classes (2 for change / no change). dropout float 0.2 Rate of the dropout (Dropout2d) after every convolution, as in the paper. 
from zeit.ai import SiameseChangeDetector

model = SiameseChangeDetector(in_channels=4)
logits = model(torch.randn(8, 4, 256, 256), torch.randn(8, 4, 256, 256))   # (8, 2, 256, 256)

docs.title: Prithvi
docs.text:
class zeit.ai.Prithvi(
    bands, n_dates, num_classes=2, variant="100M-TL", dates=None,
    latlon=None, band_map=None, reflectance_scale=1.0,
    freeze_encoder=False, pretrained=True,
)

Prithvi-EO-2.0 (Szwarcman et al., 2024), the vision transformer NASA and IBM pretrained on HLS time series, ported from the authors' prithvi_mae.py: with their weights, its encoder gives their tokens. A decoder of zeit's brings the 16 × 16 tokens back to a class per pixel, with the pixels' own bands. Takes windows (batch, bands, dates, H, W) in the cube's units, NaN where missing, H and W multiples of 16 (14 for the 600M models); gives logits (batch, num_classes, H, W); encode gives the encoder's tokens. zeit.ai.train fills in the bands, dates, units and place from the samples. Tutorial: Prithvi.

Parameter Type Default Description bands list of str required The cube's bands, in order; the six HLS bands (blue, green, red, narrow nir, swir1, swir2) are found by name. n_dates int required Dates of the windows (Prithvi was pretrained on 4; any number works). num_classes int 2 Classes of the decoder. variant str "100M-TL" "tiny-TL", "100M-TL", "300M", "300M-TL", "600M" or "600M-TL" (TL: the model also encodes the dates and the place). dates list None The dates, for the TL models. latlon tuple None Latitude and longitude (degrees) of the place, for the TL models. band_map dict None {Prithvi band: cube band} for bands whose names are not recognized. reflectance_scale float 1.0 Factor bringing the bands to reflectance times 10,000 (1e4 for reflectance from 0 to 1). freeze_encoder bool False Train the decoder only. pretrained bool True Start from the authors' weights, downloaded once from Hugging Face (129 MB to 2.6 GB, checked by SHA-256; ZEIT_WEIGHTS names a folder with a local copy). 
from zeit.ai import Prithvi

model = Prithvi(["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir1", "swir2"], n_dates=4, num_classes=3,
                dates=["2023-03-01", "2023-06-01", "2023-09-01", "2023-12-01"], latlon=(-10.5, -55.2))
logits = model(x)    # x: (batch, 6, 4, 224, 224) -> (batch, 3, 224, 224)

GeoFoundationViT, its name before zeit 1.7 (a wrapper of Prithvi-100M through transformers), builds a Prithvi with a deprecation warning; its model_id names a Prithvi-EO-2.0 repository.
