Parameter Type Default Description probs DataArray, ndarray or path required (class, y, x) probabilities in [0, 1], e.g. zeit.classify(..., probability=True).probability. window_size int 9 The neighbourhood, odd. neigh_fraction float 0.5 The fraction of the neighbourhood's highest logits that make its mean. smoothness float or list 20.0 The prior's variance, one or one per class: higher smooths more. n_jobs int -1 Threads.

Returns the smoothed probabilities, of the input's kind. As in the method, they no longer sum to one: the class of a pixel is their argmax over class.

land_cover = zeit.classify(stack, rf, probability=True)
probs = zeit.smooth_probs(land_cover.probability, window_size=9, smoothness=20)
label = (probs.fillna(-1).argmax("class") + 1).where(probs.notnull().any("class"))   # 1 = the first class; NaN where no data
label = zeit.mmu_sieve(label, min_size=11)            # then no patch under ~1 ha

docs.title: desawtooth_classes
docs.text:
zeit.spatial.desawtooth_classes(
    data, max_length=1, *, nodata="auto", n_jobs=-1,
)

Temporal consistency of yearly (or any) classifications: in each pixel's series, a run of at most max_length dates of one class between two runs of another, the same before and after (forest, pasture, forest), takes that class (forest, forest, forest). The runs are those of the series given: forest, pasture, crop, pasture, forest with max_length=1 only changes the crop. NoData dates stay and do not break a run. Also exported as zeit.desawtooth_classes.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, ndarray or path required Classes (time, y, x) (a DataArray's time anywhere; numpy: time first) or one series. max_length int 1 The longest excursion removed, in dates. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" The map's NoData (NaN for floats), a number, or none. n_jobs int -1 Threads.

docs.title: Zones and vectors
docs.text: Vector layers and maps on one grid: the area of each pixel, a layer burned on a grid, a map's patches as polygons and a layer's zones measured on maps. A layer is a GeoDataFrame or a vector file path (reprojected to the maps' CRS); a map is a DataArray or a raster path. Janus' Python history writes its zonal statistics, rasterize and polygonize runs as calls to these functions.

docs.title: pixel_area
docs.text:
zeit.vector.pixel_area(da, *, samples=128)

The area of each pixel of a grid, in m². On a geographic CRS and on a projection that does not preserve areas it is the geodesic area on the CRS's ellipsoid (Karney's algorithm, as GDAL's OGR_G_GeodesicArea), measured at the nodes of a grid of at most samples + 1 a side and bilinearly interpolated; on an equal-area projection it is the transform's area; without a CRS, the transform's in grid units squared. Also exported as zeit.pixel_area. (accuracy still weighs the rows of a geographic map by their area on the authalic sphere.)

Parameter Type Default Description da DataArray, Dataset or path required A raster (only its grid is used). samples int or None 128 Nodes a side of the measured grid; None measures every pixel.

Returns a (y, x) DataArray of m² on the grid of da.

docs.title: rasterize
docs.text:
zeit.vector.rasterize(vector, like, burn=1, *, layer=None, all_touched=False, name=None)

Burns a layer on the grid of like (rasterio's rasterize: the features in reading order, a later one over an earlier one; a pixel is burned when its centre is inside the feature, or when the feature touches it with all_touched). Also exported as zeit.rasterize.

Parameter Type Default Description vector GeoDataFrame or path required The layer. like DataArray, Dataset or path required The grid of the result. burn number or str 1 1 (or another number): that value, uint8 where it fits (0 elsewhere). "id": the feature's number, 1, 2... counting every feature read (int32, no data 0). An attribute: its value (an integer field as int32, no data -2³¹; a real one as float64, no data NaN) or, for a text, a class numbered from 1 in sorted order (uint8, int32 from 255 classes; no data 0) named in the flag_values and flag_meanings attributes. Features with no geometry or no value are left out. layer str None The layer of a multi-layer file. all_touched bool False Burn every pixel a feature touches. name str None The result's name. 
crops = zeit.rasterize("fields.gpkg", ndvi, "crop")          # classes 1, 2... by name
zeit.save_raster(crops, "fields.tif")
print(dict(zip(crops.attrs["flag_values"], crops.attrs["flag_meanings"].split())))

docs.title: polygonize
docs.text:
zeit.vector.polygonize(
    raster, *, band=None, connectivity=4, min_area_ha=0.0, min_pixels=None,
    simplify=0.0, classes=None, years=False,
    mean_of=None, mean_band=None, mean_name="mean",
)

The patches of a map (pixels of one value connected 4- or 8-wise, no data left out) as polygons, from GDAL's polygonizer. Also exported as zeit.polygonize.

Parameter Type Default Description raster DataArray or path required A 2-D map. band int None The band (1-based) of a file. connectivity int 4 4 or 8. min_area_ha, min_pixels float, int 0.0, None A minimum patch, in hectares (the pixel's area is taken at the grid's centre) or in pixels: smaller patches are merged by mmu_sieve into the neighbour they share the longest border with, and one with no neighbour to join is left out. simplify float 0.0 Simplification tolerance in metres (a geographic CRS: degrees at 111,320 m), keeping the topology. classes dict None Class names by value: a class column. years bool False The values are decimal years: a date column (YYYY-MM-DD; a whole year as itself). mean_of, mean_band, mean_name map, int, str None, None, "mean" Another map put on this grid, whose mean in each patch is the mean_name column.

Returns a GeoDataFrame in the raster's CRS with value, class, date, area_ha and perimeter_m (on the CRS's ellipsoid), pixels, the mean and geometry, those asked for.

patches = zeit.polygonize("landcover_2020.tif", connectivity=8, min_area_ha=1, classes={1: "forest", 2: "pasture"})
patches.to_file("patches.gpkg", layer="polygons", driver="GPKG")

docs.title: zonal_stats
docs.text:
zeit.vector.zonal_stats(
    zones, rasters, *, bands=None, labels=None, layer=None, id_field=None,
    all_touched=False, stat="mean", window=None,
)

The statistics of continuous maps in each zone. Each feature is a zone, its pixels those whose centre is inside it (or that it touches, with all_touched; a pixel in several features counts in each). In each map the zone's values, no data left out, give n, mean, std (population), min, p10, p25, median, p75, p90 (linear interpolation) and max. Also exported as zeit.zonal_stats.

Parameter Type Default Description zones GeoDataFrame or path required The layer, reprojected to the maps' CRS. rasters map or list required Maps on one grid: paths, DataArrays (2-D, or with a leading time/band dimension whose layers are maps) or (path, band[, label]) tuples. bands int or list None The band (1-based) of each file. labels list[str] None A label for each map (default: the file's name, the tuple's label, the layer's coordinate). layer str None The layer of a multi-layer file. id_field str None The attribute that names the zones in the id column (default: the feature id). all_touched bool False Also the pixels a zone touches. stat str "mean" The statistic of the wide table. window tuple None Pixel window (x0, y0, x1, y1) of the maps.

Returns ZonalTables(long, wide, transitions): long has id, fid, date (the map's label) and the ten statistics, a row per zone and map; wide has id, fid, pixels (the zone's, valid or not) and a <stat>_<label> column per map; transitions is None.

docs.title: zonal_areas
docs.text:
zeit.vector.zonal_areas(
    zones, rasters, *, kind="classes", names=None, bands=None, labels=None,
    layer=None, id_field=None, all_touched=False, transitions=None, window=None,
)

The pixels and area of each class (or year) of class maps in each zone, and the transitions between two maps. The zones are those of zonal_stats; each pixel counts with its true area (see pixel_area, measured over the zones' extent) in the class of its value rounded (halves away from zero) or, with kind="years", in its year. Pixels with no data are left out. Also exported as zeit.zonal_areas.

Parameter Type Default Description zones, rasters, bands, labels, layer, id_field, all_touched, window As in zonal_stats. kind str "classes" "classes" or "years". names dict None Class names by value (the class column and the ha_<name> columns). transitions (int, int) None The positions of two maps: the area of each change from the first to the second.

Returns ZonalTables(long, wide, transitions): long has id, fid, date, value, class (year), pixels, area_m2, area_ha and percent of the zone's counted area, a row per zone, map and class; wide has id, fid, pixels and an ha_<class> column per class (_<label> after it with several maps); transitions has id, fid, from, from_class, to, to_class, pixels, area_m2 and area_ha.

t = zeit.zonal_areas("municipalities.gpkg", sorted(glob("lc_*.tif")), names={1: "forest", 2: "pasture"}, transitions=(0, -1))
t.to_csv("tables/")     # zonal_long.csv, zonal_wide.csv and transitions.csv (if any), the folder created

ZonalTables.to_csv(folder) writes the tables as DataFrame.to_csv(path, index=False) does and returns the paths written.

docs.title: train_classifier
docs.text:
zeit.train_classifier(
    data, samples, *, label="class", model=None, date=None,
    folds=None,
)

Trains a classifier on the features of data at sample points. The features of a pixel are what it holds off y/x: the bands of a map, every date (and band) of a cube, the maps of a Dataset (phenology or LandTrendr metrics…), or, for a zeit.ccdc result with date, the model of the segment covering that date: each band's coefficients (the intercept moved to the date, a0 + c1 t, as CCDC classifications use it) and RMSE. Loaded on first use (scikit-learn).

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, Dataset or path required What to classify (see above). samples GeoDataFrame or path required Points with their class. Points in another CRS are reprojected; points outside the data or on a pixel with a missing feature are left out. label str "class" The column holding the class (names or numbers). model classifier None Any scikit-learn classifier; default a random forest of 100 trees (random_state=42). date date None CCDC segments: the date whose models are the features. folds SpatialFolds, list, str None A cross-validation: a spatial_folds of the samples, each sample's fold (labels, or a column of samples), or a method of spatial_folds ("blocks", "buffer", "clusters", "knndm", run on the samples kept with data; blocks balanced by label). Each sample is predicted by a copy of model fitted without its fold (and a buffer's neighbours).

Returns the fitted model, with the feature names in zeit_features_, the training features in zeit_train_ (for aoa), their classes in zeit_y_ and the samples' coordinates in zeit_xy_ (their CRS in zeit_crs_). With folds, the folds of the samples kept in zeit_folds_ (train_di and aoa use them) and the cross-validation in zeit_cv_: a DataFrame of observed, predicted and fold, indexed as the samples.

docs.title: classify
docs.text:
zeit.classify(data, model, *, date=None, probability=False)

Classifies every pixel with a trained model. The features are taken as in train_classifier, and reordered by name to the model's zeit_features_. A lazy cube stays lazy. Loaded on first use (scikit-learn).

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, Dataset or path required The features (see train_classifier). model classifier required A fitted classifier, e.g. from train_classifier. date date None CCDC segments: the date whose models are the features. probability bool False Also return each class's probability (predict_proba).

Returns an xarray.Dataset: label (y, x), 1 for the first class of model.classes_, 2 for the second… (0: a missing feature), with the names in its flag_meanings (the legend of zeit.plot); probability (class, y, x) with probability=True; the class coordinate holds the classes.

segments = zeit.ccdc(cube, qa="fmask")
rf = zeit.train_classifier(segments, "samples.gpkg", label="class", date="2020-07-01")
land_cover = zeit.classify(segments, rf, date="2020-07-01", probability=True)
land_cover.label.zeit.plot()                                   # legend: the class names
zeit.save_raster(land_cover, "results/land_cover")             # label.tif, probability.tif

stack = zeit.load_raster("s2_2022.tif")                         # any cube: each date and band a feature
classes = zeit.classify(stack, zeit.train_classifier(stack, points))

docs.title: aoa
docs.text:
zeit.aoa(
    data, train=None, *, model=None, weights=None, folds=None,
    distance="euclidean", lpd=False, date=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

Where a model can be applied (Meyer & Pebesma 2021): the dissimilarity index (DI) of each pixel to the training data, and the area of applicability (AOA), where it is no more dissimilar than the training data are to each other, as CAST's aoa (the same DI as CAST 1.0.4, to 1e-13). The predictors are scaled by the training data's means and standard deviations and weighted by their importance; a pixel's DI is its distance to the nearest training point over the mean distance between training points. The threshold is the upper whisker (75% quantile + 1.5 IQR, at most their largest) of the training points' own DI, each the distance to the nearest point of another cross-validation fold. A model's predictions outside the AOA are extrapolations: its validation says nothing about them. The nearest training points are found in a k-d tree up to 9 predictors (as CAST's FNN), from a matrix product beyond, the distances exact either way: with 2000 training points and 100,000 pixels, CAST takes 1.2 s with 8 predictors and 5.8 s with 64; Zeit 0.45 s and 1 s on one thread, 0.04 s and 0.3 s on 19 (benchmarks/vs_originals/aoa.py).

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, Dataset, DataFrame or array required What the model is applied to: anything classify takes, its features matched to the training's by name, or a table of points (predictors in columns). train DataFrame, array or TrainDI None The training data (points × predictors), or a train_di result to reuse; none with model. model classifier None A model from train_classifier: its training data (zeit_train_), its folds when it was trained with folds (zeit_folds_; CAST's useCV) and, unless weights says otherwise, its feature_importances_ as the weights. weights str, dict or list None The predictors' weights: None (the model's importance, else all 1), "importance", a dict by name or a list. Negative weights count as 0; a predictor of weight 0 is ignored, even missing. folds list or SpatialFolds None Each training point's cross-validation fold (any labels; None/NaN: in none), or a spatial_folds result (a buffer's neighbours are left out of each point's DI, as CAST's CVtrain). Spatially clustered samples should be given spatial folds, or the threshold is too strict. distance str "euclidean" "euclidean" or "mahalanobis" (CAST's method = "MD"): the Euclidean distance once the scaled predictors are whitened by their covariance in the training data, so correlated predictors (eight years of NDVI) do not count the same information several times. The weights then only say which predictors are used (0: left out): the distance does not change with their scale. With a TrainDI, its own. lpd bool False Also the local point density: how many training points are within the threshold's DI. date date None CCDC segments: the date whose models are the features. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns, for a map, an xarray.Dataset georeferenced as the data: DI (y, x) float32; AOA (y, x), 1 inside, 0 outside, 255 where a feature is missing; LPD (y, x) with lpd=True; the threshold, mean_distance and distance in its attributes. For points, a DataFrame of DI, AOA (NaN where a predictor is missing; CAST calls those inside) and LPD. With either distance the DI is CAST's to 1e-13; it is computed by blocks of pixels against every training point, the nearest ones exactly.

rf = zeit.train_classifier(stack, "samples.gpkg", label="class")
land_cover = zeit.classify(stack, rf)
applicable = zeit.aoa(stack, model=rf)                          # weighted by the forest's importance
land_cover["label"] = land_cover.label.where(applicable.AOA == 1, 0)
zeit.save_raster(applicable, "results/aoa")                      # DI.tif, AOA.tif

# samples in clusters (sites, polygons): their spatial cross-validation folds
applicable = zeit.aoa(stack, model=rf, folds=samples["site"], lpd=True)

docs.title: train_di
docs.text:
zeit.train_di(
    train=None, *, model=None, weights=None, folds=None,
    distance="euclidean", n_jobs=-1,
)

The dissimilarity of the training data to itself and the AOA's threshold, as CAST's trainDI, to reuse with aoa(data, train=td) on several images.

Parameter Type Default Description train DataFrame or array None The training data (points × predictors); points with a missing value are left out. None with model. model classifier None As in aoa. weights str, dict or list None As in aoa. folds list None As in aoa. distance str "euclidean" As in aoa. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns a TrainDI: features, center, scale, weight, train (scaled and weighted; whitened for the Mahalanobis distance), mean_distance, train_di (each training point's DI), threshold, distance and whiten (the matrix that whitens a scaled point, or None).

docs.title: error_profile
docs.text:
zeit.error_profile(
    model=None, *, train=None, observed=None, predicted=None,
    folds=None, weights=None, distance="euclidean", metric=None,
    window=5, calibration="monotone", k=6, n_jobs=-1,
)

How a model's error grows with the dissimilarity of the data to its training data, as CAST's errorProfiles (Meyer & Pebesma 2021), and the map of the error to expect where it is applied. The training points of a cross-validation, each predicted by a model fitted without its fold, are sorted by their DI (their distance to the nearest point of another fold); those within the AOA's threshold give the error metric in a moving window of window points, at the DI of the window's middle point, and a curve that only grows (only falls, for the accuracy) is fitted to the windows. The windows are CAST 1.0.4's to 1e-13, but for one difference: a window whose points are all of one class and all predicted right has accuracy 1 here and 0 in CAST. The curve is a P-spline with its coefficients kept monotone by an asymmetric penalty (Bollaerts, Eilers & van Mechelen 2006), its smoothness by generalised cross-validation, in the core; CAST's scam gives a curve within 1% of the metric's range of it on the test case.

Parameter Type Default Description model classifier None A model from train_classifier(..., folds=...): its cross-validation (zeit_cv_), training data and folds. train DataFrame or array None For a model of any kind: the training predictors (points × predictors)… observed array None …each training point's value or class… predicted array None …its prediction by a model fitted without its fold… folds list or SpatialFolds None …and the folds (as in train_di). weights str, dict or list None As in aoa. distance str "euclidean" As in aoa. metric str None "rmse" or "mae" (values), "accuracy" (classes); default "accuracy" for a classifier or observations that are not numbers, else "rmse". window int 5 The moving window's points. calibration str "monotone" "monotone" (CAST's scam) or "linear" (CAST's lm). k int 6 The monotone curve's B-splines (CAST's k). n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an ErrorProfile: points (the windows' DI and metric), threshold, the curve (call the profile on DI values), .predict(zeit.aoa(...)) (the error expected in each pixel inside the AOA, a georeferenced (y, x) DataArray; outside=True also beyond, the curve going on as a line), .save(path) and ErrorProfile.load(path) (JSON), and .plot().

rf = zeit.train_classifier(stack, samples, label="class", folds="knndm")
profile = zeit.error_profile(rf)                                   # accuracy against the DI
applicable = zeit.aoa(stack, model=rf)
expected = profile.predict(applicable)                              # the accuracy to expect, inside the AOA
profile.plot()

docs.title: Spatial cross-validation
docs.text: Points near each other are alike: a random k-fold validation tests a model on points next to its training points and says it is better than it is where it will be applied. Spatial folds hold out whole regions, as blockCV's (Valavi et al. 2019): blocks of a grid, a point and its neighbours within a buffer, or clusters of the points; or they mimic the area to predict, as CAST's kNNDM (Linnenbrink et al. 2024). They serve to choose a model and to calibrate its area of applicability (train_di, aoa); the accuracy of the map is still that of a probability sample (accuracy; Wadoux et al. 2021).

docs.title: spatial_folds
docs.text:
zeit.spatial_folds(
    samples, *, method="blocks", k=5, size=None, shape="hexagon",
    selection="random", label=None, iterations=100,
    space="geographic", data=None, prediction_points=None,
    samplesize=1000, clustering="hierarchical", maxp=0.5,
    candidates=100, seed=0, n_jobs=-1,
)

Cross-validation folds of sample points that keep the test points away from the training points, as blockCV's cv_spatial, cv_buffer and cv_cluster, and CAST's knndm.

kNNDM puts the points in q clusters, merges them into k folds of about equal size, and keeps the q (of up to candidates, from k to the number of points: q = n is a random k-fold) whose distances from each point to the nearest point of another fold (Gj*) are distributed most like those from the area to predict to the nearest point (Gij), by the W statistic (the integral of the absolute difference of their distribution functions). On CAST's own example (500 clustered points), zeit's W is CAST's when measured on CAST's folds, and its own folds match better (W 0.57 against CAST's 0.69 on 1000 points, in 0.18 s against 2 s); the distances are searched in the k-d tree of aoa, in the core.

Parameter Type Default Description samples GeoDataFrame or path required The points. Distances are in their CRS's units; a geographic CRS is replaced by its UTM zone (with data, the points are first taken to its CRS). method str "blocks" "blocks": the points in blocks of a grid, the blocks in k folds. "buffer": leave-one-out, each point tested without its neighbours within size in the training. "clusters": k clusters by k-means, of the coordinates or of the predictors (space="feature"). "knndm": kNNDM, for the area in data or prediction_points. k int 5 The number of folds (not for the buffer). size float None The blocks' size (a square's side; for hexagons, the distance between neighbouring centres) or the buffer's radius, in the CRS's units. For blocks, None takes the median range of data's spatial autocorrelation (autocorrelation_range). shape str "hexagon" "hexagon" or "square". selection str "random" How blocks go to folds: "random" (the most balanced of iterations draws), "systematic" (in rows) or "checkerboard" (squares, k=2). label str None A column of samples with the classes: the random draws then balance each class across the folds. iterations int 100 Random draws of the blocks' folds; the one closest to a k-th of the points (of each class) in every fold is kept. space str "geographic" For clusters and kNNDM: "geographic" (the coordinates) or "feature" (the predictors in data, standardised by the points'). data DataArray, Dataset or path None The predictors (anything classify takes), for size=None, space="feature" and kNNDM's area (its cells with every predictor). prediction_points GeoDataFrame or path None kNNDM's prediction points, instead of a sample of data's cells. samplesize int 1000 kNNDM: about how many of data's cells, on a regular grid, are the area to predict. clustering str "hierarchical" kNNDM: Ward's "hierarchical" clustering (once for every q; its memory grows as the square of the points) or "kmeans" (one fit per q, slower). maxp float 0.5 kNNDM: the largest share of the points a fold may hold. candidates int 100 kNNDM: how many numbers of clusters q are tried, spaced geometrically from k to the number of points. seed int 0 The random draws' seed. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns a SpatialFolds: folds (each point's fold, -1 in none: never tested, always trained on), points, size, blocks (the blocks' polygons and folds, for "blocks") exclude (each point's neighbours, for "buffer") and, for kNNDM, W, q and distances (Gij, Gj, Gjstar). It is a scikit-learn splitter (split, get_n_splits), for cross_val_predict or GridSearchCV, and train_di and aoa take it as folds (the buffer's neighbours left out of each point's DI, as CAST's CVtrain). .plot() draws the points by fold; .plot(kind="distances"), kNNDM's distributions of the distances.

folds = zeit.spatial_folds(samples, data=stack, k=5, label="class")    # hexagons as large as the autocorrelation
folds.plot()
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict
predicted = cross_val_predict(rf, x, y, cv=folds)
applicable = zeit.aoa(stack, model=rf, folds=folds)

matched = zeit.spatial_folds(samples, method="knndm", data=stack, k=10)   # like the map's distances
matched.plot(kind="distances")

docs.title: autocorrelation_range
docs.text:
zeit.autocorrelation_range(
    data, *, sample=5000, cutoff=None, boundaries=None, model="best",
    seed=0, n_jobs=-1,
)

The range of each band's spatial autocorrelation, as blockCV's cv_spatial_autocor: the empirical semivariogram of a sample of pixels and the model fitted to it that fits best (as automap's autofitVariogram, which blockCV calls) of the spherical, exponential and Gaussian, γ(h) = nugget + sill f(h/scale), by weighted least squares (weights Nh/h², as gstat). The pairs are counted in the core, in parallel: 5000 pixels take 0.05 s on 8 threads (blockCV: 1.6–2.7 s). On white noise averaged over windows of 300, 700 and 1500 m (correlated up to that distance), the ranges are 0.98–1.02 times blockCV 4.0.1's at 700 and 1500 m, and 0.89–0.99 times at 300 m (a range of three pixels, where Zeit's best model was the Gaussian). blockCV chose the spherical on every map, whose range both report alike.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, Dataset or path required Anything classify takes; a geographic CRS's pixels are measured in their UTM zone. sample int 5000 Pixels with a value drawn per band. cutoff float None The largest distance of a pair; default 0.35 of the map's diagonal (as automap). boundaries list None The upper ends of the bands of distance; default automap's, 2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 15, 25, 35, 50, 65, 80 and 100% of cutoff: finer at short distances, where a short range shows. model str "best" "best" (the least weighted squared error of the three), "spherical", "exponential" or "gaussian". seed int 0 The sample's seed. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns a DataFrame by band: range (where the points are about independent: the spherical's range, where it reaches its sill; the exponential's and the Gaussian's practical range, where they reach 95% of it, 3 and 1.73 times their scale; blockCV reports gstat's range parameter, which for those two is the scale, and it also tries Stein's Matérn, which Zeit does not), model, scale, nugget, sill (above the nugget) and pixels; in attrs, the median range and each band's semivariogram (variograms, a DataFrame of distance, gamma and pairs).

docs.title: extract_water_mask
docs.text:
zeit.masks.extract_water_mask(
    segments, green="green", swir="swir1", threshold=500.0,
)

Persistent water from CCDC models: water reflects a little in green and almost nothing in SWIR, so a pixel is water when its green level is above its SWIR level and the SWIR level is below threshold. The levels are those of each pixel's first segment at its middle (a0 + c1 t). Also exported as zeit.extract_water_mask.

Parameter Type Default Description segments Dataset required A zeit.ccdc result. A numpy stack in the layout of older versions ((segments, parameters, rows, cols)) is still accepted, with integer band positions. green str or int "green" The green band. swir str or int "swir1" The SWIR band (SWIR1 or SWIR2). threshold float 500.0 Highest SWIR level of water (reflectance × 10000).

Returns a uint8 (y, x) map, 1 = water, georeferenced for a Dataset.

water = zeit.extract_water_mask(segments)

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Accuracy assessment and area estimation, and labelling reference points by eye, have a page of their own: Validation.

docs.title: Pre-processing
docs.text: Clean time series before analysing them: put Landsat and Sentinel-2 in one series, flag clouds and shadows that the QA band missed, smooth noise, remove one-off spikes, and unmix pixels into the fractions of their materials.

docs.title: Landsat and Sentinel-2 in one series
docs.text:
A dense series that mixes Landsat and Sentinel-2 has a step wherever the sensor changes, which CCDC or BFAST read as a break. There are two ways to remove it:

  • HLS (Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2, NASA): both sensors processed alike from level 1 (the same atmospheric correction and cloud mask, view and sun angles normalized, a common 30 m grid) and Sentinel-2 adjusted to Landsat 8's bands. build_time_series reads it from Planetary Computer, both products in one call: collection=["hls2-l30", "hls2-s30"] with the bands named by role. This is the way to go wherever HLS covers the dates (from 2013 for Landsat 8, 2015 for Sentinel-2).
  • nbar and bandpass_adjust on cubes you already have (Landsat Collection 2 and Sentinel-2 L2A): HLS's view-angle normalization and its bandpass step, in that order (bandpass_adjust(nbar(cube, angles)), as in HLS). Neither is the atmospheric correction, so only part of the step goes away. nbar needs the per-pixel sun and view angles; bandpass_adjust does not.
  • spectral_adjust goes the other way, Landsat and MODIS to Sentinel-2A's bands (FORCE's spectral adjustment), and predicts the red edge bands Landsat does not have.

Measured over the Libya-4 desert site (2022–2023, Planetary Computer, pairs of Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2 observations at most a day apart, median of the area):

Pairs Sentinel-2 / Landsat, by band (blue ... SWIR2) L2A and Collection 2, as they come 21 1.14, 1.07, 1.09, 1.05, 1.09, 1.13 L2A after bandpass_adjust 21 blue and red about a third closer (differences 0.030 → 0.021 and 0.042 → 0.031), the rest about the same HLS (S30 and L30) 27 1.01, 0.99, 0.99, 1.00, 1.01, 0.99

The rest of the L2A step comes from the steps bandpass_adjust does not do: Sen2Cor and LaSRC correct the atmosphere differently, and the view geometry differs.

grid = dict(source="planetary_computer", bbox=bbox, start_date="2019-01-01", end_date="2024-12-31",
            apply_cloud_mask=True, resolution=30, epsg=32722)
hls = zeit.build_time_series(collection=["hls2-l30", "hls2-s30"],
                             bands=["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir1", "swir2"], **grid)
result = zeit.ccdc(hls.sel(band=["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir1", "swir2"]))

docs.title: nbar
docs.text:
zeit.nbar(
    data, angles=None, *, sensor=None, sza="scene", bands=None, params=None,
    nodata="auto", chunks=None, n_jobs=-1, return_cfactor=False,
)

Normalizes reflectance to what a sensor at nadir would see with the sun at a chosen zenith (NBAR, nadir BRDF-adjusted reflectance), by the c-factor method of Roy et al. (2016, Remote Sensing of Environment 176:255-271; 2017, 199:25-38). Each band is multiplied by c = ρ(sza_norm, view 0) / ρ(sza, vza, raa), where ρ is the MODIS Ross-Thick / Li-Sparse-Reciprocal model f_iso + f_vol·K_vol + f_geo·K_geo with three fixed parameters per band (Roy et al. 2016, Table 5, the global MODIS values; the HLS User Guide v2.0, Table 4, applies the same to OLI and MSI), evaluated at the pixel's observed solar zenith, view zenith and relative azimuth (view minus sun azimuth). It is the view-angle step of HLS, and goes before bandpass_adjust. HLS cubes are refused (already normalized).

Written from the papers. The implementation follows the equations of the papers and the HLS User Guide, not any other implementation (FORCE's, HLS's...): the checks are the published parameters, analytic values of the kernels and the c-factor, and the properties of the model (see tests/test_nbar.py). It is compared against the HLS product itself (the same method, the same parameters): for HLS L30 against Landsat Collection 2 of the same scene, the median ratio of HLS's NBAR to the USGS reflectance in every bin of view zenith and azimuth is within 0.0083 of Zeit's c in every band (0.01 and 0.02 tolerances), slope 0.98-1.07; for Sentinel-2 the angles from sentinel2_angles give c within 0.003 (std) of the c from HLS's own angles (fidelity). The kernels are those that Matsuoka et al. (2016, ISPRS Annals III-7:3-10) write after Wanner et al. (1995) and Lucht et al. (2000), with Li-Sparse's h/b = 2 and b/r = 1.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray or path required Surface reflectance (time, band, y, x) or (band, y, x), in memory or dask. Bands are found by role: coastal, blue, green, red, rededge1-rededge3, nir (B08), nir08 (B8A, OLI's band 5), swir1, swir2, named as Earth Search or Planetary Computer name them (swir16, B04...). Sentinel-2's B08 is normalized (it has MODIS's NIR parameters); bands without a role (B09, QA, the angles) are copied. angles Dataset, DataArray or None None Sun and view angles in degrees, SZA, SAA, VZA, VAA, on exactly the cube's grid and dates, (time, y, x) ((y, x) for a cube without time); nothing is resampled and a mismatch is an error. None takes bands of the cube with those names. Where to get them: HLS carries them (scaled by 0.01); Landsat Collection 2 has Level-1 angle bands (USGS credentials); Sentinel-2 has a 5 km grid in each tile's MTD_TL.xml, which sentinel2_angles turns into per-pixel angles on the cube's grid. VZA and VAA may have a band dimension (sentinel2_angles(..., view_band="each")): each band is then normalized with its own view geometry (the bands to normalize must all have one). A pixel with a missing angle, or a zenith outside 0-90°, is NaN. sensor str or list None As for bandpass_adjust. Only checks the sensors (Landsat 4-9, Sentinel-2) and keeps the Collection 2 names SR_B1... from being read as OLI's on Landsat 4, 5 and 7 (pass bands=). sza float, list, "scene" or "hls" "scene" The normalized solar zenith: a number of degrees (or one per date); "scene", the mean of each date's observed solar zenith over the pixels whose angles are valid (Roy et al. 2016, 2017; with dask the angles are read once ahead of the computation); or "hls", the NBAR_SOLAR_ZENITH tag as an attribute or coordinate of the cube (HLS computes it from the day and latitude with overpass times its guide does not give, so Zeit does not). The view is always nadir. Roy et al. advise against a normalized zenith far from the observed ones. bands dict None The cube's band of each role, when its names are not the usual ones. params dict None {role: (f_iso, f_geo, f_vol)} replacing the parameters of those roles (reflectance 0-1). nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Missing values besides NaN (the raster's NoData; 0 for integers without one). They stay missing. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; otherwise the result is lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads (the processors zeit may use by default). return_cfactor bool False Also return the c-factors (time, band, y, x) of the normalized bands. They are not clipped; in a Landsat's field of view they stay within 0.95-1.05.

Returns the cube with the same dimensions, coordinates, type (integers are rounded) and georeferencing, lazy if the input is, plus a nbar_sza coordinate (each date's normalized zenith). attrs["nbar"] says what was done, attrs["nbar_bands"] which bands, and a normalized cube is refused a second time. With return_cfactor, (nbar, cfactor).

Limits. The red edge parameters are the linear interpolation between MODIS's red (645 nm) and NIR (858 nm) of Roy, Li and Zhang (2017, Remote Sensing 9:1325, Eq. 3); the paper found that interpolation not particularly suited to the red edge (a POLDER test), so treat the red edge result as less certain. The parameters are MODIS's snow-free ones: mask snow before. A pixel's c-factor is not clipped, so a geometry far from the model's range gives an extreme c: inspect return_cfactor. Speed: about 10 million pixels per second on one thread and 40-55 million on eight, for the ten bands at once or one.

angles = xr.Dataset({"SZA": sza, "SAA": saa, "VZA": vza, "VAA": vaa})   # degrees, (time, y, x), the cube's grid
cube_nbar = zeit.nbar(cube, angles)
mixed = zeit.bandpass_adjust(cube_nbar)          # HLS's order: view angles first, then the bandpass
nbar, c = zeit.nbar(cube, angles, sza=35, return_cfactor=True)

docs.title: sentinel2_angles
docs.text:
zeit.sentinel2_angles(
    source, like, *, view_band="B06", chunks=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

The sun and view angles of every pixel of a Sentinel-2 cube, from the MTD_TL.xml of its tiles, in the form nbar takes. ESA gives each tile's angles as 23 × 23 grids with a 5 km step (Geometric_Info/Tile_Angles): the sun's zenith and azimuth, and the view zenith and azimuth of every band and detector. The grids start at the tile's upper left corner (the ULX, ULY of Tile_Geocoding) and run east (columns) and south (rows); the XML has no origin of its own, only the steps. A detector's grid is NaN where its swath does not reach, so a cell where two swaths overlap has two values.

How the grids become pixels (written from ESA's product description and Roy et al. 2017, Remote Sensing of Environment 199:25-38, Sec. 3.2, "bilinear interpolation from the 5 km grid values", the way HLS does it for its Sentinel-2 product):

  • Detectors are fused first, cell by cell: the mean of the zeniths and the circular mean of the azimuths of the detectors that cover the cell. A cell is valid if any detector covers it.
  • Bilinear interpolation to the pixel centres, over the valid corners of the cell only (their weights rescaled to sum to one). A pixel between the last valid node of a swath and the next, invalid one takes the valid corner's value (flat, within one 5 km cell); a pixel with no valid corner, or outside the 23 × 23 grid, is NaN. Azimuths are interpolated through their sine and cosine, so 0°/360° is no seam.
  • The CRS may differ: if like is not in the tile's CRS (the neighbouring UTM zone, or HLS's grid, which uses the northern zone with negative northings for southern tiles), the pixel centres are projected to the tile's.
Parameter Type Default Description source STAC item, path, URL, XML text or list required The tile metadata of each date of like: an Earth Search item (asset granule_metadata) or a Planetary Computer item (granule-metadata, signed with planetary_computer), as a pystac Item or its dict; the path or URL of an MTD_TL.xml; or the XML. A list gives one per date, in the order of like.time; an entry may itself be a list of the tiles that make that date's mosaic (a pixel takes the first tile that has angles there). A source sensed more than a day from its date in like is an error. like DataArray required The cube the angles must match: its CRS, y, x (pixel centres) and time. With view_band="each" it also gives the bands. view_band str "B06" The band whose view angles every band takes: "B06" (the second red edge band) is HLS's choice, one view geometry for all bands. "each" gives each Sentinel-2 band of like its own VZA and VAA (a band dimension), which nbar uses band by band. Any other band name ("B08", "red"...) takes that one for all. chunks dict, "auto" or None None None computes now unless like is dask (then lazy, with its chunks); otherwise lazy with those chunks. In memory, one 10980 × 10980 tile is four float32 images of 480 MB per date: use lazy for many dates. n_jobs int -1 Threads of the in-memory computation (strips of rows).

Returns an xarray.Dataset with SZA, SAA, VZA, VAA in degrees (float32, azimuths 0-360 clockwise from north, (time, y, x)) on exactly the coordinates of like.

Against HLS. HLS S30 uses the same grids: over a whole tile, Zeit's solar angles are 0.015° from HLS's (the Level-1C against the Level-2A metadata) and the view zenith has a standard deviation of 0.05° from it. At the borders between detectors HLS gives each pixel its detector's angles (a step of 20-60° in azimuth) where this blends the two over one 5 km cell; the c-factors differ by 0.0027 (std, 0.015 at most).

Speed. A whole 10980 × 10980 tile at 10 m, four layers, takes 4.3 s on one thread and 2.2 s on eight (Windows 11, memory bound beyond that); lazily it is computed with the cube's chunks.

items = sorted(search.item_collection(), key=lambda i: i.datetime)   # Earth Search sentinel-2-l2a items, one per date
cube = zeit.build_time_series(source="earth_search", collection="sentinel-2-l2a", ...)
angles = zeit.sentinel2_angles(items, cube)            # same order as cube.time
cube_nbar = zeit.nbar(cube, angles)
each = zeit.sentinel2_angles(items, cube, view_band="each")   # a view geometry per band

docs.title: topographic_correction
docs.text:
zeit.topographic_correction(
    cube, dem, *, sun_zenith="scene", sun_azimuth="scene", method="c", sample=None,
    min_slope=5.0, min_sample=100, bands=None, nodata="auto", n_jobs=-1,
)

Takes the modulation of the relief's illumination out of surface reflectance, by the C-correction (Teillet, Guindon & Goodenough 1982, Canadian Journal of Remote Sensing 8:84-106) or SCS+C (Soenen, Peddle & Coburn 2005, IEEE TGRS 43:2148-2159). A pixel facing the sun is brighter than one facing away, whatever it is made of; the correction flattens that so that a classifier or an index sees the cover and not the slope. Written from the published formulas, not from any implementation, and computed in the Rust core (zeit._core.topocorr).

  1. Slope and aspect of the DEM by Horn's (1981, Proceedings of the IEEE 69:14-47) 3 × 3 kernel, in the cube's projected units (metres; a foot-based CRS is converted). The slope is atan(|∇z|), the aspect the direction the surface faces, clockwise from north. A geographic CRS is an error: reproject the cube and the DEM to the scene's UTM zone first.
  2. Illumination cos i = cos sz · cos s + sin sz · sin s · cos(saz − a), with the sun's zenith sz and azimuth saz and the slope s and aspect a.
  3. The line ρ = b + m · cos i, fitted by least squares over the sample pixels of each band and date, and c = b / m.
  4. The correction ρ_H = ρ · (cos sz + c) / (cos i + c) (method="c") or ρ_H = ρ · (cos s · cos sz + c) / (cos i + c) (method="scs+c"; the sun-canopy-sensor geometry, for forests on steep slopes, which leaves a flat pixel's value times cos s on a slope).

It is multiplicative, so the units of the reflectance do not matter (scaled integers, 0-1, percent). It is an empirical flattening: Lambertian surface, the same cover on every slope, no diffuse or adjacent-terrain light, and a DEM about as fine as the image. FORCE's own C-factor, which is tied to its atmospheric correction's radiation terms, is a different step.

Parameter Type Default Description cube DataArray or path required Reflectance (time, band, y, x), (band, y, x), (time, y, x) or (y, x) in a projected CRS. A dask cube is read into memory (the line needs a whole date). NaN and the nodata values stay missing and stay out of the fit. dem DataArray or path required Elevation in metres (y, x) on exactly the cube's grid (same size and coordinates). It is never resampled: a mismatch is an error that suggests dem.rio.reproject_match(cube). A NaN or NoData cell makes the slope of its eight neighbours NaN, and those pixels are left as they are. sun_zenith, sun_azimuth number, sequence, DataArray, Dataset or "scene" "scene" Degrees, azimuth clockwise from north. A number, one per date, or a per-pixel DataArray (y, x) / (time, y, x) on the cube's grid and dates. "scene" reads the cube's own bands SZA and SAA (per pixel; the angle bands are never corrected), else a coordinate or attribute sun_zenith (or sun_elevation or STAC's view:sun_elevation, zenith = 90 − elevation) and sun_azimuth. The output of sentinel2_angles, or a DataArray with an angle dimension, may be given as either one and then serves both. A zenith outside 0-90° or missing leaves that pixel as it is. method "c" or "scs+c" "c" The correction above. sample boolean DataArray or array None (y, x) or (time, y, x): the pixels the lines are fitted on (say the vegetated, clear ones), used as given. None: the pixels with a finite reflectance and cos i and a slope of at least min_slope. min_slope float 5.0 Degrees. Flat terrain has the same cos i (cos sz) everywhere and says nothing about the relief; in a mostly flat scene it would pull the line through one cluster. Below the limit a pixel is still corrected (its factor is 1). min_sample int 100 Fewest sample pixels for a line. bands list None The bands to correct; the default is all but SZA, SAA, VZA, VAA. The others are copied. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Missing values besides NaN (the raster's NoData; 0 for integers without one). n_jobs int -1 Threads.

Returns the cube as float32 with the same dimensions, coordinates and georeferencing, missing values NaN, and a coordinate topo_c ((time, band) or (band,)): the c of every band and date, NaN where the band was copied. attrs["topocorr"] says the method and where the sun came from.

Guards. A band of a date is copied unchanged, with a warning that names it and why, when it has fewer than min_sample sample pixels, cos i has no variance, or the line's slope m is zero or negative (the reflectance does not rise with illumination: the topography does not drive it, or the sample is wrong). A pixel is left as it is when its cos i + c is below 0.01 (a deep shadow under a poorly fitted c), when cos sz + c (or cos s · cos sz + c) is not positive, when its sun angle is missing, or when its slope is NaN. The cells on the DEM's edge replicate the nearest cell and take the one-sided difference over one cell, so they have a slope; a flat cell has aspect 0.

Against R. RStoolbox's topCor(method = "C"), given Zeit's slope and aspect, gives the same corrected values to 4e-7 relative when the line is fitted on the same pixels (a 100 × 100 image, which RStoolbox samples whole); on a 1000 × 1000 image RStoolbox fits on a random sample of 10000 pixels (and so a slightly different c, a different one in each run) and the two differ by 0.3-4.5% at most, 1-2e-4 on average in reflectance (see the benchmarks). Slope and aspect agree with gdaldem (inside: 2.5e-4° in slope, the float32 of GDAL's output) and terra::terrain (8e-6°).

dem = rioxarray.open_rasterio("dem.tif").squeeze(drop=True).rio.reproject_match(cube)
flat = zeit.topographic_correction(cube, dem, sun_zenith=38.5, sun_azimuth=142.0)
flat = zeit.topographic_correction(cube, dem, sun_zenith=angles, method="scs+c")   # angles from sentinel2_angles
flat.topo_c                     # the c of each band (and date)

docs.title: bandpass_adjust
docs.text:
zeit.bandpass_adjust(
    data, *, sensor=None, etm=None, bands=None, scale="auto",
    nodata="auto", chunks=None,
)

Takes Sentinel-2 reflectance to the bands of Landsat 8's OLI with the bandpass adjustment of HLS (Claverie et al. 2018): one line per band and Sentinel-2 unit, OLI = slope × MSI + intercept, from the HLS v2.0 User Guide (Table 5; S2A and S2B are also the v1.4 values, S2C has its own). OLI is the reference, as in HLS: Landsat 8 and 9 stay as they are (HLS applies no adjustment between them). Landsat 7 (ETM+) and 4-5 (TM) are left alone unless etm is given; then the lines of Roy et al. (2016, Table 2, surface reflectance) take them to OLI. Those were fitted on pre-collection data, and Landsat Collection 2 surface reflectance is generally used across sensors without them (see Earth Engine's FAQ on cross-sensor harmonization). It is one step of HLS, not HLS (see above); HLS products are refused, since their Sentinel-2 dates are already adjusted.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, path or list required Surface reflectance (time, band, y, x) or (band, y, x), in memory or dask. Or a list of cubes on the same grid (one per collection): each is adjusted and they are joined into one series sorted by time, with the bands they share matched by role and named after it (blue ... swir2), whatever each catalog calls them, and the coordinates they share. sensor str or list None Each date's sensor: by default the cube's platform coordinate (which build_time_series keeps from STAC) or attribute; or one name for every date ("sentinel-2a", "S2B", "landsat-8", "LANDSAT_7"...), or one per date. With a list of cubes, one of these per cube. A Sentinel-2 date of unknown unit is adjusted as S2A, with a warning. etm "rma", "ols" or None None Landsat 7 and 4-5: left as they are, or taken to OLI with the reduced major axis or least squares lines of Roy et al. (2016). TM is treated as ETM+, as in Earth Engine's harmonization tutorial (no TM lines are published). bands dict None The cube's band of each role (coastal, blue, green, red, nir, swir1, swir2), when its names are not the usual ones (red, B04, SR_B4...). With a list of cubes, one dict for all or one per cube. scale "auto" or float "auto" What the reflectance is multiplied by in the data: 10000 for integers or values above 2, else 1 (a lazy cube is checked on a small window). The intercepts are in reflectance. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Missing values besides NaN (the raster's NoData; 0 for integers without one). They stay missing. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; otherwise the result is lazy.

Returns the cube with the same dimensions, coordinates, type and georeferencing (a list: the joined series), lazy if the input is. Bands without a line (the red edge, QA bands) are copied. attrs["bandpass_adjusted"] says what was done, and an adjusted cube is refused a second time.

Sentinel-2's NIR. HLS adjusts the narrow NIR, B8A (nir08 on Earth Search, B8A on Planetary Computer), the band that matches OLI's band 5. B08, the broad NIR (nir on Earth Search, B08), has no line: it is left as it is, with a warning. Load B8A, or pass bands={"nir": ...} when a band is B8A under another name.

s2 = zeit.build_time_series(collection="sentinel-2-l2a", bands=["B02", "B03", "B04", "B8A", "B11", "B12"], **grid)
landsat = zeit.build_time_series(collection="landsat-c2-l2",
                                 bands=["blue", "green", "red", "nir08", "swir16", "swir22"], **grid)
mixed = zeit.bandpass_adjust([s2, landsat])      # one series: blue, green, red, nir, swir1, swir2

docs.title: spectral_adjust
docs.text:
zeit.spectral_adjust(
    data, *, sensor=None, bands=None, scale="auto", nodata="auto",
    chunks=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

Takes Landsat 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 and MODIS (Terra and Aqua) surface reflectance to the ten bands of Sentinel-2A (blue, green, red, the three red edge bands, the broad and the narrow NIR, SWIR1 and SWIR2), the red edge and the broad NIR being predicted, since those sensors do not have them. It is FORCE's spectral adjustment (FORCE 3.11, David Frantz, GPL-3.0-or-later; the method and the tables are those of Scheffler, Frantz and Segl 2020, Remote Sensing of Environment 241:111723). Each sensor has 50 clusters of spectra and a global one, each with a linear regression of the ten Sentinel-2A bands on the six of the sensor (blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2) and an intercept. For each pixel the spectral angle to the centre of every cluster gives a weight, 1 - angle / 15° (0.00001 beyond 15°); the closest clusters, at most ten, are kept while their weight is above that of 4°, or above that of 12° and the global cluster's, and the prediction is the average of their regressions weighted by those weights (the global cluster fills in where fewer than ten are close, and takes over where none is). All ten bands are rewritten, not only the new ones: Landsat 8's blue is not Sentinel-2A's. This is not bandpass_adjust, which takes Sentinel-2 towards OLI with a line per band and predicts no band; Sentinel-2 dates pass through here unchanged.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray or path required Surface reflectance (time, band, y, x) or (band, y, x), in memory or dask, with blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1 and SWIR2 (found by role, as bandpass_adjust does). Sentinel-2 dates are passed through (their ten bands, named blue green red rededge1 rededge2 rededge3 nir nir08 swir16 swir22 or B02 ... B12). sensor str or list None Each date's sensor: by default the cube's platform coordinate (which build_time_series keeps from STAC) or attribute; or one name for every date ("landsat-8", "LC09", "LND05", "terra", "MOD02"...), or one per date. Landsat 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 are told apart, and MODIS Terra from Aqua. Any other sensor is an error that names the date. bands dict None The cube's band of each role (blue, green, red, nir, swir1, swir2; for MODIS swir1 is band 6 and swir2 band 7; and the ten Sentinel-2 names for Sentinel-2 dates), when its names are not the usual ones. scale "auto" or float "auto" What the reflectance is multiplied by in the data: 10000 for integers or values above 2, else 1. The method works on reflectance times 10000 (its intercepts are not scale-free): the data are converted to that and the result back to the data's scale. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Missing values besides NaN (the raster's NoData; 0 for integers without one). A pixel with a missing band is missing in all ten. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; otherwise the result is lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads (the processors zeit may use by default). force_search bool False FORCE's first search as it is (cluster 9 skipped, the global cluster a possible first pick), so that the values truncated to integers are FORCE's in every pixel.

Returns (time, band, y, x) (or (band, y, x)), float32, with the same coordinates and georeferencing and ten bands named as Earth Search names them, so that compute_indices finds the ones it uses: blue, green, red, rededge1, rededge2, rededge3, nir (B08), nir08 (B8A), swir16, swir22. Lazy if the input is. attrs["spectral_adjusted"] says what was done for each sensor, and an adjusted cube is refused a second time.

Where it differs from FORCE. The arithmetic is FORCE's (its tables are generated from its source and checked, and with force_search=True the integer outputs equal FORCE's, 100% of 49 million values per sensor), with one difference on purpose: FORCE's first search for the closest cluster skips cluster 9 (it tests s != 9 where the other searches leave out the global cluster, 50) and may pick the global cluster first. Here the global cluster is never the first pick and cluster 9 competes in every search, as in the second search and in the paper. On synthetic spectra of mixed land covers this changes 1.6-2.3% of the observations beyond one unit of the integer reflectance (see Against the Original Implementations). FORCE writes integers truncated toward zero and never reads the nodata value (its QA mask decides); here the output is float and not truncated.

landsat = zeit.build_time_series(collection="landsat-c2-l2",
                                 bands=["blue", "green", "red", "nir08", "swir16", "swir22"], **grid)
s2like = zeit.spectral_adjust(landsat)           # blue ... swir22, plus rededge1-3 and nir08
ndvi = zeit.compute_indices(s2like, ["NDVI"])    # nir is B08, as on Sentinel-2
rededge = s2like.sel(band="rededge2") / s2like.sel(band="rededge1")   # the red edge, which Landsat does not measure

docs.title: tasseled_cap
docs.text:
zeit.tasseled_cap(
    data, components=('brightness', 'greenness', 'wetness'), *,
    coefficients="crist1985", sensor=None, bands=None, nodata="auto",
    chunks=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

The Tasseled Cap of a reflectance cube: brightness (soil, built-up), greenness (green vegetation) and wetness (moisture, shade) as fixed weighted sums of the six reflective bands (blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2), in the scale of the data. The default is what FORCE's TSA does (TC-BRIGHT, TC-GREEN, TC-WET, FORCE 3.11, David Frantz, GPL-3.0-or-later): the matrix of Crist (1985, Remote Sensing of Environment 17:301-306) for every sensor, in float32 with the six products added in the band order, so that FORCE's values truncated to integers are those of this function on the same integers. "sensor" gives each date the matrix published for its sensor instead. "disturbance" is FORCE's TC-DI, brightness - greenness - wetness of the same matrix, not the standardized disturbance index of Healey et al. (2005), which scales each component by the mean and standard deviation of the forest of the scene.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray or path required Reflectance (time, band, y, x) or (band, y, x), in memory or dask, with blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1 and SWIR2 (found by role, as spectral_adjust does). Integers are accepted. For Sentinel-2 the NIR is B8A (nir08), FORCE's NIR for that sensor; a cube with B08 only is used with a warning. components str or list ("brightness", "greenness", "wetness") What to compute, in this order: "brightness", "greenness", "wetness", "disturbance", or the names of a dict of coefficients. coefficients str, dict or array "crist1985" "crist1985" (FORCE's, every sensor); "sensor" (the matrix of each date's sensor, below); "huang2002", "baig2014" (one matrix for every date); a dict {component: six numbers (blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2)}; or an array (components, 6) whose rows are named by components. sensor str or list None Each date's sensor for coefficients="sensor": by default the platform coordinate or attribute of the cube; or one name for every date ("landsat-8", "LC09", "sentinel-2a"...), or one per date. bands dict None The cube's band of each of the six roles (blue, green, red, nir, swir1, swir2) when its names are not the usual ones. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Missing values besides NaN (the raster's NoData; 0 for integers without one). A pixel with a band missing is missing in every component. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; otherwise the result is lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads for an in-memory cube (a dask cube is parallel by its chunks).

Returns (time, band, y, x) (or (band, y, x)), float32, whose band coordinate names the components, lazy if the input is. attrs["tasseled_cap"] says which matrix each sensor got, and a Tasseled Cap is refused a second time. Take one component for landtrendr or the others with .sel(band="wetness"). compute_indices also has TCB, TCG, TCW and TCD, with Crist's matrix, for the reflectance cubes it takes.

The matrices. Coefficients for blue, green, red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2. Those of Crist (1985), Huang et al. (2002) and Baig et al. (2014) are equal to the table of RStoolbox's tasseledCap except for the two signs noted below; RStoolbox has no matrix for Sentinel-2.

Sentinel-2. "sensor" gives Sentinel-2 dates Crist's matrix, as FORCE does. The matrix published for MSI (Shi and Xu 2019, IEEE JSTARS 12:4038-4048) weighs all 13 bands of the L1C top-of-atmosphere product, B1, B9 and B10 included, which an L2A cube does not have, so it is not offered as a six-band matrix.

Sensor Paper Derived for Brightness Greenness Wetness Landsat 4, 5 TM (and every sensor, by default) Crist (1985) reflectance factors (surface) 0.2043 0.4158 0.5524 0.5741 0.3124 0.2303 -0.1603 -0.2819 -0.4934 0.7940 -0.0002 -0.1446 0.0315 0.2021 0.3102 0.1594 -0.6806 -0.6109 Landsat 7 ETM+ Huang et al. (2002), Int. J. Remote Sensing 23:1741-1748 at-satellite reflectance 0.3561 0.3972 0.3904 0.6966 0.2286 0.1596 -0.3344 -0.3544 -0.4556 0.6966 -0.0242 -0.2630 0.2626 0.2141 0.0926 0.0656 -0.7629 -0.5388 Landsat 8 OLI (and 9) Baig et al. (2014), Remote Sensing Letters 5:423-431 top-of-atmosphere reflectance 0.3029 0.2786 0.4733 0.5599 0.5080 0.1872 -0.2941 -0.2430 -0.5424 0.7276 0.0713 -0.1608 0.1511 0.1973 0.3283 0.3407 -0.7117 -0.4559

Only Crist's matrix was derived for surface reflectance. The others were derived for top-of-atmosphere or at-sensor reflectance, and applying them to surface reflectance (as one does with Collection 2 or L2A cubes) is common practice but approximate; so is applying one matrix to every sensor, which is what FORCE does. RStoolbox's table for Landsat 5 TM has +0.0002 and +0.6806 for the SWIR1 weight of greenness and wetness, the opposite signs of Crist's table and FORCE's; Zeit follows the paper.

Against FORCE and RStoolbox. The integer outputs equal FORCE's in every observation computed (100% of 11.7 to 19.7 million values for each of a Sentinel-2A and Landsat 8, 7 and 5 synthetic cubes), and the matrices of ETM+ and OLI equal RStoolbox's to 1e-7 (see Against the Original Implementations).

landsat = zeit.build_time_series(collection="landsat-c2-l2",
                                 bands=["blue", "green", "red", "nir08", "swir16", "swir22"], **grid)
tc = zeit.tasseled_cap(landsat)                                      # as FORCE
tc = zeit.tasseled_cap(landsat, ["wetness"], coefficients="sensor")  # the matrix of each date's sensor
lt = zeit.landtrendr(tc.sel(band="wetness"))

docs.title: improphe
docs.text:
zeit.improphe(
    coarse, fine, *, by="auto", seasons=(1, 91, 181, 271, 365),
    kernel_size=2500.0, texture_size=330.0, pc_variance=0.975,
    force=False, pca=None, nodata="auto", chunks=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

Sharpens a coarse field, or the scenes of a coarser sensor, to the pixels of a finer one: each pixel's value is the weighted mean of the coarse values at the pixels of its neighbourhood that look like it in the fine data. It is FORCE's CF-ImproPhe (a continuous field with a layer for each year, such as a 500 m phenology metric, sharpened with the Sentinel-2 or Landsat scenes of that year) and L2-ImproPhe (Landsat 30 m scenes sharpened with Sentinel-2 10 m), FORCE 3.11 (David Frantz, GPL-3.0-or-later), the method of Frantz, Stellmes, Roeder, Udelhoven, Mader and Hill (2016, IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing 54(7):4153-4164).

The fine scenes (of the year, or all of them for L2) are averaged in the seasonal windows of the year, which gives one spectrum of windows x bands values per pixel; principal components keep 97.5% of their variance and are standardized, and the largest standard deviation of the components in a square of radius texture_size is the fine texture. Around each pixel, in a circle of radius kernel_size, a neighbour is kept if the mean absolute difference S of its components to the pixel's is under one of the five thresholds 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4: the smallest that keeps at least 0.5% of the circle's pixels (the pixel itself counts). The weight of a kept neighbour is 1 / (S T U), where T is the neighbour's fine texture and U the standard deviation of its coarse values in the texture square, each of the three factors rescaled over the kept neighbours to 1 + exp(25 x - 7.5) with x from 0 to 1 (a value of 0 counts 1). A pixel with no neighbour (no fine data) keeps its coarse value; a pixel without a coarse value is NaN.

Parameter Type Default Description coarse DataArray or path required What to sharpen, on any grid of the same CRS (nearest neighbour onto the fine grid, as FORCE's read does; for an integer factor that is the replication of each pixel). With by="year": (year, y, x) or (year, field, y, x); the layer dimension is year, or time with one date per year, or band named by the years. With by=None: scenes (time, band, y, x) or (time, y, x). NaN and the NoData value are missing. fine DataArray or path required The fine reflectance (time, band, y, x) with a datetime time coordinate, NaN where missing (mask clouds first). Any scale; with force=True the seasonal means are cut to integers, which is FORCE's only for reflectance times 10000. Its grid is the output's. by "year", None or "auto" "auto" "year": CF-ImproPhe, each year with the fine scenes of that year. None: L2-ImproPhe, each coarse scene with the seasonal means of all the fine scenes. "auto": a year dimension means "year", several dates in a year mean None, else it asks. seasons sequence of int (1, 91, 181, 271, 365) The days of the year that limit the seasonal windows (FORCE's SEASONAL_WINDOW), n + 1 for n windows, in FORCE's 365-day calendar. A limit larger than the next makes a window that crosses the new year (the days of the neighbouring years count). A window with no scene at a pixel takes the mean of all of them. kernel_size float 2500.0 Radius of the circle, in map units (FORCE's KERNEL_SIZE), cut to whole pixels of fine; a multiple of the pixel size is expected (FORCE refuses others; here a warning). The default suits 10 m pixels (250 pixels). texture_size float 330.0 Radius of the square of the texture, in map units (FORCE's KERNEL_TEXT), 33 pixels at 10 m. pc_variance float 0.975 Fraction of the variance the components keep. force bool False FORCE's arithmetic to the letter (below). pca str or None None The components: "principal" (the paper's) or "force" (FORCE's projection, below); None takes FORCE's with force=True and the principal ones otherwise. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Values that mean missing besides NaN: the raster's NoData of each input (0 for an integer fine without one, as tasseled_cap), a number for both, or None. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None in memory; a dask input is loaded in any case. n_jobs int -1 Threads (the processors zeit may use by default).

Returns float32, the layers of coarse on the grid and coordinates of fine: (year, [field], y, x) or (time, [band], y, x). attrs["improphe"] says the variant, the radius and texture radius in pixels, the minimum number of neighbours, the number of components (per year, or once) and force. A year (CF) or the whole series (L2) with no fine data gives the coarse values themselves.

# CF-ImproPhe: a yearly 500 m field (year, y, x) with the Sentinel-2 cube of the same years, 10 m pixels
sharp = zeit.improphe(lsp_500m, sentinel2, by="year", kernel_size=500, texture_size=60)
# L2-ImproPhe: Landsat scenes (time, band, y, x) at 10 m from the same cube
l8_10m = zeit.improphe(landsat, sentinel2, by=None, kernel_size=300, texture_size=60)
# FORCE's arithmetic, to compare with its outputs after truncating to integers
same_as_force = zeit.improphe(lsp_500m, sentinel2, force=True, kernel_size=500, texture_size=60)

Where it differs from FORCE. The kernel (the neighbours, the thresholds, the weights and their order of summation) is FORCE's, in float32 and float64 as its own. With force=False, two differences are deliberate, and a third is a FORCE quirk that is left out:

  • The components. FORCE projects the data on the transposed matrix of eigenvectors that GSL returns (gsl_blas_dgemm(NoTrans, Trans, ...) in pca-cl.c), that is on its rows and not its columns: its "components" are a rotation of the data that is not the principal axes, and the signs of GSL's eigenvectors change the distances. By default Zeit projects on the eigenvectors (the paper's PCA; with that projection the sign of an eigenvector does not matter) and takes them from a symmetric eigensolver. With force=True the eigenvectors are those of GSL 2.7's gsl_eigen_symmv, ported literally (Householder reduction, implicit QR, selection sort), and the projection is FORCE's. pca="force" takes FORCE's projection alone, with float means. Neither projection is better throughout on the synthetic data of the benchmarks: FORCE's was up to 2.8 times better in one year of a CF field and somewhat worse in others, and with float means (other eigenvector signs) it lost that gain and was 38% worse in the other year; the principal components do not depend on the signs, so they are the default.
  • The seasonal means. FORCE keeps them as 16-bit integers, truncated toward zero, and excludes the upper limit of every window, so day 365 (and 366) is in no window of the default seasons. By default the means are floats and the last window includes its upper limit. force=True reproduces both.
  • An empty year. If a year has no fine data FORCE copies the coarse field for that year and returns from the whole function, leaving the later years at 0. Zeit copies it for that year and goes on with the others.

FORCE writes int16, the result truncated toward zero, and where it does not predict it writes the coarse value as it is (an L2 scene pixel that its QAI screens, a pixel without fine data), 0 (a CF pixel whose coarse value is NoData) or the NoData value (an L2 pixel whose scene is NoData). Zeit returns float and gives NaN wherever the coarse value is missing, and the coarse value where there is no fine data.

Agreement with FORCE. On synthetic Sentinel-2A (10 m), Landsat 8 (30 m) and field (30 m) data, zeit.improphe(..., force=True) truncated to integers equals FORCE's built against GSL's reference CBLAS in every value (2 x 88,065 pixels for CF and 12.5 million values for L2, at radii of 10 and 20 pixels and two sets of seasons); FORCE as the reference build links it, to OpenBLAS, differs in the last bits of the eigenvectors and the results in 0.001-0.003% of the values by 1 or, rarely, more. The tables, and what the transposed projection costs in accuracy, are in Against the Original Implementations. FORCE 3.11.00's own L2IMP does not start as released (it never fills in the settings of the secondary sensors), so that comparison used a copy of its build with those settings filled in.

Cost and memory. The work for every year or scene is the circle of radius kernel_size around each pixel (pi h^2 neighbours of a few components each): on 6 threads of a desktop, 8e5 pixels/s of one year or scene at a radius of 10 pixels, 6e4 at 50, and 25 times the cost of 50 at the default 250 (minutes for a 1000 x 1000 tile). Zeit is 1.2 to 2.4 times as fast as FORCE's compute stage on the same data (see the benchmarks). Everything is in memory (the cube, the coarse field and the result), with no chunking: the components' statistics are those of the whole extent and the circle reaches kernel_size beyond any block. A dask input is computed first; for a large area the caller works a tile at a time, with a margin of kernel_size.

docs.title: sentinel2_resmerge
docs.text:
zeit.sentinel2_resmerge(
    cube, *, method="regression", clear=None, force=False, bands=None,
    scale="auto", nodata="auto", n_jobs=-1,
)

The 20 m bands of Sentinel-2 (red edge 1-3, B8A, SWIR1, SWIR2) at 10 m, predicted from the 10 m green, red and broad NIR: FORCE's resolution merge of its Level 2 processing (resmerge-ll.c, FORCE 3.11, David Frantz, GPL-3.0-or-later). FORCE's third option, STARFM (the USDA's code), is not part of it. The input is a cube already on the 10 m grid, where each 20 m pixel is four equal pixels: that is how FORCE gets them (it reads the 20 m files into the 10 m buffer with GDAL's RasterIO, whose resampling is the nearest neighbour), and a nearest-neighbour reproject_match of the 20 m bands gives the same.

method="regression" fits, for each pixel and each of the six bands, y = c0 + c1 green + c2 red + c3 NIR by least squares over the 5 x 5 pixels around it (GSL's gsl_multifit_linear: the singular value decomposition of the column-balanced matrix, singular values at or below epsilon times the largest dropped) and evaluates it at the pixel. The pixel is in its own window; pixels with no data are left out, and a window with fewer than 25 pixels is filled with rows (1, 0, 0, 0) and y = 0 (FORCE's: it pulls the fit towards zero at the borders and next to gaps); clouds and shadows are kept in the window. method="improphe" is ImproPhe's weighted mean with spectral instead of temporal similarity: the pixels of the disc of radius 2 that are not cloud, shadow or no data and whose mean absolute difference of green, red and NIR (reflectance) to the pixel is under 0.0025, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02 or 0.025 are the neighbours; the smallest of those cutoffs that has at least 3 of them is used, and each band is the mean of the neighbours' values weighted by 1 / (1 + exp(25 x - 7.5)), x the difference rescaled over the neighbours of the cutoff. It is faster than the regression.

Parameter Type Default Description cube DataArray required Reflectance (time, band, y, x) or (band, y, x), each date on its own, all bands on the 10 m grid, with green red nir rededge1 rededge2 rededge3 nir08 swir16 swir22 (nir is B08, nir08 B8A) or B03 B04 B08 B05 B06 B07 B8A B11 B12. Other bands pass through. In memory (a lazy cube is computed). method "regression" or "improphe" "regression" FORCE's RES_MERGE = REGRESSION or IMPROPHE. clear boolean array None Broadcastable to (time, y, x): True where the pixel is not cloud or shadow. By default every pixel with data is. Pixels that are not clear are not predicted. force bool False FORCE's arithmetic (below). bands dict None The cube's band of each of the nine roles, when its names are not the usual ones. scale "auto" or float "auto" What the reflectance is multiplied by in the data (10000 for integers or values above 2, else 1). The thresholds of "improphe" are in reflectance and the regression's coefficients are not scale-free, so a cube in 0-1 and one in 0-10000 give the same. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Missing values besides NaN: the raster's NoData (0 for an integer cube without one), a number or None. A pixel with a missing value in any of the nine bands is FORCE's "off": left out of the windows and not predicted. n_jobs int -1 Threads (the processors zeit may use by default).

Returns float32, as cube, with the six bands predicted at the pixels that are neither off nor cloud or shadow, and every other value as it was. attrs["sentinel2_resmerge"] says the method.

s2 = zeit.build_time_series(collection="sentinel-2-l2a", resolution=10, ...)   # the 20 m bands by nearest neighbour
sharp = zeit.sentinel2_resmerge(s2, method="regression", clear=cloud_free)
fast = zeit.sentinel2_resmerge(s2, method="improphe", clear=cloud_free)

Where it differs from FORCE. FORCE's regression writes each prediction into the band before the next pixel's window reads it (row-major with one thread; with OpenMP's several it is a race, so its output depends on the thread schedule). With force=False every window reads the original values, the pixels run in parallel and the output is float32, not truncated. force=True is FORCE's arithmetic: the values are taken as reflectance times 10000 (a cube in another scale is converted and rounded), predictions are truncated to integers ((short)(v * 10000)) held in float32, and for "regression" the sweep is FORCE's, in place, row-major, on one thread. The feedback is not a detail: on the synthetic scene of the benchmark the two differ by 11-20 digital numbers on average and up to 490 (the windows of force=True read smoothed predictions where those of force=False read the blocks of the 20 m bands), and force=False matches an independent least squares (numpy's lstsq, 216 pixels) to 1e-4 digital numbers. For "improphe" there is no feedback: the two modes differ by the truncation.

Agreement with FORCE. force=True equals the code of FORCE 3.11.00 in every value, for both methods, on a synthetic 500 x 500 scene with no-data pixels, clouds, shadows, constant spectra (a rank deficient fit) and zeros (6 bands x 245,534 pixels per method): the C harness is FORCE's own functions on plain arrays, linked to the real GSL 2.7 and its reference CBLAS, run on one thread (see Against the Original Implementations). FORCE has no module that runs this on an ARD tile; it runs only inside force-l2ps.

docs.title: pansharpen
docs.text:
zeit.pansharpen(
    ms, pan, method="gsa", *, ratio=None, weights=None, intensity_bands=None,
    kernel=None, gain="regression", nodata="auto", n_jobs=-1,
)

Multispectral bands on the grid of a finer panchromatic band, for any sensor: any number of bands with any names, any pair of resolutions with a ratio above 1 (whole or not: Landsat 8's 15 m band 8 and 30 m bands give 2, 2.5 m and 10 m give 4, 1.5 m and 6.5 m give 4.33), taken from the grids' georeferencing. The CBERS-4A WPM (a 2 m pan; blue, green, red and NIR at 8 m) is one example; Landsat 8/9 (band 8), Sentinel-2 (10 m with 20 m or 60 m bands) and any other pair of rasters are others. The bands are resampled to the pan's grid with the cubic kernel of the warp of load_raster(like=) and the pan's detail is injected by one of four methods, written from their papers (the equations, the references and the choices the papers leave open are in rust/zeit-core/src/pansharpen.rs). No unit is converted: the output has those of ms (digital numbers, radiance or reflectance).

"gsa" (default) is the Gram-Schmidt adaptive of Aiazzi, Baronti and Selva (2007, IEEE TGRS 45(10):3230-3239): F_k = MS_k + g_k (P' - I), g_k = cov(MS_k, I) / var(I), P' the pan matched to the mean and deviation of I, and I the intensity, the regression (with an intercept) of the pan reduced to the bands' resolution on the bands. "brovey" is the ratio transform, F_k = MS_k P / I: with weights, I is their mean (the pan in the units of the bands); without them the pan's response is unknown and I is fitted by the regression through the origin with weights not negative, which absorbs a gain between pan and bands and gives bands outside the pan's range a weight near 0. "hpf" is the high-pass filter of Schowengerdt (1980) with the kernel and modulation of Gangkofner, Pradhan and Holcomb (2008, PE&RS 74(9):1107-1118): F_k = MS_k + gain sd(MS_k) / sd(LP) (P - LP), LP the box mean of the pan (side 2 floor(ratio / 2) + 1, the box that matches the bands' cell: 3 for ratio 2, 5 for 4), computed in O(1) per pixel; by default (gain="regression", zeit's choice) each band gets its least squares slope on LP instead of the paper's modulation sd(MS_k) / sd(LP) (gain=1.0), which over-sharpens bands that the pan does not explain and did not beat the cubic resampling in ERGAS on the benchmark scenes. "pca" replaces the first principal component by the pan matched to it (to compare with products made so, such as the INPE's CB4A-WPM-PCA-FUSED-1).

Bands outside the pan's range (the NIR or the SWIR for a visible pan; the pan's spectral response is not an input). GSA and the fitted Brovey estimate the intensity by regression, so such a band gets a weight near 0 in I, and in GSA a gain g_k that follows its covariance with I: little detail goes in. The Brovey ratio multiplies every band by P / I whatever the band (a known weakness of the ratio form: prefer GSA). HPF has no intensity and gives every band detail in proportion to its spread (the default gain="regression" damps the bands that the pan does not explain; the paper's modulation, gain=1.0, does not). PCA takes the first component of all the bands, which a band the pan does not see can dominate. intensity_bands chooses the bands that enter the estimate of the intensity (GSA, PCA, fitted Brovey), by label of the band coordinate or by position, with no names assumed; the others are still sharpened. All four methods work from 1 band except "pca", which needs 2 (and at least 2 in intensity_bands).

Sources.
