docs.text: Trend tests, phenology, pattern matching, segmentation and clustering.

docs.title: mann_kendall
docs.text:
zeit.mann_kendall(
    data, *, method="hamed_rao", alpha=0.05, lag=None, period=1,
    min_valid=4, dates=None, band=None, nodata="auto", chunks=None,
    n_jobs=-1,
)

Mann-Kendall trend test and Theil-Sen slope for every pixel, a Rust port of pymannkendall. One function for every input, like bfast_monitor: it reads what data is and returns an xarray.Dataset with one variable per metric, georeferenced when the input is. All parameters but data are keyword-only. It replaces zeit.trend.run_mann_kendall_dask, run_mann_kendall_image and DataArray.zeit.run_mann_kendall; the accessor form is now DataArray.zeit.mann_kendall. Tutorial: Trend Analysis.

data is any input of the BFAST family: a raster load_raster reads, a (time, y, x) cube (a dask cube stays lazy), a (time, band, y, x) cube or Dataset with band=, a numpy array or one pixel's series. No dates are needed: the test runs on the order of the observations, so the slope is per time step (one value per year gives a slope per year).

Parameter Type Default Description data path, DataArray, Dataset, ndarray, list or pd.Series required The series to test, one value per time step. method str "hamed_rao" "original", "hamed_rao" (autocorrelation-corrected, for annual composites), "yue_wang" or "seasonal" (Hirsch & Slack, pools period season slots). alpha float 0.05 Significance level. lag int None Lags used by the autocorrelation corrections. None: all. period int 1 Observations per cycle, for "seasonal" (e.g. 23 for 16-day data). min_valid int 4 Pixels with fewer valid values are NaN. dates list None Date of each time step. Not needed: the test only uses the order of the observations. band str or int None The index to use in a (time, band, y, x) cube or a Dataset. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation besides NaN, as in bfast_monitor. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; "auto" or a dict keeps them lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an xarray.Dataset of (y, x) float32 maps (no y/x dims for one pixel; lazy for a dask cube or chunks=):

Variable Meaning trend 1 increasing, -1 decreasing, 0 no significant trend. h 1 if significant at alpha, else 0. p Two-sided p-value. z Standardised test statistic. tau Kendall's tau. s, var_s Mann-Kendall score and its (corrected) variance. slope Theil-Sen slope, per time step (per period for "seasonal"). intercept Intercept of the robust line. 
annual = zeit.load_raster("LT_Stack_NDVI_Rondonia.tif")   # one NDVI value per year
mk = zeit.mann_kendall(annual)
browning = (mk.h == 1) & (mk.trend == -1)
zeit.save_raster(mk, "mk_rondonia")                       # slope.tif, p.tif, ...

# 16-day composites tested directly: 23 observations per year
mk16 = zeit.mann_kendall(ndvi_16d, method="seasonal", period=23)

# One series
zeit.mann_kendall([0.41, 0.44, 0.39, 0.47, 0.52, 0.49, 0.55, 0.58, 0.61, 0.60]).slope.item()

docs.title: ar_trend
docs.text:
zeit.ar_trend(
    data, *, time="step", harmonics=0, period=None, gaps="exact",
    min_valid=0, dates=None, band=None, nodata="auto", chunks=None,
    n_jobs=-1,
)

Linear trend with AR(1) errors, fitted by REML, for every pixel: remotePARTS's fitAR (Ives et al. 2021, Remote Sensing of Environment 266, 112678), on the Rust core. The series is intercept + slope * t (plus harmonics, for sub-annual data) and its errors follow an AR(1) process whose coefficient rho is estimated with the trend, so the t-test of the slope accounts for the autocorrelation of the series. A parametric alternative to mann_kendall, and the per-pixel step of parts. Same inputs and outputs as mann_kendall.

Parameter Type Default Description data path, DataArray, Dataset, ndarray, list or pd.Series required The series, as for mann_kendall. time str "step" "step": t = 1, 2, ... as remotePARTS (slope per time step); "year": decimal years of the dates (slope per year). harmonics int 0 Pairs of harmonics (cos, sin) of the seasonal cycle in the design. period float None Observations per cycle of the harmonics, for time="step"; from the dates when not given. gaps str "exact" "exact": observations k dates apart are correlated by rho**k; "ignore": the valid observations are taken as consecutive, as remotePARTS's fitAR. min_valid int 0 Pixels with fewer valid values are NaN (at least the design's columns + 2). dates list None Date of each time step (needed for time="year"). band str or int None The index to use in a (time, band, y, x) cube or a Dataset. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation besides NaN. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; "auto" or a dict keeps them lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an xarray.Dataset of (y, x) float32 maps: for each coefficient (intercept, slope, cos1, sin1, ...) its value and _se, _t, _p (two-sided); rho, mse (the variance of the innovations) and loglik.

ar = zeit.ar_trend(annual)                        # slope per year for annual composites
greening = (ar.slope > 0) & (ar.slope_p < 0.05)
ar16 = zeit.ar_trend(ndvi_16d, time="year", harmonics=2)   # 16-day data, slope per year

docs.title: parts
docs.text:
zeit.parts(
    data, *, trend=None, response="slope", classes=None,
    covariates=None, mask=None, partsize=1500, npart=None, ncross=6,
    nugget="ml", correlation="exponential", range=None, shape=None,
    fit_n=1000, scaled=False, seed=0, time="step", harmonics=0,
    period=None, gaps="exact", dates=None, band=None, nodata="auto",
    n_jobs=-1,
)

The regional test of the pixels' trends by PARTS (remotePARTS's fitGLS_partition, Ives et al. 2021). Counting the pixels with a significant trend says little about a region: neighbouring pixels are correlated, and thousands of tests are run at once. PARTS answers the regional questions with valid p-values: does the mean trend of the region differ from 0, do the trends differ between land-cover classes, do they depend on a covariate. It fits each pixel's trend (ar_trend), fits the spatial correlation of the pixels to the correlations of their residual series (fitCor), and then a GLS of the trends on the design in random partitions of the pixels, combined into a t-test of each coefficient and a chi-square test of the design, both corrected for the correlation between partitions.

A step-by-step guide with figures, a worked example and the pitfalls: Regional Trends (PARTS).

Distances are in the cube's units: give a cube in projected coordinates. The results match remotePARTS's to 1e-10 for a given nugget; remotePARTS 1.0.4 crosses the partitions after the first without their nugget, which Zeit does not.

Parameter Type Default Description data path, DataArray, Dataset or ndarray required A (time, y, x) cube, in projected coordinates. trend Dataset None An ar_trend result to test instead of fitting it. response str "slope" The variable of the trend tested. classes (y, x) layer None Classes (land cover, ...): a mean trend per class, and the chi-square test that they differ. covariates dict None {name: (y, x) layer}: their effects on the trend (with a mean), and the chi-square test of them. mask (y, x) layer None The pixels tested (a region of interest). partsize int 1500 Pixels per partition (remotePARTS uses 1500 to 3000). npart int None Partitions; all the pixels by default. A few hundred are often enough: the correlation between partitions bounds what more of them gain. ncross int 6 Partitions crossed to measure the correlation between partitions. nugget "ml" or float "ml" Each partition's maximum-likelihood nugget, or a given one. correlation str "exponential" "exponential", exp(-d / range), or "exponential_power", exp(-(d / range) ** shape). range float None The correlation's range when known; fitted to the residuals when None. shape float None The shape of "exponential_power", when known. fit_n int 1000 Pixels sampled to fit the correlation. scaled bool False Distances divided by their largest in each matrix (remotePARTS's default distm_scaled), or in the cube's units. seed int 0 Seed of the samples and partitions. time str "step" As for ar_trend. harmonics int 0 As for ar_trend. period float None As for ar_trend. gaps str "exact" As for ar_trend. dates list None Date of each time step. band str or int None The index to use in a (time, band, y, x) cube or a Dataset. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation besides NaN. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns a PartsResult: table (a DataFrame of the coefficients: estimate, se, t, p), p_chisqr (the chi-square test of the design against a single mean, None without classes or covariates; remotePARTS floors it at 1e-6), f, df1, df2, correlation (the function and its parameters), nuggets, partitions (each partition's coefficients and nugget), npart, partsize, n_pixels.

res = zeit.parts(annual, classes=landcover, partsize=1500, npart=200)
print(res)                       # the mean trend of each class, and whether they differ
res.table.loc["class 3", "p"]
zeit.parts(annual, mask=roi)     # does the region's mean trend differ from 0?

docs.title: emerging_hotspots
docs.text:
zeit.emerging_hotspots(
    data, radius=1, *, shape="square", lag=1, reference="date",
    alpha=0.05, trend="hamed_rao", band=None, nodata="auto",
    n_jobs=-1,
)

Emerging hot spot analysis (ESRI's Space Time Pattern Mining; R sfdep's emerging_hotspot_analysis): where the values cluster high (hot spots) or low (cold spots), and how that changed over the dates. For each date, the Getis-Ord Gi* z-score of each pixel (Getis & Ord 1992): the sum of its neighbourhood (the pixel among it) against the mean, the neighbourhood the pixels within radius at that date and the lag dates before. A hot spot is a date whose Gi* is significantly positive, a cold spot significantly negative. Then the Mann-Kendall test of each pixel's Gi* series, and its pattern as ESRI's documentation defines them:

Code Pattern Definition (hot spots; the cold ones, negative, alike) 1 new hot at the last date only 2 consecutive one run of hot dates, at the end 3 intensifying hot on 90 % of the dates or more, the last one too, its Gi* rising significantly 4 persistent the same, without a significant trend 5 diminishing the same, its Gi* falling significantly 6 sporadic hot at the last date, on and off before, never cold 7 oscillating hot at the last date, cold at some date before 8 historical hot on 90 % of the dates, not at the last 0 no pattern

Where two definitions hold, the first of the table. Each date's Gi* is computed from row prefix sums, a few operations a pixel whatever the radius's area, and the trends in parallel.

The Gi* equals sfdep 0.2.5's (include_gi = TRUE, queen neighbours, k the lag) to 1e-14, and the trend test Kendall's to its single precision (tests/data/make_hotspots_sfdep_fixtures.R). sfdep's patterns differ: it takes the significance of each Gi* from 199 permutations and has rules of its own (it calls sporadic a pixel not significant at the last date); Zeit's follow ESRI's definitions with the normal p-values of the Gi. As sfdep's, the Gi of a date measures the dates before it in its neighbourhood against that date's mean: with a lag, a rise everywhere lowers it (reference="cube" measures every date against the whole cube's). On a grid of 50 x 50 cells and 12 dates, sfdep takes 13 minutes (28 s with 9 permutations); Zeit 4 to 7 ms (benchmarks/vs_originals/hotspots.py).

Parameter Type Default Description data path, DataArray, Dataset or ndarray required One variable as a (time, y, x) cube (an index, a count, an anomaly). Missing values are left out of the sums and statistics. radius int 1 The neighbourhood in pixels: with shape="square" the (2 radius + 1)² pixels around (1: the 8 neighbours, queen contiguity, sfdep's default); with "circle" those whose centres are within it. shape str "square" "square" or "circle". lag int 1 The dates before each date in its neighbourhood (sfdep's k, ESRI's neighbourhood time step). reference str "date" "date": each date's Gi* against that date's mean and standard deviation (as sfdep: a place hot against the others at that date); "cube": against the whole cube's (a date high everywhere is hot everywhere). alpha float 0.05 The significance of the Gi* (two-sided, normal) and of its trend. trend str "hamed_rao" The trend test of the Gi* series: "hamed_rao" (the Gi* of consecutive dates share neighbours, so their series are autocorrelated), "original" Mann-Kendall (ESRI's and sfdep's) or "yue_wang". band str or int None The index to use in a (time, band, y, x) cube or a Dataset. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation besides NaN. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an xarray.Dataset: category (y, x) int8, the pattern's code (-128 with fewer than 3 dates; flag_values and flag_meanings, the names in zeit.emerging_hotspots.PATTERNS); gi (time, y, x), the Gi* z-scores, and p, their p-values; trend_z, trend_p and tau, the trend test of the Gi*; n_hot and n_cold, the dates a significant hot or cold spot.

loss = -zeit.load_raster("ndvi_annual.tif")                  # (time, y, x): where the losses concentrate
ehs = zeit.emerging_hotspots(loss, radius=3, shape="circle")
ehs.category.zeit.plot()                                       # legend: the patterns
new_fronts = ehs.category.isin([1, 2, 3])                     # new, consecutive, intensifying hot spots

docs.title: FORCE time series analysis
docs.text: Six functions ported from the higher-level time series analysis of FORCE 3.11.00 (Frantz 2019, Remote Sensing 11, 1124; GPL-3.0-or-later). They are the steps of FORCE's TSA after the interpolation (interpolate and standardize are in Pre-processing): spectral-temporal metrics and their folds by period, linear trends, change-aftereffect-trend, clear-observation statistics and polar phenology metrics. Each runs on any input of the BFAST family (a (time, y, x) cube in memory or dask, a raster, a numpy array, one pixel's series) and returns floats, not FORCE's int16 scaled by 10000. Tutorial: FORCE's time series analysis chain. Agreement with FORCE on 10,000 pixels: Against the original implementations.

docs.title: temporal_metrics
docs.text:
zeit.temporal_metrics(
    data,
    metrics=('min', 'p25', 'median', 'p75', 'max', 'mean', 'std'), *,
    by=None, ddof=1, dates=None, band=None, nodata="auto",
    chunks=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

Statistics of each pixel's series, over all of it or by period: FORCE's spectral-temporal metrics (STM; Müller et al. 2015) and their folds (FBY, FBQ, FBM, FBW, FBD). The series can have any spacing; NaN marks a missing observation.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, Dataset, path, ndarray, list or pd.Series required A (time, y, x) cube, a (time, band, y, x) cube or Dataset with band=, a numpy array with dates=, or one pixel's series. metrics sequence of str ("min", "p25", "median", "p75", "max", "mean", "std") min, max, range, iqr, mean, std, skew, kurtosis (excess), count (valid observations), median and pNN for any integer percentile 0-100 (R-7, as np.nanpercentile). by str None None: the statistics of the whole series. "year", "quarter", "month", "week" or "doy": those of each period (the dates are needed). ddof int 1 Degrees of freedom of std: the divisor is n - ddof (1 is the sample deviation, as FORCE's STD). dates list None Date of each time step, for inputs that carry none. band str or int None The index to use in a (time, band, y, x) cube or a Dataset. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation besides NaN, as in mann_kendall. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; otherwise the result is lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an xarray.DataArray (metric, y, x), or (metric, <by>, y, x) with by, with the names of the metrics in metric. Float32 for float32 input, else float64. Pixels without a valid observation are NaN (0 for count). The periods are the years from the first to the last date, 1-4, 1-12, 1-52, 1-365, all of them, the empty ones NaN. The week is min(ceil(doy / 7), 52) and the day of the year counts 365 days, 29 February sharing day 60 with 1 March, so that a calendar day is the same day of the year in every year (FORCE's calendar).

Differences from FORCE. skew (M3 / sigma^3, the population deviation) and kurtosis (excess) are NaN in a series with fewer than 2 distinct values, where FORCE leaves them undefined; std with n <= ddof is NaN. The output is not rounded to int16.

stm = zeit.temporal_metrics(ndvi, ["p10", "median", "p90", "std"])        # (metric, y, x)
yearly = zeit.temporal_metrics(ndvi, ["mean", "max"], by="year")           # (metric, year, y, x)

docs.title: linear_trend
docs.text:
zeit.linear_trend(
    data, *, conf=0.95, tail="two", dim=None, band=None,
    nodata="auto", chunks=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

The linear trend of each pixel's series: FORCE's TRY, TRQ, TRM, TRW and TRD, depending on the series (the yearly, quarterly, monthly, weekly or daily folds of temporal_metrics). A least-squares line on the position of each step along dim (0, 1, 2..., counting the missing steps too, so the slope is per step: per year for a yearly series), with a t-test of the slope. A pixel with fewer than 3 valid steps is NaN.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, path, ndarray, list or pd.Series required A (time, y, x) cube, or a series along another axis such as the (metric, year, y, x) result of temporal_metrics(..., by="year"). conf float 0.95 Confidence level of the test of the slope. tail str "two" "two", "left" (is the slope significantly negative?) or "right". dim str None The axis of the series: "time" (default when it exists) or another, such as "year". A metric axis of length 1 is dropped; with more, choose one with .sel(metric=...). band str or int None The index to use in a (time, band, y, x) cube or a Dataset. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation besides NaN. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; otherwise the result is lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an xarray.Dataset of (y, x) maps:

Variable Meaning mean, offset Mean of the valid steps; the fit at the first step. slope Slope per step. pct_gain, abs_gain The slope times the number of steps, as a percentage of the offset (0 unless the offset is positive) and as is. rsq R squared, 0-1 (FORCE writes it times 10000). sig -1, 0 or 1: the slope is significantly negative, not significant, or positive. rmse, mae, maxe Root mean square, mean absolute and largest absolute residual. num, len Valid steps, and steps.

Differences from FORCE. The critical value is the exact quantile of Student's t with num - 2 degrees of freedom, tabled once per degrees of freedom; FORCE iterates Hill's approximation to a tolerance of 1e-4, so sig can differ only where the t-value is that close to the limit.

yearly = zeit.temporal_metrics(ndvi, ["mean"], by="year")
trend = zeit.linear_trend(yearly)                    # trend.slope: NDVI per year
greening = trend.sig == 1

docs.title: cat
docs.text:
zeit.cat(
    data, *, penalty=False, conf=0.95, tail="two", dim=None,
    band=None, nodata="auto", chunks=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

The change-aftereffect-trend of each pixel's series (CAT; Hird et al. 2016): FORCE's CAY, CAQ, CAM, CAW and CAD. The change is the greatest loss between a valid step and the valid one before it (positive for a loss; a series that only rises keeps its smallest rise). The series is split at that step, and the trend of linear_trend is fit to the whole series (total_), to the steps before the change (before_, from the first up to two before the change step, as FORCE defines it) and from the change step on (after_). A part without valid steps is NaN; one with fewer than 3 has only its mean, num and len.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, path, ndarray, list or pd.Series required As for linear_trend. penalty bool False Weight each loss by what the series has lost by the next valid step (FORCE's CHANGE_PENALTY), which discounts a dip the series recovers from. conf float 0.95 Confidence level of the test of the slopes. tail str "two" "two", "left" or "right". dim str None The axis of the series, as for linear_trend. band str or int None The index to use in a (time, band, y, x) cube or a Dataset. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation besides NaN. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; otherwise the result is lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an xarray.Dataset of (y, x) maps: change (the greatest loss), loss (the change as a percentage of total_offset, 0 unless that is positive), change_time (the coordinate of dim at the change: the date, the year, the month..., NaN or NaT when there is none) and the twelve variables of linear_trend for each part, prefixed total_, before_ and after_: 39 in all. A pixel with fewer than 2 valid steps is NaN.

Differences from FORCE. With penalty, FORCE compares the penalized value of each candidate with the unpenalized change of the best one so far, mixing two scales; Zeit compares penalized with penalized, and returns the winner's unpenalized change, as FORCE. The two can pick another step (15% of the pixels on yearly folds, 70% on monthly ones in the benchmark). The t quantile is exact, as in linear_trend.

yearly = zeit.temporal_metrics(ndvi, ["mean"], by="year")
ch = zeit.cat(yearly, penalty=True)                  # ch.change_time: the year of the greatest loss
ch.after_slope                                       # the recovery after it, per year

docs.title: clear_observations
docs.text:
zeit.clear_observations(
    data, *, months=1, metrics=('count', 'mean', 'max'), start=None,
    end=None, dates=None, band=None, nodata="auto", chunks=None,
    n_jobs=-1,
)

The clear-sky observations of each pixel in windows of months, and the gaps between them: FORCE's CSO (Ernst et al. 2018). An observation is valid where the value is finite (NaN and NoData are cloud or missing), or True in a boolean cube. In each window the intervals, in days, run from the start of the window to the first valid observation, between consecutive ones, and from the last to the end of the window. A window without a valid observation has one interval, as long as the window, and a count of 0. The dates are needed and must not decrease.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, path, ndarray, list or pd.Series required A cube of any values (valid where finite), or a boolean cube (True: clear). months int 1 The length of a window in months, 1 to 12. metrics sequence of str ("count", "mean", "max") count (the valid observations) and, of the intervals in days, the metrics of temporal_metrics: min, max, range, iqr, mean, std, skew, kurtosis, median, pNN. start, end date None The windows begin on the first day of the month of start and go on until the one that holds end, which is included whole. Default: the first and last date. dates list None Date of each time step, for inputs that carry none. band str or int None The index to use in a (time, band, y, x) cube or a Dataset. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation besides NaN. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; otherwise the result is lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an xarray.DataArray (metric, window, y, x), with window the first day of each window and window_end (along window) its end, exclusive. Float32 for float32 input, else float64.

Differences from FORCE. FORCE mixes the number of observations n with the number of intervals k: its standard deviation divides by n - 1, its skewness and kurtosis by n, and its quantiles are taken over the first n of the k intervals (reading stale memory when observations share a day). Here every metric but count is over the same k intervals; count, min, max, range and mean equal FORCE's, the others differ where n != k. In a window without a valid observation FORCE writes 0 for std, skew, kurtosis and the quantiles; here std, skew and kurtosis are NaN. FORCE leaves out the last window when it starts in the month the range ends in (December's, with 1-month windows); Zeit keeps it.

cso = zeit.clear_observations(ndvi, months=3, metrics=["count", "max"])    # (metric, window, y, x)
longest_gap = zeit.clear_observations(ndvi.notnull(), metrics=["max"])     # a boolean cube works too

References: Müller, H., Rufin, P., Griffiths, P., Barros Siqueira, A. J., & Hostert, P. (2015). Remote Sensing of Environment, 156, 490-499 (STM). Hird, J. N., Castilla, G., McDermid, G. J., & Bueno, I. T. (2016). IEEE JSTARS, 9, 3372-3383 (CAT). Ernst, S., Lymburner, L., & Sixsmith, J. (2018). Remote Sensing, 10, 1570 (CSO). The full list, with the interpolation's, is in the tutorial.

docs.title: polar_metrics
docs.text:
zeit.polar_metrics(
    data, metrics=('VSS', 'VPS', 'VES', 'VSA', 'RMR', 'IGS'), *,
    start=0.2, mid=0.5, end=0.8, adaptive=True, dates=None, band=None,
    nodata="auto", chunks=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

The polar phenology metrics of each pixel and year: FORCE's POL (polar-hl.c, Frantz), which implements and extends the polar metrics of Brooks et al. (2020). Each date of a regular series is a vector: the value is the radius and the day of the year the angle. The mean of all the vectors is the long-term mean vector; the opposite direction, the time of least activity, starts the phenological year. Along each year's season the values are accumulated and divided by their total, and the dates where that fraction reaches start, mid and end are the start, middle and end of the season; the rest of the 39 metrics (dates, lengths, values, amplitudes, integrals and rates) come from those points. Only what the requested metrics need is computed. The series must be regular, a constant step of whole days (the output of interpolate with step=, FORCE's TSI) and cover at least 2 years; a missing step (NaN) is filled by linear interpolation in time, as FORCE does.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, path, ndarray, list or pd.Series required A (time, y, x) cube of a non-negative index (negative values count as 0), a numpy array with dates=, or one pixel's series. metrics sequence of str ("VSS", "VPS", "VES", "VSA", "RMR", "IGS") Any of the 39 names in the table below, upper or lower case. start, mid, end float 0.2, 0.5, 0.8 The fractions of the season's accumulated value that mark its start, middle and end (FORCE's POL_START_THRESHOLD, POL_MID_THRESHOLD and POL_END_THRESHOLD), each between 0 and 1. adaptive bool True Fine-tune the start of each year's season from its own mean vector, not the long-term one (FORCE's POL_ADAPTIVE). dates list None Date of each time step, for inputs that carry none. band str or int None The index to use in a (time, band, y, x) cube or a Dataset. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation besides NaN, as in mann_kendall. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; otherwise the result is lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an xarray.DataArray (metric, year, y, x): one band per calendar year from the first date's to the last's, float32 for float32 input, else float64, unrounded (FORCE writes truncated int16). A season belongs to the year it ends in when the long-term start of the year is before day 182, else to the year after it begins, so a series of n years has n - 1 seasons and one year (the first or the last) is NaN. A series need not start on 1 January: a season whose start of the year is before the first date (or has no step in the series) is NaN, and the seasons whose start is in the series are measured as usual (FORCE, which looks for the first start for ever, finds no season at all in that case and writes 0 for every metric); a season cut short by the end of the series is measured from the steps it has, as in FORCE. linear_trend of one metric along year is FORCE's TRO of it and cat its CAO.

The 39 metrics. A date counts days from 1 January of the band's year (365 days a year, 29 February sharing day 60 with 1 March). Data is the unit of the input.

Name Meaning Unit DEM date of the early minimum (first step of the season with a non-zero accumulated fraction) days DLM date of the late minimum (the step after the last one with the fraction 1: the start of the next season) days DPS date of the peak (first maximum of the growing season) days DSS, DMS, DES date of the start, the middle and the end of the season (the fraction reaches start, mid, end) days DEV, DAV, DLV date of the mean vector of the early (start to mid), whole (start to end) and late (mid to end) growing season days LTS, LGS, LGV length of the total season (DLM - DEM), of the growing season (DES - DSS) and between the early and late mean vectors (DLV - DEV) days VEM, VLM value at the early and at the late minimum data VPS value at the peak data VSS, VMS, VES value at the start, the middle and the end of the season data VEV, VAV, VLV length of the early, whole and late mean vector (the mean, not the sum, of the points of the window) data VBL base level, (VEM + VLM) / 2 data VGM, VGV mean and standard deviation (n - 1) of the growing season data VGA green amplitude, peak minus (VSS + VES) / 2 data VSA seasonal amplitude, peak minus base level data VPA peak amplitude, peak minus the value at the middle data DPY start of the phenological year (long-term, the same every year; negative when it falls before 1 January of the band's year) days DPV shift of the season's own start from DPY (0 without adaptive) days IST seasonal integral, above the base level data × year IBL base integral, under the base level data × year IBT total integral of the season data × year IGS green integral, above the green level in the growing season data × year IRR, IFR rising and falling integral (the sum of the rises and of the falls) data × month RAR, RAF average rate of rise (early growing season) and of fall (late growing season); the sum of the rates over all the steps of the window, as FORCE data / month RMR, RMF maximum rate of rise (early growing season) and of fall (late growing season) data / month

Differences from FORCE. All are deliberate.

  • Dates count from 1 January of the band's year, FORCE's from 1 January of the first year of the series (continuous days). A linear trend along year is then directly the change per year; FORCE subtracts 365 from the slope of a date (its in_ce) to get the same. To compare with FORCE's rasters add 365 * i to the dates of year i (FORCE also writes the slope of a date times 1000).
  • What FORCE leaves undefined is NaN. FORCE casts a NaN to int16 and writes garbage (0 on x86): a season whose accumulated total is 0 (a pixel of zero index), a season without steps, the mean vector or rate of a window without steps, VGM without a step, VGV with fewer than 2. Nothing is clipped to 16 bits (FORCE wraps an integral past 32767).
  • DPV is 0 without adaptive, where FORCE writes -DPY (a start it never set).
  • STANDARDIZE_POL does nothing in FORCE and does not exist here: use standardize.
tsi = zeit.interpolate(ndvi * 10000, "rbf", step=16)           # FORCE's TSI
pol = zeit.polar_metrics(tsi, ["DSS", "DES", "VPS", "IGS"])    # (metric, year, y, x)
sos_trend = zeit.linear_trend(pol.sel(metric="DSS"))           # days per year, along year

Reference: Brooks, B.-G. J., Lee, D. C., Pomara, L. Y., & Hargrove, W. W. (2020). Monitoring broadscale vegetational diversity and change across North American landscapes using land surface phenology. Forests, 11(6), 606. doi:10.3390/f11060606.

docs.title: phenology
docs.text:
zeit.phenology(
    data, *, curve="beck", method="threshold", weights=None,
    dates=None, annual=True, max_seasons=None, whittaker_lambda=10.0,
    apply_whittaker=True, apply_hants=False, hants_frequencies=3,
    hants_threshold=0.1, min_season_length=0, min_amplitude=0.0,
    min_pixel_amplitude=0.1, season_retry=True, band=None,
    nodata="auto", chunks=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

Land surface phenology, written from the papers (Whittaker: Eilers 2003; HANTS: Roerink et al. 2000; the curves of Beck 2006, Elmore 2012, Gu 2009, Klosterman 2014, Zhang 2003, Jönsson & Eklundh and Fisher 2006), not from the code of R phenofit, which stays a useful reference to compare outputs with: smooths each pixel's series (Whittaker or HANTS), splits it into seasons, fits a curve to each season and extracts 19 transition metrics plus the fit's R² and RMSE, every pixel in parallel in the Rust core. One function for every input, like bfast_monitor (the same data table), with dates at any spacing. It replaces zeit.phenology.run_phenology_dask and DataArray.zeit.run_phenology; the accessor form is now DataArray.zeit.phenology, and the engine module is internal (zeit._phenology). Tutorial: Phenology.

The day numbering of the core (days since January 1st of the first year) and the first year are computed from the dates, so no day-of-year array is needed.

Parameter Type Default Description data path, DataArray, Dataset, ndarray, list or pd.Series required A vegetation-index series with dates (see bfast_monitor). curve str or int "beck" Fitted curve: "beck", "elmore", "gu", "klos", "zhang", "ag" or "dl" (or its integer code). method str or int "threshold" "threshold", "derivative", "gu" or "klosterman" (or its integer code). Recorded in attrs; every metric family is computed whatever the method. weights DataArray or array None Per-observation reliability weights in [0, 1], aligned with the data (e.g. from qc_sentinel2_scl). dates list None Date of each time step, for numpy input and series without dates. annual bool True True: one value per calendar year, (year, y, x), dates as day of year. False: one value per detected season, (season, y, x), dates as days since January 1st of the first year (attrs["base_year"]). max_seasons int None Years (with annual) or seasons per pixel. Default: the number of years in the series. whittaker_lambda float 10.0 Whittaker smoothness. apply_whittaker bool True Smooth with Whittaker before fitting. apply_hants bool False Smooth with HANTS (harmonics) instead. hants_frequencies int 3 HANTS harmonics. hants_threshold float 0.1 HANTS outlier threshold. min_season_length int 0 Drop seasons shorter than this many days. min_amplitude float 0.0 Drop seasons with a smaller amplitude. min_pixel_amplitude float 0.1 Skip pixels whose whole series varies less than this (water, urban). season_retry bool True Retry pixels with no season once with a relaxed trough threshold. band str or int None The index to use in a (time, band, y, x) cube or a Dataset. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation besides NaN, as in bfast_monitor. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; "auto" or a dict keeps them lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an xarray.Dataset with 21 variables, each (year, y, x) (annual=True, year coordinate from the first year) or (season, y, x) (season = 1, 2, …): TRS2.sos, TRS2.eos, TRS5.sos, TRS5.eos, TRS6.sos, TRS6.eos, DER.sos, DER.pos, DER.eos, UD, SD, DD, RD, Greenup, Maturity, Senescence, Dormancy, LOS, POP, R2, RMSE (see the 19 metrics). NaN where no season was found. The names contain dots, so select them with brackets: pheno["TRS5.sos"]. The result is georeferenced and lazy for a dask cube or chunks=; save_raster writes one GeoTIFF per metric with one band per year (2019, 2020, …) or season.

ndvi_16d = zeit.regularize_time_series(ndvi, freq="16D", method="median")   # (time, y, x)
pheno = zeit.phenology(ndvi_16d, curve="beck", min_season_length=45, min_amplitude=0.15)
sos = pheno["TRS5.sos"]                         # (year, y, x), day of year
late = sos.sel(year=2021) - sos.sel(year=[2019, 2020]).mean("year")
zeit.save_raster(pheno, "pheno_out")            # TRS2.sos.tif, ..., one band per year

# Double cropping: up to 3 seasons per pixel instead of one value per year
seasons = zeit.phenology(ndvi_16d, annual=False, max_seasons=3)

docs.title: Pattern matching (TWDTW)
docs.text: Tutorial: Pattern Matching.

docs.title: twdtw
docs.text:
zeit.twdtw(
    data, patterns, *, band=None, steepness=0.1, midpoint=50.0,
    cycle="year", max_elapsed=None, nodata="auto", chunks=None,
    n_jobs=-1,
)

Classifies time series by Time-Weighted Dynamic Time Warping (Maus et al. 2016): each pattern, a typical series of a class, is matched against every pixel's series, and the class of a pixel is the pattern with the lowest distance. The distance is that of the R package twdtw (checked against it to 1e-12): the pattern may match any stretch of the series, each pair of matched observations costs their Euclidean distance plus a logistic time weight

\[ w(\Delta t) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\text{steepness}\,(\Delta t - \text{midpoint})}} \]

of the days \(\Delta t\) between them, and dates a pixel has no value for are left out of its series. One function for every input; it replaces classify_twdtw, run_twdtw and run_twdtw_batch.

Input Example Where the dates come from A cube (time, y, x), or (time, band, y, x) for several bands; anything load_raster reads ndvi Its time coordinate. A dask cube stays lazy. One pixel: a pandas.Series (or a DataFrame, one column per band) indexed by dates series Its index

Patterns are {name: series}: a pandas.Series indexed by dates, a DataFrame with one column per band, or a DataArray with time (and band). With several bands, the cube's bands are taken by the patterns' column names.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, path, pd.Series or pd.DataFrame required The series to classify (see the table above). patterns dict required {name: pattern}, one per class. Names cannot hold spaces. band str None A cube with a band dim and one-band patterns: the band to classify. steepness float 0.1 Steepness of the logistic time weight, per day. midpoint float 50.0 Days apart at which a pair costs half a unit more (R's time_weight = c(0.1, 50)). cycle str or None "year" "year": the days between dates are counted between days of the year, around it (31 December and 1 January are a day apart), so a pattern of one year matches the same season of any year. None: between the dates themselves. max_elapsed float None Pairs farther apart than this many days are never matched. None: no limit. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation: the raster's NoData (0 for integer data without one), a number, or None. chunks "auto", dict None Inputs read from disk: None reads into memory; otherwise the result is lazy. n_jobs int -1 Threads. -1: all the cores but one, or every core of a cluster job (how they are counted).

Returns an xarray.Dataset:

Variable Dims Meaning label (y, x) The class: 1 for the first pattern, 2 for the second… (0: no observation). Its flag_meanings hold the names, which zeit.plot shows in the legend. distance (y, x) TWDTW distance to that pattern. High values mean no pattern fits well. distances (pattern, y, x) Distance to every pattern. pattern_value, pattern_time (pattern, pattern_step[, band]) The patterns, so that zeit.plot(cube, fit=result) draws the best one aligned with a clicked pixel's series. save_raster skips them. 
patterns = {"soy": soy, "pasture": pasture, "forest": forest}   # pandas Series indexed by dates
classes = zeit.twdtw(ndvi, patterns)
classes.label.zeit.plot(basemap="satellite")                     # legend: soy, pasture, forest
unknown = classes.label.where(classes.distance < 3, 0)          # 0 where nothing fits
zeit.plot(ndvi, fit=classes)                                     # click a pixel: its best match
zeit.save_raster(classes, "twdtw")                               # label.tif, distance.tif, distances.tif

docs.title: Segmentation (SNIC)
docs.text: Tutorial: Segmentation.

docs.title: snic
docs.text:
zeit.snic(
    data, *, spacing=10, compactness=0.5, seeds=None,
    grid="rectangular", padding=None, tile_size=None,
    random_state=None, nodata="auto", n_jobs=-1,
)

SNIC superpixels of an image or a whole cube: every value of a pixel off its y/x (each band, each date) is one feature, so two pixels are alike when their whole trajectories are, as sits_segment(seg_fn = sits_snic()). Given the same seeds, labels match the reference C implementation. It replaces run_snic (the engine, still in zeit.segmentation) and the accessor's run_snic.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, ndarray or path required (y, x), (band, y, x), (time, y, x) or (time, band, y, x), read into memory. Pixels with any missing feature are left unlabelled (-1). spacing float or pair 10 Seed spacing in pixels. compactness float 0.5 Regularity of the segments, in data units. Higher is more compact. seeds (n, 2) array None Explicit (row, col) seeds; overrides the grid. grid str "rectangular" "rectangular", "diamond", "hexagonal" or "random". padding float or pair None Seed-free margin. Default spacing / 2. tile_size int or pair None Segment tiles of this size independently, in parallel. random_state int None Seed for grid="random". nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation. n_jobs int -1 Threads.

Returns an xarray.Dataset: labels (y, x) (georeferenced; -1 unlabelled), means (segment, ...) with the cube's dims and coordinates ((segment, time, band) for a (time, band, y, x) cube), and n_pixels, centroid_x, centroid_y (segment) (map coordinates). save_raster writes the labels; snic_to_polygons makes polygons.

seg = zeit.snic(ndvi, spacing=8, compactness=0.3)          # ndvi: (time, y, x)
zeit.save_raster(seg, "results/snic")                       # labels.tif
polygons = zeit.snic_to_polygons(seg, include_means=True)   # one column per date

docs.title: snic_to_polygons
docs.text:
zeit.segmentation.snic_to_polygons(
    result, transform=None, crs=None, include_means=False,
)

Converts SNIC labels to a GeoDataFrame, one polygon per segment, like sits_segment(). Also exported as zeit.snic_to_polygons.

Parameter Type Default Description result Dataset or SnicResult required Output of zeit.snic (its transform, CRS and feature names are used) or of the engine run_snic. transform Affine None Geotransform of a SnicResult (identity: pixel coordinates); taken from a Dataset. crs None Coordinate reference system of a SnicResult; taken from a Dataset. include_means bool False Add each segment's mean features as columns, named by the cube's coordinates (2022-01-01_ndvi, …; f0, f1, … for a SnicResult).

docs.text:

    shape, spacing, padding=None, type="rectangular",
    random_state=None,

The seed grids of the R snic package, as (n, 2) (row, col) positions. Also exported as zeit.snic_grid.

Parameter Type Default Description shape (int, int) required Image (rows, cols). spacing float or pair required Seed spacing. padding float or pair None Seed-free margin. type str "rectangular" Grid type, as in zeit.snic's grid. random_state int None Seed for "random".

docs.title: texture
docs.text:
zeit.texture(
    data, *, features=None, window=7, levels=32, distance=1, lo=None,
    hi=None, summary="median", n_jobs=-1,
)

Texture features of an image in a moving window, inputs for a classifier where fields, pastures, orchards and forests differ in texture but not in spectrum. The grey-level co-occurrence matrix's properties (Haralick et al. 1973) are scikit-image's graycomatrix(..., angles=[0, pi/4, pi/2, 3pi/4], symmetric=True, normed=True) and graycoprops for each pixel's window (cut by the image's edges), averaged over the four angles: equal to 1e-12, and 78 times faster on one thread (benchmarks/vs_originals/texture.py). Three of spfeas's window statistics (Graesser et al. 2012) complete them. A cube is summarized over time first.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray or ndarray required A map (y, x), or a cube (time, y, x) summarized by summary. features str or list None All twelve, or any of: contrast, dissimilarity, homogeneity, asm, energy, correlation, entropy (base 2), glcm_mean, glcm_variance, and the window's mean, std and gradient (mean Sobel magnitude). window int 7 The window's side in pixels (odd). levels int 32 Grey levels (2-254) the values are quantized to over [lo, hi]. distance int 1 The pairs' distance in pixels. lo, hi float None The range quantized; default the image's 2nd and 98th percentiles. summary str "median" A cube's summary: "median", "mean", "min", "max", "std" or "amplitude" (95th - 5th percentile). n_jobs int -1 Threads.

Returns an xarray.DataArray (feature, y, x), the map's coordinates kept; NaN where a window has no valid pair.

tex = zeit.texture(ndvi, summary="max", window=7, features=["contrast", "entropy", "std"])
stack = xr.concat([ndvi.median("time").expand_dims(feature=["ndvi"]), tex], "feature")  # predictors

docs.title: som
docs.text:
zeit.som(
    data, *, x=3, y=3, sample=50000, num_iters=None,
    algorithm="online", sigma=1.0, learning_rate=0.5,
    decay="linear_decay_to_zero", neighborhood="gaussian",
    topology="rectangular", init="random", seed=42, nodata="auto",
    chunks=None, n_jobs=-1,
)

Clusters the pixels of a map or a cube with a self-organizing map. Every value a pixel holds off its y/x is a feature (each date of an index, each band of each date, each map of a Dataset), so pixels share a neuron when their whole trajectories are alike. The SOM is trained on a random sample of the pixels by the SOM engine (a bit-for-bit port of minisom), then every pixel goes to its best-matching neuron. Tutorial: Clustering.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, Dataset, ndarray or path required A map, a stack, a (time, y, x) or (time, band, y, x) cube (in memory or dask), a Dataset of maps (e.g. phenology metrics), or anything load_raster reads. The features should share a scale: the distance adds them up as they are. x, y int 3, 3 Neurons of the grid: x * y clusters. Small grids cluster; large ones (10 × 10 and up) explore the data. sample int or None 50000 Pixels to train on, drawn at random among those with every feature; None: all of them. num_iters int None "online": single-sample updates (default 20 passes over the sample). "batch": passes (default 20). algorithm str "online" "online" or "batch" (parallel). On small grids the batch update can leave neurons empty; the online one does not, and is about as fast on 50,000 samples. sigma, learning_rate float 1.0, 0.5 Initial neighbourhood radius (grid units) and learning rate. decay str "linear_decay_to_zero" Online: how the learning rate falls. Ending at 0 lets the prototypes settle; minisom's default, "asymptotic_decay", ends at a third of it, and the last samples seen still pull them (on 30,000 Rondônia trajectories: a mean distance 10% larger, prototypes up to twice as far from their pixels' mean). Or "inverse_decay_to_zero". neighborhood str "gaussian" "gaussian", "mexican_hat", "bubble" or "triangle". topology str "rectangular" "rectangular" or "hexagonal". init str or None "random" Initial prototypes: "random" (sample pixels), "pca" (first two principal components; poor on a grid one neuron wide) or None (minisom's random unit vectors). seed int 42 Seed of the sample, the initial weights and the sample order. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value marking a missing observation. Pixels with a missing feature get no neuron. chunks "auto", dict None A raster path: read lazily. n_jobs int -1 Threads.

Returns an xarray.Dataset: label (y, x) (the neuron, 1 to x * y; 0 without one; the grid positions i_j in flag_meanings), distance (y, x) (to the neuron's prototype: large where the map represents the pixel poorly), prototypes (neuron, ...) with the cube's dims and coordinates (prototypes.sel(neuron=3) is a series over time) and n_pixels (neuron); the grid position of each neuron in the i/j coordinates and the sample's mean distance in attrs["quantization_error"]. Georeferenced as the input; a lazy cube stays lazy. With sample=None and the same arguments, the prototypes are the engine's and label is SOM.predict + 1.

ndvi = zeit.load_raster("LT_Stack_NDVI_Rondonia.tif")     # (time, y, x)
clusters = zeit.som(ndvi, x=2, y=2, sample=30_000)
clusters.prototypes.sel(neuron=1).plot()                  # one typical trajectory
clusters.label.zeit.plot()                                # the cluster map
zeit.plot(ndvi, fit=clusters)                             # click a pixel: its series and its prototype

docs.title: clean_samples
docs.text:
zeit.clean_samples(
    data, samples, *, label="class", x=None, y=None, num_iters=None,
    algorithm="online", sigma=1.0, learning_rate=0.5,
    decay="linear_decay_to_zero", neighborhood="gaussian",
    topology="rectangular", init="random", seed=42, date=None,
    nodata="auto", n_jobs=-1,
)

Checks labelled samples with a SOM before a classifier is trained on them, as sits_som_clean_samples of the R sits package: a SOM is trained on the features of the samples (read as train_classifier reads them), and a sample whose class differs from the majority class of its neuron is suspicious.

Parameter Type Default Description data as in train_classifier required What the classifier will be trained on. samples GeoDataFrame or path required Points with their class, reprojected when in another CRS. label str "class" The column holding the class. x, y int None Neurons of the grid; by default a square grid of about 5 * sqrt(n) neurons for n samples. date date None CCDC segments: the date whose models are the features. num_iters, algorithm, sigma, learning_rate, decay, neighborhood, topology, init, seed, nodata, n_jobs As in som.

Returns the samples as given (GeoDataFrame, same CRS), with neuron (0: outside the data or a missing feature), neuron_class (the neuron's majority class), purity (the share of the neuron's samples in that class) and keep (the sample's class is its neuron's; False without a neuron).

checked = zeit.clean_samples(stack, "samples.gpkg", label="class")
print(checked[~checked.keep])                              # the suspicious ones
rf = zeit.train_classifier(stack, checked[checked.keep], label="class")

docs.title: SOM
docs.text:
class zeit.ai.SOM(
    x, y, input_len, sigma=1.0, learning_rate=0.5,
    decay_function="asymptotic_decay",
    neighborhood_function="gaussian", topology="rectangular",
    random_seed=42, sigma_decay_function="asymptotic_decay",
)

The engine of zeit.som, for samples you arrange yourself: a self-organizing map in Rust (online and batch, the batch one multi-threaded), an operation-by-operation port of Python minisom 2.3: with the same random_seed and arguments the trained codebook is bit-for-bit identical to MiniSom.train (algorithm="online") or MiniSom.train_batch_offline (algorithm="batch"), 30–190 times faster. Tutorial: Clustering.

Parameter Type Default Description x, y int required Grid size. input_len int required Features per sample. sigma float 1.0 Initial spread of the neighbourhood function. learning_rate float 0.5 Initial learning rate. decay_function str "asymptotic_decay" "asymptotic_decay", "inverse_decay_to_zero" or "linear_decay_to_zero". neighborhood_function str "gaussian" "gaussian", "mexican_hat", "bubble" or "triangle". topology str "rectangular" "rectangular" or "hexagonal". random_seed int 42 Seed of the numpy.random.RandomState used for initialisation and sample order (the same draws as minisom). sigma_decay_function str "asymptotic_decay" "asymptotic_decay", "inverse_decay_to_one" or "linear_decay_to_one". Method Description random_weights_init(data) / pca_weights_init(data) Initialise the weights from random samples / from the first two principal components. train(data, num_iters, n_jobs=-1, algorithm="online", random_order=False, use_epochs=False) Train on (samples, features), continuing from the current weights. "online": num_iters single-sample updates (epochs with use_epochs=True). "batch": num_iters passes over the data, parallel with n_jobs, same result for any n_jobs. predict(data, n_jobs=-1) Flat index i * y + j of each sample's best-matching unit. winner(x) Grid coordinates (i, j) of one sample's best-matching unit. quantization(data, n_jobs=-1) / quantization_error(data, n_jobs=-1) Best-matching codebook vector of each sample / mean distance to it. get_weights() Codebook, shape (x, y, input_len). filter_noisy_samples(data, labels, n_jobs=-1) Boolean mask of samples to keep: False where a sample's label disagrees with the majority label of its neuron. 
from zeit.ai import SOM

som = SOM(x=10, y=10, input_len=X.shape[1], sigma=1.5)
som.random_weights_init(X)
som.train(X, num_iters=20, algorithm="batch")    # 20 passes, multi-threaded
clusters = som.predict(X)

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
How accurate is a map, and how much area really changed? Draw a stratified random sample of the map, label it by eye, and get the error matrix, the accuracies and the error-adjusted area of each class with their confidence intervals, following the good practices of Olofsson et al. (2014).

The three functions work on any map: classes from classify, ai.predict, twdtw or som, a raster made elsewhere, or a map of events from extract_events or agreement (stratified as "no change" and "change"). Areas come from each pixel's size, in hectares (in a geographic CRS, the area of each row on the sphere); dask maps are read lazily, a row strip at a time. Tutorial: Accuracy & Area.

events = zeit.extract_events(zeit.landtrendr(ndvi))
design = zeit.sampling_design(events, expected_ua={"change": 0.7, "no change": 0.95})
points = zeit.stratified_sample(events, design=design)
s = zeit.interpret(cube, points, map=events, save="reference.gpkg")   # label each point by eye
acc = zeit.accuracy(events, s)
print(acc)                                 # overall, user's, producer's, mapped and estimated areas

docs.title: sampling_design
docs.text:
zeit.sampling_design(
    data, *, expected_ua=0.75, std_error=0.01, n=None,
    alloc="proportional", min_per_stratum=50, bins=None,
    nodata="auto",
)

How many points the map needs to reach a target standard error of the overall accuracy (Olofsson et al. 2014, eq. 13), and how many in each stratum. The strata are the map's classes. Also exported as zeit.sampling_design.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, Dataset or path required The map to assess: classes (integers; names from its flag_meanings), or a map of events. expected_ua float or dict 0.75 The user's accuracy you expect of each stratum: one value, or stratum name (or code) → value. Hard classes (0.6) need more points than easy ones (0.95). std_error float 0.01 Target standard error of the overall accuracy. n int None Total number of points; computed from expected_ua and std_error when None. alloc str or dict "proportional" "proportional" (to the area of each stratum), "equal", "neyman" (to area × expected standard deviation), or stratum → number of points. min_per_stratum int 50 Strata that would get fewer points get this many, taken from the larger ones, so the total stays n. Olofsson et al. recommend 50–100 for rare classes such as change. 0 disables. bins sequence of float None Strata as intervals [a, b) of the map's values. For a map of events, periods of yod ([2000, 2010, 2020]), next to "no change". nodata "auto", float or None "auto" Value outside every stratum: the map's NoData, a number, or none. A map of events keeps its 0 as "no change".

Returns a pandas.DataFrame with one row per stratum (indexed by its code): name, pixels, area, weight (share of the area), expected_ua and n. attrs holds the total n, the std_error, how points were allocated and the area_unit ("ha", or "pixels" without a CRS).

design = zeit.sampling_design(classes, expected_ua={"forest": 0.9, "pasture": 0.85, "deforestation": 0.6})
design.attrs["n"]                                           # e.g. 641
zeit.sampling_design(events, n=300, bins=[2000, 2010, 2020])  # no change, 2000-2009, 2010-2019

docs.title: stratified_sample
docs.text:
zeit.stratified_sample(
    data, n=None, *, design=None, bins=None, nodata="auto", seed=42,
    **design_kwargs,
)

Draws the points: a simple random sample of pixels within each stratum, without replacement. The same map and seed give the same points in memory or lazily, whatever the chunks. Also exported as zeit.stratified_sample.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray, Dataset or path required The map, as for sampling_design. n int None Total number of points, allocated as sampling_design does. design DataFrame None The table of sampling_design; its n column is used as is. bins, nodata None, "auto" As for sampling_design. seed int 42 Seed of the draw. design_kwargs Passed to sampling_design when there is no design (expected_ua, alloc, min_per_stratum...).

Returns a geopandas.GeoDataFrame of points at the centres of the sampled pixels, in the map's CRS, with stratum (code), stratum_name, row and col. Keep the stratum column: accuracy weighs the points by it.

docs.title: interpret
docs.text:
zeit.interpret(
    data, samples=None, *, classes=None, save=None, rgb=None,
    band=None, series=None, chips="year", chip_size=33, fit=None,
    map=None, strata=None, blind=True, interpreter=None, basemap=None,
    zoom=120, height=480, block=None, open=True,
)

Labels the reference points by eye, one after the other, in the viewer of zeit.plot with another layout: the queue of points and a form on the right, the map centred on the current point, a strip of image chips around it (one per year, the median of its dates), and the point's series below (a click on it dates the change). Each label is written to save at once; calling interpret again with the same file resumes where it stopped. In a notebook the viewer is shown right away and the returned object follows it live; in a script it opens in its own window and returns when the window is closed. Also exported as zeit.interpret.

Parameter Type Default Description data DataArray or path required The imagery: a (time, band, y, x) cube (rgb picks the image's bands), or a (time, y, x) index. samples GeoDataFrame or path None The points, e.g. from stratified_sample. Not needed to resume from save. classes list of str None The reference classes; keys 1–9 pick them. Default: the classes of map. save path None .gpkg, .geojson or .parquet written after every label; an existing file is resumed. rgb three band names None The bands of the image, e.g. ["swir1", "nir", "red"] (default: red, green, blue). band band name None One band to show instead of an RGB image. series band name(s) or DataArray None What the chart shows: bands of data (e.g. "nbr"), or a (time, y, x) cube of the same area. Default: the image's bands. chips "year", "month", "date", int or None "year" One chip per year (the median of its dates), month, date, every n images, or none. A click on a chip shows that image. chip_size int 33 Side of a chip, in pixels. fit result Dataset None A result of zeit drawn over the series, as in zeit.plot (landtrendr, ccdc, extract_events...). map DataArray, Dataset or path None The map being assessed. Its value at the point is shown, and the Review tab gives its accuracy. strata DataArray, Dataset or path None The map the points were stratified by, when it is not map (see accuracy). blind bool True Hide what map and fit say at a point until it is labelled, and the review until every point is: the reference should not be swayed by the map. interpreter str None Name recorded with each label (default: the login name). basemap str None A web map under the data, as in zeit.plot. zoom int 120 How many pixels across the map shows around a point. height int 480 Height of the map in a notebook, in pixels. block, open None, True Outside a notebook, as in zeit.plot: wait for the window to close (default: yes in a script); "native", "browser", or False to only serve the page.

Returns an Interpretation:

Attribute Meaning samples The points with ref, ref_date, confidence (high, medium, low), note, status (todo, done, skipped), interpreter and labelled_at. progress Points done, skipped and in the queue (total). accuracy(map=None, **kwargs) accuracy of map (default: the map given) from the labelled points. zeit.accuracy(map, interpretation) works too. save(path=None), close() Write the labels; close the window. Key Action 1–9 Class Enter Save and go to the next point without a label s Skip the point (cloudy, no imagery...) n / p Next / previous point d Date of the change = the image shown h / m / l Confidence high / medium / low ← →, Space Previous / next image, play

A click on the series sets the date of the change; a click on a point of the map goes to it. The Review tab (with map) shows the overall, user's and producer's accuracies and the areas, with their intervals, and the error matrix in points: a click on a cell (say, map "change", reference "no change") lists its points to look at again.

points = zeit.stratified_sample(loss, n=300)
s = zeit.interpret(landsat, points, rgb=["swir1", "nir", "red"], series="nbr", map=loss,
                   fit=lt, save="reference.gpkg")
acc = s.accuracy(date_tolerance=1)

docs.title: accuracy
docs.text:
zeit.accuracy(
    map, samples, *, reference="ref", strata=None, bins=None,
    date_tolerance=None, reference_date="ref_date", confidence=0.95,
    estimator="direct", nodata="auto",
)

The map's error matrix in proportions of area, its overall, user's and producer's accuracies and the error-adjusted area of each class, each with a confidence interval. The estimators are Stehman's (2014) for stratified random sampling; with the map's classes as strata they are Olofsson et al. (2014), eqs. 4–11, checked against the paper's example and against R's sits_accuracy. Also exported as zeit.accuracy.

Parameter Type Default Description map DataArray, Dataset or path required The map to assess (classes, or events). samples GeoDataFrame, path or zeit.interpret session required The reference points, in any CRS. Points without a reference label are left out (and counted). reference str "ref" Column with the reference class: names of the map's classes, their codes, or for a map of events "change"/"no change" (or True/False, 1/0). A class the map never gives is kept (its user's accuracy is NaN, its area estimated). strata DataArray, Dataset or path None The map the sample was stratified by, when it is not map: a sample of one map assesses another (Stehman 2014). Default: map's classes. bins sequence of float None Classes of map as intervals of its values, as in sampling_design. date_tolerance float None Maps of events: also compare dates. Of the points both call change, the share whose years (of the map's date and reference_date) are at most this far apart. reference_date str "ref_date" Column with the reference date of the change. confidence float 0.95 Level of the confidence intervals. estimator str "direct" How the areas are estimated: "direct" (the sample alone: Stehman 2014), "difference" (the mapped area plus the estimated area of the reference minus the map's) or "ratio" (the mapped area times the estimated ratio of the reference's area to the map's). See Model-assisted estimators. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" As for sampling_design.

Returns an Accuracy object; print(acc) gives a summary.

Attribute Meaning overall estimate, se, ci_low, ci_high of the overall accuracy. users, producers The same, per class (rows). area Per class: mapped (area the map gives it; inside the strata when strata is on the map's grid, the population the sample was drawn from), estimate (error-adjusted area), se, ci (half-width of the interval), ci_low, ci_high, in area_unit. confusion Error matrix in proportions of area: map classes in rows, reference classes in columns. counts The error matrix in points. date With date_tolerance: within (estimated share of the change points whose dates agree), within_se, mean_difference (years), n. n, n_unlabelled Points used, and points left out for having no label. estimator How area was estimated. to_dataframe() User's, producer's and area in one table. 
acc = zeit.accuracy(events, points, date_tolerance=1)
acc.area.loc["change", ["estimate", "ci"]]         # hectares of change, ± the 95% interval
acc.users.loc["change"]                            # how often a mapped change is real
acc.producers.loc["change"]                        # how much of the real change the map finds

# The same reference points assess another algorithm's map, weighed by the first map's strata
acc_ccdc = zeit.accuracy(zeit.extract_events(segments, band="nir", event_type="loss"), points, strata=events)

Points chosen by hand are not a sample

The estimates assume the points were drawn at random within the strata (or across the whole map). Field points or points picked on the screen give an error matrix, but not unbiased accuracies or areas. accuracy warns when the points have no stratum column and weighs them as if they were stratified by the map.

docs.title: Model-assisted estimators
docs.text:
The direct estimator uses the sample alone: the share of each class in the reference, weighed by the area of each stratum. The map, though, is known everywhere, and its classes agree with the reference at most points. The model-assisted estimators use it (Särndal et al. 1992; Stehman 2013; McRoberts et al. 2018):

  • difference: the mapped area of the class, plus the estimated area where the reference has it minus the area where the map has it (the map's net error). Its variance is that of the differences, small where the map is right.
  • ratio: the mapped area of the class, times the estimated ratio of the area the reference gives it to the area the map gives it (the combined ratio estimator, Cochran 1977). NaN for a class no sample point is mapped as.

They matter when the strata are not the map's classes, as with a sample stratified by another map or by a map of change, and most for rare classes and changes: on the fixture of the tests (a sample of 190 points stratified by an older alert map), the 95% interval of "Forest -> Pasture" is ±17.6 ha by the direct estimator and ±3.4 ha by the difference estimator, around 22 ha. With the map's classes as strata the three estimators give the same areas. The accuracies (user's, producer's, overall) are the same whatever the estimator. All three are R's survey package's (svytotal, svyratio) to 1e-10.

acc = zeit.accuracy(the_map, points, strata=alerts, estimator="difference")

docs.title: transitions
docs.text:
zeit.transitions(
    map_from, map_to, samples, *, reference_from="ref_from",
    reference_to="ref_to", strata=None, confidence=0.95,
    estimator="direct", nodata="auto",
)

The area of each transition between two dates of a map of classes ("Forest -> Pasture"; "Forest -> Forest" where nothing changed), with its confidence interval, from a reference sample labelled with the class at each date. Each pair of classes is a class of a map of transitions, assessed as accuracy assesses a map: error matrix of the transitions, user's and producer's accuracies, and the error-adjusted areas by the direct, difference or ratio estimator. Also exported as zeit.transitions.

Parameter Type Default Description map_from DataArray or path required The map of classes at the first date. map_to DataArray or path required The map of classes at the second date, on the same grid. samples GeoDataFrame, path or zeit.interpret session required The reference points, in any CRS, with the reference class at each date. Points without both are left out (and counted). reference_from str "ref_from" Column with the reference class at the first date (names of the maps' classes or their codes). reference_to str "ref_to" Column with the reference class at the second date. strata DataArray, Dataset or path None The map the sample was stratified by (classes of one date, a map of change...). Default: the transitions themselves. confidence float 0.95 Level of the confidence intervals. estimator str "direct" "direct", "difference" or "ratio", as for accuracy. nodata "auto", float or None "auto" As for sampling_design.

Returns an Accuracy object whose classes are the transitions "<from> -> <to>": those the maps have and those the reference adds.

tr = zeit.transitions("lc_2015.tif", "lc_2022.tif", points, strata="change_2015_2022.tif",
                      estimator="difference")
tr.area.loc["Forest -> Pasture", ["mapped", "estimate", "ci"]]   # hectares, ± the 95% interval

docs.title: Xarray Accessor
docs.text:
import zeit registers a .zeit accessor on every xarray.DataArray (and, to save or show results, on every xarray.Dataset). Its methods run the compiled (Rust) algorithms over Dask chunks, so they work on cubes larger than memory and on clusters. On a dask-backed cube the algorithms are lazy: call .compute(), or write the result with save_raster or to_zarr_optimized. An in-memory cube gives an in-memory result.

Chunk in space, never in time

Each pixel needs its whole history, so keep time (and band, for CCDC) in a single chunk: cube.chunk({"time": -1, "y": 512, "x": 512}). See Parallel & Cloud Processing.

Method Input dims Output Parameters as in landtrendr (time, y, x) xr.Dataset of vertices zeit.landtrendr ccdc (time, band, y, x) xr.Dataset of segments zeit.ccdc bfast_monitor (time, y, x) xr.Dataset of metrics zeit.bfast_monitor bfast_lite (time, y, x) xr.Dataset of metrics zeit.bfast_lite bfast (time, y, x) xr.Dataset of metrics zeit.bfast mann_kendall (time, y, x) xr.Dataset of metrics zeit.mann_kendall ar_trend (time, y, x) xr.Dataset of metrics zeit.ar_trend parts (time, y, x) PartsResult zeit.parts phenology (time, y, x) xr.Dataset of metrics, by year or season zeit.phenology twdtw (time, y, x) or (time, band, y, x) xr.Dataset of classes and distances zeit.twdtw smooth (time, ...) the smoothed DataArray zeit.smooth snic (..., y, x) xr.Dataset of labels and means zeit.snic som (..., y, x) xr.Dataset of clusters and prototypes zeit.som tmask (time, band, y, x) clear (time, y, x) zeit.tmask save any with y, x (also on a Dataset) writes a raster, returns its path zeit.save_raster plot any with y, x (also on a Dataset) the viewer, a window or a figure zeit.plot to_zarr_optimized any with y, x writes a Zarr store below

Each algorithm method returns an xr.Dataset with one variable per output, selected by name: result.slope, result["TRS5.sos"].

docs.title: landtrendr
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.landtrendr(**kwargs)

LandTrendr on this (time, y, x) cube: the same as zeit.landtrendr(cube, **kwargs), with the same keyword arguments (direction, max_segments, nodata, fitted, …) and the same xarray.Dataset of vertices. The years come from the time coordinate. A dask-backed cube stays lazy and is computed block by block.

ndvi = ndvi.chunk({"time": -1, "y": 512, "x": 512})
lt = ndvi.zeit.landtrendr(max_segments=6)                  # direction="loss": NDVI drops
loss = zeit.extract_events(lt, min_magnitude=2000)         # still lazy
zeit.save_raster(loss, "results/")                         # computed while written

docs.title: ccdc
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.ccdc(**kwargs)

CCDC on this (time, band, y, x) cube of reflectance × 10,000: the same as zeit.ccdc(cube, **kwargs), with the same keyword arguments (qa, bands, max_segments, conseq_anom, …) and the same xarray.Dataset of segments. The dates come from the time coordinate. A dask-backed cube stays lazy and is computed block by block, with time and band in one chunk.

cube = cube.chunk({"time": -1, "band": -1, "y": 512, "x": 512})
segments = cube.zeit.ccdc(qa="fmask")       # QA band by name; still lazy
zeit.save_raster(segments, "ccdc_out/")      # computed while written

docs.title: bfast_monitor
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.bfast_monitor(monitor_start, **kwargs)

BFAST Monitor on this (time, y, x) cube: the same as zeit.bfast_monitor(cube, monitor_start, **kwargs), with the same keyword arguments (order, h, period, alpha, nodata, …) and the same xarray.Dataset of metrics. start_time and frequency come from the time coordinate unless given. A dask-backed cube stays lazy.

ndvi_16d = ndvi_16d.chunk({"time": -1, "y": 512, "x": 512})
bfm = ndvi_16d.zeit.bfast_monitor("2022-01-01")    # still lazy
zeit.save_raster(bfm, "results/bfm")               # computed while written

DataArray.zeit.mann_kendall(**kwargs)

Mann-Kendall test and Theil-Sen slope on this (time, y, x) cube: the same as zeit.mann_kendall(cube, **kwargs), with the same keyword arguments (method, alpha, lag, period, …) and the same xarray.Dataset of metrics.

docs.title: parts
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.parts(**kwargs)

The regional test of this cube's trends by PARTS: the same as zeit.parts(cube, **kwargs).

docs.title: phenology
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.phenology(**kwargs)

Phenology on this (time, y, x) cube: the same as zeit.phenology(cube, **kwargs), with the same keyword arguments (curve, annual, max_seasons, weights, …) and the same xarray.Dataset of 21 metrics. The day numbering and the first year come from the time coordinate.

pheno = ndvi_16d.zeit.phenology(curve="beck", weights=weights)
sos = pheno["TRS5.sos"]                  # (year, y, x), day of year

docs.title: twdtw
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.twdtw(patterns, **kwargs)

TWDTW classification of this cube: the same as zeit.twdtw(cube, patterns, **kwargs), with the same keyword arguments (steepness, midpoint, cycle, max_elapsed, …) and the same xarray.Dataset. A dask-backed cube stays lazy.

classes = ndvi.zeit.twdtw({"soy": soy, "pasture": pasture})

docs.title: smooth
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.smooth(**kwargs)

Smoothing of this cube along time: the same as zeit.smooth(cube, **kwargs) (method, lmbda, weights, …).

smooth = ndvi.zeit.smooth(lmbda=100)

docs.title: snic
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.snic(**kwargs)

SNIC superpixels of this map or cube: the same as zeit.snic(da, **kwargs). The cube is loaded into memory.

seg = ndvi.zeit.snic(spacing=8, compactness=0.3)

docs.title: som
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.som(**kwargs)

Self-organizing map clusters of this map or cube: the same as zeit.som(da, **kwargs).

clusters = ndvi.zeit.som(x=3, y=3)

docs.title: tmask
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.tmask(**kwargs)

Tmask on this (time, band, y, x) cube: the same as zeit.tmask(cube, **kwargs).

clear = cube.zeit.tmask(green="green", swir="swir1")

docs.title: Saving and showing results
docs.text:
The results of the algorithms are Datasets; .zeit.save and .zeit.plot write or show them (or any map or cube) without leaving a chain of calls:

zeit.landtrendr(ndvi).zeit.save("results/lt")               # one GeoTIFF per variable
zeit.extract_events(lt).yod.zeit.plot(basemap="satellite")  # one map
lt.zeit.plot()                                              # a selector of the variables

docs.title: save
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.save(path, **kwargs)

Dataset.zeit.save(path, **kwargs)

Writes this map, cube or result: the same as zeit.save_raster(data, path, **kwargs), with its keyword arguments (nodata, dtype, compress, driver, …). A Dataset with a path without extension becomes a folder with one GeoTIFF per variable; with .tif, one multiband raster. Returns the Path written. A lazy result is computed while it is written.

docs.title: plot
docs.text:
DataArray.zeit.plot(**kwargs)

Dataset.zeit.plot(**kwargs)

Shows this map, cube or result: the same as zeit.plot(data, **kwargs), with its keyword arguments (var, fit, basemap, vector, static, save, …): the interactive viewer in a notebook, a window in a script, a figure with static=True or save=. A Dataset opens with a selector of its variables.

docs.title: to_zarr_optimized
