DataArray.zeit.to_zarr_optimized(
    store_path, chunk_size={'y': 512, 'x': 512},
)

Rechunks the array spatially and writes it to a Zarr store with consolidated metadata, locally or to object storage (s3://, gs://). With a Dask-backed array, this is the step that triggers the computation, and every worker writes its own chunks.

Parameter Type Default Description store_path str required Local path or fsspec URL. chunk_size dict {"y": 512, "x": 512} Chunk sizes of the stored array. 
mk.slope.zeit.to_zarr_optimized("s3://my-bucket/ndvi_slope.zarr")

docs.title: Benchmarks & Validation Suite
docs.text: Welcome to the Zeit Fidelity & Performance Validation Suite. This section provides a comprehensive empirical evaluation of the algorithms implemented in Zeit, assessing both scientific fidelity (how faithfully Zeit reproduces the original tools and published papers it ports) and computational performance (single-core speedup and multi-core CPU scaling).

docs.title: Executive Summary & Mission
docs.text:
Earth Observation (EO) time-series analysis has historically suffered from fragmented software ecosystems. Canonical algorithms were originally authored across diverse, often proprietary or single-threaded environments:

  • LandTrendr was authored in proprietary IDL (Kennedy et al. 2010).
  • CCDC was authored in MATLAB with a compiled Fortran GLMnet lasso (Zhu & Woodcock 2014).
  • BFAST, Phenology, and TWDTW gained widespread adoption through R packages (bfast, phenofit, dtwSat/twdtw).
  • Deep learning models for satellite time-series (TempCNN, LightTAE, U-TAE) were scattered between R sits and standalone PyTorch repositories; Zeit's TempCNN and LightTAE are written from the papers and the authors' code.
  • Researchers have frequently relied on cloud platforms like Google Earth Engine (GEE), trading off local control, customization, and queue times for scalability.

Zeit was engineered to unify these algorithms into a modern, cloud-native architecture written in a high-performance compiled core (C++ with Eigen3 and OpenMP up to 1.7, Rust from 2.0) and PyTorch (zeit.ai), exposed through Python, Dask, and Xarray. The compiled core's timings in this section were taken with the Rust core of zeit 2.3, which gives the same results as the C++ one (see Performance).

docs.title: The Validation Mandate
docs.text:
To verify that Zeit can serve as a drop-in, scientifically reliable replacement for these reference implementations, we subjected Zeit to a rigorous battery of 13 benchmark comparisons (plus one bonus architectural verification). Every algorithm was evaluated against the authentic reference tool across millions of observations, testing:

  1. Numerical and Statistical Fidelity: Do Zeit outputs match the reference tools down to floating-point tolerance, identical breakpoint positions, and matching model categories?
  2. Execution Efficiency: How much faster is Zeit on a single core, how effectively does it scale across threads, and how does local desktop processing compare against distributed cloud platforms like Google Earth Engine?

docs.title: Key Performance Indicators
docs.text: Tested Algorithms 13 + 1 13 canonical tools + 1 bonus segmentation port (U-TAE) Algorithm Parity 100% Exact vertex/label/codebook match on LandTrendr, SNIC, SOM, TWDTW; CCDC with identical segment dates and categories Phenology, Start of Season 4.1 d 90th-percentile error of Beck's TRS5 on a synthetic cube with known truth (10.7 d in Zeit 1.x) Max Single-Core Speedup 30,000× The fastest of the newer ports against its R original (see Against the Originals) Vs. Google Earth Engine 19.4× Compute throughput on full 54.7M px Landsat tile, 8 threads (0 queue delay)

docs.title: Speed and Fidelity at a Glance
docs.text:
Every port is held to two standards at once: it must give the reference tool's answer, and it must give it faster. The chart lines both up for each algorithm. Hover over (or tab to) a row for the exact numbers; the full matrix follows below.

Single-core speedup over the reference tool, and how closely Zeit reproduces it

Same task, one thread on each side. Log scale: each grid line is ten times the one before. A light extension shows the range over several workloads.

Zeit faster Range across workloads Zeit slower Identical output Equal within 1e-7 Close: same method, small numerical differences Algorithm · reference Fidelity Speedup, one core (log scale) 1× 10× 100× LandTrendr IDL original (GDL) Identical 232× CCDC MATLAB original (Octave) Identical 218×–260× TWDTW R twdtw / dtwSat ≤ 1e-7 72× Mann-Kendall Python pymannkendall Identical 65×–75× SOM Python minisom Identical 42×–67× BFAST Monitor R bfast::bfastmonitor Identical 16.9× BFAST R bfast::bfast Close 13.2× BFAST Lite R bfast::bfastlite Close 5.2× SNIC C reference (snic.c) Identical 1.8×–3.5× Presto Official nasaharvest/presto ≤ 1e-7 1.17× U-TAE Official utae-paps Identical 1.08× Siamese CNN Official FC-Siam-diff (Daudt et al.) ≤ 1e-7 1.07×–1.16×

Thirteen of the sixteen ports return the reference tool's own output, bit for bit or to floating-point rounding, and the fifteen measured on a single core are all faster before any parallelism (U-TAE by 8%, the Siamese detector by 7–16%, Presto by 17%). The three "close" ports fit curves or search for breaks with numerical optimisers, where tiny differences in the starting point or in the stopping rule move a date by a few days (Fidelity has the details). The deep-learning ports run the same PyTorch operations as their references, so they gain little; Prithvi, measured on 14 threads and on the GPU, ties with its reference.

The ports added since (emerging hot spots, recovery metrics, EWMACD, unmixing, Bayesian smoothing, area of applicability) are timed against their R originals with the Rust core on a page of their own: Against the Original Implementations.

Status Definitions

  • compared: Exact numerical or statistical benchmark against the official reference tool or canonical implementation.

docs.title: Hardware & Test Environment
docs.text:
All performance benchmarks were measured on a modern workstation environment:

Benchmark Workstation (Intel Core i5)
  • CPU: Intel Core i5-13600K (14 physical cores: 6 P-cores + 8 E-cores, 20 logical threads)
  • RAM: 64 GB DDR5
  • Operating System: Windows 11 Pro 64-bit
  • R Environment: R 4.4.2 (CRAN `bfast`, `phenofit`, `twdtw`, `torch` 0.17.0, `sits` 1.5.2)
  • Python Environment: Python 3.12.8, PyTorch 2.14.0, Zeit 0.18.0+
  • GDL / Octave: GDL 1.1.2 (native Windows), GNU Octave 11.3 (compiled Fortran GLMnet)

SOM (re-validated in Zeit 0.21.0 after the bit-exact minisom port) was measured on an AMD Ryzen 7 7730U laptop (8 cores / 16 threads, Windows 11, Python 3.10, NumPy 1.26, minisom 2.3.6). Its speedups are ratios measured on that same machine.

docs.title: 1. Parity Demands Meticulous Porting, Not High-Level Mimicry
docs.text:
Empirical validation demonstrates that reproducing published remote sensing algorithms requires rigorous line-by-line fidelity to author reference implementations rather than high-level approximations:

  • LandTrendr: Replicating Kennedy et al. (2010) with 100% vertex year agreement (330/330 series) required reproducing subtle source behaviors: fitting on the despiked series, in-place take_out_weakest2 mutation, whole-ladder Levenberg-Marquardt fallback, flat-line non-significance fallback, and single-precision F-test p-value tie-breaking.
  • CCDC: Matching Zhu & Woodcock (2014) across 350 pixels (599 models, 249 breaks) required MATLAB datenum coordinate alignment and bisquare Tmask outlier detection. The lasso, once a port of the Fortran GLMnet, is now written from the paper (Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010): segment dates, categories and observation counts stay exact, and the coefficients agree within the tolerances of the parity test.
  • SNIC: Achieving bit-for-bit label parity with Achanta & Süsstrunk (2017) required reproducing priority queue heap tie-breaking order, while resolving upstream heap underflow crashes on edge-case inputs.
  • SOM: Reproducing Python minisom codebooks bit-for-bit required matching its RandomState draw sequence, NumPy's pairwise summation inside the distance norm, argmin tie-breaking on square-rooted distances, and sample-order accumulation in the batch update. An earlier Zeit variant that only resembled the batch algorithm (different decay, no learning rate, epoch-based num_iters) agreed with minisom at just ARI = 0.39 and ran 6–10× slower on the same call; the exact port is identical and 41–67× faster on one core.

Across all families, Zeit delivers 100% bitwise and statistical parity with the authoritative reference implementations.

docs.title: 2. High-Performance Local Processing Beats Cloud Queues
docs.text:
The prevailing assumption in remote sensing has been that massive spatial workflows require distributed cloud infrastructure like Google Earth Engine. Our full Landsat tile benchmark demonstrates otherwise:

  • Zeit processing 54,731,482 pixels (41 years) on a single desktop PC completed in 103.92 seconds (526,693 pixels/sec) on 8 of its 20 threads.
  • Google Earth Engine's distributed cluster executed active server compute on ~38M pixels in 1,396 seconds (27,213 pixels/sec), with an additional 5.08 hours of cloud queue latency.
  • Zeit delivered 19.4× higher compute throughput than GEE's server cluster, with zero queue overhead and zero network egress costs.

LandTrendr on a full Landsat tile: a desktop PC against Google Earth Engine

54.7 million pixels × 41 years on an Intel Core i5-13600K; about 38 million active pixels on Earth Engine's batch workers. Top: throughput while computing. Bottom: the time from submitting the job to having the result.

Zeit, 8 threads Zeit, 1 thread Google Earth Engine Waiting in Earth Engine's queue Compute throughput, pixels per second 0 200k 400k 600k Google Earth Engine batch workers (EECU) 27k Zeit, 1 thread desktop PC 85k Zeit, 8 threads desktop PC 527k Time to the result, minutes: queue + compute 0 60 120 180 240 300 360 Google Earth Engine batch workers (EECU) queue: 5.1 h 5.47 h Zeit, 1 thread desktop PC 10.7 min Zeit, 8 threads desktop PC 1.7 min

When both sides run in parallel, the gap stays wide for the statistical tools, whose reference implementations pay for each worker with an interpreter, and closes for the deep-learning models, which run on the same tensor libraries:

Who finishes first in parallel

Wall-clock time of Zeit with 8 threads (20 for the neural networks, which run on PyTorch) and of the reference with its own parallel framework (19 R or Python workers, or intra-op threads for the neural networks). Each row is its own workload; log scale.

Zeit, 8 threads Reference, all workers Algorithm · workload Wall-clock time, in parallel (log scale) Zeit finishes 10 ms 100 ms 1 s 10 s 100 s Mann-Kendall 5,000 series 3.6 ms 20.1 s 5,552× sooner BFAST Monitor 20,000 series 10.0 ms 5.0 s 499× sooner TWDTW 3,000 series 2.1 ms 189 ms 89× sooner BFAST 400 series 239 ms 3.3 s 14× sooner BFAST Lite 2,000 series 1.5 s 4.6 s 3.1× sooner U-TAE batch of 32 126 ms 125 ms tied

docs.title: 3. Phenology: written from the papers
docs.text:
Zeit's phenology is written from the papers (Whittaker: Eilers 2003; HANTS: Roerink et al. 2000; the curves of Beck 2006, Elmore 2012, Gu 2009, Klosterman 2014, Zhang 2003, Jönsson & Eklundh, Fisher 2006), not from the code of R phenofit. R phenofit remains a useful reference to compare outputs with, but the earlier comparison on the real EVI raster no longer applies and was not redone, nor was the speed comparison with it.

What was measured is the error against a known truth: a synthetic cube of 2,000 pixels (5 years of 16 days, half with one season a year and half with two, with clouds, weights and gaps), the truth being the 50% crossings of the generator. The error of TRS5 at the start of season in the single-season pixels, median / 90th percentile in days:

Curve Zeit 1.x (derived from phenofit) Current Zeit Beck 2.43 / 10.7 1.50 / 4.12 Elmore 1.71 / 7.28 1.51 / 4.23 Gu 1.90 / 8.55 1.80 / 4.99 Klosterman 1.94 / 8.84 1.74 / 4.97 Zhang 1.71 / 7.51 1.50 / 4.12 Asymmetric Gaussian 1.95 / 10.5 1.70 / 5.15 Double logistic 1.73 / 8.39 1.49 / 4.15

docs.title: The end of season stays at the same level (Beck: 1.43 / 4.63 d). With 4 jobs, on the cube, Beck takes 0.25 s, Gu 0.68 s and Klosterman 0.79 s (Zeit 1.x: 0.27, 1.58 and 3.56 s); on the real EVI raster (638 pixels, 575 dates), Beck takes 0.30 s and Gu 0.95 s.

docs.title: Algorithmic Fidelity & Scientific Validation
docs.text: This page details the methodology, test suites, and quantitative results measuring how faithfully zeit reproduces the canonical algorithms and published reference implementations it ports.

docs.title: Validation Methodology
docs.text:
To ensure transparent and reproducible validation, Zeit benchmarks its 8 core algorithm families (14 implementations) across four rigorous evaluation pillars, ranging from controlled ground-truth injection to bit-for-bit source parity and 25-year satellite raster joins:

The 4 evaluation strategies (pillars) used across Zeit algorithm families to guarantee mathematical and numerical fidelity.

  1. Pillar 1: Controlled Ground-Truth Injection (Statistical Algorithms):
  2. Evaluated Algorithms: BFAST (Classic), BFAST Monitor, BFAST Lite, and TWDTW.
  3. Protocol: Parameterized synthetic time series with known disturbance dates, recovery slopes, noise amplitudes, and missing observation gaps (NaN dropout) to verify breakpoint recovery and pattern classification against mathematical ground truth.
  4. Pillar 2: Direct Source-Level Port Parity (Original Codebases):
  5. Evaluated Algorithms: LandTrendr, CCDC, SNIC, and SOM.
  6. Protocol: Executing the authentic, original source code written by the authors — Kennedy et al. (2010) IDL source (fit_trajectory_v2.pro / tbcd_v2.pro) executed via GNU Data Language (GDL 1.1.2), Zhu & Woodcock (2014) MATLAB source (TrendSeasonalFit_v12_30Line.m) with its bundled GLMnet lasso executed unmodified under GNU Octave 11.3, Achanta & Süsstrunk (2017) canonical C reference (snic.c, EPFL), and Python minisom (Vettigli) for SOM — validating model dates, vertex coordinates, superpixel segment labels, and SOM codebooks (CCDC's coefficients within the tolerances given in section 2; the rest bit for bit).
  7. Pillar 3: Architectures Written from the Authors (Deep Learning):
  8. Evaluated Algorithms: TempCNN, LightTAE (LTAE), and Official U-TAE.
  9. Protocol: TempCNN and LightTAE are written from the papers and the authors' code, not ported from R sits, so their weights are no longer compared with sits's: the two are compared by accuracy on sits's samples_modis_ndvi (12 dates, 4 classes; 5 seeds, the same 80/20 split on both sides). Official U-TAE is run against the authors' code with the same weights, testing forward-pass outputs for floating-point equivalence on identical input tensors.
  10. Pillar 4: Synthetic Cube with Known Truth (Phenology Extraction):
  11. Evaluated Algorithms: Phenology Extraction (Beck, Elmore, Gu, Klosterman, Zhang, asymmetric Gaussian and double logistic curves).
  12. Protocol: A synthetic cube of 2,000 pixels (5 years of 16 days, half of the pixels with one season a year and half with two), with clouds, weights and gaps. The truth is the 50% crossings of the generator; the error is that of TRS5 in the single-season pixels, as median / 90th percentile in days. Zeit's phenology is written from the papers, not from phenofit's code, so it is no longer compared with phenofit's outputs record by record; the comparison with the earlier Zeit 1.x, derived from phenofit, is in section 4.

docs.title: 1. LandTrendr (Kennedy et al. 2010)
docs.text: LandTrendr simplifies annual satellite time series into straight-line segments using an iterative regression ladder and F-test model complexity selection.

docs.title: Canonical IDL Source Parity
docs.text:
Zeit (rust/zeit-core/src/landtrendr.rs; C++ up to 1.7, with the same results) faithfully replicates the canonical Kennedy et al. (2010) IDL source (fit_trajectory_v2.pro / tbcd_v2.pro) executed via GNU Data Language (GDL 1.1.2). To achieve bit-for-bit fidelity with the original IDL implementation, Zeit reproduces all canonical core behaviors:

  1. Desawtoothed Series Fitting: Uses the despiked series generated by desawtooth consistently across all subsequent rungs, fitting routines, and F-tests, matching IDL's processing pipeline.
  2. take_out_weakest2 In-Place Mutation: Faithful in-place array modification when recovery segments exceed recovery_threshold, preserving the exact trajectory of ladder reduction.
  3. Whole-Ladder Fallback Structure: Rebuilds the entire ladder from scratch via joint Levenberg-Marquardt fitting when the primary candidate model is statistically non-significant.
  4. Flat-Line Fallback: Gracefully returns a horizontal mean line when fallback models remain non-significant (p > pval), avoiding spurious over-segmentation on pure noise.
  5. Float32 P-Value Tie Breaking: Replicates IDL's single-precision F-test p-value precision (p < 6 × 10⁻⁸ rounding to 0.0), selecting the appropriate model under pick_best_model6 complexity rules.

docs.title: Verification & Parity Results
docs.text:
Across both original and expanded test batteries: - 30 / 30 original scenarios achieved 100% identical vertex years. - 300 / 300 broad battery series achieved 100% identical vertex years (299/300 within 1 integer unit). - Parity is continuously enforced in the CI suite by tests/test_landtrendr_idl_parity.py across 14 GDL-derived edge cases.

The Single Residual Tie Edge Case

The only non-identical value out of 300 series occurred on a stable series where a segment spanned exactly 1 / threshold years. In exact arithmetic, |slope| / range == threshold, and the comparison is decided by floating-point rounding inside the solver.

docs.title: 2. CCDC (Zhu & Woodcock 2014)
docs.text: CCDC models surface reflectance across multiple spectral bands using harmonic regressions, detecting breaks when consecutive residuals exceed a Chi-square threshold.

docs.title: MATLAB Parity and the Clean-Room Lasso
docs.text:
Zeit (rust/zeit-core/src/ccdc.rs) follows the canonical MATLAB codebase (TrendSeasonalFit_v12_30Line.m) by Zhu & Woodcock (2014). Until the swap the lasso was a port of the GLMnet Fortran solver bundled with it, and the results matched the MATLAB's coefficients to about 5e-10. That solver is GPL-2.0-only, so the lasso is now written from the paper (Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010, coordinate descent; rust/zeit-core/src/lasso.rs), and CCDC is no longer bit for bit with the MATLAB.

  • Lasso swap (before against after, 2,812 pixels). Same number of segments, same start, end and break dates (exactly), same category and same num_obs in every pixel; change_prob is the same. The RMSE of the optical bands differs by a median of about 5e-6 (absolute) and the harmonic coefficients by a median of 0 (p99 about 2e-4; the largest 0.03 on a coefficient near zero).
  • Against the MATLAB (11 cases, LASSO_THRESH = 1e-8). Same segments, category, num_obs and change_prob, and the same predictors kept by the lasso in every segment of every band. The predicted value at the start, middle and end of a segment differs by at most 0.234 (reflectance x 10000), 0.2% of the segment's RMSE; the harmonic coefficients by at most 0.035; the RMSE by 7.9e-4. The intercept a0 is collinear with the trend c1 on the datenum axis, so the two differ together (c1 by at most 1.3e-5 per day) and their sum, the prediction, stays. The MATLAB's single precision leaves 1e-3 to 1e-2 of noise in the RMSE of a constant band; the new fit gives 0.
  • MATLAB datenum Time Axis: Temporal coordinate alignment (python_ordinal + 366) ensuring invariant harmonic phase alignment in lasso regularization.
  • Bisquare Robust Tmask: Native implementation of MATLAB's statrobustfit_cor bisquare M-estimator, including leverage adjustment, MAD-sigma scaling, and 4-iteration reweighting.
  • Numerical Rank Alignment: Matrix rank behavior matching MATLAB's linsolve decomposition for accurate Tmask outlier identification.

docs.title: Verification & Parity Results
docs.text: • Segment dates, categories and observation counts are exact. Coefficients, RMSE and magnitude are compared within tolerances (tests/test_ccdc_matlab_parity.py): the model through its predictions at the segment's start, middle and end (atol 0.5), c1 (atol 1e-4), the harmonics (atol 0.1), the RMSE (rtol 1e-4, atol 0.01) and the magnitude (atol 0.25), about twice the largest differences measured.

docs.title: 3. BFAST Family (Verbesselt et al.)
docs.text:
The BFAST suite represents one of the most widely used statistical change detection families.

  • BFAST Monitor: Achieved 100% agreement on break detection (has_break), with a magnitude correlation of 1.000. The test battery specifically verified that Zeit reproduces R's documented ~44% false-positive rate when evaluating pure Gaussian noise under history="all", confirming fidelity even in known edge cases.
  • BFAST Lite: Achieved 100% agreement on break counts. Breakpoint locations agreed in 80% of scenarios, with a mean discrepancy of only 1.6 observations in remaining series. The evaluation harness resolved a potential 0-indexed (Python) vs. 1-indexed (R) convention mismatch.
  • BFAST Classic (Iterative STL): Achieved 87.5% exact agreement on trend break counts. Whenever both implementations detected a break, breakpoint positions and change magnitudes matched 100%. Minor discrepancies stem from slight differences in how seasonal Loess smoothers handle NaN gaps in Zeit vs. R.

docs.title: 4. Phenology Extraction
docs.text:
Phenology extraction fits parametric curves (Beck, Elmore, Gu, Zhang, asymmetric Gaussian, double logistic) to multi-year vegetation index time series and derives critical transition dates (Start of Season, End of Season, Peak, Maturity, Senescence, Dormancy).

Zeit's phenology is written from the papers (Whittaker: Eilers 2003; HANTS: Roerink et al. 2000; Beck et al. 2006; Elmore et al. 2012; Gu et al. 2009; Klosterman et al. 2014; Zhang et al. 2003; the asymmetric Gaussian of Jönsson & Eklundh; the double logistic of Fisher et al. 2006), not from the code of R phenofit, so it is no longer comparable with phenofit's outputs record by record. The earlier comparison on the real 25-year EVI raster (against phenofit) no longer applies and was not redone. What was measured is the error against a known truth, on a synthetic cube of 2,000 pixels (5 years of 16 days, half of the pixels with one season a year and half with two, with clouds, weights and gaps). The truth is the 50% crossings of the generator; the table gives the error of TRS5 in the single-season pixels, as median / 90th percentile in days, for Zeit 1.x (derived from phenofit) and for the current Zeit.

5. Time-Weighted Dynamic Time Warping (TWDTW)
docs.text:
TWDTW (Maus et al. 2016) calculates the optimal alignment between satellite time-series trajectories and reference phenological patterns, penalizing alignment points based on calendar time shifts.

  • Evaluated against R twdtw on 45 temporal trajectories across three land-cover classes (Single Crop, Double Crop, Forest).
  • 100% Classification Agreement: Zeit and the original R package produced identical land-cover classifications for all tested series.
  • Distance Metric Correlation: With the earlier engine's own time weight, the raw distances had a Pearson correlation of 0.9381. Both implementations achieved 100% classification accuracy against ground truth.
  • Identical distances (zeit.twdtw, 0.41): with R twdtw's logistic weight and its day-of-year cycle, zeit.twdtw gives R twdtw 1.0.1's distances to 1e-12 on one- and two-band series, cloudy dates and patterns inside four-year series (tests/test_twdtw_api.py, fixtures from R in tests/data).

docs.title: 6. Self-Organizing Maps (SOM)
docs.text:
• zeit.ai.SOM is an operation-by-operation port of Python minisom 2.3.6: same numpy.random.RandomState draws for initialization and sample order, NumPy's pairwise summation for the distance norm, argmin tie-breaking on the square-rooted distance, and the same neighborhood, decay and update expressions. The batch trainer accumulates each neuron's numerator and denominator in sample order, exactly like MiniSom.train_batch_offline, so its output does not depend on n_jobs.
  • Evaluated with identical seed and random_weights_init on both sides, on 5 Gaussian clusters (1,500 samples, 5×5 grid; 20,000 samples, 10×10 grid), for MiniSom.train (sequential and random order) and MiniSom.train_batch_offline (1 thread and all threads):
    • Codebook: max |wZeit − wminisom| = 0.0 in all 6 scenarios.
    • BMU assignments: 100% agreement (ARI = 1.0); quantization errors identical.
  • The unit tests cover 67 further configurations (all four neighborhood functions, rectangular and hexagonal topologies, every decay function, random/PCA initialization, 1–150 features) against stored minisom outputs.
  • Earlier result (superseded): before this port, Zeit ran its own Batch SOM variant (exponential sigma decay, no learning rate, and num_iters counted full-data epochs instead of single-sample updates), which gave ARI = 0.394 against minisom and was 6–10× slower on the same call.

docs.title: 7. Deep Learning (zeit.ai)
docs.text: TempCNN and LightTAE are written from the papers and from the authors' code (Pelletier et al. 2019, temporalCNN; Sainte Fare Garnot & Landrieu 2020, lightweight-temporal-attention-pytorch). They are no longer ports of R sits, and weights trained in sits do not load into them, so the forward-pass comparison with sits that was made for the earlier port no longer applies.

docs.title: TempCNN & LightTAE (accuracy vs. R sits)
docs.text:
Measured on samples_modis_ndvi of sits (12 dates, 4 classes), with the same 80/20 split on both sides and 5 seeds, the mean accuracy was:

sits, with its defaults Zeit, the authors' defaults Zeit, the pipeline's defaults (150 epochs) TempCNN 0.879 ± 0.027 0.839 ± 0.031 0.861 ± 0.024 LightTAE 0.902 ± 0.016 0.892 ± 0.020 0.915 ± 0.011

The authors' defaults for TempCNN (20 epochs, patience 0, 5% of the samples for validation) stop early on a set as small as this one.

docs.title: Bonus Finding: Official U-TAE Segmentation Architecture
docs.text: During code inspection, zeit.ai.utae contains the full U-Net + LTAE2d segmentation model from the official VSainteuf/utae-paps GitHub repository (Garnot & Landrieu 2021). - Comparing Zeit against the official reference repository on both standard and irregular temporal padded sampling paths yielded an exact numerical match (max abs diff = 0.0).

docs.title: 8. SNIC Superpixel Segmentation (Achanta & Süsstrunk 2017)
docs.text: SNIC (Simple Non-Iterative Clustering; Achanta & Süsstrunk, CVPR 2017) partitions an image or multi-spectral time-series cube into compact, contiguous, boundary-adhering regions of similar pixels (superpixels). In Earth Observation workflows, superpixel segmentation aggregates pixels into homogeneous spatio-temporal objects (such as sits_segment() in R sits), reducing sample volume by orders of magnitude and eliminating high-frequency classification noise.

docs.title: Direct Source-Level Parity
docs.text:
Zeit implements the canonical SNIC algorithm in Rust (rust/zeit-core/src/snic.rs; C++ up to 1.7, with the same labels), evaluated directly against the authors' original C reference implementation (snic.c, EPFL):

  • Bit-for-Bit Label Identity: Given identical seed coordinates, Zeit produces 100% identical segment labels (res.labels), matching the reference C implementation pixel for pixel.
  • Exact Heap Tie-Breaking: When adjacent boundary pixels yield identical distance metrics to competing candidate clusters, Zeit reproduces the exact priority queue tie-breaking order of the reference implementation. Tests in tests/test_snic.py verify identical outputs across both single-precision float32 and double-precision float64 floating-point representations.
  • Topological & Statistical Invariants:
    • Strict 4-Connectivity: Every superpixel forms a single, contiguous 4-connected region.
    • Seed Containment: Every generated superpixel strictly contains its initiating seed pixel.
    • Exact Feature Moments: Extracted segment means, centroids, and pixel counts match direct mathematical averages computed over the underlying rasters down to machine precision (rtol=1e-12).

docs.title: Upstream Bug Fixes & Edge-Case Resilience
docs.text:
Analysis of the authors' original C code (snic.c) revealed critical edge-case defects that Zeit resolves:

  1. Heap Underflow on Single Seed: In snic.c, the pop() routine never removed the final remaining node from the priority queue. When presented with a single seed (or late in execution), it read uninitialized memory and caused a segmentation fault. Zeit properly drains the priority queue, supporting single-seed segmentations and arbitrary seed counts safely.
  2. Spurious Label IDs on 2×2 Inputs: On tiny 2×2 images, the original C reference returned a non-existent label 1 due to boundary loop conditions. Zeit strictly bounds all label assignments to valid seed IDs [0, K-1].
  3. Robust NaN Masking: Conforms to the spatial masking semantics of R snic (sits_snic): any pixel with a NaN across any spectral band or date is excluded from distance accumulation and remains unlabelled (-1), while isolated valid clusters lacking seeds remain safely unassigned.

docs.title: Ecosystem Compatibility & Spatio-Temporal Cubes
docs.text:
• R snic Grid Compatibility: The snic_grid generator in Zeit matches R snic::snic_grid 1:1, supporting "rectangular", "diamond", "hexagonal", and "random" seed placement patterns with configurable boundary padding.
  • Full Trajectory Distance: While the original paper focused on 2D CIELAB photographs, Zeit natively handles 4D spatio-temporal arrays (time, band, y, x). Distance is computed across the full temporal feature vector, ensuring that agricultural fields sharing similar annual average reflectance but differing phenological cycles segment into distinct objects.
  • Deterministic Tiled Parallel Execution: For large satellite scenes, run_snic(..., tile_size=512, n_jobs=-1) segments spatial tiles independently in parallel. Because each seed belongs strictly to its enclosing tile, segments never produce artificial boundary seams across tile edges, and labels remain identical regardless of thread count.

docs.title: 9. Newer Ports Against Their Originals
docs.text:
The methods below were ported from R packages and scripts (and S-CCD written from its paper), and each is checked against the original on the same inputs. The timings, the workloads and the scripts that check the agreement on every run are on Against the Original Implementations.

  • Bayesian smoothing (zeit.smooth_probs) vs R bayesEO. Written from the paper (Camara et al. 2024, Remote Sensing 16(23):4572): it agrees with bayesEO's bayes_smooth to about 2e-3, with the same class everywhere in the tests (tests/test_postproc.py). A pixel with no probabilities stays missing.
  • Area of applicability (zeit.aoa, zeit.train_di) vs R CAST 1.0.4. The same dissimilarity index as trainDI and aoa, to 1e-13, with and without the local point density, for 8 and 64 predictors. The Mahalanobis distance (method = "MD") and a leave-one-out without the neighbours within a buffer (CVtrain) give CAST's DI to 1e-13 too, on the test cases (tests/data/make_aoa_cast_fixtures.R) and on 100,000 new points in the benchmark.
  • ImproPhe (zeit.improphe) vs FORCE 3.11.00's CF-ImproPhe and L2-ImproPhe. On synthetic Sentinel-2A (10 m, 90 dates), Landsat 8 (30 m, 24 scenes) and field (30 m) data, force=True truncated to integers equals FORCE's built against GSL's reference CBLAS in every value (176,130 CF values and 12.5 million L2 values per configuration, radii of 10 and 20 pixels, two sets of seasonal windows; also the seasonal means, components and texture, bit for bit); FORCE linked to OpenBLAS as in the reference build differs in the last bits of GSL's eigenvectors and so in 0.002-0.003% of the L2 values (by 1, up to 11 in a handful) and 0.001-0.002% of the CF ones (more, up to 0.9%, on a cube whose seasonal means are collinear). The comparison found that Rust's hypot on Windows is not correctly rounded as glibc's is, and that GSL's eigenvectors, which FORCE's transposed PCA projection makes depend on every bit, differed from the first Householder step; Zeit's port now equals GSL 2.7 in every stage. FORCE 3.11.00's L2IMP does not start as released (the secondary sensors' target sensor and products are never set); conda-forge's libgslcblas.so.0 is OpenBLAS, GSL's reference is libgslcblas.so.0.0.0. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • Sentinel-2 resolution merge (zeit.sentinel2_resmerge) vs FORCE 3.11.00's resmerge-ll.c. force=True equals FORCE's regression (resolution_merge_1, a 25-pixel least squares by GSL's SVD) and ImproPhe-like weighted mean (resolution_merge_2) in every value of the six 20 m bands (245,534 pixels each, on a 500 x 500 scene with no-data pixels, clouds, shadows, constant spectra and zeros): FORCE's functions copied verbatim into a C harness linked statically to GSL 2.7 and its reference CBLAS, run on one thread. FORCE runs it only inside force-l2ps, so there is no ARD-level program to compare with. With force=False the regression does not read earlier predictions as neighbours (FORCE's in-place sweep does, in an order that is a race on several threads) and differs from force=True by 11-20 digital numbers on average. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • Sentinel-2 parallax cloud test and cloud buffer (zeit.parallax_clouds, zeit.cloud_displacement_index, zeit.buffer_mask) vs FORCE 3.11.00's cloud_parallax and buffer_. The cloud mask (262,144 pixels) and the Cloud Displacement Index (65,536 blocks, bit for bit) equal FORCE's in every value on a synthetic 512 x 512 scene of parallax-displaced clouds, built-up patches, off, saturated and non-bright pixels, and on four more scenes; buffer_mask(force=True) equals buffer_ in every pixel at radii of 1 to 30 (FORCE's own functions copied verbatim into a C harness; only Frantz's parallax step is ported, the Fmask inputs (potential cloud pixels, variability probability, bright and saturated pixels) are inputs). With force=False the buffer keeps the True pixels within the radius of an image edge, which FORCE's loop drops. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • Spatial folds and the error profile vs R CAST 1.0.4 and blockCV 4.0.1. kNNDM's statistics (the nearest-neighbour distances Gij, Gj* and their W) equal CAST's on its own folds to 1e-9; the folds themselves are drawn by Zeit's own clustering of other candidates, and their W was as small as CAST's or smaller on the benchmark's points (tests/data/make_knndm_cast_fixtures.R). The error profile's windows of the DI and their RMSE or accuracy equal CAST's errorProfiles to 1e-14 (tests/data/make_error_profile_cast_fixtures.R); the monotone curve is a P-spline (Bollaerts et al. 2006) within about 1% of scam's. One difference is deliberate: CAST gives a window of a single class, all predicted right, an accuracy of 0 (17 of the 145 windows of the test case), Zeit gives it 1. The range of a map's autocorrelation is within 2% of blockCV's cv_spatial_autocor at ranges of 7 and 15 pixels, and 1-11% shorter at 3 pixels; each draws its own pixels.
  • Emerging hot spots (zeit.emerging_hotspots) vs R sfdep 0.2.5. The Getis-Ord Gi* of every cell and date equals sfdep's (include_gi = TRUE, queen neighbours, k the lag) to 1e-14, and the Mann-Kendall test of each series equals R Kendall's to its single precision (tests/data/make_hotspots_sfdep_fixtures.R). The patterns are not compared: sfdep takes the significance of each Gi* from permutations and has rules of its own, while Zeit follows ESRI's definitions with the normal p-values of the Gi*.
  • EWMACD (zeit.ewmacd) vs Brooks' EWMACD v1.3.0 script. With persistence=1, the flags are identical date by date, on synthetic series (tests/data/make_ewmacd_parity_fixtures.R), on 400 pixels of the paper's sample data and on the 11,000 pixels of the benchmark. With more persistence, the first disturbance is the same but a few later dates differ: there the script means to keep the previous sustained state but reads another date's flag.
  • Recovery metrics (zeit.recovery_metrics) vs R RecoverMetricsR 0.1.0. RRI, R80P, YrYr and the years to recovery agree to a relative 6e-8 (float32, Zeit's output) on series that regrow steadily. The two define the metrics a little differently (RecoverMetricsR takes the best of the 5 years after the trough where Zeit, after Frazier et al. 2018, takes years 4 and 5, and counts the years to recovery from the year after the trough), so on irregular regrowth they can differ by design.
  • Spectral unmixing vs R RStoolbox 1.0.2.2 (mesma, NNLS). With the same constraints (non-negative fractions, free sum), the fractions agree to 4e-4 (a median of 7e-5): mesma's NNLS stops at a tolerance, while Zeit's active set solves each pixel exactly, and its residual is never larger than mesma's.
  • S-CCD (zeit.sccd) vs pyxccd 1.1.0 (sccd_detect). pyxccd is Apache-2.0, but Zeit's S-CCD is written from the paper (Ye et al. 2021 and its preprint) and pyxccd only run on the same data. On series with clear changes the two agree on every break (1000 synthetic pixels of 35 years). On 4096 Landsat pixels of Rondonia (2020–2026, about 27 clear observations each), 85% of the pixels have as many breaks in both, 56% of pyxccd's breaks are on the same date in Zeit and 75% within one observation (76% on the 61 dates of the timing benchmark, which leaves out the dates without data anywhere); the magnitudes of the breaks found by both correlate at 0.99, and the near-real-time mode (monitoring, or waiting for a model) is the same in 89% of the pixels (tests/test_sccd.py, on 384 of them, from tests/data/make_sccd_pyxccd_fixtures.py). The paper leaves the filter partly open, and the differences come from there: (1) the process noise: the paper estimates it from a first filtering of the initialisation window (its Eq. 9), which Zeit does, while pyxccd's states adapt faster on irregular dates than that estimate gives; (2) the RMSE that standardizes the test: Zeit's is that of the filter's one-step-ahead predictions and comes out about 15% smaller than pyxccd's, whose definition is not documented. Zeit's extra breaks (about 20% more) have statistics near the threshold (a median of 1.5× it, against 2× for the breaks both find), where that 15% decides: with its RMSE scaled by 1.1, Zeit finds as many breaks as pyxccd. Zeit starts a model with COLD's stability test (Zhu et al. 2020, which S-CCD inherits), not CCDC's, which kept many Amazon pixels from ever starting one. The paper's temporally adjusted RMSE (from the observations nearest in the day of the year) was tried and left out: it found more breaks still, further from pyxccd.
  • FORCE's time series analysis (zeit.temporal_metrics, standardize, interpolate, linear_trend, cat, clear_observations, polar_metrics) vs FORCE 3.11.00. On 10,000 pixels the 16 metrics, the folds by year, quarter, month, week and day, the standardization and the linear and moving-average interpolation equal FORCE's int16 values (a few of 1.1 million differ by 1); the RBF and the harmonic fit to all the series are within 1 (99.98% and 99.999% equal), and the harmonic fit to part of the series, with its near-real-time dates, is equal. The trends equal FORCE's, and CAT's values are equal or within 1 (loss, where FORCE truncates the offset before dividing). Differences are deliberate: Student's t is exact where FORCE iterates Hill's approximation; the CAT penalty compares penalized with penalized drops (a literal Python port of FORCE's comparison reproduces the pixels where the step differs); CSO takes every statistic over the same k intervals and keeps the last window; skewness and kurtosis of a constant series are NaN; the pixels whose harmonic IRLS does not converge in 100 iterations are left out. The 39 polar metrics equal FORCE's, adaptive and fixed, with gaps and other thresholds (NaN where FORCE casts an undefined value); against the authors' R package (PolarMetrics 0.1.0) the eight metrics in common agree once its year start (one sample off in 60% of the pixels) and its reading of the unrotated steps are accounted for, shown with a literal port of calc_metrics. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • FORCE's spectral adjustment (zeit.spectral_adjust) vs FORCE 3.11.00. The ten Sentinel-2A bands of synthetic Landsat 8, 7 and 5 cubes (200 x 200 pixels, 136 dates, 4.9 million observations each; vegetation, soil, water, snow and urban spectra and their mixtures, plus zeros, negatives, high and near-saturated values) equal FORCE's int16 output in every value (49 million per sensor, none off by 1) when the core runs FORCE's own first search of the nearest cluster (force_search=True, truncation and 16-bit wrap as FORCE's (short)). Zeit's default departs on purpose: FORCE's first search skips cluster 9 (s != N_SIM-1, which looks like a slip for the global cluster, 50) and may pick the global cluster, so the default, where the global cluster is never the first pick and cluster 9 competes, differs beyond 1 in 2.29% (Landsat 8), 1.87% (7) and 1.60% (5) of the observations, and those are exactly the observations where the two searches differ (none beyond 1 that the two modes do not share, none the other way). MODIS is not compared: FORCE's TSA rejects it with SPECTRAL_ADJUST (the union of its bands with Sentinel-2A's has 11 bands, and the target sensor must have the same number); its tables are checked against FORCE's source by checksum. The authors' own SpecHomo is not run: its trained classifiers are 218 MB dill files (loading executes code) of undeclared license. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • Tasseled Cap (zeit.tasseled_cap) vs FORCE 3.11.00 and RStoolbox 1.0.2.2. FORCE's TC-BRIGHT, TC-GREEN, TC-WET and TC-DI (Crist 1985 for every sensor) equal Zeit's in every observation FORCE computes of synthetic Sentinel-2A (11.7 million values) and Landsat 8, 7 and 5 (19.7 million each) cubes, none off by 1 (Zeit adds the six float32 products in FORCE's order and truncates as (short)); for Sentinel-2 FORCE's NIR is B8A. RStoolbox's tasseledCap equals Zeit's matrices of OLI (Baig et al. 2014) and ETM+ (Huang et al. 2002) to 1e-7, and its Landsat 5 table differs from Crist's in the sign of the SWIR1 weight of greenness and wetness (+0.0002, +0.6806 against -0.0002, -0.6806, the paper's and FORCE's), which Zeit follows. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • Topographic correction (zeit.topographic_correction) vs terra, GDAL and RStoolbox 1.0.2.2. Written from the published formulas (Horn 1981, Teillet et al. 1982, Soenen et al. 2005), compared by outputs only, on synthetic terrain of 1000 x 1000 cells (no DEM ships with the repository). Horn's slope and aspect equal terra::terrain (8 neighbours) to 8e-6 and 5e-5 degrees and gdaldem to 2.5e-4 (slope; GDAL writes float32) and 0.09 degrees (aspect, on cells of almost no slope) inside the grid; the edge cells differ (Zeit's one-sided difference over one cell, against GDAL's -compute_edges; terra leaves them NA). RStoolbox's topCor(method = "C"), given Zeit's slope and aspect, equals Zeit's C-correction to 4e-7 relative when the line is fitted on the same pixels (a 100 x 100 image, which RStoolbox samples whole), and differs by 0.3-4.5% at most on 1000 x 1000, where RStoolbox fits on a random 10000-pixel sample. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • Global co-registration (zeit.coregister) vs AROSICS 1.14.0's COREG. A port of AROSICS' global shift (the matching window, the shifted cross power spectrum in single precision, the integer shift and its validation, the subpixel shift from the side maxima, the reliability and the structural similarity), run against AROSICS itself in its own conda environment on 11 pairs where a shift is found (value noise of 200 x 200 to 4096 x 4096 pixels with whole and fractional shifts, a uint16 image with a no-data margin, a diagonal no-data edge, odd sizes, and scikit-image's camera image moved by a subpixel shift) and 2 where neither finds one (a shift above max_shift, a constant image). The two agree on every success and failure; the integer part, the matching window, the FFT size, the reliability and the similarity before and after are equal, and the shifts differ by 2.1e-7 pixels at most (single-precision noise of two FFT libraries). The aligned images differ by one unit in the last place of float32 (by 1 in uint16). AROSICS fills the holes of an image's footprint and Zeit's window avoids them; the aligned image is on the cube's grid (AROSICS, with align_grids=False, only moves the origin). No satellite scene was available (the repository's GeoTIFFs are 25 x 25 pixels). Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • Local co-registration (zeit.coregister_local) vs AROSICS 1.14.0's COREG_LOCAL. The grid of tie points, the match of each point, the three filters and the warp, run against AROSICS itself on 7 pairs of 777 x 1001 to 2048 x 2048 pixels (a smooth field of shifts of up to 3 pixels, patches of changed texture, no data and a displaced block that are outliers, a uint16 image with a no-data margin and a diagonal edge, odd sizes, a fine grid, and scikit-image's camera warped by a field; 19 to 165 points each). The same points are placed and matched in every pair; the shifts differ by 2e-6 pixels at most (2e-3 at one point of the natural image), the windows are equal, the reliability agrees to 8e-5 and the similarity to 2e-5 (3e-4 in the 8-bit image), and with arosics_compat=True the flags of the reliability, similarity and RANSAC filters (and so the control points) are identical in every pair, with scikit-image's RANSAC and numpy's random generator reproduced in the core; the warped image from the same points differs by 0.001 at most in float32. That flag-for-flag match needed arosics_compat: AROSICS 1.14.0 assigns RANSAC's flags to the wrong rows of its table when the reliability or similarity filter has flagged a point (a pandas index misalignment), so it drops good points and keeps outliers (7 to 26 points differ in four of the pairs); Zeit's default puts the flags on the points RANSAC found. Differences in design: the overlap is the valid pixels, not the footprint polygons, and a date with fewer than 5 control points is left as it was where AROSICS corrects with their mean. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • Radiative transfer of the atmospheric correction (zeit_core::radtran, no public function yet) vs FORCE 3.11.00's own C. The pieces of radtran-ll.c (molecular and aerosol optical depth, the scattering transmittances, path reflectance, spherical albedo, the environmental weights, the phase functions, the water vapour and ozone transmittance of each of the 56 Landsat 4-8 and Sentinel-2A/B bands, the Fresnel reflection, the illumination angle and the C-factors), wavelength and E0 of table-ll.c, ozone_amount of gas-ll.c, and localtime2gmt of sunview-ll.c equal FORCE's in every value, bit for bit: 7,077,563 values of 27 functions on a grid of angles, optical depths, elevations, water vapour, ozone, bands, days, latitudes and longitudes, 0 with a difference of 1 ulp and 0 with more (FORCE's own functions compiled with its flags, gcc -O3, glibc 2.39, against Zeit's core on Windows' UCRT). The sun position (sunpos, and the zenith inside standard_sunzenith) is not a port of FORCE's sun-cl.c but a clean-room implementation from Meeus and NOAA's documentation (zeit_core::solpos): it differs from FORCE's by 0.012 degrees on average and 0.09 at most in the zenith (the FORCE harness keeps its Julian day in float32, steps of a quarter of a day, which moves the declination by up to 0.05 degrees near the equinoxes; Zeit's is the more accurate), and the daytime azimuth by 0.07 degrees on average. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • Water vapour and gas transmittance of the atmospheric correction (zeit_core::gas, no public function yet) vs FORCE 3.11.00's own C. wvp_transmitt_lut, water_vapor (the Nelder-Mead retrieval of each 60 m block from the NIR and water vapour bands, with GSL 2.7's nmsimplex2 ported in one dimension), gas_transmittance and water_vapor_from_lut of gas-ll.c equal FORCE's in every value, bit for bit: 7,076,598 values of 6 synthetic Sentinel-2 scenes (36 x 30 to 300 x 240 pixels, coarse cells of 60, 120 and 300 m, a low sun, a scene of water only; the LUT of 13 bands, the water vapour, the QAI after the fill and the gas transmittance of each band), and 300 of 300 LUT-file scenarios (daily and climatological WVP_*.txt, nodata, strict mode), 0 differences (FORCE's own gas-ll.c compiled as it is against the real GSL 2.7 and its reference CBLAS, linked statically). Zeit's retrieval is FORCE's with one OpenMP thread: with more, each thread carries its last estimate to its next pixel and FORCE's output depends on the number of threads (4 threads against 1: 8,208 of 72,000 pixels differ, 0.010 cm on average, 2.09 cm at most). Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • Dark targets and the AOD over each of them (zeit_core::aod, no public function yet) vs FORCE 3.11.00's own C. The first half of aod-ll.c: extract_dark_target (water and vegetation targets: the spectral tests, the cut by the coarse grid, the connected components and the distance to the shore, the lapsing spectra, the target and environment reflectance), the water and vegetation spectral libraries, aod_lib_to_target (the AOD that best matches each library spectrum, band by band), aod_from_target (with aod_linear_fit and the 2nd order aod_polynomial_fit of GSL 2.7's nmsimplex2 in three dimensions), aod_elev_dependency (GSL 2.7's Brent minimizer), aodfileread, and the segmentation and distance transform of imagefuns-cl.c, equal FORCE's in every value, bit for bit: 161,773 values of 6 synthetic Sentinel-2 scenes (120 x 90 to 480 x 440 pixels with 150 to 300 m cells; lakes, a river cut by the grid, vegetation, cloud, shadow and no-data regions, 0 to 741 candidate targets) with the target lists, the library AOD, the fitted AOD, coefficients and R2, and the elevation factors, plus 9,703 values of 300 random lists of targets for the elevation dependency, 200 of 200 AOD-file scenarios and 104,133 values of the segmentation and distance transform, 0 differences (FORCE's own aod-ll.c compiled as it is, one OpenMP thread, against the real GSL 2.7 linked statically). The shadow type is disabled in FORCE 3.11.00 and is here too. FORCE's scene-average environment reflectance is a sum per OpenMP thread and its loop over targets hands each thread one set of work arrays, so its output can depend on the number of threads (on the large scene, 4 threads against 1 gave the same targets and AOD); Zeit's is FORCE with one thread. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • The AOD map (zeit_core::aod::compile_aod, with zeit_core::gdal_grid; no public function yet) vs FORCE 3.11.00's own C and GDAL 3.9.3. The second half of aod-ll.c: aod_map, interpolate_aod_map and compile_aod. FORCE interpolates the per-cell mean AOD with GDAL's GDALGridCreate (algorithm invdist, default options), which takes GDAL's AVX path: float arithmetic, 16 points at a time into 8 lanes, and the CPU's reciprocal approximation rcpps instead of a division; Zeit ports that path (gdalgrid.cpp, gdalgridavx.cpp, MIT) lane by lane and executes the same rcpss instruction. Equal to the real GDAL bit for bit in 143,903 cells of 240 random grids (1 x 1 to 60 x 50 cells, 0 to 600 points, a dynamic range of seven decades), and compile_aod equal to FORCE's own in 51,690 values of 16 runs on 11 synthetic scenes (four ordinary ones, one target, one target on a 2 x 2 grid, only water, only vegetation, targets that all fail the fit, no target and all cloud: the fallback; with and without an AOD file and with the AOD estimation off): the final AOD map per band and cell, the interpolation marks, the scene AOD, the scale height and the elevation factors, 0 differences. The result depends on the CPU: Intel's and AMD's rcpps tables differ, so GDAL (and FORCE) give AOD maps that differ by about 1e-3 on the two; Zeit is GDAL's on the same CPU (an Intel i5-13600K here, WSL and Windows), and on a non-x86 architecture the reciprocal is exact and the map differs from GDAL's by that much. Only the AVX path is ported (GDAL uses the SSE one, with 4 lanes, with GDAL_USE_AVX=NO or without AVX). GDAL's threads split the rows, and each cell is computed from all the points in the same order: the result does not depend on GDAL_NUM_THREADS. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • The topography of the atmospheric correction (zeit_core::topo, no public function yet) vs FORCE 3.11.00's own C. topo-ll.c whole: the ocean detection, the smoothing of the DEM below 30 m, slope and aspect (Horn's method in float, in radians times 10000), the elevation statistics and the binned DEM, the illumination angle and its QAI flag, the sky view factor, cfactor_topography (the C-factor, theoretical or from a regression over a 3 km neighbourhood of similar pixels) and average_elevation_cell, equal FORCE's in every value, bit for bit: 11,620,508 values of 14 synthetic scenes (flat, ramp, cone, valley, mountains at 5, 10, 20, 30 and 250 m, no-data holes and frame, an ocean with its no-data coast, a QAI with off pixels and flags already set, nothing on, DEMs above 9 km and below -500 m where FORCE fails and so does Zeit, 3 km and finer coarse cells, a sun that changes over the grid): every field of top_t, the QAI afterwards, atc->dem, the C-factor and the average elevation of every coarse cell, 0 differences (FORCE's own topo-ll.c compiled as it is, one OpenMP thread; the atan, atan2, sqrt, cos and sin of Windows' libm and glibc's gave the same bits). FORCE's warp of the DEM file (GDAL, bilinear by default) is outside the core: both sides get the same DEM on the grid of the scene. The average elevation is a sum of doubles per OpenMP thread in FORCE, so its last bits can depend on the number of threads (4 against 1 gave the same bits on the large scene); Zeit's is FORCE with one thread. This is not zeit.topographic_correction, which is unchanged. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • The atmosphere of the coarse grid (zeit_core::atc, sunview, atmo, no public function yet) vs FORCE 3.11.00's own C. atc-ll.c (allocate_atc: every field of atc_t after init_atc, init_atc_xy and init_atc_xyz, the Henyey-Greenstein terms, the environmental weighting, the wavelengths, the solar irradiances, the 50 bricks with their bands, size, resolution, no-data and band domains), sunview-ll.c (sun_target_view, viewgeo and view_angle: the sun and view angles of every coarse cell with their cosines, sines and tangents, the nadir line of a Landsat swath, the Sentinel-2 view angle grids with cells without data that set pixels off, the range of the cosines, the low sun flag) and, from atmo-ll.c, interpolation_weights, interpolate_coarse, atmo_angledep (the phase functions, the gas transmittances, the average elevation, the molecular optical depth at that elevation, the Fresnel reflection), atmo_elevdep (the 256 elevation bins of 15 families and the aerosol flag of the QAI) and apply_aoi, equal FORCE's in every value, bit for bit: 81,850,920 values of 13 synthetic scenes (Landsat at 100 and 30 m, in the north, south and west, in summer and with the sun below the horizon, grids with more columns than rows and the other way round; Sentinel-2 at 10, 20 and 60 m up to a whole tile of 22 x 22 cells and 13 bands; with and without an AOD map, the environmental weighting and the multiple scattering; about 1,500 interpolation pixels a scene), 0 differences, none at 1 ulp (FORCE's own atc-ll.c and sunview-ll.c compiled as they are and the functions of atmo-ll.c copied verbatim, one OpenMP thread; the exp, log, sin, cos, tan, acos and atan2 of Windows' libm and glibc's gave the same bits; Zeit with 4 threads gave the same fields as with 1). Not FORCE's, and the same on both sides: the sun position (sun-cl.c is not opened: Zeit's clean-room sunpos, handed to the C harness as a table), the warp of map coordinates to longitude and latitude (an affine map) and brdf_factor (brdf-ll.c is not ported: 1 for every band, the factor it starts from), so the sun angles are not FORCE's bits. The three earlier harnesses were run again with the completed Atc: the same counts, 0 differences. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • The surface reflectance and the Level 2 products (zeit_core::l2, no public function yet) vs FORCE 3.11.00's own radiometric_correction. The rest of atmo-ll.c (surface_reflectance with the topographic, BRDF and environmental terms, background_reflectance with its three rings of exponential moving averages, compile_l2_boa, _qai, _dst with cloud_distance, _vzn with the inverse distance weighting of GDAL, _hot, _aod, _wvp, compile_level2 and radiometric_correction in FORCE's order: atmo_angledep, compile_aod, atmo_elevdep, water_vapor, cfactor_topography, apply_aoi, the products), equal to FORCE's in every value, bit for bit: 139,889,050 values of 13 synthetic scenes (Landsat at 30 and 100 m, Sentinel-2 at 10, 20 and 60 m up to a 1200 x 1200 tile with 13 bands; TOA reflectance from the radiative transfer for soil, lakes, dark vegetation, cloud (opaque, unsure, cirrus), shadow and snow, a DEM with relief and an ocean; with doatmo, dotopo, doenv, domulti, dobrdf, erase_cloud, doaod on and off, an area of interest, an AOD map and the fallback, high AOD, low sun, all the optional products), 0 differences: the atc after the correction (the water vapour, the AOD, 18 coarse bricks, 15 families of 256 bricks), the final QAI, the BOA of every band, the DST, VZN, HOT, AOD and WVP products, the gaseous transmittance maps. The C side is FORCE's own radiometric_correction (the object files FORCE's make built for force-l2ps, with the real GSL 2.7 and GDAL 3.9.3, one OpenMP thread); not FORCE's, and the same on both sides: the sun position (Zeit's clean-room sunpos as a table), the map to longitude and latitude, the DEM warp and brdf_factor (not ported: a factor of the view zenith and the band). The comparison found that wvp_transmitt of the C is NaN for a sun below the horizon (the port gave a finite value: fixed). The four earlier harnesses were run again: the same counts (81,850,920; 11,620,508; 7,076,598; 51,690), 0 differences. Details in Against the Original Implementations.
  • PARTS (zeit.ar_trend, zeit.parts) vs R remotePARTS 1.0.4. The GLS, each partition's fit and nugget and the combined coefficients match to 1e-8; the AR(1) fits match fitAR to about 1e-6, the correlation's range fitCor to 1e-5, and the chi-square p-value to 1e-6 (rust/zeit-core/tests/remoteparts.rs). remotePARTS 1.0.4 computes the correlation between partitions after the first without their nugget; Zeit uses each partition's own, so the two agree for a fixed nugget=. Details in Regional Trends: parity with remotePARTS.
  • BEAST (zeit.beast) vs R Rbeast 1.0.2. Zeit's BEAST is a port of Rbeast's C code, with its generic kernels (cputype = "sse"), its random number generator and its float32 arithmetic. From the same seed it runs the same chain and returns the same float32 outputs, to the last bit. That holds for the season, the trend, their credible intervals, the changepoints and their probabilities, the slope, the amplitude and the fit, on the Nile, Rbeast's simulated series, its Yellowstone NDVI with gaps, its irregular Ohio Landsat series (beast.irreg), a short series, and the uniform and constant priors (tests/data/make_beast_fixtures.R). Two outputs differ on purpose. The slope's interval is the mean over the chains, per unit of time; Rbeast sums it over the chains, per time step. And with one chain, Zeit gives the mode, median and percentiles of the number of changepoints, which Rbeast leaves at 0. Rbeast's default AVX2 kernels sum in another order, so their chain departs from the generic one after a few hundred iterations and the two agree in distribution only. Each pixel of a cube is fitted as beast() fits one series; beast123() carries its random stream from one pixel to the next.

docs.title: 10. NBAR Against HLS (zeit.nbar, zeit.sentinel2_angles)
docs.text:
This one is a validation against a product, not against another implementation: HLS v2.0 applies the same method, the c-factor of Roy et al. (2016, 2017) with the same fixed MODIS parameters, and publishes the NBAR reflectance and the angles it used. It does not publish the reflectance before the NBAR, so the test cannot compare the two states of one scene. Zeit's NBAR is written from the papers and the HLS User Guide, never from HLS's or FORCE's code; the product is used only through its outputs. python benchmarks/vs_originals/nbar_hls.py (network: Planetary Computer and Earth Search; results in benchmarks/results/nbar-hls.json) does the following.

  • HLS L30 against Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 of the same scene and day. HLS.L30.T23LKC.2023214T131426.v2.0 (Landsat 9, 2023-08-02, 0% cloud) and LC09_L2SP_221071_20230802_02_T1, both LaSRC (scale 2.75e-05, offset -0.2 for the USGS product), read onto HLS's 30 m grid (nearest neighbour) in three windows of 1000 × 1000 pixels chosen for their spread of view zenith (the lowest, the middle and the highest median, clear and with angles), 2.2 to 2.9 million valid pixels per band. Zeit computes the c-factor from HLS's own angle bands (0.01°, fill 40000) with the file's NBAR_SOLAR_ZENITH (44.0496°) as the normalized zenith, and the ratio R = NBAR_HLS / SR_USGS of each pixel is binned by view zenith (1°) and relative azimuth (six sectors of 60°); the table compares the median of R with the median of Zeit's c in the 15 bins with at least 300 pixels.
Band c range median R median c largest |median R - median c| tolerance slope of R-1 on c-1 (bins) after each window's own offset coastal 1.004-1.029 1.0135 1.0149 0.0057 0.02 1.04 0.0039 blue 1.004-1.029 1.0145 1.0148 0.0053 0.02 1.04 0.0049 green 1.005-1.035 1.0182 1.0178 0.0045 0.01 1.03 0.0050 red 1.005-1.031 1.0155 1.0160 0.0083 0.01 1.07 0.0081 NIR 1.004-1.031 1.0170 1.0156 0.0014 0.01 0.98 0.0024 SWIR1 1.005-1.031 1.0175 1.0157 0.0026 0.02 1.03 0.0043 SWIR2 1.005-1.030 1.0166 1.0156 0.0049 0.02 1.06 0.0057

Every bin of every band is inside the tolerance (0.01 for green, red and NIR, 0.02 for the rest) and the slope is between 0.98 and 1.07 (0.9-1.0 on the individual pixels), so the c-factor has the right sign, size and dependence on the geometry. The test sees c between 1.004 and 1.035 because Landsat's field of view is narrow (view zenith 0.6-8.5°) and the azimuth in this scene is about 240° from the sun's (far from the hot spot); it would not catch a mistake that only matters near the hot spot.

  • HLS S30 against Sentinel-2 L2A (Sen2Cor). HLS.S30.T23LKC.2023204T132241.v2.0 against S2A_23LKC_20230723_0_L2A of Earth Search (the item that the tile metadata below belongs to), three windows of 1000 × 1000 pixels at 30 m, Zeit's c from sentinel2_angles (B06's view angles, as HLS does) and the file's NBAR_SOLAR_ZENITH (45.8260°). HLS S30 is bandpass-adjusted after the NBAR (the slope and offset are in the file's tags), which is undone before the ratio. Sen2Cor and LaSRC correct the atmosphere differently, so R carries a processor offset that is not the geometry's (the medians of R are 0.84 in the coastal band, 0.94 in blue, 0.96 in red, 0.98 in B8A): against the c alone, the largest difference between bin medians passes 0.03 in B8A (0.012), red edge 3 (0.024) and SWIR1 (0.026), and does not in B08 (0.035), red edge 2 (0.041), red (0.042), SWIR2 (0.077), red edge 1 (0.090) and the visible and coastal bands (0.08-0.25), where aerosol dominates. With each window's own offset removed (what is left of the disagreement is the geometry's), the largest difference is 0.010-0.012 in the red edge, B08 and B8A, 0.016-0.021 in SWIR1, SWIR2 and red (all inside 0.03), and the slope of the bin medians is 1.16-1.20 (1.13-1.32 in the pixels) from the red edge to SWIR2, 1.3 in red. The visible bands do not pass (green 0.033, blue 0.072, coastal 0.119, slopes 1.4-2.2): their R changes from window to window with the aerosol more than with the view geometry (c changes by 0.035 across the three windows), so the S30 test says little about them.

  • sentinel2_angles against HLS S30's angle bands. HLS reads the same ESA 5 km grids (from the Level-1C metadata). Over the whole tile (a decimated read, 366 × 366 pixels, 134 thousand pixels) Zeit's angles minus HLS's: the solar zenith +0.015° on average (std 0.004, maximum 0.029) and the solar azimuth +0.013° (maximum 0.028), a constant that is the difference between the Level-1C and Level-2A metadata's sun grids (the means in HLS's tags, 44.763° and 37.577°, against the Level-2A file's 44.778° and 37.590°); the view zenith -0.002° on average (std 0.053°, 99% of the pixels within 0.25°, maximum 0.48°); the view azimuth -0.4° on average (std 6.7°, 99% within 31°, maximum 64°). The view differences are at the borders of the detectors: HLS gives each pixel the angles of its detector, a step of 20-60° in azimuth at each border, where Zeit's fused 5 km grid changes smoothly over the cell between two detectors (a fifth of the tile is in cells that no single detector covers). In the cells that one detector covers, taking that detector's own grid instead of the fused one agrees with HLS to a std of 0.013° in zenith and within 1° in azimuth for 99.4% of the pixels. The c-factors from the two sets of angles (the same normalized zenith) differ by -0.0001 on average, with a standard deviation of 0.0027, 99% of the pixels within 0.010 and a maximum of 0.015 (blue, red, red edge 1, B8A and SWIR1 alike). Choosing the detector of each pixel by the largest weight in the cell's four corners (flat in the cells no detector covers) agrees with HLS within 1° in azimuth for 96% of the pixels, but its c differs from HLS's just as much (standard deviation 0.0029): where the detector chosen is not HLS's, the error is as large as the blend's, so Zeit keeps the smooth fusion, which has no sharp border to get wrong. HLS's own rule for the cells between two detectors (it seems to extend one detector's grid) was not recovered from the outputs.

Not checked: the forward/backward overlap test of Roy et al., a Landsat scene other than this one, a geometry near the hot spot or with a large view zenith, and the Landsat angle bands (Level-1, USGS credentials). The step is not tested for snow.

docs.title: Siamese Change Detector (zeit.ai.siamese)
docs.text:
Up to zeit 1.6 the detector was a small network of zeit's own (one pooling, no skip connections), compared only with a conceptual analog in R sits (DTW). It is now FC-Siam-diff, written from Daudt et al. (2018), and compared with the authors' SiamUnet_diff (rcdaudt/fully_convolutional_change_detection, which publishes no license; it is run, not copied):

  • Same weights, same outputs. The reference's weights copied into zeit's model give the same log-probabilities to 5.6e-16 in float64 (4.8e-7 in float32), and the same labels, for 3 to 13 bands and windows of 16 to 130 pixels, odd sizes included (the decoder pads them back as the authors' code does). The decoder's stride-1 transposed convolutions are plain convolutions in zeit, with their kernels flipped.
  • Trained the same way, as accurate. Same initial weights, data, order, augmentation and deterministic kernels, on synthetic scenes with 3-20 px clearings and 1-2 px roads under another illumination: F1 of the change class 0.979 (zeit) against 0.971 (reference) over five seeds, the same label on 99.5-99.9% of the test pixels. zeit runs both dates through the encoder in one pass, so in training batch normalization takes the statistics of both dates together, where the authors' code takes them per date; over six further seeds the two trained alike (F1 0.969 against 0.970). The old zeit network got 0.903, with one seed collapsing to 0.64.
  • Speed. On one CPU thread, 1.07× (inference, 32 windows of 64²) to 1.16× (training, 8 windows of 256²) the reference; 0.95-1.21× on 14 threads and 0.96-1.10× on the GPU. The old network was 2-3.4× slower than the reference at these sizes.

docs.title: Presto (zeit.ai.presto)
docs.text: Ported from nasaharvest/presto (MIT) and compared with its encoder and the authors' input construction (construct_batch_presto_input), with their pretrained weights. zeit reads the bands in the cube's units (reflectance, dB, kelvin, metres) with NaN where missing; the reference gets the same values, normalized and masked by its own code. The encodings agree to 1.2e-6, and are identical in three of the five cases (every input; the six HLS bands under zeit's names; Sentinel-1 and -2 with 30% cloudy dates; 3 dates; 24 dates, half cloudy). zeit encodes 1.17× faster on one CPU thread and 1.32× on 14; on the GPU it is 16× faster, because the reference's month_to_tensor takes Python's max over a CUDA tensor, one device synchronization per element.

docs.title: Prithvi-EO-2.0 (zeit.ai.prithvi)
docs.text: Up to zeit 1.6, GeoFoundationViT loaded Prithvi-100M through transformers and the remote code of its repository, which no longer runs (TypeError: 'NoneType' object cannot be interpreted as an integer); it then fell back, silently, to an untrained convolution. It is replaced by zeit.ai.Prithvi, Prithvi-EO-2.0's encoder ported from the authors' prithvi_mae.py (Apache-2.0), without transformers or timm. With the weights of each of the six published models (tiny-TL, 100M-TL, 300M, 300M-TL, 600M, 600M-TL), loaded as the authors' inference.py loads them, the tokens of the last layer agree to 7.9e-7 of the largest value: four dates of 224 × 224 with and without dates and place, three dates, one date, and windows of 112 × 112 (positions interpolated bicubically, as theirs; 112 is a multiple of the 600M models' patches of 14 and of the others' 16). The speed is the reference's, 0.98-1.05× on 14 CPU threads and 1.00-1.11× on the GPU, for all six models (the 600M-TL on the CPU varied from run to run on this machine, 19 to 35 s for four windows, for both; its fastest runs tie, 19.0 s against 18.9 s): the same PyTorch operations. The decoder from the tokens to a class per pixel is zeit's own and has no reference.

docs.title: Performance & Parallel CPU Scaling
docs.text:
This page documents the computational performance of zeit across single-core CPU execution, multi-core CPU scaling, and distributed cloud comparison (Google Earth Engine), measured on an Intel Core i5-13600K workstation (20 logical threads).

Measured with the Rust core of zeit 2.3

Zeit's side of every table on this page was measured with the Rust core of zeit 2.3, in October 2026, on the same workloads as before. Two kinds of rows keep their earlier numbers: the deep-learning model U-TAE, which runs on PyTorch and not on the compiled core, and SNIC, whose published workload could not be rebuilt exactly. The reference tools (R, GDL, Octave, snic.c) were timed on this same machine in September 2026 and not again; minisom, first timed on another computer, was timed again here. The multi-thread runs use 8 of the 20 logical processors, leaving the rest to the machine; the reference tools' parallel runs use 19 workers. The scripts are in benchmarks/vs_references/ and the results in benchmarks/results/vs-references-rust.json.

The recovery metrics, the majority filter, the temporal consistency and the emerging hot spots gain least: their work per pixel is a few comparisons or sums, so reading and writing memory, not the processors, sets their pace. The sieve and SOM's online training are sequential by nature.

Windows' power throttling

Windows 11 moves a process it deems in the background, as a benchmark run from a terminal is, to the efficiency cores at a low clock after a few seconds of work (power throttling, or EcoQoS). One-thread timings came out up to 2.4 times slower for it. The benchmark scripts take their processes out of power throttling, so the times are of the computation.

docs.title: Multi-Core CPU Scaling
docs.text: Zeit implements parallel execution in its compiled core (n_jobs, the Rust core's own threads), avoiding Python Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) contention and inter-process communication (IPC) overhead. Going from 1 thread to 8 on an Intel Core i5-13600K, most modules run 6–7× faster (the per-module gains are in the table above).

The Python IPC Penalty on Mann-Kendall

On a batch of 5,000 short time series, running Python's standard multiprocessing.Pool(19) caused execution time to explode from 4.06 seconds (sequential) to 20.11 seconds (parallel) — a 5× slowdown (0.20× speedup). The operating system overhead of pickling objects, IPC socket transfers, and process synchronization dwarfed the actual statistical computation. In contrast, Zeit's threads share memory with sub-microsecond synchronization overhead, achieving a true 4.87× speedup on 8 threads (down to 3.62 milliseconds).

docs.text:
A central design goal of Zeit is eliminating cloud lock-in for regional and continental-scale analyses. We evaluated LandTrendr performance on an entire Landsat tile:

  • Environment: Intel Core i5-13600K (desktop PC, 20 logical processors, 64 GB RAM); Zeit on 1 thread and on 8.
  • Reference: Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud batch cluster executing on a full tile (P232/R67, 1985–2025, ~38 million active pixels).
