docs.title: Change detection methods compared
docs.text:
The seven change-detection families answer related but different questions. The figures below all come from their tutorials.

Annual · retrospectiveLandTrendrStraight segments through yearly values. Best for forest disturbance and recovery over decades.

Dense · retrospectiveCCDCHarmonic models of the seasonal cycle, multi-band. Dates changes within the year and describes the new state.

Dense · near real timeS-CCDCCDC's models carried forward by a Kalman filter: one update per new image, and the changes still in progress.

Regular · retrospectiveBFAST Lite / BFASTStatistically optimal number of breaks in trend and season. Single index.

Annual or regular · retrospectiveBEASTBayesian model averaging of trend and season: the probability of each changepoint, and of each number of them.

Regular · near real timeBFAST MonitorIs the newest data consistent with the stable past? The basis of many alert systems.

Irregular · monitoringEWMACDControl charts on every observation after a training period: disturbances, gains and recoveries, cloudy dates welcome.

LandTrendr CCDC S-CCD BFAST Lite / BFAST BEAST BFAST Monitor EWMACD Input 1 index, 1 value per year Up to 7 bands, every clear observation Up to 7 bands, every clear observation 1 index, regular series 1 index, annual or regular (irregular dates put on a grid) 1 index, regular series 1 index, every observation, irregular dates Models the season? No (annual values) Yes (harmonics) Yes (harmonics, filtered) Yes (harmonics) Yes (harmonics), or none Yes (harmonics) Yes (harmonics of the training years) Detects Abrupt and gradual change, recovery Abrupt change, any time of year Abrupt change, and changes in progress at the last date Breaks in trend (and season, for BFAST) Changepoints in trend and season, with their probability The first break after a date Disturbances, gains and recoveries after the training years Typical use Forest disturbance history Land-cover change mapping and classification Monitoring as images arrive Retrospective break analysis Retrospective analysis, with its uncertainty Alerts Monitoring subtle and abrupt change Speed per pixel Very fast Moderate Fast Moderate Slow (an MCMC per pixel) Very fast Very fast

Combine methods

The methods complement each other. A common pattern is Mann-Kendall to find where a region is trending, then LandTrendr or CCDC to find when and how abruptly it changed there. Another is Tmask to clean the data before CCDC. See the User Guide for every workflow.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: A few conventions run through the whole library. Learn them once and every tutorial and API page will read the same way. If something in Zeit surprises you, the answer is most likely on this page.

docs.title: Images become time series
docs.text:
A satellite revisits the same place again and again. Stack the images of one area in date order and you get a data cube with three axes: time, rows and columns. Now read the cube along its time axis at a single pixel, and you have that pixel's time series: how its reflectance (or a vegetation index such as NDVI) evolved.

Real Landsat NDVI over Rondônia, Brazil. The circled pixel stays at about 0.8 while it is forest, then drops to 0.3–0.5 after being cleared in 2003. Data: annual Landsat NDVI composites exported from LT-GEE on Google Earth Engine.

Nearly every algorithm in Zeit works one pixel at a time. It reads a pixel's time series, fits a model to it, and returns a few numbers (a break date, a trend slope, a class). Run over every pixel, those numbers become maps. Because pixels are independent, the work splits cleanly across CPU cores and across machines.

docs.title: Array shapes
docs.text:
What Shape Notes A single pixel (time,) 1-D NumPy array or list. A single-band cube (time, rows, cols) The default input for almost everything. zeit.load_raster reads a GeoTIFF with one band per date into this shape, with the dates in a time coordinate and the georeferencing in .rio. A multi-band cube (time, band, rows, cols) What build_time_series returns (as an xarray DataArray), and what zeit.ccdc takes. Per-pixel results xarray.Dataset of (rows, cols) maps One variable per output, with the cube's coordinates and CRS: result.slope, result["TRS5.sos"]. Outputs with several values per pixel add a leading dim, such as (vertex, y, x) or (year, y, x).

An exception

The deep-learning models follow PyTorch conventions (for example (batch, channels, time) for TempCNN). Their pages say so explicitly.

docs.title: Dates: each family has its own convention
docs.text:
This is the single most common source of confusion, because each algorithm keeps the time convention of the software it was ported from:

Algorithm What you pass Example LandTrendr Nothing for a cube with dates (read from its time coordinate); integer years for a numpy array or a single series years=np.arange(1985, 2025) CCDC Nothing for a cube with dates (read from its time coordinate); any dates for a numpy array or an unnamed stack dates=["2020-01-15", "2020-01-31", ...] Tmask Python ordinal days (date.toordinal()) date(2020, 7, 1).toordinal() → 737607 BFAST, BFAST Monitor, BFAST Lite Nothing for a cube with dates: the regular series of R's ts, start_time (fractional year) and frequency (observations per year), is read from them. Both for a series without dates. start_time=2010.0, frequency=23 for 16-day composites Mann-Kendall Nothing. The slope is per time step, so use one value per year for a per-year slope (or method="seasonal"). Phenology Nothing for a cube with dates (read from its time coordinate); any dates for a numpy array or a single series dates=pd.date_range("2019-01-01", periods=69, freq="16D") TWDTW Nothing for a cube with dates (read from its time coordinate); patterns are series indexed by dates, matched by day of year around the year pd.Series(values, pd.date_range("2021-01-01", periods=23, freq="16D")) SNIC, SOM Nothing. Time is just another feature.

Converting from pandas / xarray timestamps:

import pandas as pd

t = pd.to_datetime(cube.time.values)

years    = t.year.values                                   # LandTrendr (numpy input)
ordinals = [d.toordinal() for d in t.date]                 # Tmask

docs.title: Values and scale factors
docs.text:
Most surface-reflectance and index products are stored as integers scaled by 10,000 (so NDVI 0.73 is stored as 7300). Zeit keeps each reference algorithm's own assumptions:

  • CCDC and Tmask expect reflectance × 10,000. Their thresholds (the lasso penalty, the cloud tests) are defined on that scale. Pass 0–1 floats and results will be wrong. Tmask has a scale_factor argument if your data is already 0–1.
  • LandTrendr works on any scale, but min_magnitude in extract_events is in the same units as your data (1500 for NDVI × 10,000, 0.15 for plain NDVI).
  • Trend, BFAST and phenology work on any scale. Slopes and magnitudes come back in the units you put in.

docs.title: Missing data
docs.text:
• Use NaN for missing observations in float arrays. Most algorithms skip NaNs per pixel.
  • zeit.landtrendr, zeit.ccdc, the BFAST family, zeit.mann_kendall and zeit.phenology also leave out the raster's NoData value and, for integer data without one, 0 (how Earth Engine exports masked pixels). Set nodata= to another value, or nodata=None to treat only NaN as missing.
  • CCDC uses its own QA codes (Fmask convention: 0 clear, 1 water, 2 shadow, 3 snow, 4 cloud, 255 fill). See CCDC.

docs.title: Ways to call an algorithm
docs.text:
The change-detection, trend and phenology algorithms each have a single entry point for every form of data. zeit.landtrendr, zeit.ccdc, zeit.bfast_monitor, zeit.bfast_lite, zeit.bfast, zeit.mann_kendall and zeit.phenology read what they are given and return the same xarray.Dataset (of vertices, segments or metrics), georeferenced when the input is:

flowchart LR
    A["One pixel's series"] --> L["<code>zeit.landtrendr(data)</code><br/><code>zeit.ccdc(data)</code><br/><code>zeit.bfast_monitor(data, ...)</code><br/>…"]
    B["NumPy array or cube in memory"] --> L
    C["GeoTIFF bigger than RAM<br/>(read lazily, block by block)"] --> L
    D["Xarray / Dask cube"] --> L
    L --> E["xarray.Dataset"]
Data Use it when Example One pixel Exploring, plotting, testing parameters on a few series zeit.landtrendr(values, years=years), zeit.ccdc(df), zeit.mann_kendall(values) Array or cube The data fits in memory zeit.landtrendr(cube), zeit.ccdc(cube, qa="fmask"), zeit.phenology(cube) Raster file A GeoTIFF too big for memory. It is read and computed in blocks. zeit.landtrendr("stack.tif", chunks="auto"), zeit.bfast_monitor("ndvi_16d.tif", "2022-01-01", chunks="auto") Dask cube Lazy cubes (STAC, Zarr), clusters, cloud storage zeit.landtrendr(cube), cube.zeit.ccdc(), cube.zeit.bfast_lite() CLI Scripts, cron jobs and HPC schedulers, no Python needed zeit landtrendr ..., zeit ccdc ..., zeit bfast-monitor ..., zeit mann-kendall ...

All run the same compiled (Rust) code; only the way the data is read and the result is computed changes. A dask cube gives a lazy result, computed when you call .compute() or write it with save_raster; in-memory data gives an in-memory result.

Each function also has an accessor form, available on every xarray object once you import zeit: cube.zeit.landtrendr(), cube.zeit.bfast_monitor("2022-01-01"), … See the Xarray accessor reference for the full list of methods.

docs.title: Parallelism
docs.text:
• n_jobs controls the threads of the compiled core. The default -1 uses all cores but one, so your machine stays responsive; in a job of a cluster (Slurm, PBS, LSF), every core the job was given. n_jobs=1 runs single-threaded, which is handy for debugging. ZEIT_NUM_THREADS sets the count for every call, and zeit doctor shows what was found (details).
  • Dask splits a cube into spatial chunks and processes them in parallel, on one machine or a cluster. Always keep the time axis in a single chunk (chunks={"time": -1, "y": 512, "x": 512}), because each pixel needs its whole history.
  • With Dask, leave n_jobs at -1: the blocks running at once share the core's threads instead of multiplying them, and in a dask.distributed worker -1 is the worker's threads.
  • The pre-built wheels are multi-threaded on every system, macOS included.

More in Parallel & Cloud Processing.

docs.title: Faithful ports, validated
docs.text: Each algorithm is a port of a specific reference implementation (the original IDL LandTrendr, the MATLAB CCDC, R's bfast and so on; phenology, the Bayesian smoothing of probabilities and the QA weights are written from papers and product documentation instead). Parameters keep their original names and defaults where possible, so published parameter choices carry over. The Benchmarks section documents how each port was compared with its reference, and where it differs on purpose.

docs.title: Contributing to Zeit
docs.text: We welcome contributions from the community. Whether you are fixing bugs, improving documentation, or adding new features, your help is appreciated.

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text: To start contributing to the Zeit codebase, you will need to set up a local development environment.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.9+
  • A Rust toolchain (stable, from rustup) for the compiled core.

docs.title: Setup Instructions
docs.text:
1. Fork and Clone: Fork the repository on GitHub and clone your fork locally. 

    git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/zeit-cdts.git
cd zeit-cdts

  2. Install in Editable Mode with Dev Dependencies: Install the package so that changes to the Python code are immediately reflected without needing to reinstall. 

    pip install -e .[dev]
    Note: changes to the Rust code (rust/) need a rebuild of the compiled core: python setup.py build_rust --inplace --release (or pip install -e . again).

The compiled core is two Rust crates in rust/: zeit-core holds the algorithms, zeit-py their Python bindings (PyO3), built as zeit._core.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
We use pytest for running our test suite. Ensure that all tests pass before submitting a pull request.

To run the tests with coverage reporting, execute:

pytest --cov=zeit tests/

The Rust core has unit tests of its own, and is checked with clippy and rustfmt:

cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p zeit-core --release
cargo clippy --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --release --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --all --check

docs.title: Building the docs locally
docs.text:
Documentation lives in docs/ and is built with Material for MkDocs:

pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve        # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build        # link and anchor problems are reported as warnings

docs.title: API signatures
docs.text:
Every entry in docs/api/*.md starts with a marker such as <!-- sig: zeit.metrics.extract_events -->. The signature block under it is generated from the code, and the parameter table is checked against it:

python docs/scripts/sync_api.py           # regenerate signature blocks
python docs/scripts/sync_api.py --check   # report undocumented or unknown parameters, wrong defaults

Run it whenever you add, rename or change a parameter.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
The figures in docs/assets/figures/ are produced by running Zeit itself:

python docs/scripts/make_figures.py              # all figures
python docs/scripts/make_figures.py ccdc_fit     # just one

Synthetic figures need only Zeit. The real-data figures (LandTrendr, Mann-Kendall, SNIC, SOM) need the Rondônia annual NDVI stack (Landsat NDVI composites for 1985–2024, exported from LT-GEE on Google Earth Engine); set ZEIT_DOCS_RONDONIA to its path. Set ZEIT_DOCS_FONT_DIR to a folder with the Inter font files to match the site's typeface.

docs.title: Writing style
docs.text:
• Start each tutorial with a one-sentence lead, the "at a glance" box and a real result figure.
  • Explain what the method is for before how it works, and how it works before the code.
  • Keep code examples runnable against the current API; prefer real outputs to invented ones.
  • Put validation details and implementation notes in a collapsible ??? info block, and link to Benchmarks for the full comparison.

docs.title: Pull Request Process
docs.text:
1. Create a new branch for your feature or bug fix.
  2. Ensure your code follows professional Python standards.
  3. Add tests for any new functionality in the tests/ directory.
  4. Update documentation if necessary.
  5. Submit a pull request on GitHub, clearly describing the changes and referencing any related issues.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: Ready-made container images with Zeit, GDAL, PyTorch and JupyterLab. Use them to share an identical environment across a team, or to run Zeit workers on a cluster.

docs.title: Published images
docs.text:
Each zeit version is published on the GitHub Container Registry, built from the two Dockerfiles below, with zeit.ai and JupyterLab:

docker pull ghcr.io/sacridini/zeit-cdts:2.3.0        # CPU, amd64 and arm64 (also :latest)
docker pull ghcr.io/sacridini/zeit-cdts:2.3.0-gpu    # CUDA, amd64 (also :latest-gpu)

On a cluster, Apptainer runs them without root: apptainer pull zeit.sif docker://ghcr.io/sacridini/zeit-cdts:2.3.0, then apptainer exec zeit.sif zeit doctor (--nv for the GPU image). See Zeit on a Cluster.

docs.title: Official Docker Images
docs.text:
We provide two Dockerfiles, built the same way but on different base images:

  • Dockerfile — based on the official PyTorch image with CUDA support (pytorch/pytorch:2.1.2-cuda12.1-cudnn8-devel), for GPU hosts.
  • Dockerfile.cpu — based on the slim, multi-arch python:3.11-slim image with a CPU-only PyTorch wheel, for machines without an NVIDIA GPU. Because it has no CUDA dependency, this one builds and runs natively on Apple Silicon (arm64) Macs, with no emulation.

Both images include: * A Rust toolchain to build Zeit's compiled core, and GDAL. * Python dependencies and the Zeit package installed in editable mode. * JupyterLab for interactive data science.

docs.title: Building and Running
docs.text: To build the Rust core, install PyTorch, and launch a JupyterLab environment, you can use one of the two provided Compose files, depending on whether your host has an NVIDIA GPU.

docs.title: GPU hosts (NVIDIA + Linux/Windows)
docs.text:
docker-compose.yml reserves an NVIDIA GPU for the container (deploy.resources.reservations.devices), so it requires the NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed on the host in addition to Docker itself.

  1. Ensure you have Docker, Docker Compose, and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed on your system.
  2. Navigate to the root directory of the Zeit repository.
  3. Run the following command:
docker-compose up --build

docs.title: CPU-only hosts (including macOS)
docs.text:
Warning

The default docker-compose.yml will fail to start on any machine without an NVIDIA GPU — this includes every Mac, since Docker Desktop on macOS has no GPU passthrough. Use docker-compose.cpu.yml instead, which builds Dockerfile.cpu and drops the GPU reservation entirely.

docker-compose -f docker-compose.cpu.yml up --build

This builds a separate, CUDA-free image (Dockerfile.cpu) and runs it entirely on CPU. On Apple Silicon Macs it builds as a native arm64 image — no amd64 emulation, unlike running the default Dockerfile would require. torch.cuda.is_available() is False inside this container, since it has no GPU acceleration at all; it does not have access to the host's Metal/MPS GPU either, since Docker containers can't pass that through. For MPS acceleration on a Mac, use the native pip install path from the installation guide instead of Docker.

Multi-threaded on every Mac chip

Zeit's compiled core starts its own threads, with no OpenMP runtime, so it runs on all the container's cores whatever the host chip, as it does in a native macOS install.

docs.title: Accessing the container
docs.text:
Either command builds the image and starts a Jupyter server. By default, the server runs on port 8888. You can access it by navigating to http://localhost:8888 in your web browser.

The command used by the container is configured to allow root access and disables the automatic browser launch, making it ideal for headless server environments.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: One command installs Zeit with pre-compiled wheels for Windows, macOS and Linux. Build from source only if you want to change the Rust core.

docs.title: Standard Installation
docs.text:
The easiest way to install Zeit is via Python's package manager, pip. We provide pre-compiled binaries (wheels) for Windows, macOS, and Linux (x86_64 and aarch64, glibc 2.28 or newer), supporting Python 3.9 and newer. Because we distribute pre-compiled binaries, you do not need a compiler (Rust or any other) installed on your machine for the standard installation. The wheels run the compiled core on all your cores on every system, macOS included.

pip install zeit-cdts

This command automatically installs all required Python dependencies, including xarray, dask, scikit-learn, rasterio, and pystac-client. The deep learning of zeit.ai needs PyTorch, a large download, which comes with the ai extra:

pip install "zeit-cdts[ai]"

Since 2.3, PyTorch is optional

Up to zeit 2.2, pip install zeit-cdts installed PyTorch too. Code that uses zeit.ai now needs pip install "zeit-cdts[ai]" (or PyTorch installed by other means, such as the build for a GPU's CUDA from pytorch.org); without it, import zeit.ai says so. Everything else needs no PyTorch.

macOS: Apple Silicon vs. Intel

Prebuilt wheels are published for whichever architecture GitHub Actions' macos-latest runner uses at build time, which is Apple Silicon (arm64) as of this writing. If pip install zeit-cdts on an Intel Mac reports no matching distribution, pip will fall back to building from source automatically — see Installing from Source below for the Rust toolchain that requires.

docs.title: Verifying the Installation
docs.text:
Once installed, confirm the package and its CLI are working:

python -c "from importlib.metadata import version; print(version('zeit-cdts'))"
zeit --help

docs.title: Optional Dependencies
docs.text:
To look at maps and time series with zeit.plot (matplotlib for figures, anywidget for the interactive viewer in notebooks):

pip install zeit-cdts[plot]
pip install pywebview   # optional: show the viewer in a native window outside notebooks

The embeddings of TESSERA and AlphaEarth need nothing extra: geotessera, which reads TESSERA, is installed with zeit on Python 3.12 or newer (it does not support older ones).

For development and running tests, you can install the optional development dependencies:

pip install zeit-cdts[dev]

docs.title: Caches
docs.text:
What zeit downloads is kept in one folder, with a subfolder per kind: weights (the pretrained weights of zeit.ai), embeddings (TESSERA and AlphaEarth downloads), tiles (the tiles a tile run built or received), map-tiles (the basemaps of zeit.plot), l1c (the Sentinel-2 .SAFE directories of zeit.download_l1c) and dem (the DEM mosaics of zeit.download_dem). The folder is, from the first that is set:

Folder ZEIT_CACHE_DIR as given XDG_CACHE_HOME $XDG_CACHE_HOME/zeit Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\zeit elsewhere ~/.cache/zeit

On a cluster, point ZEIT_CACHE_DIR at the scratch space (export ZEIT_CACHE_DIR=/scratch/$USER/zeit-cache): the home directory's quota is small, and some compute nodes see it read-only. zeit doctor shows each folder and whether it can be written. A cache that zeit 2.2 or older filled in ~/.cache/zeit keeps being used there until ZEIT_CACHE_DIR is set.

On a computer without internet access (the compute nodes of many clusters), fill the cache beforehand where there is access, with zeit fetch: zeit fetch weights, zeit fetch tiles urls.txt, zeit fetch embeddings .... Without it, zeit says what it could not reach and which zeit fetch downloads it. The weights can also come from a folder of copies, named by ZEIT_WEIGHTS.

docs.title: Installing from Source
docs.text: If you need to modify the Rust core, use the latest unreleased features, or build the package on an unsupported architecture, you will need to install Zeit from the source.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.9+
  • A Rust toolchain (stable), installed with rustup: 
    curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh   # Linux and macOS
    On Windows, run rustup-init.exe from rustup.rs; it also offers to install the Visual Studio build tools Rust links with.
  • macOS only: the Xcode Command Line Tools, for the linker. Install them first if you haven't already: 
    xcode-select --install

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository from GitHub: 

    git clone https://github.com/sacridini/zeit-cdts.git
cd zeit-cdts

  2. Install the package in editable mode: 

    pip install -e .

This builds the compiled core (zeit._core) from the Rust crates in rust/ (zeit-core, the algorithms; zeit-py, their Python bindings) with setuptools-rust, in release mode. After changing the Rust code, rebuild it in place with:

python setup.py build_rust --inplace --release

The core is multi-threaded on every system, macOS included, with no extra library: it starts its own threads, so there is no OpenMP to install or enable.

docs.title: GPU Acceleration for zeit.ai
docs.text:
The deep learning models in zeit.ai (UTAE, LTAE/LightTAE, TempCNN, Presto, Siamese Change Detector, Prithvi) are plain PyTorch nn.Modules and run on whatever device you move them to — none of them hard-code CUDA.

  • NVIDIA GPUs (Linux/Windows): pip install "zeit-cdts[ai]" installs PyTorch's build with CUDA support on Linux; on Windows, and for a given CUDA version, install torch first as pytorch.org says. Use torch.device("cuda") as usual.
  • Apple Silicon (any M-series chip): PyTorch's Metal (mps) backend gives you native GPU acceleration on macOS — no CUDA or extra install needed, since it ships in the same torch package: 
    device = torch.device("mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu")
model = model.to(device)
    Every tutorial in AI & Deep Learning picks "cuda" vs. "cpu" in its example — swap in the snippet above on macOS to use the GPU.
  • CPU fallback: works everywhere, just slower.

On a cluster, see Zeit on a Cluster (--gres=gpu:1, and the GPU container image with Apptainer's --nv).

Docker and MPS

The Docker image is built on a CUDA base image and has no access to Apple's Metal APIs. To use mps acceleration on macOS, install Zeit natively with pip rather than through Docker.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
In five minutes you will build a small image time series, run LandTrendr on every pixel, and get a map of when the vegetation was lost. Nothing is downloaded: the data is generated in the script, so you can see exactly what goes in and what comes out.

You needPython 3.9+ and pip install zeit-cdts TimeAbout 5 minutes You will learnThe input shape, one algorithm call, and how to read its output

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install zeit-cdts

Wheels are published for Windows, macOS and Linux, so no compiler is needed. See Installation for GPU support, Docker, and building from source.

docs.title: 2. Make a tiny image time series
docs.text:
Real analyses start from a stack of images: one layer per date. Here we fake one, a 120 × 120 pixel patch of forest observed once a year from 1990 to 2024, with two clearings added:

  • a field cleared in 2003 that stays as pasture;
  • a patch cleared in 2016 that then starts to regrow.

Values are NDVI (a vegetation index: about 0.85 for dense forest, 0.3 for pasture) multiplied by 10,000, which is how most satellite products store it.

import numpy as np
import zeit

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
years = np.arange(1990, 2025)                      # 35 annual observations
n_years, rows, cols = len(years), 120, 120

# A forest (NDVI ~0.85) with noise...
stack = 0.85 + rng.normal(0, 0.03, (n_years, rows, cols))
# ...a field cleared in 2003 that stays as pasture,
stack[years >= 2003, 20:60, 15:70] = 0.35 + rng.normal(0, 0.04, (np.sum(years >= 2003), 40, 55))
# ...and a patch cleared in 2016 that starts to regrow.
regrow = np.clip((years - 2016) * 0.06, 0, 0.4)[:, None, None]
after = (years >= 2016)[:, None, None]
stack[:, 70:105, 50:110] = np.where(after, 0.30 + regrow, stack[:, 70:105, 50:110])
stack = (stack * 10000).astype(np.float32)         # NDVI x 10000, like most products

print(stack.shape)   # (35, 120, 120) -> (time, rows, cols)

The one shape to remember

Almost every Zeit function takes an array shaped (time, rows, cols): the first axis is the date, the last two are the image. zeit.load_raster reads a GeoTIFF with one band per year into this shape, with the years in a time coordinate and the georeferencing in .rio.

docs.title: 3. Run LandTrendr on every pixel
docs.text:
LandTrendr simplifies each pixel's history into a few straight segments. The breakpoints between segments, called vertices, mark the moments when something changed.

lt = zeit.landtrendr(stack, years=years)

That one call fits all 14,400 pixels in parallel, in Rust. A numpy array has no dates, so years gives the year of each layer. By default (direction="loss") LandTrendr looks for drops in the index, i.e. vegetation loss on NDVI. Use direction="gain" for indices where disturbance makes the value go up.

lt is an xarray.Dataset: the year and fitted value of each vertex (vertex_year, vertex_value), their number (n_vertices) and how well each fit follows its data (rmse).

docs.title: 4. Turn the fit into a map of events
docs.text:
The vertices are compact but not yet a map. extract_events scans each pixel's segments and keeps the largest loss:

loss = zeit.extract_events(lt, min_magnitude=1500)

years_found, n_pixels = np.unique(loss["yod"], return_counts=True)
print({int(y): int(n) for y, n in zip(years_found, n_pixels)})
# {0: 10095, 1990: 2, 1997: 1, 1998: 1, 2001: 1, 2002: 2199, 2015: 2100, 2022: 1}

loss is an xarray.Dataset of 2-D maps, all shaped (rows, cols):

Variable Meaning yod Year of the vertex where the loss begins, i.e. the last year before the drop. 0 means no event. magnitude How much the index fell (here in NDVI × 10,000). duration How many years the fall took. 1 means abrupt. pre_val, post_val Index value before and after the event. rate magnitude / duration. dsnr magnitude divided by the fit's RMSE: a signal-to-noise ratio.

So the output reads: about 2,200 pixels lost vegetation right after 2002, and about 2,100 right after 2015. Those are the two clearings (2003 and 2016). Only six pixels out of 14,400 were flagged by noise.

yod is the year before the change

LandTrendr places a vertex on the last stable year and the next vertex on the first disturbed one. yod reports the first of the two, so the first year in which the loss is visible is loss["yod"] + 1. Keep this in mind when comparing with LT-GEE, whose change maps report the start vertex year plus one.

docs.title: 5. Look at the result
docs.text:
Left: the last image. Middle: the yod map, one color per event year. Right: one pixel from each clearing, with LandTrendr's fitted segments. The 2016 clearing's regrowth shows up as a rising segment after the drop. This figure is produced by the exact code on this page.

To plot it yourself:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

yod = (loss["yod"] + 1).where(loss["yod"] > 0)   # first year of loss
plt.imshow(yod, cmap="plasma")
plt.colorbar(label="First year of loss")
plt.show()

docs.title: Explore it interactively
docs.text:
zeit.plot shows any cube or result (install it with pip install zeit-cdts[plot]). In a notebook it is an interactive viewer: space plays the years, the arrow keys step through them, and clicking a pixel shows its series with LandTrendr's fit. In a script, the same viewer opens in its own window.

cube = zeit.load_raster(stack, start_year=1990)   # the same array, with its years
zeit.plot(cube, fit=lt)                           # page through the years, click a pixel
zeit.plot(loss)                                   # the event maps, with a variable selector

See Plotting and Exploring Results for basemaps, static figures and more.

docs.title: 6. Use your own data
docs.text:
Swap the synthetic stack for a real one. Any GeoTIFF with one band per year works:

ndvi = zeit.load_raster("my_ndvi_1990_2024.tif", start_year=1990)   # (time, y, x)

lt = zeit.landtrendr(ndvi)                       # years from the time coordinate
loss = zeit.extract_events(lt, min_magnitude=1500)

zeit.save_raster(loss, "lt_results")             # one GeoTIFF per map: yod.tif, magnitude.tif, ...

start_year is only needed when the file does not name its bands by year: a stack whose bands are described as yr1990, yr1991, … (like the LT-GEE export in the LandTrendr tutorial) is read without it. The cube carries its georeferencing, so the results do too: save_raster writes georeferenced, compressed GeoTIFFs that open directly in QGIS or ArcGIS.

Don't have a stack yet? Build one from a cloud catalog with build_time_series, or from Google Earth Engine with download_gee_timeseries.

docs.text:

    Shapes, dates, scale factors and the different entry points (pixel, array, file, xarray, CLI).

    Core concepts

  • Do it on real Landsat data

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
Step-by-step tutorials for every part of Zeit. Each one starts with what the method is for and a real output, explains how it works in plain language, then walks through the code and how to read the results.

New here?

Do the Quickstart first, and skim Core Concepts for the conventions (array shapes, dates, scale factors) that every tutorial uses. Unsure which method fits your question? See Choosing an Algorithm.

docs.title: Change detection
docs.text:
Find where and when the land surface changed.

Annual dataLandTrendrDisturbance and recovery history from one image per year. Maps of year, magnitude and duration.

After a disturbanceRecovery metricsYears to recovery, R80P, RRI and the year-on-year recovery of every disturbed pixel.

Dense dataCCDCHarmonic models of every clear observation. Dates changes and describes the land before and after.

Dense data · near real timeS-CCDCCDC carried forward by a Kalman filter: the breaks, and the changes still in progress at the last image.

Regular seriesBFASTSeparate breaks in the trend from breaks in the seasonal cycle.

Near real timeBFAST MonitorTest new observations against a stable history. The basis of alert systems.

Irregular seriesEWMACDControl charts on every observation: disturbances, gains and recoveries, cloudy dates welcome.

Regular seriesBFAST LiteThe optimal number of breaks in a whole series, in a single fast pass.

Annual or regular seriesBEASTTrend and season averaged over thousands of models: how probable each changepoint is, and how many there were.

docs.title: Time-series analysis
docs.text:
Trends, seasons, patterns and objects.

TrendsMann-KendallSignificant greening and browning, with a robust slope per pixel.

Regional trendsPARTSIs the region, or each land-cover class, really trending? A test that accounts for correlated pixels.

Space-time patternsEmerging hot spotsGetis-Ord Gi* at every date and its trend: new, intensifying, persistent, sporadic hot and cold spots.

SeasonsPhenologyStart, peak and end of every growing season, and 16 more metrics.

Spectral mixturesSpectral unmixingThe fraction of each material in every pixel and date, with endmembers of your own.

ClassificationTWDTWMatch each pixel to reference patterns, tolerating shifts in timing.

ClusteringSOMFind the typical trajectories in a landscape without labels.

SegmentationSNICGroup pixels with similar histories into fields and patches.

docs.title: Deep learning
docs.text:
PyTorch models for classification and change detection, checked against their reference implementations (TempCNN and LightTAE are written from the authors' papers and code).

Pixel classificationTempCNNA fast 1-D convolutional baseline for pixel time series.

After classifyingPost-processing & AoABayesian smoothing, a minimum mapping unit, and the area where the model can be applied.

Model Task Tutorial Overview Available models, data loading, loss functions Deep Learning TempCNN Pixel time-series classification (convolutional) TempCNN LTAE / LightTAE Pixel time-series classification (attention) LTAE & LightTAE Presto Pretrained pixel time-series model: few samples, gaps, embeddings of a cube Presto U-TAE Segmentation of whole image patches over time UTAE Siamese Change detection between two dates Siamese Change Detector Prithvi Fine-tuning the Prithvi-EO-2.0 foundation model Prithvi Any classifier Smoothing the class map, a minimum mapping unit, the area of applicability Post-processing & AoA

docs.title: Getting and preparing data
docs.text:
Cloud catalogsSTAC Data CubesLazy cubes from Earth Search, Planetary Computer or Brazil Data Cube; compositing and smoothing.

Cloud maskingTmaskCatch the clouds and shadows that single-image masks miss.

  • Sentinel-2 Level 1C to Surface Reflectance: zeit.level2 on a scene on disk or downloaded by name: the atmospheric correction with Zeit's own Fmask, the products (boa, qai, dst, ...), how to read the QAI flags, and how it compares with FORCE and ESA's L2A.
  • Preparing Images: co-registration, NBAR, the spectral adjustment of Landsat and MODIS to Sentinel-2, the Tasseled Cap, the 20 m bands at 10 m, ImproPhe and pansharpening, each with when to use it.
  • FORCE's Time Series Analysis Chain: interpolation, spectral-temporal metrics (temporal_metrics), land surface phenology (polar_metrics), trends and change.
  • Plotting & Exploring Results: zeit.plot for maps, dense time series and pixel fits, in a notebook or a window.
  • Google Earth Engine: harmonised Landsat composites prepared on Google's servers.
  • Embeddings (TESSERA, AlphaEarth): the yearly embeddings of foundation models as a cube: classify from few samples, find similar places, follow change year to year.
  • Parallel & Cloud Processing: from one core to a cluster, with Dask and Zarr.
  • Zeit on a Cluster (HPC, Slurm): installing on a cluster, a job array over the tiles with zeit slurm, time limits, nodes without internet access.

docs.title: Accuracy & Area
docs.text:
A change map says that 18,000 ha were deforested. How sure is that number? Counting the pixels of a map gives a biased area: every map has omission and commission errors, and they rarely cancel. The good practice is to label a random sample of the map, estimate the error matrix in proportions of area, and correct the area with it. That gives an unbiased area with a confidence interval, which is what reports such as REDD+ or a paper's results need.

AnswersHow accurate is the map? How much area really changed, ± how much? InputAny map of classes or of events, and reference labels at sample points OutputOverall, user's and producer's accuracies and error-adjusted areas, with confidence intervals ReferenceOlofsson et al. (2014), Remote Sensing of Environment 148; Stehman (2014), IJRS 35

docs.title: Why counting pixels is not enough
docs.text:
A map's area of a class is the number of its pixels times their size. It counts every false alarm as change and misses every change the map did not find. Both errors happen in every map, and they do not cancel: a change map usually misses more change (forest cleared slowly, small clearings, a cloudy year) than it invents, so its mapped area of change is too small.

The fix is to measure the errors on a sample and correct the area for them. In the numerical example of Olofsson et al. (2014), which zeit reproduces to the hectare, the map shows 18,000 ha of deforestation; corrected with a sample of 640 points, the estimate is 21,158 ha, between 15,000 and 27,316 ha with 95% confidence. The map missed a quarter of the deforestation, and the stable classes absorbed it.

Mapped area (orange diamond) and error-adjusted estimate with its 95% confidence interval (blue), in thousand hectares, for the example of Olofsson et al. (2014). The mapped areas of the two rare classes fall well inside the intervals, but the estimates move them by 18% and 13%: what the map calls change is not what is on the ground.

The interval is as important as the estimate. A ± 6,158 ha interval on 21,158 ha says the sample was too small to pin the area of deforestation down to better than ± 30%; with more points in the right strata, the interval shrinks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Stratify by the map

Each class of the map is a stratum. Rare classes, change above all, get a sample of their own.

sampling_design

Draw the sample

Points at random inside each stratum, as many as the design asks for.

stratified_sample

Label the points

Decide what is really there, from better imagery or the field: the reference.

interpret

Estimate

Weigh each point by its stratum's area: accuracies and areas, with intervals.

accuracy

The same steps work for any map, from zeit or not, and for maps of events: these are stratified as "no change" and "change" (or, with bins, as periods of the year of change).

Steps 1 and 2 on real data. Left: forest loss since 2015 found by LandTrendr over 44,000 ha of Rondônia (orange), and a stratified sample for a standard error of 0.015. Right: change covers 4% of the map, so a sample proportional to area would put 9 of its points there, too few to measure the user's accuracy of change. min_per_stratum=50 (the default) takes 41 points from "no change" and gives them to "change".

docs.title: 1. Make the map of events
docs.text:
import zeit

ndvi = zeit.load_raster("LT_Stack_NDVI_Rondonia.tif")
loss = zeit.extract_events(zeit.landtrendr(ndvi), min_magnitude=1500)

Any change algorithm works the same way: zeit.extract_events gives the same maps for CCDC, BFAST and the others, and zeit.agreement combines them. A map of classes works too: the label of zeit.classify, any land-cover GeoTIFF with its class codes (names come from the raster's flag_meanings, when it has them).

Assess the map you will report. If you clean it before publishing (a minimum mapping unit, a mask), clean it first and sample the cleaned map, since the sample measures the errors of the map it was drawn from.

docs.title: 2. Size and draw the sample
docs.text:
design = zeit.sampling_design(loss, expected_ua={"change": 0.7, "no change": 0.95}, std_error=0.01)
print(design)        # per stratum: name, pixels, area (ha), weight, expected_ua, n

points = zeit.stratified_sample(loss, design=design)
points.to_file("loss_points.gpkg")

How many points. expected_ua is your guess of each stratum's user's accuracy and std_error the standard error you want for the overall accuracy. Together they set the total sample size (Olofsson et al. 2014, eq. 13):

\[ n = \frac{\left(\sum_i W_i S_i\right)^2}{S(\hat O)^2 + \frac{1}{N}\sum_i W_i S_i^2}, \qquad S_i = \sqrt{U_i\,(1 - U_i)} \]

where \(W_i\) is the share of the map's area in stratum \(i\), \(U_i\) its expected user's accuracy, \(S(\hat O)\) the target standard error and \(N\) the number of pixels. Two things follow. Classes expected to be mapped well need fewer points than hard ones, so it pays to guess expected_ua honestly rather than leave the default 0.75. And the size grows with the inverse square of the standard error: halving it takes about four times the points.

Sample size for the map of Olofsson et al. (2014). With the expected user's accuracies of the paper, a standard error of 0.01 takes 641 points (the paper's number); assuming 0.75 everywhere would ask for almost three times as many.

How to spread them. alloc decides how the points go to the strata:

alloc Points per stratum When "proportional" (default) In proportion to its area Good overall accuracy and area of the large classes "equal" The same number in every stratum Good user's accuracy of every class, rare ones included "neyman" In proportion to area × expected standard deviation The smallest variance of the overall accuracy a dict As given, e.g. {"change": 100, "no change": 300} Your own compromise

Whatever the allocation, min_per_stratum (50 by default; Olofsson et al. recommend 50 to 100) raises the small strata to that many points, taken from the large ones, and the total stays the same. This is what makes the user's accuracy of rare change measurable at all.

Strata by period. A map of the year of change can be stratified by period, so that the estimates come out per period too:

design = zeit.sampling_design(loss, bins=[1985, 2000, 2010, 2025], expected_ua=0.7)

Each [a, b) interval of years is a stratum, plus "no change".

stratified_sample draws the points at random inside each stratum (seed= makes the draw repeatable, in memory or lazy, whatever the chunks) and returns them at the centres of their pixels, with their stratum, stratum_name, row and col. Keep those columns: zeit.accuracy uses stratum to weigh the points.

docs.title: 3. Label the points
docs.text:
s = zeit.interpret(landsat, points, rgb=["swir1", "nir", "red"], series="nbr",
                   map=loss, fit=zeit.landtrendr(ndvi), save="loss_reference.gpkg")

zeit.interpret goes through the points one by one: the map is centred on each, a strip of chips shows the place every year, and the chart its series. Press 1 or 2 for the class, click the chart (or press d on the image where the change appears) to date it, and Enter to save and move on. Each label is written to loss_reference.gpkg at once: close the window and run the same line tomorrow to go on.

By default it is blind: what the map and LandTrendr say at a point shows only once you have labelled it. A reference swayed by the map would only measure how much you agree with it. When every point has a label, the Review tab shows the accuracies, and a click on a cell of the error matrix (say, map "change", reference "no change") lists those points to look at again.

QGIS, Collect Earth or field visits work as well: what zeit.accuracy needs is a ref column (and ref_date for dates) in the points.

Write the labelling rules down before you start

The reference is only as good as its definitions. Decide, and write in your methods, what counts as change (a clearing? a degraded canopy? a crop harvest?), the period it must happen in, how much of the pixel must change, and which imagery is the reference (Landsat chips, Sentinel-2, very-high-resolution images, field visits). Points you cannot decide can stay without a label: zeit.accuracy leaves them out and says how many, but many of them in one stratum bias its estimate.

docs.title: 4. Estimate accuracy and area
docs.text:
acc = s.accuracy(date_tolerance=1)          # or zeit.accuracy(loss, "loss_reference.gpkg", date_tolerance=1)
print(acc)

The summary looks like this one, of the numerical example in Olofsson et al. (2014): a map of 10 million 30 m pixels in four classes and 640 labelled points:

Accuracy of the map, from 640 reference points:
  overall: 0.947 ± 0.018 (95% CI)

                         user's     producer's mapped (ha)    estimated (ha)
class
deforestation     0.880 ± 0.074  0.749 ± 0.213      18,000    21,158 ± 6,158
forest_gain       0.733 ± 0.101  0.847 ± 0.254      13,500    11,686 ± 3,756
stable_forest     0.927 ± 0.040  0.935 ± 0.034     288,000  285,770 ± 15,510
stable_nonforest  0.963 ± 0.021  0.962 ± 0.018     580,500  581,386 ± 16,281

With date_tolerance, a last line gives the share of the change points whose dates agree.

docs.title: Reading the error matrix
docs.text:
The counts of the sample are not the error matrix of the map. The strata were sampled at different rates (in the example, 75 points for 200,000 deforestation pixels, 325 for 6.45 million stable non-forest pixels), so each point stands for a different area. The estimators weigh each count by its stratum's share of the map, \(W_i\), divided by the stratum's sample size \(n_{i\cdot}\):

\[ \hat p_{ij} = W_i\,\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i\cdot}} \]

\(\hat p_{ij}\) is the estimated share of the whole map that the map calls \(i\) and is really \(j\). Everything else comes from that matrix:

Estimator Says Overall accuracy \(\hat O = \sum_j \hat p_{jj}\) Share of the area mapped correctly User's accuracy of \(i\) \(\hat U_i = \hat p_{ii} / \hat p_{i\cdot}\) Of the area mapped as \(i\), the share that is \(i\). Low: false alarms (commission) Producer's accuracy of \(j\) \(\hat P_j = \hat p_{jj} / \hat p_{\cdot j}\) Of the area that is \(j\), the share mapped as \(j\). Low: missed change (omission) Area of \(j\) \(\hat A_j = A \cdot \hat p_{\cdot j}\) The error-adjusted area: the column total times the map's area

Left: the 640 points as counted. Right: the same matrix in estimated shares of the map's area. The 2 deforestation points the map put in stable non-forest weigh 0.40% of the area, because that stratum is huge; with the 1 in stable forest, they are why the producer's accuracy of deforestation (0.75) is much lower than its user's accuracy (0.88).

The figure shows the main lesson of area estimation: a few omission errors in a large stratum outweigh many points in a small one. The 2 deforestation points among the 325 of stable non-forest (0.6% of that stratum) stand for 0.40% of the whole map, a sixth of all the deforestation, and they make up two thirds of the variance of its area. To narrow the interval of the area of change, sample the strata where change hides, not only the change stratum. Olofsson et al. suggest a "buffer" stratum: a ring of pixels around the mapped change, where missed change is most likely. Add it as a class of the map you stratify (a dilation of the change map does it) and give it its own points.

The standard errors follow Stehman (2014): for an estimated proportion,

\[ \widehat{SE}(\hat p_{\cdot j}) = \sqrt{\sum_i W_i^2\,\frac{\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i\cdot}}\left(1-\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i\cdot}}\right)}{n_{i\cdot}-1}} \]

and the ratio estimators (user's and producer's accuracies) have theirs. Intervals are \(\pm z\,\widehat{SE}\), \(z = 1.96\) for confidence=0.95.

docs.title: What accuracy returns
docs.text:
print(acc) is the summary; every number is also a table:

Attribute Content acc.overall estimate, se, ci_low, ci_high of the overall accuracy acc.users, acc.producers The same four columns, one row per class acc.area mapped, estimate, se, ci (the half-width), ci_low, ci_high, in acc.area_unit (hectares) acc.confusion The error matrix in proportions of area, \(\hat p_{ij}\) (rows: map, columns: reference) acc.counts The error matrix of the sample, \(n_{ij}\) acc.date With date_tolerance: within (share of the change points whose dates agree), within_se, mean_difference (years) and n acc.to_dataframe() One row per class with all of the above, for a paper's table 
acc.area.loc["change", ["estimate", "ci_low", "ci_high"]]
acc.to_dataframe().to_csv("accuracy.csv")

docs.title: Assessing other maps with the same points
docs.text:
The reference describes the ground, not the map, so one set of labelled points assesses every map of the same area: LandTrendr, CCDC, the agreement of both. Pass the map the sample was drawn from as strata, so the points keep their weights:

ccdc_loss = zeit.extract_events(zeit.ccdc(cube), band="nir", event_type="loss")
acc_ccdc = zeit.accuracy(ccdc_loss, "loss_reference.gpkg", strata=loss)

This is the fair way to compare algorithms: the same points, labelled once, without knowing which map they would favour. The intervals of the second map are wider than if it had been sampled on its own strata, since its errors are not where the sample concentrated.

docs.title: Transitions between two dates
docs.text:
A map of classes at two dates says how much forest became pasture. Label each point with the class at each date (two columns, ref_from and ref_to), and zeit.transitions estimates the area of every transition, "Forest -> Pasture" as well as "Forest -> Forest", each with its interval:

tr = zeit.transitions("lc_2015.tif", "lc_2022.tif", points, strata="lc_2015.tif")
tr.area.loc["Forest -> Pasture", ["mapped", "estimate", "ci"]]

Changes are rare, so a sample stratified by one date's classes has few points in them, and their intervals are wide. Stratify by a map of change instead (the transitions themselves, or another product's alerts), and pass it as strata.

docs.title: When the strata are not the map: model-assisted estimators
docs.text:
The error-adjusted areas above use the sample alone (the direct estimator). The map is known everywhere, though, and the model-assisted estimators use it: estimator="difference" takes the mapped area and corrects it by the map's net error estimated from the sample; estimator="ratio" multiplies it by the estimated ratio of the reference's area to the map's. With the map's classes as strata the three agree; with other strata, and for rare classes or changes, the model-assisted intervals are narrower when the map is good:

tr = zeit.transitions("lc_2015.tif", "lc_2022.tif", points, strata="alerts.tif", estimator="difference")

On the fixture of the tests (190 points stratified by an older alert map), the 95% interval of the area cleared is ±17.6 ha by the direct estimator and ±3.4 ha by the difference estimator. The three are checked against R's survey package to 1e-10.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
What makes the estimates wrong

  • Points chosen by hand. The estimators need a probability sample. Points picked where change is obvious, or moved to a "cleaner" pixel, are not one. Points without a stratum column are weighed as a stratified sample of the map, and zeit.accuracy warns about it.
  • Labels that saw the map. A reference interpreted with the map in view agrees with it more than the ground does. Keep zeit.interpret blind.
  • The wrong strata. With a sample drawn on one map and assessed on another, pass the first as strata. Otherwise every point is weighed by the wrong area.
  • Empty strata. A stratum without labelled points is left out, with a warning, and the estimates then cover only the rest of the area.
  • Reporting the mapped area. It is a pixel count, not an estimate. Report the error-adjusted area and its interval.

docs.title: What to report
docs.text:
Following Olofsson et al. (2014), a paper or a report should give enough to repeat the estimate:

  1. The sampling design: strata, their areas, the sample size of each and how it was chosen (print(design)).
  2. The response design: the reference imagery, the labelling rules, who labelled and whether it was blind.
  3. The error matrix in proportions of area (acc.confusion), not only in counts.
  4. User's, producer's and overall accuracies with their confidence intervals.
  5. The error-adjusted area of each class with its confidence interval, next to the mapped area.

Validation checked against the reference implementations

zeit.accuracy reproduces the numerical example of Olofsson et al. (2014) (areas, accuracies and their intervals) and R's sits_accuracy to 1e-9. With a sample stratified by one map assessing another, its 95% intervals cover the true accuracy in about 95% of repeated samples.

docs.title: Deep Learning
docs.text:
When you have labelled examples, neural networks usually give the most accurate land-cover and change maps. zeit.ai provides PyTorch implementations of the architectures most used for satellite image time series, ported layer for layer from their reference code so that trained weights are interchangeable.

Install

zeit.ai needs PyTorch, which comes with the ai extra: pip install "zeit-cdts[ai]" (since zeit 2.3; for a GPU, see GPU Acceleration).

A typical result. A TempCNN trained for 30 epochs on noisy, cloud-contaminated NDVI series of four classes. Forest and pasture are separated perfectly; the remaining errors are between single and double cropping, whose second season is weak in many samples. See the TempCNN tutorial.

docs.title: Available models
docs.text:
Model Task Input Dedicated Tutorial Written from LTAE & LightTAE Per-pixel time series classification (Batch, Time, Bands) LTAE & LightTAE Garnot & Landrieu (2020) and the authors' code TempCNN Per-pixel time series classification (Batch, Bands, Time) TempCNN Pelletier et al. (2019) and the authors' code Presto Pretrained per-pixel model: classification from few samples, embeddings (Batch, Time, Bands), the cube's units Presto Official nasaharvest/presto encoder, same weights UTAE Spatio-temporal segmentation (whole-patch class map) (Batch, Time, Bands, H, W) UTAE Official VSainteuf/utae-paps reference (bit-for-bit exact) Siamese Change Detector Bi-temporal change detection (two dates) Two (Batch, Bands, H, W) images Siamese Change Detector FC-Siam-diff, same outputs as the authors' code with the same weights Prithvi Segmentation from the pretrained Prithvi-EO-2.0 foundation model (Batch, Bands, Time, H, W), the six HLS bands Prithvi Official prithvi_mae.py encoder, same weights

Choosing a model:

  • Have a long, well-sampled per-pixel time series and want the best accuracy? Try LightTAE first, and TempCNN as a faster/simpler baseline.
  • Few labelled samples, gappy series or several sensors (Sentinel-1 and -2)? Fine-tune the pretrained Presto.
  • Need a class map over a spatial patch, not just individual pixels? Use UTAE.
  • Have exactly two dates and want a change map between them? Use the Siamese Change Detector.
  • Have very few labelled windows of HLS-like data? Fine-tune the pretrained Prithvi foundation model.

docs.title: From a cube to a map
docs.text: The models take tensors; zeit.ai takes them from a cube and labelled samples to a georeferenced map in three calls, as train_classifier and classify do for a random forest.

docs.title: 1. Samples
docs.text:
import zeit
from zeit import ai

cube = zeit.load_raster("s2_2022.tif")          # (time, band, y, x), dates in the band names
samples = ai.samples(cube, "samples.gpkg", label="class")
samples                                          # SampleSet(2140 pixels: 1712 train, 428 val; 23 dates x 4 bands; ...)

The samples are points or polygons with a class column, in any CRS. For the pixel models (TempCNN, LightTAE, Presto) each sample is one pixel's series, (time, band), and a polygon gives every pixel it covers. For the patch models (UTAE, SiameseChangeDetector, Prithvi) pass patch= a size in pixels: each sample is the window around a point or a polygon (large polygons are tiled by windows), with every labelled pixel in it. Patch models learn best from polygons: a window around a point has a single labelled pixel.

Two things happen here that are easy to get wrong by hand:

  • Validation in spatial blocks. A fifth of the samples is kept for validation (split=0.2), but by whole blocks of 64 × 64 pixels (split_by="block", block_size=64). Neighbouring pixels are nearly the same, so a validation set of pixels drawn at random next to the training ones measures how well the model remembers, not how well it generalizes.
  • Normalization. Each band is scaled by its 2% and 98% quantiles in the training samples, as sits does, and the same scaling is applied when predicting. Missing values become 0 after it; fill gaps first (e.g. with zeit.smooth) if clouds are frequent.

docs.title: 2. Train
docs.text:
model = ai.train(ai.TempCNN, samples, epochs=50)
model.zeit_history_[-1]                          # {'epoch': 31, 'train_loss': ..., 'val_loss': ..., 'val_accuracy': 0.94}

train builds the model from its class with the samples' numbers of bands, dates and classes (other arguments of the model pass through, e.g. dropout_rate=0.3), trains it with Adam, stops when the validation loss has not improved for 10 epochs and keeps the best epoch. It runs on the GPU when there is one (device="auto"). loss="focal" helps with imbalanced classes.

docs.title: 3. Predict
docs.text:
classes = ai.predict(model, cube, probability=True)
classes.label.zeit.plot()                         # the class map, with its legend
classes.zeit.save("results/classes")              # label.tif, probability.tif
ai.save(model, "tempcnn_2022.pt")                 # with what predict checks

predict checks the bands (by name) and the dates against the training samples, normalizes the cube as they were and classifies every pixel. zeit.classify(cube, model) does the same. A lazy cube stays lazy and is classified block by block. Patch models slide windows of the training size over the image, overlapping by a quarter (overlap=), and average each pixel's probabilities over the windows, weighted down towards their edges, so the map has no seams.

TempCNN, LightTAE and the Siamese and ViT models are built for the number of dates they were trained on, so the cube to classify needs as many (the same composites of another year, for instance). UTAE takes the positions of the dates at each call and classifies any series.

Model samples(..., patch=) Dates when predicting TempCNN, LightTAE, Presto None (pixels) as many as in training UTAE a multiple of 8 (default U-Net) any SiameseChangeDetector 16 or more; the data is a pair (before, after) a pair Prithvi a multiple of 16 (224 as pretrained), the six HLS bands as in training

For change detection with the Siamese model, the data is a pair of images and the classes are e.g. change and same:

pair = (zeit.load_raster("s2_2021.tif"), zeit.load_raster("s2_2023.tif", like="s2_2021.tif"))
samples = ai.samples(pair, "change_polygons.gpkg", label="class", patch=64)
model = ai.train(ai.SiameseChangeDetector, samples)
change = ai.predict(model, pair)

docs.title: A loop of your own
docs.text:
The models are ordinary nn.Modules. For a training loop of your own, the SampleSet is a PyTorch Dataset: each item is a dict with x (normalized), y and positions (days since the first date, for the positional encodings):

from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

loader = DataLoader(samples.train, batch_size=64, shuffle=True)
for batch in loader:
    logits = model(batch["x"].permute(0, 2, 1))   # TempCNN takes (batch, band, time)
    ...

To run a model over a whole cube in windows, STACCubeDataset cuts a (lazy) cube into windows that cover it, with the missing values left as NaN and each window's position:

from zeit.ai import STACCubeDataset

dataset = STACCubeDataset(cube, patch_size=64, stride=48)
item = dataset[0]          # {"x": (time, band, 64, 64), "valid", "positions", "row", "col"}

docs.title: Loss functions for imbalanced classes
docs.text:
Imbalanced classes are very common in change detection and land-cover classification (where the class of interest is often a small minority of pixels). zeit.ai.losses provides three specialized loss functions used throughout the per-model tutorials:

from zeit.ai.losses import FocalLoss, TverskyLoss, ContrastiveSiameseLoss

# Down-weights easy examples, focuses training on hard-to-classify pixels
criterion = FocalLoss(alpha=0.25, gamma=2.0)

# Tunable trade-off between False Positives (alpha) and False Negatives (beta);
# setting beta > alpha penalizes missed changes more than false alarms
criterion = TverskyLoss(alpha=0.3, beta=0.7)

# For metric-learning style training of twin encoders (see the Siamese tutorial)
criterion = ContrastiveSiameseLoss(margin=2.0)

With zeit.ai.train, loss="focal" is the focal loss, ignoring unlabelled pixels; any of these can be passed as loss= too. FocalLoss and TverskyLoss apply to any model's classifier logits ((B, C, H, W) or (B, C) vs. integer labels). ContrastiveSiameseLoss is specific to twin-encoder architectures — see the Siamese Change Detector tutorial.
