docs.title: BEAST (Bayesian changepoints)
docs.text:
Most change detection methods choose one model of a series: so many breaks, at these dates. BEAST does not choose. It samples thousands of models of the trend and the season, with every number and position of changepoints, keeps each in proportion to how well it fits, and averages them. What comes out says how sure each answer is: the probability of a changepoint in each year, of each number of changepoints, and a trend with its 95% interval.

AnswersDid the trend or the season change, when, and how sure is it? How many changes were there? InputOne index: an annual series, or a sub-annual one (regular, or irregular dates put on a regular grid) OutputTrend and season with credible intervals, the probability of a changepoint at each date, the most probable changepoints with their probability and jump ReferenceZhao et al. (2019), Remote Sensing of Environment 232; a port of the R package Rbeast's C code

What BEAST produces. Two real pixels of a Landsat annual NDVI series of Rondônia, Brazil, 1985 to 2024. Top: the NDVI of each year, BEAST's trend (blue, the average over the sampled models) with its 95% interval, and LandTrendr's single fit (dashed orange); the inset gives the probability of each number of changepoints. Bottom: the probability of a trend changepoint in each year; each label is a listed changepoint's probability, summed over the years around it. A: a forest cleared in 1999, a changepoint BEAST is sure of, and a rise in 2012 it gives 60%. B: a forest left standing, where no changepoint reaches 15% and none at all is the most probable answer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
BEAST (a Bayesian estimator of abrupt change, seasonal change and trend) writes a series as

\[ y(t) = T(t) + S(t) + \varepsilon(t) \]

where the trend \(T\) is a sequence of straight (or polynomial) segments, the season \(S\) a sequence of harmonic segments, each with its own number of harmonics, and \(\varepsilon\) Gaussian noise. A model is a choice of the changepoints of each component and of the order of each segment.

  1. A prior over the models. Any number of trend changepoints from 0 to 10, and of season changepoints, at any date, with segments no shorter than a minimum (half a period for the season), 1 to 5 harmonics per season segment, a flat or a sloping trend per segment. The coefficients of each model have a Gaussian prior whose precision is itself estimated.
  2. Reversible-jump MCMC. A Markov chain walks through the models: it adds a changepoint, removes one, moves one, merges two, or changes an order, and accepts the step in proportion to the marginal likelihood of the new model against the old one. With the coefficients integrated out, a model with one more changepoint has to fit enough better to be kept: the prior is the penalty, there is no threshold to set.
  3. Average over the models. After a burn-in, every few iterations the chain's current model is kept: 8000 samples per chain, 3 chains, by default. The trend and the season are the means of those models' fits, with their 95% intervals. The probability of a changepoint at a date is the share of samples with a changepoint there; the probability of k changepoints, the share with k of them.
  4. List the changepoints. From the probabilities by date, the most probable changepoints are picked: each peak, with the probabilities of the dates around it summed, the interval of dates it spans and the jump of the component there.

The answer is a distribution, not one model. When the data are clear, it is concentrated: a changepoint at 100%, two changepoints at 90%. When they are not, it says so: a changepoint at 40%, as likely two as three changepoints. That is the difference with BFAST, BFAST Lite and LandTrendr, which return the best model and its dates, however close the second best was.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text: The annual data are the stack of the LandTrendr tutorial: one Landsat NDVI value per year, 1985 to 2024, × 10,000, over about 50 km of Rondônia, Brazil, from LT-GEE's medoid composites. The tutorial follows two pixels, then maps a 300 × 300 pixel window (9 × 9 km) around the first.

docs.title: 1. Run BEAST on one pixel
docs.text:
import zeit

ndvi = zeit.load_raster("LT_Stack_NDVI_Rondonia.tif")   # (40 years, y, x), dated 1985-01-01 ... 2024-01-01
a = ndvi.isel(y=913, x=306)                               # pixel A

res = zeit.beast(a, season="none")                        # one value a year: a trend, no season

An annual series has no season to fit, so season="none". The dates become decimal years, and since they are a year apart the grid is the series itself: 40 steps of one year. With Rbeast's defaults (8000 samples, 3 chains), one pixel takes 0.06 s.

docs.title: 2. Read the changepoints
docs.text:
found = res.trend_cp.notnull()
res[["trend_cp", "trend_cp_prob", "trend_cp_abrupt"]].where(found, drop=True).to_dataframe()
res.trend_cp_ci.where(found, drop=True)                   # the interval of dates of each

     trend_cp  trend_cp_prob  trend_cp_abrupt     95% interval
tcp
0      1999.0          0.999          -1748.7     1998.0 – 2000.0
1      2012.0          0.596            374.7     2008.8 – 2013.8
2      2017.0          0.345            118.1     2013.6 – 2020.5
3      1991.0          0.298            -95.0     1988.6 – 1995.3
4      2005.0          0.136             19.4     2002.2 – 2008.7

The changepoints come most probable first. In 1999 the NDVI of pixel A fell from 0.85 to 0.61, a clearing: every sampled model has a changepoint there (0.999), the trend drops by 0.175, and the interval holds it to 1998–2000. In 2012 the NDVI rose from 0.59 to 0.74 and stayed higher: 60% of the models put a changepoint there, the others account for it with a steeper slope. The changepoints of 2017, 1991 and 2005 are each in a minority of the models; they are not changes BEAST is willing to vouch for.

How many changepoints? trend_ncp_prob answers:

res.trend_ncp_prob.values[:7].round(2)     # P(0, 1, 2, ... changepoints)
# [0.  , 0.18, 0.33, 0.28, 0.15, 0.05, 0.01]
float(res.trend_ncp), int(res.trend_ncp_mode)   # (2.6, 2): 2.6 on average, 2 most likely

Two changepoints are the most likely (33%), three almost as likely (28%), and one, the clearing alone, has 18%. A method that chooses one model would report one of these answers; BEAST reports all three with their weights.

LandTrendr on the same pixel (dashed orange in the figure) puts its vertices in 1985, 1990, 1991, 1998, 1999 and 2024: the same clearing, then a single line of regrowth from 1999 to 2024, across the step of 2012. It is one good model; BEAST's trend is the average of many, and its interval (the blue band) widens where they disagree, around 2012 and 2017.

The trend's slope and its sign come per date:

float(res.trend_slope[-1]), float(res.trend_slope_pos_prob[-1])   # (42.3, 0.64)

At the end of the series the trend rises by 42 (NDVI × 10,000) a year, and 64% of the models have it rising: the regrowth is still going on, more likely than not.

Pixel B, a forest 2 km to the south-west, is the other case. No changepoint is the most likely answer (54%), the mean is 0.74, and the most probable date, 2002, has 15%: BEAST does not claim a change it cannot see. Its trend is a slow rise of 0.04 NDVI over the 40 years, as LandTrendr's single segment. Its R² is low, 0.40, which is right: once the trend is drawn, there is little but noise left to explain.

docs.title: 3. Map the window
docs.text:
Every pixel of a cube runs in parallel, each from the same seed (so a pixel's result does not depend on the others or on the threads):

win = ndvi.isel(y=slice(763, 1063), x=slice(156, 456))     # 300 x 300 pixels around A
res = zeit.beast(win, season="none", samples=2000, chains=2)

ncp = res.trend_ncp                                  # mean number of trend changepoints
first = res.isel(tcp=0)                              # the most probable changepoint of each pixel
sure = first.trend_cp_prob > 0.5
when = first.trend_cp.where(sure)                    # its year, where more likely than not
jump = first.trend_cp_abrupt.where(sure) / 1e4       # and its jump, in NDVI

zeit.save_raster(res[["trend_ncp", "r2"]], "results/beast")

BEAST is a few hundredths of a second per annual pixel, and its cost grows with the samples, the chains and the length of the series: a map is where the samples are worth cutting. With 2000 samples and 2 chains (the defaults of Janus' BEAST tool), the window's 90,000 pixels take about a minute on 19 threads; with Rbeast's 8000 samples and 3 chains, five to six times as long. Fewer samples make the probabilities noisier by a percent or two, not different: on pixel A, 2012 has 61% instead of 60%.

Result of this tutorial, over the 300 × 300 pixel window. From left: the NDVI of 2024; the mean number of trend changepoints; the year of each pixel's most probable changepoint, where its probability is above 0.5; and the jump of the trend there, in NDVI. A and B are the pixels above.

Over the window, a pixel has 2.0 trend changepoints on average (the median; a tenth of the pixels have fewer than 1.6, a tenth more than 3.0). 67% of the pixels have a changepoint more likely than not, 39% one above 0.9, and 93% of those are drops: the history of this frontier is one of clearings. Their years follow the field edges, and a few years hold many of them: 2004 (8.5% of the window), 2006 (7.8%) and 2003 (6.2%). The drops have a median of 0.1 NDVI, a tenth of them more than 0.22. The rises, in 5% of the window (green in the last map), are smaller, a median of 0.04. The median R² is 0.6.

docs.title: 4. Compared with LandTrendr
docs.text:
LandTrendr on the same window finds a loss of 0.2 NDVI or more (its greatest, from extract_events) in 34% of the pixels; BEAST has a drop of 0.1 or more with a probability above 0.5 in 33%. The two date the loss within a year of each other in 43% of LandTrendr's, and that depends on how fast the loss was:

LandTrendr's loss lasts Share of its losses With a BEAST drop within a year 1 year 53% 70% (81% of those over 0.3 NDVI) 2 years 12% 26% 3 to 4 years 12% 15% 5 years or more 24% 6%

A clearing is a changepoint in both. A slow decline is a vertex of LandTrendr's, which draws straight segments between vertices, but a slope for BEAST, which has no reason to add a changepoint where a sloping segment fits: read trend_slope and trend_slope_pos_prob for those, not the changepoints.

docs.title: 5. A series with seasons
docs.text:
With several values a year, BEAST fits a season too, and changepoints of its own. The series here is MODIS EVI every 16 days, January 2001 to December 2025 (575 dates), at 250 m over western France: the series of Janus' BFAST guide, and its first pin, a field.

evi = zeit.load_raster("EVI_Series_ID_EU_150-X026-Y027_2001_2025.tif")   # dates from the band names
px = evi.isel(y=153, x=435)

res = zeit.beast(px, deltat=1 / 23)          # a 16-day grid; the season's period is one year

The MODIS dates are 16 days apart within a year and 13 or 14 across the new year, so the series is not regular to BEAST, which then puts it on a grid of its own choosing: half a month, 24 steps a year. deltat=1/23 keeps one step per composite instead. The pixel takes about a second.

Trend and season, apart. Top: the EVI on the 16-day grid and BEAST's fit, trend plus season. Middle: the trend, its 95% interval and the probability of a trend changepoint at each date. Bottom: the season and the probability of a season changepoint. Until 2012 the field has one sharp peak a year, in spring; from 2013 its level is lower and its season a gentler wave.

The pixel's EVI (38 of its 575 dates missing) has a sharp peak each spring until 2012; from 2013 its level is lower and its season a gentler wave. BEAST splits the change between its components. The trend drops by 0.036 in April 2013 (2013.26, probability 0.95). The season changes at the start of 2013 (probability 0.92): until 2012 it needs four harmonics on average (3.95) to draw the sharp peak, after 2014 one or two (1.5), and its range shrinks from −0.08…+0.22 to −0.08…+0.08. The season has changepoints of its own later, in 2022 and 2023 (0.92 and 0.89), when its shape changes again.

The trend also steps up in 2006.74 and back in 2007.74, up again in 2008.35 (each 0.99 or 1.0): the whole of 2007 sits higher, a year whose level is unlike the others, as a field that changes crops gives, and the trend takes it. With up to 10 changepoints allowed, the trend has 9.3 on average. Whether those steps are changes is a question for the prior:

res3 = zeit.beast(px, deltat=1 / 23, tcp_minmax=(0, 3))
# the drop of April 2013 remains (2013.26, probability 0.96, jump -0.041);
# 2006.74 falls to 0.45 and nothing else is above 0.5

The drop of 2013 is what both answers share, at 0.95 and 0.96; the steps of 2006–2008 hold only while the prior lets the trend spend changepoints on single years. On crop land, set tcp_minmax and tseg_minlength for the changes you are after.

docs.title: Other inputs
docs.text:
The same function takes a raster on disk, a numpy array, one pixel as a pandas.Series, or values with numeric times; a dask cube stays lazy and is computed block by block (all inputs):

# a GeoTIFF of 16-day composites larger than memory, block by block
res = zeit.beast("ndvi_16d.tif", deltat=1 / 23, chunks="auto", samples=2000, chains=2)

# one pixel as a pandas Series with dates (irregular: averaged onto a monthly grid)
res = zeit.beast(series, deltat=1 / 12)

# numeric times in any unit: a monthly series counted in months, a season of 12
res = zeit.beast(values, times=months, period=12)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect season "harmonic" "none" for annual series (a trend alone). deltat from the dates The step of the regular grid. A regular series keeps its own; otherwise the nearest of a day, half a month, a month and a week to the mean spacing, as Rbeast. Set it: 1/23 for 16-day composites, 1/12 monthly, 1 annual. period 1 with dates The season's period, in the units of the times. tcp_minmax, scp_minmax (0, 10) The least and most changepoints of the trend and of the season. The most is part of the prior: lower it when you know a series changes rarely. tseg_minlength, sseg_minlength half a period, or 3 steps The shortest segment, in steps. torder_minmax (0, 1) Flat or sloping trend segments; (0, 2) allows curves. sorder_minmax (0, 5) The harmonics of a season segment. samples, chains, burnin, thin 8000, 3, 200, 5 The MCMC. More samples and chains steady the probabilities and cost time in proportion. seed 42 The same seed gives the same result, in Zeit and in Rbeast. ci True The 95% intervals of the trend, the season and the slope. max_missing_rate 0.75 A series missing more of its grid is not fitted (NaN everywhere).

All parameters and every output are in the API reference. In Janus, the same algorithm is the BEAST (Bayesian changepoints) tool: its fit and changepoints on the chart, and maps of the number of changepoints and of the most probable one (its guide).

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• Read the probability with the date. A changepoint is a date and how many of the models have it. Threshold the probability for a map (0.5: more likely than not), and keep it as a layer: it is the confidence a single-model method cannot give.
  • Set deltat. BEAST works on a regular grid. With dates that are not exactly regular (16-day composites across the new year, or an annual series dated on 1 July, whose decimal years shift by a day in leap years), the grid is chosen from the mean spacing, and for an annual series that is a month: 469 monthly steps for 40 values, more than 75% missing, and the pixel is not fitted. deltat=1 (annual), 1/23 (16-day), 1/12 (monthly) avoid it.
  • The prior is part of the answer. With up to 10 trend changepoints, a busy series is allowed to use them: on fields whose crop changes from year to year, the trend steps up and down with the crops. Lower tcp_minmax or raise tseg_minlength when such steps are not what you are looking for.
  • On a long, flat series, read the mode, not the mean. Many sampled models add a changepoint of almost no jump somewhere in a long stable series, each date at a low probability, and together they raise the mean number of changepoints: on the stable forest of example 28 (460 16-day dates) the mean is 3.4 and the mode 1, with no changepoint above 15% (Rbeast gives the same). trend_ncp_mode, trend_ncp_prob and the probability of each changepoint say more than trend_ncp.
  • A season needs observations all year. With only dry-season images (Landsat in the Amazon: none from November to April), there is little to fit a season on, and a clearing can be taken as a change of the season rather than of the trend. For such data, an annual composite and season="none", or S-CCD and CCDC on every observation, fit better.
  • season_amp is Rbeast's amplitude: the sum of the squared coefficients of the harmonics, so a sine of amplitude 0.2 gives 0.04. Compare it between dates of a pixel, or take its square root.
  • Budget the time. A long sub-annual series costs a second a pixel with the default samples. Map a window or an ROI first, with 2000 samples and 2 chains.

About this implementation

Zeit's BEAST is a port of the C code of Rbeast 1.0.2 (Kaiguang Zhao, GPL ≥ 2): the same sampler, random number generator and single-precision arithmetic as Rbeast's beast() and beast.irreg() with its generic kernels (cputype = "sse"). From the same seed it runs the same chain and returns the same float32 outputs, to the last bit. That is checked in the tests on six series (the Nile, Rbeast's simulated series, its Yellowstone NDVI with gaps, its irregular Ohio Landsat series, a short series and other priors), and holds on the two pixels of this tutorial: pixel A and the EVI field give the same numbers in R, with dump.ci = TRUE (Rbeast leaves the intervals out by default, and drawing them changes the chain). Rbeast's default AVX2 kernels sum in another order, so their chain drifts apart from the generic one after a few hundred iterations and the results agree in distribution only. On one series of 360 months, Rbeast with AVX2 takes 0.13 s and Zeit 0.19 s, as fast as Rbeast's generic kernels; on a cube of 10,000 pixels × 144 months, Zeit is 1.5 times faster than Rbeast's beast123() on one thread and 1.9 times on 19 (Against the Original Implementations). Each pixel is fitted from the seed, as beast() fits one series; beast123() carries its random stream from one pixel to the next. Two outputs differ on purpose: the slope's interval is the mean over the chains, in the slope's units (Rbeast sums it, per time step), and with one chain Zeit still gives the mode, median and percentiles of the number of changepoints. See Algorithm Fidelity.

For a single best model of the breaks in trend and season of a regular series, see BFAST and BFAST Lite; for the segments of an annual series with their recovery, LandTrendr; for a trend's significance alone, Mann-Kendall.

docs.title: BFAST
docs.text:
The classic BFAST algorithm splits a time series into trend, seasonal and remainder components, and looks for breaks in the trend and in the seasonal cycle separately. Use it when you need to know not only that something changed but whether it was the level of the vegetation or its seasonal behaviour.

AnswersDid the trend break, the season, or both? When, and by how much? InputA regular series of one index OutputTrend and season breaks, largest trend jump and its time ReferenceVerbesselt et al. (2010), R package bfast

What BFAST finds. A synthetic 16-day NDVI series with a 0.18 drop in mid-2011. BFAST detects one trend break with magnitude −0.18 and no seasonal break. The components are drawn from the detected breakpoints, for illustration.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
BFAST decomposes the series as

\[ Y_t = T_t + S_t + e_t \]

(trend, season, remainder) and alternates between two segmented regressions until neither changes:

  1. Trend step. Remove the current seasonal estimate and fit a piecewise-linear trend, choosing the number and position of breaks (Bai & Perron, with BIC).
  2. Season step. Remove the trend and fit a piecewise harmonic model, again choosing its breaks.

The first seasonal estimate comes from an STL decomposition, as in R. Before each break search, a stability test (OLS-MOSUM) checks whether there is any evidence of change at all. If there isn't, no break is reported.

Compared with BFAST Lite, classic BFAST is slower (several iterations per pixel) but separates trend breaks from seasonal breaks.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
import zeit

# ndvi_16d: (time, y, x) DataArray of 16-day composites starting in January 2010
ndvi_16d = ndvi_16d.chunk({"time": -1, "y": 256, "x": 256})

result = zeit.bfast(
    ndvi_16d,               # start_time 2010.0 and frequency 23, from the dates
    h=0.15,                 # minimum segment size, fraction of the observations
    max_breaks_trend=5,     # break slots reported for the trend
    max_breaks_season=5,    # break slots reported for the season
).compute()

n_trend = result.n_trend_breaks
n_season = result.n_season_breaks
jump = result.magnitude                  # largest trend jump, 0 if none
when = result.break_time                 # fractional year of that jump

The same function takes a GeoTIFF larger than memory (zeit.bfast("ndvi_16d.tif", chunks="auto")), a numpy array or a single pixel (all inputs), and runs from the shell as zeit bfast. zeit.save_raster(result, "results/bfast") writes one georeferenced GeoTIFF per metric.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
The xarray.Dataset has one (y, x) map per metric:

Variable Meaning n_trend_breaks Number of trend breaks at convergence. n_season_breaks Number of seasonal breaks at convergence. magnitude Size of the largest jump in the trend (difference between the fitted levels either side). 0 if there is no trend break. Matches R's bf$Magnitude. break_time Fractional year of that jump, NaN if none. Matches R's bf$jump$x. n_iter Iterations until convergence (or max_iter). n_valid Valid observations used. valid 1.0 if the series was long enough to fit (more than 2 × frequency observations). trend_breakpoint_idx_1 … _k 0-based index (in the whole series, gaps included) of the last observation before each trend break, NaN past n_trend_breaks. season_breakpoint_idx_1 … _k Same for seasonal breaks. trend_magnitude_1 … _k The jump of the trend at each trend break; magnitude is the largest. trend_break_date_1 … _k Date of the first observation after each trend break.

Seasonal amplitude changes are hard to detect

The stability test sums residuals, so a change that only makes the seasonal cycle larger or smaller averages out and is rarely significant. This is a property of the method (R behaves the same way), not a bug. If amplitude changes matter to you, look at CCDC or phenology metrics.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect start_time, frequency from the dates Regular time axis: first observation and observations per year. order 3 Number of harmonics in the seasonal model. h 0.15 Minimum segment size, as a fraction of the observations. max_iter 10 Maximum trend/season iterations. level 0.05 Significance level of the stability pre-test. Set 1.0 to always search for breaks. max_breaks_trend, max_breaks_season 5 Break slots in the output. Implementation notes, validation and performance

Scope. The iterative trend/season loop with BIC-selected breaks (the default of breakpoints() when breaks = NULL), the STL "periodic" seasonal seed, and the OLS-MOSUM stability pre-test. Differences from R: only season = "harmonic" (R's default is "dummy"), only decomp = "stl", and internal NaN gaps are linearly interpolated only to build the STL seed. The segmented fits skip NaNs as usual.

Validation. Compared with R 4.4.2, bfast 1.7.2 and strucchangeRcpp 1.5.4 on four scenarios (trend break, seasonal-amplitude break, no break, both). Break positions, magnitudes (to 4 decimals) and iteration counts matched. With the pre-test disabled (level=1.0) both implementations find the seasonal break at the same observation; with the default level both suppress it.

Performance. A single call takes about 25 ms for 300 observations with 2 iterations, versus about 106 ms in R (about 4×). With n_jobs=-1 on a 20-thread machine, 2,000 pixels take about 4 s instead of 25 s single-threaded.

docs.title: BFAST Lite
docs.text:
Find how many structural changes happened in a whole time series, and when. BFAST Lite splits each pixel's history into the statistically optimal number of segments, each with its own trend and seasonal cycle, in a single fast pass.

AnswersHow many breaks does this series have, and where are they? InputA regular series of one index; gaps as NaN OutputNumber of breaks and the index of each break per pixel ReferenceMasiliūnas et al., R package bfast (bfastlite)

What BFAST Lite produces. A synthetic 16-day NDVI series with a drop in 2010 and a partial recovery from 2015. BFAST Lite finds both breaks. The blue lines are a trend-plus-season model refitted within each segment, for display.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
BFAST Lite fits the model response ~ trend + harmonics to the series and searches for the set of breakpoints that minimises the total error, using the Bai & Perron dynamic program. Adding breaks always lowers the error, so the number of breaks is chosen with an information criterion (LWZ by default) that penalises extra segments. Each segment must hold at least a fraction h of the observations.

Unlike the classic BFAST, it needs no seasonal decomposition and no iteration, and it handles missing values natively. Unlike BFAST Monitor, it looks at the whole series retrospectively.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
import zeit

# ndvi_16d: (time, y, x) DataArray of 16-day composites starting in January 2010
ndvi_16d = ndvi_16d.chunk({"time": -1, "y": 256, "x": 256})

result = zeit.bfast_lite(
    ndvi_16d,               # start_time 2010.0 and frequency 23 (16-day steps), from the dates
    h=0.15,                 # each segment holds >= 15% of the observations
    max_breaks=5,           # report at most 5 breaks per pixel
).compute()

n_breaks = result.n_breaks
first_break = result.breakpoint_idx_1                  # NaN where n_breaks == 0

To turn a break index into a date, for a series without gaps:

first_break_time = result.attrs["start_time"] + first_break / result.attrs["frequency"]   # fractional year

The same function takes a GeoTIFF larger than memory (zeit.bfast_lite("ndvi_16d.tif", chunks="auto")), a numpy array or a single pixel (all inputs), and runs from the shell as zeit bfast-lite. zeit.save_raster(result, "results/bfl") writes one georeferenced GeoTIFF per metric.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
The number of breaks varies by pixel, so the output reserves max_breaks slots and fills the unused ones with NaN. The xarray.Dataset has one (y, x) map per metric:

Variable Meaning n_breaks Number of breaks chosen by the criterion (0 if none). rss Residual sum of squares of the selected model. lwz Value of the LWZ criterion that was minimised. n_valid Valid (non-NaN) observations used. valid 1.0 if the series had enough observations to fit. breakpoint_idx_1 … _k 0-based index of the last observation before each break, in chronological order, NaN past n_breaks. magnitude_1 … _k The model after each break minus the model before it, both on the first observation after the break. break_date_1 … _k Date of the first observation after each break, NaT past n_breaks.

Indices count every observation

Break indices refer to the whole series, missing observations included, so cube.time[idx] is the date of the last observation before the break even when the pixel has gaps. break_date_k already gives the first date after it, and extract_events turns the breaks into a map of one event per pixel, as for LandTrendr and CCDC.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect start_time from the dates Time of the first observation, as a fractional year. frequency from the dates Observations per year. order 3 Number of seasonal harmonics. h 0.15 Minimum segment size as a fraction of the valid observations. Larger values forbid short segments. max_breaks 5 Number of break slots in the output. Implementation notes, validation and performance

Scope. The default breaks="LWZ" model selection over response ~ trend + harmon, with the segment RSS table computed from recursive residuals (O(n²) rather than O(n³)).

Validation. Compared with R's bfastlite() on six scenarios (a single break, no break, two candidate breaks, NaN gaps, monthly data, non-default h). All six matched n_breaks and every break position exactly; rss differed by 1e-6 to 1e-7.

Performance. On 300 pixels of 150 observations, R bfastlite() took 34.5 ms per pixel and Zeit 11.2 ms single-threaded (about 3×). With n_jobs=-1 on 15 of 16 cores, 20,000 pixels took 45.5 s instead of 249.3 s single-threaded (a further 5.5×). The gain is smaller than BFAST Monitor's because the dynamic program is real computation on both sides, not interpreter overhead.

  • Bai, J., & Perron, P. (2003). Computation and analysis of multiple structural change models. Journal of Applied Econometrics, 18(1), 1–22. doi:10.1002/jae.659
  • Liu, J., Wu, S., & Zidek, J. V. (1997). On segmented multivariate regression. Statistica Sinica, 7(2), 497–525.
  • Brown, R. L., Durbin, J., & Evans, J. M. (1975). Techniques for testing the constancy of regression relationships over time. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 37(2), 149–163.

docs.title: BFAST Monitor
docs.text:
Near-real-time change detection. BFAST Monitor learns what "normal" looks like for each pixel from a stable history period, then checks every new observation against it and reports the first moment the pixel stops behaving normally. This is the logic behind many operational deforestation alert systems.

AnswersIs something changing now, compared with the stable past? Since when? InputA regular series of one index, e.g. 16-day NDVI composites OutputBreak date, magnitude and a has-break flag per pixel ReferenceVerbesselt et al. (2012), R package bfast

What BFAST Monitor produces. A synthetic 16-day NDVI series with 12% missing observations. The model is fitted on the history period (2010–2015) and projected forward. A drop is injected in May 2017 (2017.4). BFAST Monitor flags it at 2017.57, once enough evidence has accumulated to be statistically significant.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Fit the history. For each pixel, observations before monitor_start are fitted with a regression made of a linear trend plus order seasonal harmonics.
  2. Monitor. For each later observation, the residual against that model is computed. A moving sum of residuals (the OLS-MOSUM process) is compared with a boundary that widens over time.
  3. Flag. The first time the process crosses the boundary is the detected break. If it never crosses, the pixel is stable.

Because the test accumulates evidence, a single cloudy outlier does not trigger an alarm, but a persistent shift does, usually within a few observations.

Time is regular, not calendar-based

Like R's ts objects, BFAST uses a synthetic, regular time axis: observation i is at start_time + i / frequency. Zeit reads both from the cube's dates (frequency from their median spacing, start_time from the first date), so composite your data to a fixed step first (regularize_time_series) and use NaN for gaps. For a series without dates, give start_time as a whole year (e.g. 2010.0) so the harmonics align with the calendar.

docs.title: 1. Prepare a regular series
docs.text:
import zeit

# cube from build_time_series(...), see "STAC Data Cubes"
ndvi = (cube.sel(band="nir") - cube.sel(band="red")) / (cube.sel(band="nir") + cube.sel(band="red"))
ndvi_16d = zeit.regularize_time_series(ndvi, freq="16D", method="median")   # (time, y, x)
ndvi_16d = ndvi_16d.chunk({"time": -1, "y": 256, "x": 256})

16-day composites give frequency=23 observations per year, monthly data frequency=12. Zeit infers it from the dates.

docs.title: 2. Monitor
docs.text:
result = zeit.bfast_monitor(
    ndvi_16d,
    "2022-01-01",               # history before, monitoring from here on (or 2022.0)
    h=0.25,                     # MOSUM window, fraction of the history length
    period=10,
    alpha=0.05,
).compute()                     # a dask cube gives a lazy result
result.attrs["start_time"], result.attrs["frequency"]   # e.g. (2010.0, 23), read from the dates

docs.title: 3. Read the output
docs.text:
The result is an xarray.Dataset with one (y, x) map per metric, on the grid and CRS of the cube:

has_break = result.has_break == 1
break_time = result.breakpoint      # fractional year, NaN if none
magnitude = result.magnitude        # median residual in the monitoring period
Variable Meaning breakpoint Fractional-year time of the first detected break, NaN if none. breakpoint_idx 0-based index of that observation in the input series. magnitude Median residual over the monitoring period: size and direction of the shift. Negative means lower than expected (e.g. vegetation loss on NDVI). sigma Residual standard error of the history fit. n_history Valid observations used to fit the history. has_break 1.0 if a break was detected, else 0.0. valid 0.0 if the history was too short to fit; the other metrics are then NaN.

A typical alert map keeps breaks that also go in the expected direction:

alerts = has_break & (magnitude < -0.1)

docs.title: Save the maps
docs.text: zeit.save_raster(result, "results/bfm")        # breakpoint.tif, magnitude.tif, ... georeferenced

docs.title: Other inputs
docs.text:
The same function takes a raster on disk, a numpy array or a single pixel (all inputs):

# A GeoTIFF larger than memory, with its dates in the band names: read and computed block by block
bfm = zeit.bfast_monitor("ndvi_16d.tif", "2022-01-01", chunks="auto")
zeit.save_raster(bfm, "results/bfm")

# A numpy (time, y, x) array or one pixel's series without dates: give the time axis
bfm = zeit.bfast_monitor(ndvi_numpy, 2022.0, start_time=2010.0, frequency=23)
px = zeit.bfast_monitor(values, 2022.0, start_time=2010.0, frequency=23)

From the shell: zeit bfast-monitor.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect monitor_start required Start of the monitoring period: a date or a fractional year. start_time from the dates Time of the first observation, as a fractional year. frequency from the dates Observations per year. order 3 Number of seasonal harmonics. h 0.25 MOSUM window as a fraction of the history. Must be 0.25, 0.5 or 1.0. period 10 How far ahead, in history lengths, the boundary is valid. Must be 2, 4, 6, 8 or 10. alpha 0.05 Significance level. min_valid 10 Minimum valid history observations.

h and period index a table of simulated critical values (from strucchangeRcpp), so other values raise an error instead of being silently extrapolated.

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
Choose a genuinely stable history

This port uses history="all": the whole pre-monitoring period is assumed stable. If that history contains a disturbance, the model is wrong and false alarms follow. In tests on pure noise at alpha=0.05, R's own bfastmonitor(history="all") flagged about 44% of series, and Zeit matched it (about 42%). Pick a disturbance-free history window, require a minimum magnitude, and treat single-pixel detections with caution.

  • Use at least 2–3 years of history so the seasonal cycle is well estimated.
  • Combine with a spatial filter (for example apply_mmu_filter) to drop isolated alerts.
  • For a retrospective analysis of the whole series, use BFAST Lite instead.
Implementation notes and validation

Scope. Only bfastmonitor()'s default monitoring process (type="OLS-MOSUM") with history="all" is ported. R's default history="ROC" (reverse-CUSUM trimming of unstable history) and history="BP" are not. The design matrix matches bfastpp(): response ~ trend + harmon.

Validation. Compared directly with R's bfastmonitor() on six scenarios: a mid-series break, no break, an early break, NaN gaps in the history, monthly data, and non-default h/period. All six matched to floating-point tolerance (identical breakpoint_idx, n_history; differences of 1e-11 to 1e-13 in breakpoint, magnitude, sigma). See Benchmarks.
