docs.title: CCDC
docs.text:
Continuous Change Detection and Classification models the seasonal rhythm of every pixel from all available clear images, and flags the moment that rhythm breaks. It detects changes at any time of year and describes what the land looks like before and after.

AnswersDid this pixel change, on what date, and into what? InputDense multi-band reflectance (× 10,000) plus QA codes OutputStable segments with start, end and break dates plus harmonic coefficients ReferenceZhu & Woodcock (2014), ported from the original MATLAB

What CCDC produces. A synthetic Landsat pixel observed every 16 days from 2008 to 2021, with about a third of the images lost to clouds. A forest is converted to pasture in mid-2014. CCDC fits one harmonic model per stable period (blue) and detects the break on the first clear observation after the change (orange). Note how the seasonal amplitude also changes after the break.

docs.title: How CCDC works
docs.text:
Vegetation follows a yearly cycle, so a pixel's reflectance rises and falls with the seasons. CCDC describes that cycle with a small harmonic model (a trend line plus sine and cosine waves) fitted to all clear observations:

\[ \hat{\rho}(t) = a_0 + c_1 t + \sum_{k=1}^{3} \left[ a_k \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi k t}{T}\right) + b_k \sin\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi k t}{T}\right) \right], \qquad T = 365.25 \text{ days} \]

Each new observation is compared with the model's prediction. If six consecutive observations (by default) all deviate more than a chi-squared threshold, in several bands at once, CCDC declares a break, closes the current model, and starts a new one after it. The model coefficients are also useful by themselves. They describe the "average" appearance of each stable period and make excellent features for land-cover classification.

Compared with LandTrendr, CCDC uses every clear image instead of one per year, works on several bands together, and can date a change to within a few weeks. The price is that it needs dense, well-masked data.

docs.title: 1. Load a dense stack
docs.text:
CCDC works on all clear Landsat-like observations. It expects:

  • Bands Blue, Green, Red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2 (optionally a thermal band), as surface reflectance × 10,000. The original's thresholds are defined on that scale, so convert 0–1 reflectance first. For Landsat Collection 2 Level 2 digital numbers, reflectance × 10,000 is 0.275 * DN - 2000.
  • Dates for every observation. A cube carries them in its time coordinate, so there is nothing to pass.

zeit.load_raster reads a stack as a georeferenced (time, band, y, x) cube. Here each date has the 6 spectral bands and Landsat's QA_PIXEL band, named 2008-01-05_blue, 2008-01-05_green, …, 2008-01-05_qa_pixel (how save_raster writes a cube). A cube from build_time_series, or a folder of single-date files read with pattern=, works the same way.

import numpy as np
import zeit

cube = zeit.load_raster("landsat_dense_stack.tif", validate="ccdc")
cube.dims          # ('time', 'band', 'y', 'x')
cube.band.values   # array(['blue', 'green', 'red', 'nir', 'swir1', 'swir2', 'qa_pixel'], ...)

validate="ccdc" warns when the series looks unfit for CCDC (too few dates, values that do not look scaled). For a stack interleaved by date without band names, see Processing large areas.

docs.title: 2. Build the QA codes
docs.text:
CCDC uses the Fmask codes of the original implementation:

Code Meaning Used for fitting? 0 clear land yes 1 water yes 2 cloud shadow no 3 snow handled separately 4 cloud no 255 no observation / fill no

For Landsat Collection 2, decode the QA_PIXEL bit flags:

qa_pixel = cube.sel(band="qa_pixel").values.astype(np.uint16)   # (time, y, x)

qa = np.zeros(qa_pixel.shape, dtype=np.uint8)          # 0 = clear land
qa[(qa_pixel & (1 << 7)) != 0] = 1                     # water
qa[(qa_pixel & (1 << 4)) != 0] = 2                     # cloud shadow
qa[(qa_pixel & (1 << 5)) != 0] = 3                     # snow
qa[(qa_pixel & (1 << 3)) != 0] = 4                     # cloud
qa[(qa_pixel & 1) != 0] = 255                          # fill

reflectance = cube.drop_sel(band="qa_pixel")           # blue ... swir2

1 means water, not cloud

A mask with 0 = clear, 1 = cloudy is wrong for CCDC: code 1 is water, which is treated as a valid observation. Mark clouds with 4. If you only have a boolean clear mask (for example from Tmask), use qa = np.where(clear, 0, 4).

CCDC already runs its own Tmask screening internally to catch clouds the QA band missed, as the original does. If the stack already holds a band of Fmask codes, there is nothing to decode: name it, zeit.ccdc(cube, qa="fmask"), and it is left out of the spectral bands.

docs.title: 3. Try one pixel
docs.text:
Start with a single pixel to see what CCDC returns. zeit.ccdc takes one pixel's (time, band) series as readily as the whole cube:

row, col = 200, 310
px = zeit.ccdc(reflectance.isel(y=row, x=col), qa=qa[:, row, col])

px[["t_start", "t_end", "t_break"]].to_dataframe().dropna(subset=["t_start"])

For the pixel in the figure above this gives two segments:

           t_start      t_end    t_break
segment
1       2008-01-05 2014-07-16 2014-08-17     <- forest; breaks on 2014-08-17
2       2014-08-17 2021-12-26        NaT     <- pasture; no further break

Each segment has its first and last date (t_start, t_end), the date of the break that ended it (t_break, NaT if none), and for each band the RMSE of the fit (rmse) and the 8 harmonic coefficients (coefs), as in the original code. A pixel you already have as a table works too: a pandas.DataFrame indexed by date, one column per band, zeit.ccdc(df, qa="fmask").

docs.title: 4. Run the whole stack
docs.text:
segments = zeit.ccdc(reflectance, qa=qa, max_segments=6)

Every pixel runs in parallel in Rust. The result is an xarray.Dataset on the grid and CRS of the cube.

docs.title: 5. Read the output
docs.text:
segments has one slot per segment (up to max_segments):

Variable Dims Content t_start, t_end (segment, y, x) First and last date of each segment; NaT past the last one t_break (segment, y, x) Date of the break that ended the segment; NaT if none n_segments (y, x) Number of segments rmse (segment, band, y, x) RMSE of each band's fit coefs (segment, band, coef, y, x) The 8 coefficients of each band: a0 (intercept), c1 (slope), then a1, b1, a2, b2, a3, b3 (cos/sin for 1, 2 and 3 cycles per year)

Unused segment slots are NaT and NaN. To map the date of the first change:

first_break = segments.t_break.isel(segment=0)         # (y, x), NaT = no change
print(f"{first_break.notnull().mean().item():.1%} of pixels changed")
year_of_change = first_break.dt.year                   # NaN = no change

zeit.save_raster(first_break, "results/ccdc_first_break.tif")   # decimal years, NaN = no change
zeit.save_raster(segments, "results/ccdc")             # t_start.tif, ..., coefs.tif

save_raster writes dates as decimal years (2014-08-17 → 2014.62) and the whole result as one GeoTIFF per variable, with coefs.tif holding one band per segment, band and coefficient (1_blue_a0, 1_blue_c1, …).

docs.title: 6. Predict a cloud-free image for any date
docs.text:
Because each model describes the full seasonal cycle, you can evaluate it on any day, including days with no image at all. predict_synthetic_image picks the segment active on that date for every pixel:

synthetic = zeit.predict_synthetic_image(segments, "2019-07-15")   # (band, y, x)
zeit.save_raster(synthetic, "results/synthetic_2019-07-15.tif")

This is a clean way to fill gaps or build seasonal mosaics. On a single pixel's result (px) it returns one value per band, so a loop over dates draws model curves like those in the figure above.

docs.title: 7. Classify the segments
docs.text:
The model of each segment is a compact description of the land cover during that period. zeit.train_classifier takes, for every pixel, the model of the segment covering a date (each band's coefficients, the intercept moved to that date, and its RMSE) at labelled points; zeit.classify labels every pixel:

rf = zeit.train_classifier(segments, "samples.gpkg", label="class", date="2019-07-01")
land_cover = zeit.classify(segments, rf, date="2019-07-01")
land_cover.label.zeit.plot()                         # the legend names the classes
zeit.save_raster(land_cover, "results/ccdc_classes")

The same functions classify any cube or Dataset of metrics; see the API reference.

docs.title: Tuning the parameters
docs.text:
The defaults are those of the original CCDC_Parameters.txt. Bands can be given by name or 0-based position.

Parameter Default Effect conseq_anom 6 Consecutive anomalous observations needed to confirm a break. Higher is more robust and slower to react. chi2_prob_threshold 0.99 Change probability. The break threshold is chi2inv(p, n_detection_bands). Lower is more sensitive. tmax_cg_prob_threshold 0.999999 Observations beyond chi2inv(p, …) are treated as outliers (for example missed clouds) and dropped. num_c 8 Maximum number of coefficients (4, 6 or 8). Models grow from 4 to 8 as observations accumulate. detection_bands Green to SWIR2 Bands used for detection, e.g. ["green", "red", "nir", "swir1", "swir2"]. tmask_bands Green, SWIR1 Bands used by the internal Tmask screen. thermal_band None A brightness-temperature band (°C × 100), if you have one.

A model is only started once there are at least 12 clear observations spanning a year, as in the original.

docs.title: Processing large areas
docs.text:
GeoTIFFs larger than memory. With chunks="auto", zeit.ccdc reads the file lazily and the result is computed block by block while it is written:

segments = zeit.ccdc("landsat_dense_stack.tif", qa="fmask", chunks="auto")
zeit.save_raster(segments, "results/ccdc")

The QA band must already hold Fmask codes (step 2), here a band named fmask. A stack interleaved by date without band names (for each date, 6 spectral bands then the QA band) needs its dates and the names of the bands of each date:

dates = open("dates.txt").read().split()          # one date per acquisition, e.g. 2008-01-05
segments = zeit.ccdc("landsat_dense_stack.tif", dates=dates, qa="fmask", chunks="auto",
                     bands=["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir1", "swir2", "fmask"])

The same is available as zeit ccdc.

Dask cubes and clusters. A dask-backed (time, band, y, x) cube stays lazy. Chunk only in space:

cube = cube.chunk({"time": -1, "band": -1, "y": 256, "x": 256})
segments = cube.zeit.ccdc(qa="fmask", max_segments=6)   # same as zeit.ccdc(cube, ...)
segments.to_zarr("s3://my-bucket/ccdc.zarr")

The blocks running at once share the core's threads, so n_jobs stays at its default. See Parallel & Cloud Processing.

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• Masking is everything. A missed cloud looks like a change. Use the best QA you have. CCDC's internal Tmask catches most leftovers.
  • Density matters. CCDC shines with every clear Landsat image, or harmonised Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS). Annual composites are a job for LandTrendr.
  • Detect fewer false breaks by raising conseq_anom. This is what the COLD variant does to trade sensitivity for robustness.
  • Validation. Zeit reproduces the original MATLAB segment for segment: the same dates, categories and observation counts, with the coefficients, RMSE and magnitudes within small tolerances (predictions at the start, middle and end of a segment within 0.5 reflectance units x 10000, at most 0.2% of the segment's RMSE in the cases measured). The lasso is written from the paper (Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010), not ported from GLMnet, so the results are no longer bit for bit. See Algorithm Fidelity.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Zhu, Z., & Woodcock, C. E. (2014). Continuous change detection and classification of land cover using all available Landsat data. Remote Sensing of Environment, 144, 152–171. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2014.01.011
  • Zhu, Z., et al. (2020). Continuous monitoring of land disturbance based on Landsat time series. Remote Sensing of Environment, 238, 111116. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2019.03.009
  • Original MATLAB implementation: GERSL/CCDC

docs.title: Forest Degradation (CODED)
docs.text:
Deforestation is easy to see from space: the forest is gone. Degradation is not. Selective logging opens small gaps, an understory fire scorches the lower layers, and within two years the canopy closes again. Each Landsat pixel only darkens a little, for a short time. CODED finds these events by unmixing every observation into its materials and following the result through time, then tells degradation (the land is still forest afterwards) from deforestation (it is not).

AnswersWhere and when was the forest degraded or cleared? InputEvery Landsat observation, six reflectance bands: (time, band, y, x) OutputDates, magnitudes and types of change; a strata map for sample-based area estimates ReferenceBullock, Woodcock & Olofsson (2020), Remote Sensing of Environment 238; Souza et al. (2005), Remote Sensing of Environment 98

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Spectral mixture analysis. A 30 m pixel is a mix of materials. zeit.unmix finds, for every observation, the fractions of green vegetation (GV), non-photosynthetic vegetation (NPV: dead wood, litter), soil, shade and cloud that best rebuild its spectrum, with the endmembers of Souza et al. (2005). Logging raises NPV and soil where the canopy was; the reflectance barely changes, the fractions do.
  2. NDFI. The fractions are combined into the Normalized Difference Fraction Index: (GVs − (NPV + soil)) / (GVs + NPV + soil), with GVs = GV / (1 − shade). Closed forest is near 1, damaged forest lower, bare soil and pasture below 0.
  3. Monitoring. For each pixel, a model of the NDFI (a constant plus an annual harmonic) is fitted to a training period, with its RMSE. After it, each observation is compared with the model: when consec observations in a row fall more than thresh RMSEs below it, there is a change, dated at the first of them.
  4. What came after. A new model is fitted to the min_years after each change. If it is forest, the change was degradation; if not, deforestation. Forest or not is decided by a random forest trained on land cover points (as in CODED), or else by the model's mean NDFI.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text: The example 21 builds a synthetic Landsat series by mixing known fractions: intact forest, forest selectively logged in mid-2006 (with cuts of varying intensity; the canopy closes within two years), forest cleared in mid-2008, and pasture, with a third of the observations lost to clouds.

docs.title: 1. Unmix
docs.text:
import zeit

fractions = zeit.unmix(landsat, cloud_threshold=0.05)   # gv, shade, npv, soil, cloud, rmse, ndfi

Clouds that the QA mask missed have a large cloud fraction, and cloud_threshold (CODED uses 0.05) removes them. Use every observation, not composites: degradation lasts a year or two, and a composite blurs it away.

docs.title: 2. Run CODED
docs.text:
result = zeit.coded(fractions, start=2005)                      # monitor from 2005, train on 2002-2004
result = zeit.coded(fractions, start=2005, training="lc.gpkg")   # forest or not from land cover points

result.strata is a map of forest, non-forest, degradation and deforestation (by the first change), and result.t_change, result.type and result.ndfi_change describe each change. zeit.plot(fractions.ndfi, fit=result) shows the NDFI of any pixel with the changes marked.

Parameter Default Effect train_years 3 Years that define the forest's normal state. consec 3 Observations in a row beyond the threshold. More: fewer false alarms, later detections. thresh 3 Threshold in RMSEs of the training model. Lower finds lighter degradation and more noise. min_years 3 Years after a change that define the new land cover. forest_ndfi 0.5 Without training points: forest where the model's mean NDFI is at least this.

docs.title: 3. Estimate the area
docs.text:
CODED's authors recommend using the map as strata for a sample, not as the area itself: light degradation is easily missed. The strata go straight into sampling_design, interpret and accuracy:

points = zeit.stratified_sample(result.strata, n=200, min_per_stratum=30)
s = zeit.interpret(landsat, points, rgb=["swir1", "nir", "red"], series=fractions.ndfi,
                   map=result.strata, fit=result, save="reference.gpkg")
acc = s.accuracy()

In the example the reference comes from the known truth instead of an interpreter. The map finds 51 ha of degradation and misses the lightest cuts. The sample sees them, and the estimate is 56 ± 6 ha, close to the 54 ha that were logged:

Accuracy of the map, from 200 reference points:
  overall: 0.989 ± 0.015 (95% CI)

                      user's     producer's mapped (ha) estimated (ha)
class
forest         0.979 ± 0.029  1.000 ± 0.000         219        214 ± 6
non_forest     1.000 ± 0.000  1.000 ± 0.000         108        108 ± 0
degradation    1.000 ± 0.000  0.916 ± 0.106          51         56 ± 6
deforestation  1.000 ± 0.000  1.000 ± 0.000          54         54 ± 0

About this implementation

zeit.coded follows the version of CODED described in the paper (its cdd_simple.py): a training model, monitoring by normalized residuals, and a new model after each change. The Earth Engine versions 1 and 2 use Earth Engine's CCDC for the monitoring and give similar but not identical results. The monitoring is checked against a Python implementation of the algorithm, and the unmixing against scipy.optimize.nnls. The endmembers are the ones CODED uses (Souza et al. 2005, plus a cloud endmember), for Landsat 5, 7 and 8 surface reflectance.

docs.title: Embeddings (TESSERA, AlphaEarth)
docs.text:
Foundation models for Earth observation turn a whole year of satellite images into one vector per pixel: an embedding. Two products are global, open and made at 10 m every year since 2017, TESSERA and Google's AlphaEarth Foundations. zeit reads them as a cube like any other, so the classifiers, the clustering, the segmentation and the validation of zeit work on them as they are, and adds what is particular to embeddings: looking at them, searching for places like a sample, and following each pixel's embedding from year to year.

AnswersWhat is where, from few samples? Where else looks like this? Where did the land change, year to year? InputA region and years; the embeddings are downloaded OutputA (time, band, y, x) cube of 128 (TESSERA) or 64 (AlphaEarth) dimensions ReferenceFeng et al. (2025), arXiv:2506.20380; Brown et al. (2025), arXiv:2507.22291

docs.title: What an embedding is
docs.text:
A pixel seen by Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 through one year is a few hundred numbers: a dozen bands on every clear date, radar backscatter every few days, gaps under clouds. A foundation model is a neural network trained on such series from the whole planet to squeeze them into a short vector, so that the vector keeps what tells places apart (forest from pasture, soy from maize, a city from bare soil) and drops what does not (noise, clouds, the exact dates of the images). That vector is the embedding.

1 · A year of observations of one pixel JanDec Sentinel-2 bandsSentinel-1 radar 2 · A foundation model encoder trained once, on the whole planet 3 · One vector A00A02 ⋮ A63 64 numbers (AlphaEarth) or 128 (TESSERA) 4 · Every pixel, every year x, y: 10 m cells band:A00…A63 time: 2017 … 2025

The vector of a pixel summarises how it looked through the whole year. Pixels whose vectors point the same way look alike; a pixel whose vector turns from one year to the next has changed.

The numbers of an embedding have no physical meaning on their own: A07 is not a band nor an index. What carries meaning is the direction of the vector. Two pixels whose vectors point the same way looked alike through the year; a pixel whose vector turns from one year to the next has changed. Everything zeit does with embeddings comes back to that angle, measured by the cosine similarity:

\[ \cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf a \cdot \mathbf b}{\lVert \mathbf a\rVert\,\lVert \mathbf b\rVert} \]

1 for the same direction, 0 for unrelated ones. zeit.similarity maps it against a reference, and zeit.embedding_change maps \(1 - \cos\theta\) between consecutive years.

This makes embeddings very good at some things and blind to others:

Embeddings are good at They cannot tell Classifying land cover from a few dozen samples When in the year something happened (a whole year is one vector) Finding more places like a sample, anywhere Physical quantities: NDVI, biomass, a magnitude of loss in reflectance Flagging that a pixel changed between two years, whatever the change The direction of a change (loss and regrowth both just "move") Clustering a region into its kinds of land without labels Anything before 2017

For dates within a year, physical magnitudes and the record before 2017, use the classic algorithms (LandTrendr, CCDC, BFAST) on the images themselves. The two approaches answer different questions, and zeit compares them on the same grid (see below).

docs.title: Two products, one cube
docs.text:
TESSERA AlphaEarth Foundations Dimensions 128 64 (each embedding has length 1) Cells, years 10 m, 2017–2025 10 m, 2017–2025 Made from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, Landsat and more Stored as Zarr, int8 times a scale per pixel, a group per UTM zone COGs, int8 on a fixed curve, per year and UTM zone Read through geotessera, installed with zeit (Python 3.12+) nothing: free open COGs on Source Cooperative (default); or Earth Engine Licence CC0 1.0 (attribution requested) CC-BY 4.0, attribution required

Both are read with one function, and give the same thing: a georeferenced (time, band, y, x) cube, time on January 1 of each year, band the dimensions (A00, A01...), NaN where there is no embedding. A region within a UTM zone keeps the zone's CRS and the cells the embeddings were made on, so the two products line up cell by cell:

import zeit

box = (-63.136, -10.133, -63.086, -10.083)           # 5 x 5 km of Rondônia, Brazil
emb = zeit.load_embeddings(box, source="tessera", years=range(2017, 2026))
aef = zeit.load_embeddings(box, source="alphaearth", years=range(2017, 2026))
emb.rio.transform() == aef.rio.transform()      # True: the same 554 x 549 cells of 10 m, EPSG:32720

Every figure of this page comes from these two cubes, a box of the Rondônia scene used by the LandTrendr tutorial, where cattle pasture and soy fields have kept replacing the forest since 2016.

The cube is lazy: the blocks are read when computed, a year and every dimension at a time, kept as downloaded (up to 1 GB, so that what is computed twice is downloaded once) and dequantised as they arrive. Over this box, all nine years took 38 s for TESSERA and 59 s for AlphaEarth on a home connection: 700 MB of AlphaEarth and 1.4 GB of TESSERA once in memory as float32. chunks=None reads it all at once; zeit.save_raster(emb, "emb.tif") keeps a copy that zeit.load_raster reads back, still knowing what it holds.

Regions come as bounds in longitude and latitude, a vector file or a GeoDataFrame (cells outside its polygons become NaN), or the grid of another raster:

emb = zeit.load_embeddings("municipality.gpkg", source="tessera", years=2024)
on_landsat = zeit.load_embeddings(source="alphaearth", like=landsat, years=range(2018, 2025))   # 30 m, averaged

With like= (or crs=/res=) the embeddings are put on that grid: by the nearest cell, or by the mean of the cells when the new ones are at least 1.5 times larger. A region across UTM zones needs crs=.

Check the coverage of each year

The products are global, but not every year covers every cell. Over this box, TESSERA has no 2017 embedding for 72% of the cells (AlphaEarth has all of them), so the figures below start in 2018. One line shows the share of cells without an embedding, per year:

emb.isel(band=0).isnull().mean(["y", "x"]).values      # [0.72, 0.00, 0.00, ...]

docs.title: What the cube remembers
docs.text: The cube's attributes say which embeddings it holds: product, version and variant (TESSERA has had several inference runs, and each is a space of its own), the licence and the citation. A model trained with zeit.train_classifier or zeit.ai.train records them, and zeit.classify/zeit.ai.predict refuse a cube of other embeddings rather than produce a map from vectors it was never trained on. The algorithms that fit a physical, seasonal signal (LandTrendr, CCDC, BFAST, phenology, TWDTW, indices...) refuse a cube of embeddings too: there is nothing in a yearly summary for them to fit.

docs.title: Look
docs.text:
zeit.plot(emb)

Dozens of dimensions cannot be shown at once, so zeit.plot shows the first three principal components as red, green and blue. They hold much of the variety of a region: here 69% of the variance of AlphaEarth (51%, 13% and 5%) and 70% of TESSERA's. The components are fitted once, on pixels of every year, and applied to all of them: a colour means the same embedding in 2018 and in 2025, and paging through the years shows the land changing.

The same box in 2018, 2021 and 2025, through the first three principal components of each product. Within a product, a colour is the same embedding in every year. In AlphaEarth, forest is orange (compare the similarity maps below) and fields green to cyan. A patch whose colour changes between two years changed on the ground; the change maps below date it. The colours of the two products are unrelated (each has its own components), but the patches are the same.

The viewer has two more views, picked in the panel beside the map, and computes all of them on the GPU from the vectors themselves:

  • Similarity: move the mouse, and every pixel is coloured by how much it looks like the one under the cursor (the cosine similarity of their embeddings). Click a pixel to pin it as the reference, tick keep the reference's year, and page through the years: a pasture that comes to look like the forest you pinned, or a field that stops looking like it, shows up. The chart below the map follows the cursor's pixel over the years.
  • Change: how far each pixel moved from the previous year (1 − cosine), the same distance as zeit.embedding_change.

The components can also be fitted on the visible area only: zoom into a forest, and the colours spread over its differences instead of over forest versus city. See Visualisation for the details.

docs.title: Classify from few samples
docs.text:
The embeddings were made for this. Each dimension of a year is a feature:

year = emb.sel(time="2024")                               # blocks read for training are kept for classify
rf = zeit.train_classifier(year, "samples.gpkg", label="class")
classes = zeit.classify(year, rf)

Because the model behind the embeddings has already learned what tells land covers apart, a random forest on them needs far fewer samples than one on raw bands: both papers report accurate maps from sparse labels. Then validate it as any map, with a probability sample and error-adjusted areas (Accuracy & Area):

design = zeit.sampling_design(classes.label, expected_ua=0.8)
points = zeit.stratified_sample(classes.label, design=design)

Several years at once (emb.sel(time=slice("2022", "2024"))) give the classifier how each pixel changed. Train on the same product, version and variant you classify: the cube's attributes enforce it.

Without labels, zeit.som clusters the embeddings into a few kinds of land and zeit.snic segments them into objects:

clusters = zeit.som(aef.sel(time="2025"), x=2, y=3, sample=20_000)   # six clusters

Six clusters of the 2025 AlphaEarth embeddings, found by a self-organizing map without a single label. Forest, the fields and the pasture come out as clusters of their own, and the river with its edges as others; naming them takes a look at each, not a training set.

docs.title: Find more places like these
docs.text:
forest = zeit.similarity(aef, "forest_samples.gpkg", year=2018)   # (time, y, x): cosine similarity
per_class = zeit.similarity(emb, "samples.gpkg", by="class")       # one map per class

The reference is the mean embedding of the samples (every cell of a polygon) in one year (year, the last of the cube by default), and every year of the cube is compared with it: where something like it appears, and when. With by=, each value of a column gets its own reference and its own map, under a class dimension. metric="euclidean" gives a distance instead (0 for the same embedding).

25 pixels of forest picked in 2018 (orange rings) are the reference. Left and centre: every pixel's similarity to them, in 2018 and in 2025; dark green is forest. Right: the distribution of the similarity over the box. The peak near 1, the forest, shrinks from 2018 to 2025 as it is cleared (the share of the box above 0.8 drops from 21% to 13.5%), and the pasture peak grows.

A similarity map has no fixed threshold: how similar "the same thing" is depends on the product and on how varied the samples are. Look at its distribution, as in the figure: when the samples are a coherent class, it has a clear peak near 1, and the valley before it is the threshold.

docs.title: Change from year to year
docs.text:
change = zeit.embedding_change(emb)                   # distance of each year to the year before
events = zeit.extract_events(change, min_magnitude=0.3)

embedding_change returns two maps: distance (time, y, x), how far each pixel's embedding moved (1 - cos of the angle between two years, 0 for no movement, up to 2), and noise (y, x), the median of a pixel's distances, its usual movement from year to year. With baseline="first" or a year, every year is measured against that one instead of the year before.

extract_events keeps the largest move of each pixel in the schema of the other change algorithms: yod the year before the first embedding that shows the change, date, magnitude (the distance), and dsnr (the move over the pixel's noise). An embedding summarises a year, so a clearing in the middle of a year shows partly in it and partly in the next.

docs.title: Choosing a threshold
docs.text:
Each product has its own scale. Over this box, the median pixel moved 0.037 a year in AlphaEarth and 0.082 in TESSERA, and the 99th percentile was 0.21 and 0.41. The same threshold flags very different amounts of change: at 0.2, 1.1% of AlphaEarth's pixel-years and 11% of TESSERA's; at 0.3, 0.45% and 4.0%.

Left: the year-to-year distance of every pixel and year, on a log scale. Most pixels barely move; TESSERA's whole distribution sits about twice as far out as AlphaEarth's. Dashed lines: the thresholds used below, which 1.1% (AlphaEarth) and 4.0% (TESSERA) of the pixel-years exceed. Right: a pixel cleared between 2020 and 2021. Both products jump in 2021; AlphaEarth's move stands out ten times above its usual one, TESSERA's three times.

Two ways to set it:

  • From the distribution. Plot change.distance as a histogram, as above: the bulk is year-to-year noise, and the threshold goes where its tail ends. Here, 0.2 for AlphaEarth and 0.3 for TESSERA.

  • Relative to each pixel. extract_events(change, sort_by="dsnr") keeps, for each pixel, the move that stands furthest above its usual one, and a threshold on dsnr means the same in both products. It suits places with very different usual movement (a field that changes crop every year next to a forest that does not):

    events = zeit.extract_events(change, sort_by="dsnr")
strong = events.where(events.dsnr >= 4)          # moves at least 4 times the pixel's usual one

Then check the result as any change map, with a sample and error-adjusted areas: Accuracy & Area.

docs.title: Compare with the classic algorithms
docs.text:
agree = zeit.agreement({
    "tessera": zeit.extract_events(zeit.embedding_change(emb), min_magnitude=0.3),
    "alphaearth": zeit.extract_events(zeit.embedding_change(aef), min_magnitude=0.2),
    "landtrendr": zeit.extract_events(zeit.landtrendr(ndvi), min_magnitude=2000),
}, tolerance=1)
The first year that shows each pixel's largest change, 2017–2025, by the two embedding products and by LandTrendr on annual Landsat NDVI (losses only, put on the 10 m grid). The same clearings come out in all three, with the same years: the large block of the bottom centre in 2022, the patches of the left in 2019–2021.

On this box, with the thresholds above:

Pair Pixels where both find a change ... and agree on its year (± 1) AlphaEarth and LandTrendr 15,042 12,664 (84%) TESSERA and LandTrendr 19,449 14,869 (76%) AlphaEarth and TESSERA 17,040 14,575 (86%)

The maps also differ, and for reasons worth knowing. LandTrendr was asked for losses of NDVI only; the embeddings find any change, so changes inside fields (the dark block on the right of TESSERA's map is a field in every year, and changed in 2025) show up in them and not in LandTrendr. LandTrendr works on 30 m Landsat pixels, so its map is grainier, and its record starts in 1985: its losses of 2017 (light yellow) happened between the 2016 and 2017 images, before the first embedding, so the embeddings cannot see them. And TESSERA, at 0.3, flags more pixels than AlphaEarth at 0.2, among them small edges and field margins: a higher threshold, or min_dsnr, makes it stricter.

docs.title: Embeddings of your own cube
docs.text: TESSERA and AlphaEarth are made once a year, for the years they cover. zeit.ai.presto_embeddings makes embeddings from a cube you have, of any period of up to 24 dates (monthly composites of Sentinel-2 and/or Sentinel-1, ERA5, SRTM), with the pretrained Presto encoder: 128 dimensions per pixel, tagged as Presto's, and everything on this page takes them as it takes TESSERA's.

docs.title: Earth Engine, local copies, versions
docs.text:
• AlphaEarth comes by default from its open copy on Source Cooperative: free, no account, no quota. backend="gee" reads it from the GOOGLE/SATELLITE_EMBEDDING/V1/ANNUAL collection of Earth Engine instead (start a session with zeit.gee.auth.initialize_gee()), which counts against the account's quota; each year is downloaded once into cache_dir.
  • store= reads a copy of either product: a TESSERA Zarr store (a local one needs no geotessera), or a folder with AlphaEarth's aef_index.parquet and its COGs.
  • version=/variant= choose a TESSERA run (default v1.1, the complete global one) and depth= the first dimensions of a v2 store (Matryoshka embeddings, trained to work truncated).
  • From the shell: zeit embeddings ./out --source tessera --bbox -63 -10 -62.9 -9.9 --years 2018-2024 (CLI).

docs.title: Cite
docs.text: TESSERA: Feng et al. (2025), TESSERA: Temporal Embeddings of Surface Spectra for Earth Representation and Analysis, arXiv:2506.20380 (embeddings and weights CC0; the authors ask to be cited). AlphaEarth: Brown et al. (2025), AlphaEarth Foundations: An embedding field model for accurate and efficient global mapping from sparse label data, arXiv:2507.22291; the dataset is CC-BY 4.0 and requires the attribution "The AlphaEarth Foundations Satellite Embedding dataset is produced by Google and Google DeepMind." Both are in the cube's attributes.

docs.title: Monitoring with EWMACD
docs.text:
EWMACD watches every observation of a pixel with a control chart, the tool factories use to notice when a machine drifts. A harmonic model learns the pixel's normal seasonal cycle from a few stable years. After them, the chart follows how far each new observation falls from the model, and it signals when the departures add up. Because it works date by date, it takes irregular, cloudy Landsat series as they are, without compositing, and it catches subtle, lasting changes such as thinning as well as clear-cuts.

AnswersSince when has this pixel left its normal behaviour, how far, and has it come back? InputEvery observation of one index, irregular dates welcome: (time, y, x) OutputThe flags of every date; maps of the first disturbance, its severity, the recovery, the first gain and the state at the last date ReferenceBrooks et al. (2014), IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing 52(6)

What EWMACD produces. Two real pixels of the sample data of Brooks et al. (2014): the tasseled cap angle index of loblolly pine stands in Alabama, 51 Landsat dates from 2005 to 2011. Top: the observations and the harmonic model fitted on the training years (shaded); hollow dots are training dates screened out as clouds or shadows. Bottom: the EWMA of the residuals and its control limits. Orange dots are dates flagged as disturbed. Left: a drop from early 2009, deepest in August 2010, back within the limits in December 2010. Right: a sharp drop in February 2010, most likely a harvest, still far below the model in October 2011.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Learn the normal cycle. For each pixel, a constant plus order (2) sine and cosine pairs of the day of the year is fitted to the observations of the training years. Dates more than xbar_train (1.5) standard deviations from this first fit are dropped as clouds and shadows (a Shewhart X-bar chart), and the model is fitted again without them.
  2. Compute the residuals. Every date gets its residual: observation minus model. After the training years, only gross anomalies, beyond xbar_monitor (20) standard deviations, are dropped, so that real changes stay in.
  3. Smooth them in a control chart. The exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) of the residuals, z = (1 - lmbda) * z_previous + lmbda * residual, remembers the recent dates, so that a small shift that lasts adds up while a single odd date fades. Its control limits are sigmas (3) standard deviations of the EWMA, from the training residuals.
  4. Flag. Each date's flag is the EWMA divided by its limit, truncated: 0 inside the limits, -1, -2... for a loss of one, two... limits, and positive values for a gain. A signal must last persistence (3) dates to count.

From the flags after the training years come the maps: the first disturbance, its severity, the date it came back, the first gain, and the state at the last date.

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text: The data are the sample data of the paper, a 65 x 64 pixel stack of the tasseled cap angle index (x 1000) over loblolly pine stands in Alabama, USA (Virginia Tech data repository). Its 51 dates are uneven: 11 in 2006, 4 in 2007 and 4 in 2011.

docs.title: 1. Load every date
docs.text:
import zeit

cube = zeit.load_raster("ewmacd_sample/angle_*.tif")   # one GeoTIFF per date, the date in the name
cube.sizes                                              # time: 51, y: 64, x: 65

The download is a single stack with its dates in a CSV file. Give them to load_raster:

import pandas as pd

t = pd.read_csv("Temporal Distribution with DOY.csv")
dates = pd.to_datetime(dict(year=t.Year, month=t.Month, day=t.Day))
cube = zeit.load_raster("Sample Data - Angle Index x1000 Stack.tif", dates=dates)

Use every observation, with the clouds masked as NaN, and do not composite: EWMACD needs the dates as they are. Any vegetation index works (NDVI, NBR, EVI); the paper uses the tasseled cap angle, atan(greenness / brightness).

docs.title: 2. Run EWMACD
docs.text:
The paper trains on 2005-2008 and monitors 2009-2011. train_end is the first year after the training period:

res = zeit.ewmacd(cube, train_end=2009)

list(res.data_vars)
# ['flags', 'break_time', 'severity', 'recovery_time', 'gain_time', 'state', 'sigma', 'rmse', 'r2', 'coefficients']

The 4,160 pixels take 40 ms. The training years must be stable: a pixel disturbed during them has a poor model and signals at once when monitoring starts.

docs.title: 3. Read the maps
docs.text:
Result of this tutorial. Left: the angle index on the last date; the pale patch, cleared in 2010, is most likely a harvest. Middle: the date of the first disturbance, for the pixels whose disturbance reached 3 control limits or more. Right: the state at the last date. Variable Meaning flags (time, y, x): the chart's flag at every date. 0 in control, negative a loss, positive a gain, in control limits. break_time The first disturbance after the training years, as a decimal year (NaN: none). severity Its most negative flag until it came back: -3 is three control limits below the model. recovery_time The first date back inside the limits (or above) after the disturbance. gain_time The first positive flag after the training years. state At the last date: 0 stable, 1 disturbed, 2 recovered (disturbed, then back), 3 gain. sigma, rmse, r2 The training residuals' standard deviation behind the limits, and the model's fit. coefficients (coefficient, y, x): the harmonic model's constant, sines and cosines. 
names = res.state.attrs["flag_meanings"].split()   # ['stable', 'disturbed', 'recovered', 'gain']
res.state.to_series().value_counts()               # 0: 888, 1: 636, 2: 1648, 3: 988

severe = res.break_time.where(res.severity <= -3)  # the map in the middle
zeit.save_raster(res[["break_time", "severity", "state"]], "results/ewmacd")

The maps show how sensitive the method is. 2,284 pixels (55%) have a first disturbance, and 82% of them start in the first months of 2009: half of the scene drifts below its model in the spring of 2009, by one or two limits, and most of it comes back (57% of these pixels within 2009, 86% by 2011). That is why so many pixels are "recovered" at the last date. It is a weak, widespread signal, more likely weather than management. The severe changes are fewer: 15% of the pixels have a first disturbance of severity 3 or more, grouped in stands, and 5% are at -3 or less on the last date, most of them in the harvest (85% of them have an angle index below 450 in October 2011, against a median of 574 over the scene). Filter on severity, as in the middle map, to keep the clear changes.

The pixels in gain (24%) have an index that stays above their training model, as a young stand that keeps growing would.

docs.title: 4. Look at one pixel's chart
docs.text:
With one pixel's series, the result also has the chart itself, date by date: ewma, limit and fitted (the model).

px = zeit.ewmacd(cube.isel(y=39, x=50), train_end=2009)   # the harvested pixel, right in the first figure
float(px.break_time), int(px.severity), int(px.state)     # (2010.13, -10, 1)

(px.ewma / px.limit).plot.line("o")                       # out of control beyond -1 and 1

ewma and limit are NaN on the dates that were screened out of the chart. Those dates carry the flag of the date before.

docs.title: Other inputs
docs.text:
The same function takes a raster on disk, a numpy array or a single pixel (all inputs):

# many GeoTIFFs, read and computed block by block
res = zeit.ewmacd("landsat_ndvi/*.tif", train_end=2017, chunks="auto")
zeit.save_raster(res[["break_time", "severity", "state"]], "results/ewmacd")

# one pixel's series: a pandas Series indexed by date, or values with dates=
px = zeit.ewmacd(series, train_end=2017)
px = zeit.ewmacd(values, train_end=2017, dates=dates)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect train_end required The first year after the training period. The model is fitted on the years before it. train_start first year Dates before it are left out. order 2 Sine and cosine pairs of the harmonic model. lmbda 0.3 Weight of each new residual in the EWMA, in (0, 1]. Lower: a slower, smoother chart, more weight on lasting shifts. 1 charts each date on its own. sigmas 3.0 The control limits, in standard deviations of the EWMA. Higher: fewer and later signals. persistence 3 Dates a signal must last. Counted in dates, not in time: in a cloudy year, 3 dates can span months. xbar_train 1.5 Training dates beyond this many standard deviations are screened out of the model. xbar_monitor 20.0 Later dates beyond this many standard deviations are screened as anomalies. Raise it for smooth series (see below). low None Values not above it are missing: fill values, water, bare soil.

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• Expect short false signals with the defaults. Screening the training dates at 1.5 standard deviations makes sigma smaller than the noise, so the limits are tight: the chart sees small changes, and it also signals briefly on noise. On a synthetic series of stable forest (Gaussian noise only, 145 dates, example 24), 24% of the pixels got a short signal with the defaults, nearly all of -1; 4% with persistence=6, none with persistence=12; 6% with sigmas=4 or xbar_train=2.5. With each of these settings, a thinning that lowered the index by twice the noise was still found in every pixel, a median of one or two months after it. Brooks' later scripts use half the dates of a year as the persistence.
  • Mask clouds before. Missing dates are fine. A dark date that the cloud mask missed is not: after the training years, only residuals beyond xbar_monitor are screened, and a cloud shadow is often less than that. It enters the EWMA and weighs on it for several dates (with lmbda=0.3, 70% of it remains on the next date). Mask with the QA band, or with Tmask.
  • Raise xbar_monitor for smooth series. A clear-cut larger than 20 standard deviations of a very quiet pixel is screened as an anomaly until it comes back within them, which delays the detection.
  • Check the training years. A pixel disturbed during them signals at once after them, and its r2 is low.
  • Read severity, not only break_time. The first disturbance can be a flag of -1. The deeper and longer ones are the changes worth mapping.

About this implementation

The flags are those of Brooks' EWMACD v1.3.0 R script, the paper's own; Earth Engine has the method as ee.Algorithms.TemporalSegmentation.Ewmacd. With persistence=1 they were checked date by date on synthetic series and on 400 pixels of the sample data used here. With more persistence, the first disturbance is the same, and a few later dates differ where the script, which means to keep the previous lasting state, reads another date's flag. Values not above low are missing from the start, whereas the script still fits them in its first regression. On 10,000 pixels and 71 dates, the script takes 2.8 s, and Zeit 55 ms on one thread and 7 ms on 19. See Against the Original Implementations.

For a regular series and a statistical test of the break, see BFAST Monitor. For degradation in the tropics from the fractions of each observation, see CODED.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Brooks, E. B., Wynne, R. H., Thomas, V. A., Blinn, C. E., & Coulston, J. W. (2014). On-the-fly massively multitemporal change detection using statistical quality control charts and Landsat data. IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing, 52(6), 3316–3332. doi:10.1109/TGRS.2013.2272545
  • Sample data and the EWMACD R script: Brooks, E. B., Virginia Tech. doi:10.7294/W4WD3XHK

docs.title: FORCE's Time Series Analysis Chain
docs.text:
FORCE's higher-level time series analysis turns an irregular, cloudy index series into a regular one, summarizes it by year and season, and reads trends and changes from the summaries. Zeit has each step as a function, on any cube, in memory or dask: interpolate, spectral-temporal metrics, folds, trend, change-aftereffect-trend and clear-observation statistics.

AnswersWhat does this pixel's year look like, is it trending, when did it lose most, and how well was it observed? InputOne index with clouds as NaN: (time, rows, cols), any spacing OutputA regular series, metrics by period, a trend and a change map, and gap statistics ReferencePorted from FORCE's TSA (Frantz 2019); RBF: Schwieder et al. (2016); STM: Müller et al. (2015); CAT: Hird et al. (2016); CSO: Ernst et al. (2018); polar metrics: Brooks et al. (2020)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
FORCE's chain, and the Zeit function of each step:

Step FORCE Zeit Regular series every N days TSI (RBF, linear, moving average, harmonic) zeit.interpolate Statistics of the series STM zeit.temporal_metrics Statistics by year, quarter, month, week or day FBY, FBQ, FBM, FBW, FBD temporal_metrics(..., by=) Z-score or centering STANDARDIZE zeit.standardize Linear trend of a fold TRY, TRQ, TRM, TRW, TRD zeit.linear_trend Greatest change, and the trend around it CAY, CAQ, CAM, CAW, CAD zeit.cat Clear observations and the gaps between them CSO zeit.clear_observations Land surface phenology: dates, values, integrals and rates of each season POL (and TRO, CAO of each metric) zeit.polar_metrics

The folds are the link: the yearly mean of the interpolated series is a short series of its own, and linear_trend and cat take it along its year axis.

docs.title: 1. A cloudy NDVI series
docs.text:
The example builds its own data: five years of NDVI every 5 days on a 40 × 40 grid, with a season, a slow greening, noise and 35% of the observations lost to clouds. The 10 first rows lose their vegetation in July 2020.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
import zeit

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
dates = pd.date_range("2018-01-01", "2022-12-31", freq="5D")
ny = nx = 40
doy = dates.dayofyear.values[:, None, None]
year = (dates.year.values - 2018)[:, None, None]

ndvi = 0.55 + 0.25 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (doy - 110) / 365.25) + 0.01 * year
ndvi = ndvi + rng.normal(0, 0.03, (len(dates), ny, nx))
cut = (dates >= "2020-07-01")[:, None, None] & (np.arange(ny)[None, :, None] < 10)
ndvi = np.where(cut, ndvi - 0.3, ndvi)
ndvi[rng.random(ndvi.shape) < 0.35] = np.nan                       # clouds

ndvi = xr.DataArray(ndvi.astype("float32"), dims=("time", "y", "x"), name="ndvi",
                    coords={"time": dates, "y": np.arange(ny), "x": np.arange(nx)})

With real data, ndvi = zeit.load_raster("ndvi_stack.tif") gives the same thing (and chunks="auto" keeps it lazy).

docs.title: 2. Interpolate every 16 days
docs.text:
tsi = zeit.interpolate(ndvi, "rbf", step=16)        # (time, y, x): 114 dates, no gaps

The RBF ensemble (Gaussian kernels of 8, 16 and 32 days) fills the gaps from the observations around each date. The grid is FORCE's: from the first date, every 16 days, up to the last. The other methods are "linear", "moving" and "harmonic"; the harmonic can be fit to part of the series and predict the rest (fit=("2018-01-01", "2019-12-31")), the near-real-time mode.

docs.title: 3. Spectral-temporal metrics and folds
docs.text:
stm = zeit.temporal_metrics(tsi, ["p10", "median", "p90", "std"])  # (metric, y, x)
yearly = zeit.temporal_metrics(tsi, ["mean"], by="year")           # (metric, year, y, x)

by takes "year", "quarter", "month", "week" or "doy". skew, kurtosis, iqr, range and count are metrics too. To compare each year with the others, zeit.standardize(yearly, dim="year").

docs.title: 4. Trend and change over the yearly folds
docs.text:
trend = zeit.linear_trend(yearly)                   # Dataset: slope, sig, rsq, ...
greening = trend.sig == 1
browning = trend.sig == -1

change = zeit.cat(yearly, penalty=True)             # Dataset: change, change_time, after_slope, ...
change.change_time.isel(y=0, x=0).item()            # 2020.0: the year of the greatest loss

slope is NDVI per year, because the series has one value per year. sig is 1, -1 or 0 at 95% (conf=). cat finds the greatest loss between consecutive years, then fits the trend to the whole series (total_*), before the loss (before_*) and from it on (after_*): a recovery shows as a positive after_slope. With penalty=True, a dip the series recovers from next year counts for less.

docs.title: 5. How well was it observed?
docs.text:
cso = zeit.clear_observations(ndvi, months=3, metrics=["count", "max"])    # (metric, window, y, x)
cso.sel(metric="count").mean(("y", "x"))            # clear observations per quarter
cso.sel(metric="max").mean(("y", "x"))              # the longest gap, in days

Each window is a quarter; the gaps run from the window's start to the first clear observation, between them, and from the last to the window's end. A cube of booleans (ndvi.notnull()) works too. Low counts and long gaps tell where the interpolation, and the metrics built on it, are least reliable.

docs.title: 6. Polar phenology metrics, and the trend of the start of the season
docs.text:
pol = zeit.polar_metrics(tsi, ["DSS", "DES", "VPS", "IGS"])   # (metric, year, y, x)
pol.sel(metric="DSS").mean(("y", "x"))                       # day of the year each season starts
sos = zeit.linear_trend(pol.sel(metric="DSS"))               # days per year: slope, sig, ...

Each date of the interpolated series is a vector (the NDVI as the radius, the day of the year as the angle); the mean vector gives the time of least activity, which starts the phenological year, and the values accumulated along each season give its start (DSS, 20% of the total), middle and end (DES, 80%). metrics takes any of the 39 FORCE names: dates, lengths, values, amplitudes, integrals and rates. With 5 years of data there are 4 seasons, so one year at an end of the series is NaN (here 2022, which has no complete season). The result has a year axis, so linear_trend and cat take one metric along it directly: sos.slope is the change of the start of the season in days per year (a positive slope is a later start), and with so few seasons sos.sig should be read before the slope. The series must be regular, which is what interpolate(..., step=16) gives.

Save the maps

The results are DataArrays and Datasets on the cube's grid: zeit.save_raster(trend, "results/trend") writes one GeoTIFF per variable, and zeit.save_raster(stm, ...) one per metric.

docs.title: Differences from FORCE
docs.text:
• Floats, not int16. FORCE scales its outputs by 10000 and rounds; Zeit returns floats (rsq from 0 to 1, kurtosis as is). Rounded, the values equal FORCE's to within 1 in all the comparisons below.
  • Student's t is exact. FORCE iterates Hill's approximation for the critical value of the trend's test; Zeit tables the exact quantile.
  • The CAT penalty is corrected. FORCE compares a candidate's penalized drop with the best one's unpenalized drop; Zeit compares penalized with penalized.
  • CSO over k intervals, and the last window. FORCE mixes the number of observations with the number of intervals in its standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis and quantiles, and drops the last window when it starts in the month the range ends in; Zeit takes every statistic over the same intervals and keeps the window.
  • Constant series. skew and kurtosis are NaN where FORCE leaves them undefined.
  • Polar metrics. The dates count from 1 January of each season's year (FORCE counts continuous days from the first year's), so a trend along year is the change per year; what FORCE leaves undefined and writes as 0 (a season whose total is zero) is NaN; DPV is 0 without adaptive, where FORCE writes -DPY.
  • A harmonic pixel that does not converge. The robust fit can cycle without settling; such a pixel is left out of the comparison with FORCE.
Validation

Against FORCE 3.11.00 on 10,000 pixels, the metrics, folds, standardization, linear and moving interpolation and the harmonic fit to part of the series are equal; the RBF and the full harmonic are within 1 of FORCE's int16, and the 39 polar metrics are equal. See Against the Original Implementations.

docs.title: Google Earth Engine
docs.text:
Let Google's servers do the heavy preparation (Landsat sensor harmonisation, cloud masking and compositing) and download a ready-to-use time series as GeoTIFFs. This is the quickest way to get the annual stacks LandTrendr needs.

DoesHarmonise Landsat 5/7/8/9, mask clouds, composite, download AreaWRS-2 path/row, Sentinel-2 tile, bbox, vector or raster file OutputOne GeoTIFF per composite, on a shared pixel grid NeedsAn Earth Engine account and a Google Cloud project

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Earth Engine requires the user to authenticate their machine with Google Cloud Project (GCP) credentials that have API access enabled. Every time you attempt a download, the download_gee_timeseries function handles this initialization. If your credentials expire or do not exist, a browser window will open prompting you to log in.

Note

Make sure the Google account has access to Earth Engine, and pass your Google Cloud project with project="your-project".

docs.title: Choosing the area (roi)
docs.text:
You never need to build Earth Engine objects yourself. The roi argument accepts local, offline inputs, and zeit converts them internally:

roi = "217/076"                              # a Landsat WRS-2 path/row: the tile's footprint
roi = "23KPQ"                                # a Sentinel-2 (MGRS) tile id, computed offline ('T23KPQ' also works)
roi = [-43.6, -23.1, -43.1, -22.6]           # a bounding box [min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat]
roi = "data/study_area.shp"                  # a vector file: Shapefile, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KML...
roi = "data/reference_image.tif"             # a raster file: its extent
roi = geopandas.read_file("area.gpkg")       # an in-memory GeoDataFrame (or a shapely geometry)

Files in any CRS are reprojected to lon/lat. For vector and raster inputs, the download covers their bounding box. To keep only the pixels inside a polygon, mask the result locally afterwards, for example with rasterio.mask.

Sentinel-2 tiles follow the MGRS grid: 109.8 km × 109.8 km squares in the tile's UTM zone, overlapping their neighbours by 9.8 km. zeit computes the footprint from the id alone, with no Earth Engine lookup. The calculation matches real Sentinel-2 scene footprints to within about 50 m. Tiles that straddle the 180° meridian can't be expressed as a lon/lat box and raise an error; pass a bbox for one side instead.

Landsat WRS-2 path/rows are looked up from a Landsat Collection 2 scene on that path/row, which takes one quick Earth Engine query.

What about Sentinel-1?

Sentinel-1 has no fixed tiling grid equivalent to WRS-2 or MGRS. Its relative orbit (1–175) and pass direction (ascending/descending) identify a ground track, not an area. The GRD slices in Earth Engine are not cut at the same places from one acquisition to the next. ESA's stable burst IDs exist only for SLC products, which Earth Engine doesn't provide. For a Sentinel-1 area, use a Sentinel-2 tile id, a bounding box or a vector file.

docs.title: Downloading: method="auto" (default)
docs.text:
For most areas you don't need to choose a method. With the default method='auto', zeit plans each image before downloading it and picks the fastest route that will work:

  • Direct tiled download for images up to max_direct_mb (4 GB raw by default). zeit fixes a single pixel grid for the whole region, splits it into tiles sized in bytes rather than degrees, and fetches them concurrently with ee.data.computePixels. Each tile is written straight into its place in the output GeoTIFF, so tiles line up exactly with no seams and there is no mosaicking step. Tiles are split in space first; deep stacks such as a 'dense' time series with hundreds of bands are also split by band, so they stay under Earth Engine's per-request limits (32 MB, 1024 bands).
  • Google Drive export (see Large areas) for images above that size, or when a tile hits an Earth Engine interactive compute limit (user memory limit, computation timeout), which retrying the same request cannot fix.

Concurrency adapts to your account. Earth Engine limits concurrent interactive requests per account (about 40 on a standard tier, only 2–3 for a project in noncommercial Restricted Mode). zeit starts with 4 concurrent requests, ramps up while requests succeed, and halves on every HTTP 429, so it settles just under whatever limit your account actually has.

from zeit.gee import download_gee_timeseries

# Bounding box [min_lon, min_lat, max_lon, max_lat]
my_roi = [-47.95, -15.85, -47.85, -15.75]

download_gee_timeseries(
    roi=my_roi,
    start_date='2010-01-01',
    end_date='2020-12-31',
    out_dir='./gee_direct_data',
    method='auto',             # default: direct tiled download, Drive export when needed
    composite_type='annual',   # Generates LandTrendr-style Annual Medoid Composites
    project='my-gcp-project'   # Replace with your Google Cloud Project ID
)

To download a single ee.Image you built yourself, use download_gee_image directly. It accepts the same method and exposes the tuning knobs:

from zeit.gee.downloader import download_gee_image

download_gee_image(
    image, roi, 'out.tif',
    scale=30,
    crs='EPSG:4326',           # or a projected CRS such as 'EPSG:32723'
    sub_tile_workers=16,       # upper bound on concurrent requests (adapts downward on 429)
    max_tile_mb=None,          # cap per tile request (default 32 MB); tiles are sized on the fly
)

Masked pixels are written with the GeoTIFF nodata value Earth Engine uses for the output type (-inf for float, the type minimum for signed integers, 0 for unsigned). You can force either route with method='direct' or method='drive'.

docs.title: Indices and spectral temporal metrics
docs.text:
Earth Engine computes whatever you ask on its own servers, so you can download indices instead of bands, and per-year statistics instead of every observation.

Indices instead of bands. Pass index names in indices: NDVI, EVI, SAVI, kNDVI, NBR, NDMI, NDWI, MNDWI and NDFI (from Earth Engine's unmix), alone or mixed with SR bands. They are computed on surface reflectance (the Collection 2 digital numbers scaled by 2.75e-05 and offset by −0.2), on the medoid for 'annual' and on every observation for 'dense'. One index is one sixth of the six-band download.

Spectral temporal metrics (composite_type='stm') summarize a whole year in a few bands per index: each index is computed on every clear observation, then reduced over the year on Earth Engine with one combined reducer. Choose the statistics with metrics: median, mean, std, min, max, iqr (p75 − p25), count (clear observations) or any percentile such as p10.

from zeit.gee import download_gee_timeseries

download_gee_timeseries(
    roi="23KPQ",
    start_date="2015-01-01",
    end_date="2024-12-31",
    out_dir="./stm",
    composite_type="stm",
    indices=["NDVI", "NBR", "SR_B6"],           # indices and SR bands
    metrics=["median", "p10", "p90", "iqr"],
    project="my-gcp-project",
)
# -> ./stm/landsat_stm_2015.tif ... landsat_stm_2024.tif,
#    12 bands each: NDVI_median, NDVI_p10, NDVI_p90, NDVI_iqr, NBR_median, ...

Each year is the calendar year inside start_date–end_date. To summarize one season, run one call per year with that season's dates. The band names and order match zeit.build_spectral_temporal_metrics (the STAC version), so models trained on one source can be applied to the other. Both take what to summarize in indices. Earth Engine's percentile reducer is not guaranteed to interpolate exactly like NumPy, so percentiles can differ slightly from the STAC version.

To build metrics on a collection of your own, use zeit.gee.compute_stm(collection, indices, metrics). It returns the ee.Image to pass to download_gee_image.

The indices argument was called bands up to zeit 0.25. bands= still works, with a deprecation warning.

Indices from zeit 0.25 and earlier

zeit 0.25 and earlier computed indices on the raw Collection 2 digital numbers, which carry a large offset (reflectance 0 is DN 7273). That compressed normalized differences towards zero (an NDVI of 0.71 came out as 0.33) and made EVI meaningless. Download index composites made with those versions again.

docs.title: Large areas: export to Google Drive
docs.text:
For state-level or national-scale analyses, downloading data directly over the internet in real-time might fail due to API payload limits or simply take too long.

In these cases, pass method='drive'. The zeit package will set up everything and dispatch a Task directly to Google's servers. Google will silently process and save the final file in the cloud inside your Google Drive, under the Zeit_Downloads folder.

from zeit.gee import download_gee_timeseries

# Example: Bounding box of a larger region
state_roi = [-53.11, -25.31, -44.15, -19.78]

download_gee_timeseries(
    roi=state_roi, 
    start_date='1985-01-01',
    end_date='2022-12-31', 
    out_dir='./data',  # Used only to name the files in Drive for this method
    method='drive',    # Initiates asynchronous export
    composite_type='annual',
    project='my-gcp-project'
)

# The terminal will display a message similar to:
# [landsat_medoid_1985] Task sent to Google Drive (Task ID: ABCD123456).

docs.title: Worked example: a full Landsat tile, 1985–2025, ready for LandTrendr
docs.text:
This is the complete path from "I have a WRS-2 path/row" to LandTrendr disturbance maps, all through zeit. It uses no Earth Engine objects in your code and needs no local satellite data.

LandTrendr works on one spectral index per year. NBR is the standard choice for forest loss. The pipeline has three steps: download the annual composites as NBR, read the yearly files as one cube, then run LandTrendr out-of-core and write the event maps.

import zeit
from zeit.gee import download_gee_timeseries

# 1. Annual Landsat 5/7/8/9 medoid composites -> NBR, one file per year
download_gee_timeseries(
    roi="217/076",                   # WRS-2 path/row (Rio de Janeiro); or a bbox / .shp / .gpkg / .tif
    start_date="1985-01-01",
    end_date="2025-12-31",
    out_dir="./lt_rj/annual",
    composite_type="annual",
    indices=["NBR"],                 # index computed on the medoid, which is selected on all 6 SR bands
    project="my-gcp-project",
)
# -> ./lt_rj/annual/landsat_medoid_1985.tif ... landsat_medoid_2025.tif

# 2. The yearly files as one (time, y, x) cube: the years come from the file names,
#    masked pixels (-inf) become NaN, and chunks= keeps it lazy (the tile is ~10 GB)
nbr = zeit.load_raster("./lt_rj/annual", chunks="auto")

# 3. LandTrendr and the event maps, computed block by block while they are written
lt = zeit.landtrendr(nbr, direction="loss", max_segments=6)   # an NBR drop is a disturbance
loss = zeit.extract_events(lt)
zeit.save_raster(loss, "./lt_rj/results")                     # yod.tif, magnitude.tif, ...

Three details that matter for LandTrendr

  1. -inf → NaN. Downloaded GeoTIFFs mark masked pixels (clouds, no scene that year) with the nodata value -inf. load_raster reads them as NaN, which LandTrendr treats as a missing year. If you read the files another way, convert them yourself.
  2. nodata. For float data like this NBR, zeit.landtrendr's default (nodata="auto") treats only NaN and the raster's NoData as missing, so pixels whose NBR is exactly 0 are kept. For integer stacks without a NoData value, 0 is treated as missing; pass nodata=None if 0 is a valid value there.
  3. 2012 has gaps. Landsat 5 stopped in November 2011 and Landsat 8 started in April 2013, so 2012 relies on Landsat 7 SLC-off alone and has striping gaps. LandTrendr tolerates missing years (min_observations_needed=6 by default), so this is expected, not an error.

Resuming. A download never leaves a partial file at its final path, so re-running the same call is safe. For fine-grained control, loop over the years yourself with download_gee_image and skip years whose file already exists. The composites come from zeit.gee.composites.create_annual_medoid on the collection from zeit.gee.harmonization.get_harmonized_collection: Landsat 5, 7, 8 and 9 Collection 2 surface reflectance, cloud-masked, with Landsat 5/7's bands renamed as Landsat 8/9's and no adjustment between the sensors (Collection 2 is used across them as it comes; up to 1.3, Landsat 8/9 were rescaled by a few percent with coefficients of no known source).

Tile extent. For roi="217/076", zeit looks up the tile's footprint from a Landsat Collection 2 scene and downloads its bounding box, about 2.2° × 2.0° (~8,070 × 7,330 px at 30 m). Scenes from neighbouring paths/rows that overlap the box are also used, which fills the box corners and adds observations in the overlap zones.

docs.title: How long will a download take?
docs.text:
Time is dominated by Earth Engine's server-side compute, not by your connection or CPU. Two factors decide it: how many pixels you request, and how many concurrent requests your account is allowed.

Account state Concurrent interactive requests Standard tier (paid or noncommercial within quota) about 40 Noncommercial project in Restricted Mode (quota exceeded) about 2

zeit discovers the limit on its own. It starts with 4 concurrent requests, ramps up to sub_tile_workers while requests succeed, and backs off on every HTTP 429. You'll see EE throttled concurrency: finished at 2/16 concurrent requests when the account is limited. When Earth Engine initializes, it prints a warning if your project is in Restricted Mode.

Times below are for annual medoid composites on WRS-2 217/076 (year 2020). The rows marked measured were timed on a Restricted Mode account; everything else is extrapolated from them. Years before 1999 have only Landsat 5 and compute faster, so treat totals as orders of magnitude:

Area Content Restricted Mode (~2 concurrent) Standard tier (estimated, 16 concurrent) 0.5° × 0.5° (~3.5 M px) 1 index (NBR) ~27 s / year (measured) → ~20 min for 41 years ~3–5 min 0.5° × 0.5° 6 SR bands ~77 s / year (measured) → ~50 min ~8–15 min Sentinel-2 tile 23KPQ (~15 M px) 1 index (NBR) ~2.5 min / year (measured) → ~1.5 h ~15–25 min Full WRS-2 tile 217/076 (~59 M px) 1 index (NBR) ~13 min / year (measured) → ~6–9 h ~1–2 h Full WRS-2 tile 6 SR bands ~35 min / year → ~1 day ~3–6 h

The standard-tier column assumes Earth Engine throughput scales 4–8× from 2 to 16 concurrent requests. It was not measured.

Making large downloads faster

  • Download the index, not the bands. A single NBR band is ~3× faster than 6 SR bands, and it is all LandTrendr needs.
  • Standard-tier accounts can raise concurrency. Call download_gee_image directly with sub_tile_workers=32 (up to ~40). download_gee_timeseries uses the default of 16.
  • Don't run several downloads in parallel. They all share the account-wide concurrency limit and just throttle each other.
  • For a full tile on a restricted account, consider the Drive export. download_gee_timeseries_drive submits all years at once as batch tasks, which Earth Engine computes in parallel server-side. Turnaround then depends on the batch queue, from tens of minutes to hours.

Once downloaded, the local part is fast. LandTrendr on a full tile with 41 years runs in about 1.6 minutes on a 20-thread desktop (see Performance & Scaling).

docs.title: Output format
docs.text:
Each image arrives as one GeoTIFF. The tiles it is fetched in are written directly into their place in that file, so there is nothing to mosaic afterwards. download_gee_timeseries writes one such file per year. Stacking the years into a single multi-band file for LandTrendr is the one manual step (see the worked example).

Every file written by the direct download has:

  • The same pixel grid for every year. The grid is fixed from the ROI and snapped to multiples of the resolution, so the annual files stack without resampling. The default CRS is EPSG:4326 with 30 m converted to degrees at the equator, as Earth Engine does. Pass crs="EPSG:32723" (for example) to download_gee_image for a metric grid.
  • Named bands (SR_B2 … SR_B7, or the index names) stored as band descriptions.
  • Nodata equal to the value Earth Engine uses for masked pixels: -inf for float, the type minimum for signed integers, 0 for unsigned.
  • A tiled, LZW-compressed GeoTIFF (BigTIFF when needed), written atomically: it appears at its final path only once every tile has arrived.

docs.title: What happens on the server
docs.text:
When using composite_type='annual' (the current zeit default for LandTrendr integration):

  1. Sensor Fusion: The function fetches Landsat 5, 7, 8, and 9 collections (Surface Reflectance Collection 2).
  2. Harmonization: Values from Landsat 8 and 9 (OLI) are mathematically converted to their ETM+ equivalents using coefficients from Roy et al. (2016) (see References). This ensures a perfect time series, free from sensor biases.
  3. Cloud Masking: The QA_PIXEL quality assurance band is used to filter out dense clouds and shadows across all images.
  4. Medoid Compositing: Instead of a simple median, we apply the Medoid geometric strategy to find the actual real-world pixel that best represents the season (a standard approach in eMapR/LandTrendr workflows).
  5. Download planning: The ROI's bounding box gets one pixel grid, and one request asks for the band names and data types. The image is then fetched as tiles with ee.data.computePixels, each sized on the fly as remaining work divided by the concurrency Earth Engine currently allows (between 4 and 32 MB). Tiles are split in space first, so a composite is never recomputed per band. Only deep stacks such as a 'dense' series are also split by band, to respect the 1024-band request limit.
  6. Automatic fallback: With method='auto', images larger than max_direct_mb (4 GB raw) go to a Drive export. So does any image whose tiles hit an Earth Engine interactive compute limit (user memory limit, computation timeout), which retrying the same request cannot fix.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • Roy, D. P., Kovalskyy, V., Zhang, H. K., Vermote, E. F., Yan, L., Kumar, S. S., & Egorov, A. (2016). Characterization of Landsat-7 to Landsat-8 reflective wavelength and normalized difference vegetation index continuity. Remote Sensing of Environment, 185, 57–70. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2015.12.024

docs.title: Emerging Hot Spots
docs.text:
Where do high values cluster, and is that cluster new, growing, steady or fading? Emerging hot spot analysis answers this for a cube of maps over time. For each date it asks whether a place and its neighbours are higher (a hot spot) or lower (a cold spot) than the rest. Then it reads the history of the answer and names the place's pattern: new, consecutive, intensifying, persistent, diminishing, sporadic, oscillating or historical.

AnswersWhere do high or low values cluster, and how did the clusters change over time? InputOne variable, one map per date (at least 3): (time, rows, cols). A count, a rate, a share or an index. OutputA pattern for every cell (17 classes), the Gi* of every date and the trend of that Gi* ReferenceGetis & Ord (1992); ESRI's Emerging Hot Spot Analysis; the Gi* of R sfdep

Result of this tutorial. 40 years of annual Landsat NDVI over a 50 km area of Rondônia, Brazil, as the share of each 300 m cell that is open land (NDVI below 0.7), 1985–2024. Left and middle: that share at the start and at the end. Right: the pattern of each cell. Red and orange cells are where open land clusters: in one run up to today (consecutive), or since before 1985 but less and less distinctly (diminishing). Blue cells are forest blocks: they stand out more every year as the land around them is cleared (intensifying cold spots). The numbered cells are plotted below. The analysis of the 167 × 168 cells × 40 years took 55 ms. Data: annual Landsat NDVI composites exported from LT-GEE on Google Earth Engine.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A hot spot at one date. For each cell, the Getis-Ord Gi* adds up the values of its neighbourhood (the cell itself among them) and compares the sum with what it would be if values were spread at random. The result is a z-score. Above 1.96 the neighbourhood is significantly high at the 5% level: a hot spot. Below −1.96 it is significantly low: a cold spot. One high cell among low neighbours is not a hot spot; a cluster of high cells is.
  2. A neighbourhood in space and time. radius sets the cells around (1: the 8 neighbours), and lag adds the same cells at the dates before (1: the previous date). Each date's Gi* is measured against that date's mean and spread (reference="date"), as in R's sfdep.
  3. The trend of the Gi. Each cell now has a series of z-scores, one per date. A Mann-Kendall test says whether it rises or falls significantly. By default this is the Hamed-Rao version, because consecutive Gi share neighbours and are autocorrelated.
  4. The pattern. The dates that are hot, the dates that are cold, the last date and the trend name the pattern, by the rules of ESRI's documentation:
Code Pattern The cell was… 1 new hot spot hot at the last date only. 2 consecutive hot spot hot in one unbroken run of dates that ends at the last date, and on less than 90% of the dates. 3 intensifying hot spot hot on at least 90% of the dates, the last one too, and its Gi* rises significantly. 4 persistent hot spot the same, with no significant trend. 5 diminishing hot spot the same, but its Gi* falls significantly. 6 sporadic hot spot hot at the last date, on and off before, and never cold. 7 oscillating hot spot hot at the last date, and cold at some date before. 8 historical hot spot hot on at least 90% of the dates, but not the last one. 0 no pattern none of these. −1 … −8 the cold spots the same rules with cold dates.

When two rules hold, the first in the table wins. Every rule but "historical" needs the last date to be hot (or cold). The patterns describe the clusters as they are at the end of the series. A cluster that was strong in 2003 and stopped in 2010 has no pattern unless it was hot on 90% of the dates.

The three numbered cells of the map. Top: the share of open land. Bottom: the Gi* of each year; the grey band is not significant. (1) Cleared before 1985 and still open, but the rest of the area caught up: hot every year, less and less distinctly, so diminishing. (2) Cleared around 2003: hot in one run from 2004 to the end, so consecutive. (3) Forest throughout: cold almost every year and more so as the area around it was cleared, so intensifying. The first year's Gi* is closer to 0 because the first date has no previous date to add to its neighbourhood.

docs.title: 1. Choose the variable and the cells
docs.text:
Emerging hot spot analysis was designed for counts of events in space-time bins: crimes per block per month, fires per cell per year. Raw pixels of an index are rarely the right input. Two choices go into the map above.

Cells, not pixels. A 30 m pixel is either cleared or not. Its 8 neighbours cover 90 m, much less than a clearing in Rondônia, where the settlement lots are a few hundred metres wide. The share of open land in 10 × 10 pixel cells (about 300 m) varies smoothly. With radius=1, each neighbourhood is then about 900 m across, the scale of the clearing process. It also turns 2.8 million pixels into 28,000 cells, 22,000 of them with data.

A smooth variable. Annual composites wobble from year to year: a dry year or some haze moves the NDVI of a whole region. That wobble makes the Gi* flip sign, and the patterns become sporadic and oscillating. With the raw NDVI, 40% of the cells get one of those four patterns. LandTrendr's fitted trajectories keep the clearings and drop the wobble, and with them only 10% do.

import zeit

ndvi = zeit.load_raster("LT_Stack_NDVI_Rondonia.tif")      # (time, y, x), NDVI x 10000, 1985-2024
lt = zeit.landtrendr(ndvi, fitted=True)                      # the fitted trajectory of every pixel

valid = lt.fitted.notnull()                                  # NaN where the stack has no data
open_land = (lt.fitted < 7000).where(valid)                  # 1 open land, 0 forest
share = open_land.coarsen(y=10, x=10, boundary="trim").mean() * 100        # % of each 300 m cell
n = valid.coarsen(y=10, x=10, boundary="trim").sum()
share = share.where(n >= 50)                                 # cells at least half covered by data

share is a (time, y, x) cube of 167 × 168 cells and 40 years, georeferenced like ndvi. Across the area, open land went from 12% in 1985 to 52% in 2005 and 66% in 2024.

docs.title: 2. Run the analysis
docs.text:
ehs = zeit.emerging_hotspots(share)           # radius=1, lag=1, reference="date"
Variable Meaning category (y, x) The pattern's code, from the table above. -128 where a cell has fewer than 3 dates.
