The names are in zeit.emerging_hotspots.PATTERNS. gi (time, y, x) The Gi* z-score of every cell and date. p (time, y, x) Its two-sided p-value. trend_z, trend_p, tau The trend test of each cell's Gi* series. n_hot, n_cold The number of dates the cell was a significant hot or cold spot.

The parameters that shape the result:

Parameter Default Effect radius 1 The neighbourhood in cells. With shape="square", the (2 radius + 1)² cells around: 1 is the 8 neighbours (queen contiguity). shape "square" "circle": the cells whose centres are within radius. lag 1 Dates before each date that are added to its neighbourhood. reference "date" "date": each date against its own mean and spread. "cube": against the whole cube's. See below. alpha 0.05 Significance of the Gi* and of its trend. trend "hamed_rao" The trend test of the Gi* series: "hamed_rao", "yue_wang" or "original" Mann-Kendall (what ESRI and sfdep use).

All parameters are in the API reference.

docs.title: 3. Read and save the map
docs.text:
In the map at the top:

Pattern Cells What it is here consecutive hot spot 20% Clusters cleared during the record and still open: the clearings of the 1990s and 2000s. intensifying cold spot 12% Forest blocks. They stay forest while the mean rises, so they are colder every year. diminishing hot spot 8% Clusters already open in 1985, along the main road and the first side roads. They are still open, but less exceptional every year. consecutive cold spot 7% Forest that only became significantly cold once enough land around it was cleared. sporadic hot or cold spot 9% Hot (or cold) at the end and on and off before: mostly cells at the edge of a cluster. no pattern 36% Not significant at the last date, and not hot or cold on 90% of the dates.

diminishing does not mean that less land was cleared in those cells. It means the cells are less exceptional than they were: the Gi* of a date is measured against that date's mean, and the mean rose. Read a pattern together with the values: a few series, as in the figure above, tell more than the class name.

names = zeit.emerging_hotspots.PATTERNS
ehs.category.zeit.plot()                                    # the legend names the patterns
fronts = ehs.category.isin([1, 2, 3])                      # new, consecutive, intensifying hot spots
zeit.save_raster(ehs.category, "results/hotspot_patterns.tif")
zeit.save_raster(ehs.gi, "results/gi.tif")                 # one band per date

docs.title: The reference and the lag change the answer
docs.text:
The same cube with three other settings:

Setting consecutive hot diminishing hot intensifying cold consecutive cold no pattern default: lag=1, reference="date" 20% 8% 12% 7% 36% lag=0 12% 6% 0% 16% 55% reference="cube" 56% 0% 2% 0% 24% radius=2, shape="circle" 20% 8% 13% 6% 34%

reference. With "date", a hot spot is high compared with the other places at that date. With "cube", it is high compared with every place and date of the cube. Here open land rose everywhere, so with "cube" most cells cleared at some point are above the 40-year mean at the end, and 56% of them become consecutive hot spots. Neither is wrong: "date" asks where clearing is concentrated at each date, "cube" asks where values are high in absolute terms. ArcGIS Pro makes the same choice with its "Define Global Window" parameter: its default, "Entire cube", is close to reference="cube", and "Individual time step" to reference="date" (sfdep's and Zeit's default).

lag. With lag=1, a date's Gi* sums the neighbourhood at that date and at the date before: 18 values instead of 9. A contrast that lasts gets more significant, which is why the forest blocks are cold on 90% of the dates with lag=1 (intensifying) but not with lag=0 (consecutive). The first date has no date before it, so its Gi* sums half as many values and is closer to 0. There is also a bias, the same as in sfdep. The values of the date before are measured against this date's mean. When the variable rises everywhere, the dates before sit below that mean and pull the Gi* down. Here open land rose by about 1.4 points a year against a spread of about 35 points between cells, so the bias is small, but on a fast-rising variable it is not. Use lag=0 or reference="cube" when that matters.

docs.title: Zeit, sfdep and ArcGIS
docs.text:
The Gi* of every cell and date is the same as R sfdep 0.2.5's (include_gi = TRUE, queen neighbours, k the lag) to 1e-14. The patterns are not always the same as sfdep's, for two reasons:

  • sfdep takes the significance of each Gi* from permutations (199 by default). Zeit takes it from the normal distribution of the Gi*, as ArcGIS Pro does (ArcGIS also corrects the p-values for the false discovery rate, which Zeit does not).
  • sfdep has rules of its own. For example, it can call a cell sporadic when the cell is not significant at the last date. Zeit follows the definitions of ESRI's documentation, given in the table above.

The permutations are also most of sfdep's time. On 50 × 50 cells and 12 dates, sfdep takes 13 minutes with 199 permutations (28 s with 9). Zeit takes 4 to 7 ms. See Benchmarks against the originals.

The example example 25 builds a synthetic cube of hectares cleared per 1 km cell, with a frontier that opened in 2019, an accelerating one, a steady one, a cluster cleared only in the last year and a protected area. It prints the pattern of each, with reference="date" and "cube".

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• Use cells at the scale of the process. Aggregate pixels into cells (counts, shares, means) so that a neighbourhood covers what you want to find. In a geographic CRS, cells are square only near the equator. At 10° S, these are 296 × 300 m.
  • Remove the noise first. Smooth the series (LandTrendr fits, smooth) or use counts of detected events. Otherwise the patterns describe the noise.
  • Choose the last date for your question. The patterns describe the end of the series. To describe a period that ended earlier, cut the cube there.
  • Many cells, many tests. At alpha=0.05, some cells are significant by chance. Read the map as clusters, not single cells, and check a few series.
  • Missing values (NaN, the raster's NoData) are left out of the sums and statistics. Cells with no data get -128.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Getis, A., & Ord, J. K. (1992). The analysis of spatial association by use of distance statistics. Geographical Analysis, 24(3), 189–206. doi:10.1111/j.1538-4632.1992.tb00261.x
  • Ord, J. K., & Getis, A. (1995). Local spatial autocorrelation statistics: distributional issues and an application. Geographical Analysis, 27(4), 286–306. doi:10.1111/j.1538-4632.1995.tb00912.x
  • ESRI. How Emerging Hot Spot Analysis works. ArcGIS Pro documentation, Space Time Pattern Mining toolbox. pro.arcgis.com
  • Parry, J., & Locke, D. sfdep: Spatial Dependence for Simple Features. R package version 0.2.5. CRAN
  • Hamed, K. H., & Rao, A. R. (1998). A modified Mann-Kendall trend test for autocorrelated data. Journal of Hydrology, 204(1–4), 182–196. doi:10.1016/S0022-1694(97)00125-X
  • Kennedy, R. E., Yang, Z., & Cohen, W. B. (2010). Detecting trends in forest disturbance and recovery using yearly Landsat time series: 1. LandTrendr — Temporal segmentation algorithms. Remote Sensing of Environment, 114(12), 2897–2910. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2010.07.008

docs.title: Zeit on a Cluster (HPC, Slurm)
docs.text:
A cluster gives zeit many processors and many nodes, through a scheduler and with a few habits of its own: compute nodes without internet access, a small home directory, modules that set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, time limits that stop a job midway. This page goes from installing zeit on a cluster to a job array that processes a thousand tiles, resubmits what failed and survives its time limit, with Slurm as the example.

Firstzeit doctor in a job: threads, caches, network, what to fix One nodesbatch with --cpus-per-task; zeit uses them all, without --jobs Many nodeszeit slurm writes a job array over the tiles; zeit tiles status says what is left No internetzeit fetch on the login node, into a cache the nodes see ContainersApptainer, from the image published with each version

docs.title: In a virtual environment
docs.text:
On the login node, with the cluster's Python (often module load python/3.12):

python -m venv ~/venvs/zeit
source ~/venvs/zeit/bin/activate
pip install zeit-cdts            # the algorithms, the cubes, the tiles
pip install "zeit-cdts[ai]"      # and zeit.ai, with PyTorch (gigabytes: only if you use it)

Zeit is published as wheels for Linux x86_64 and aarch64 (Grace, Graviton), for glibc 2.28 or newer (RHEL 8, Rocky 8, Ubuntu 20.04 and later). A job runs zeit with the environment's Python; activating the environment in the job script is enough.

docs.title: Where the caches go
docs.text:
What zeit downloads (the weights of zeit.ai, embeddings, tiles) goes into one cache folder, by default ~/.cache/zeit. On a cluster the home directory is small, and some compute nodes see it read-only: put the cache on the scratch space, in ~/.bashrc so that jobs inherit it:

export ZEIT_CACHE_DIR=/scratch/$USER/zeit-cache

docs.title: With Apptainer
docs.text:
Each zeit version is published as a container image, which Apptainer (formerly Singularity) runs without root:

apptainer pull zeit.sif docker://ghcr.io/sacridini/zeit-cdts:2.3.0          # CPU
apptainer pull zeit-gpu.sif docker://ghcr.io/sacridini/zeit-cdts:2.3.0-gpu  # CUDA, for zeit.ai
apptainer exec zeit.sif zeit doctor

The image brings its own Python, GDAL and glibc, so it also runs where the wheels do not install (an older glibc). Apptainer mounts the home directory and the current one; add the others with --bind /scratch.

docs.title: First: zeit doctor in a job
docs.text:
What a job gets is not what the login node has. Ask a node:

srun --cpus-per-task=16 --time=5 zeit doctor

zeit 2.3.0 (Python 3.12.8, Linux x86_64, glibc 2.28)
Threads (n_jobs=-1): 1 thread (OMP_NUM_THREADS=1; 16 of 128 processors available to this process; Slurm job 123456)
  OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK=16
  ! OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 leaves 15 of this job's processors idle (cluster modules often set it for MPI programs): set ZEIT_NUM_THREADS=16, which zeit reads first
Job: Slurm job 123456
Caches: /scratch/ana/zeit-cache (ZEIT_CACHE_DIR)
  weights     /scratch/ana/zeit-cache/weights      writable
  ...
Network:
  STAC, Earth Search                           NO: no answer in 5 s  (earth-search.aws.element84.com)
  ...
  ! This computer seems to have no internet access (...): `zeit fetch` downloads weights, embeddings and tiles.

Each line says what it found and where from. Here a module set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, which zeit would obey, and the node has no internet access: the next sections deal with both.

docs.title: On the login node
docs.text:
The login node is everyone's. Outside a job, where Slurm, PBS or LSF is installed, zeit uses at most 4 threads (fewer when many people are logged in: it divides the processors among them), says so once, and suggests a job:

RuntimeWarning: this looks like a login node of a Slurm cluster (outside a job), which everyone shares: zeit uses 4 of its 64 processors. Run the analysis in a job (srun, sbatch, `zeit slurm`). To change it, pass n_jobs (--jobs on the command line), set ZEIT_NUM_THREADS, or run `zeit config threads N` once.

Small things (looking at a cube, zeit fetch, zeit slurm) are fine there; an analysis goes in a job, srun --cpus-per-task=16 zeit ... for one that you watch.

docs.title: One node
docs.text:
Every algorithm already runs on all the processors a job is given: n_jobs=-1 (the default, --jobs on the command line) counts the job's processors (--cpus-per-task, the cgroup Slurm confines the job to), not the node's. There is nothing to set:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=landtrendr
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=32
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --time=4:00:00

source ~/venvs/zeit/bin/activate
export ZEIT_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK   # only if a module sets OMP_NUM_THREADS

zeit landtrendr nbr_stack.tif lt_out/ --max-segments 6

The same for Python code (zeit.landtrendr(cube), zeit.ccdc(...)) and for a folder of tiles on one node (zeit landtrendr tiles/ lt_out/ --tiles): the tiles are processed one after another, each with all the job's processors.

docs.title: Many nodes: a job array over the tiles
docs.text:
A region in many tiles spreads over many nodes as a job array, one task per tile (or per few tiles). zeit slurm writes the script:

zeit slurm landtrendr tiles/ lt_out/ --cpus 16 --time 2:00:00 --partition normal --max-segments 8

#!/bin/bash
# Written by `zeit slurm`: landtrendr on 412 tiles of /scratch/ana/tiles, one per task of the array.
#   submit it:    sbatch /scratch/ana/lt_out/.zeit-tiles/landtrendr.sbatch
#   follow it:    zeit tiles status /scratch/ana/lt_out
# Each task takes its tiles from SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID and every processor it is given; finished tiles
# are kept, and a task stopped at its time limit requeues itself to continue.
# --mem: suggested for 10 blocks of 512 x 512 pixels at once (a row of the widest tile, 5000 columns of 40 bands); a smaller --chunk-size, or fewer --cpus, needs less.
#SBATCH --job-name=zeit-landtrendr
#SBATCH --array=0-411
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --mem=4G
#SBATCH --time=2:00:00
#SBATCH --partition=normal
#SBATCH --output=/scratch/ana/lt_out/.zeit-tiles/logs/slurm-%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --signal=B:TERM@120
#SBATCH --requeue

exec /home/ana/venvs/zeit/bin/python -m zeit.cli landtrendr /scratch/ana/tiles /scratch/ana/lt_out --tiles --requeue --max-segments 8

It is saved as lt_out/.zeit-tiles/landtrendr.sbatch; submit it with sbatch, or write and submit at once with --submit. What each line does:

  • The split. Every task runs the same command; it finds its part from SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, the tiles k with k mod 412 equal to it. The first task keeps the split in lt_out/.zeit-tiles/split.json, so that a task submitted again later takes the same tiles.
  • The memory. A task reads a tile in blocks of --chunk-size and writes it one row of blocks at a time, so it holds a row of blocks, at most one per processor: the width of the tiles and their bands count, not their height. --mem is suggested from that, measured for LandTrendr and CCDC: 4G above for 40 years, but 119G for CCDC on tiles 5000 pixels wide with 200 dates of 6 bands, where --chunk-size 256 asks for 48G. Give your own with --mem 24G; sacct -j <job> --format=JobID,MaxRSS says what the first tasks used.
  • Fewer tasks. --tasks 50 makes 50 tasks of about 8 tiles each; --max-running 20 lets at most 20 run at once (--array=0-49%20), for a fair share of the partition.
  • The environment. The script runs zeit with the Python that wrote it, so the virtual environment needs no activation. --setup "module load gdal" adds a line before it, --sbatch=--qos=long another #SBATCH line.

docs.title: What is done, and what is left
docs.text:
zeit tiles status lt_out/

landtrendr in lt_out: 412 tiles, 405 done, 3 failed, 4 not done
  failed: tile_031 (run 4242_31): MemoryError
          log: lt_out/.zeit-tiles/logs/tile_031.log
  ...
To process the 7 left: sbatch --array=31,40,88,101,117,203,377 lt_out/.zeit-tiles/landtrendr.sbatch

The last line submits again only the tasks that have tiles left; finished tiles are never processed twice. For a tile that failed for want of memory, raise --mem in the script (or write it again with zeit slurm ... --mem 12G) before resubmitting.

docs.title: Time limits
docs.text: A task that reaches its time limit would be killed in the middle of a tile. With --signal=B:TERM@120, Slurm warns it two minutes before: zeit drops the tile at work (its unfinished files are deleted, the finished tiles stay) and, with --requeue, puts the task back in the queue, where it continues with its tiles left. A task that did not finish a single tile in its time does not requeue itself (its time limit is too short for one tile); zeit tiles status shows it.

docs.title: Other schedulers
docs.text: PBS and LSF arrays do not tell a task how many there are: give the part with --shard, zeit landtrendr tiles/ out/ --shard $PBS_ARRAY_INDEX/50 for an array of 50. Everything else (the split, the record, zeit tiles status, SIGTERM) is the same. On a node that does not confine its jobs, the threads follow the job's processors from NCPUS (PBS Pro), PBS_NUM_PPN (Torque) or LSB_DJOB_NUMPROC (LSF), as they follow SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK (or, without --cpus-per-task, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE) on Slurm.

docs.title: Compute nodes without internet access
docs.text:
Download beforehand, on the login node, what zeit would download while running, into the cache the compute nodes see (ZEIT_CACHE_DIR on the scratch space):

zeit fetch weights prithvi-300m-tl                       # the weights of zeit.ai
zeit fetch tiles urls.txt                                # the tiles of a list of URLs
zeit fetch embeddings emb/ --source tessera --bbox -63.2 -10.1 -62.8 -9.7 --years 2020-2024

The job then runs zeit landtrendr urls.txt out/ --tiles (or the job array of zeit slurm) as if it had the network: each tile is in the cache. Tiles built from STAC or Earth Engine (zeit.stac_tiles, zeit.gee_tiles) are fetched the same way, in Python, with zeit.fetch_tiles(sources). A node that cannot reach something zeit needs says so, with the zeit fetch command for it, instead of a connection error.

docs.title: GPUs for zeit.ai
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=6:00:00

source ~/venvs/zeit/bin/activate        # installed with zeit-cdts[ai]
python train_tempcnn.py

With the container, the GPU image and --nv, which passes the node's driver into it:

apptainer exec --nv --bind /scratch zeit-gpu.sif python train_tempcnn.py

Fetch the weights of the pretrained models (Presto, Prithvi) on the login node first, with zeit fetch weights.

docs.title: Zeit uses one thread
docs.text: A module exported OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 (common: it is the right value for MPI programs). Zeit warns once, and zeit doctor shows it. Set ZEIT_NUM_THREADS, which zeit reads first and other programs ignore: export ZEIT_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK.

docs.title: "Disk quota exceeded" in the home directory
docs.text: The caches went to ~/.cache/zeit. Set ZEIT_CACHE_DIR to the scratch space (see Where the caches go), and move the old cache there if it is worth keeping.

docs.title: pip install compiles zeit, and fails for want of Rust
docs.text:
There is no wheel for this computer: an older glibc than 2.28 (ldd --version: CentOS 7 has 2.17), or another architecture. Either use Apptainer, or install Rust in your home directory, without root, and let pip compile zeit:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y --profile minimal
source ~/.cargo/env
pip install zeit-cdts

Its dependencies (rasterio, PyTorch) need wheels for that glibc as well; on CentOS 7 the container is the simpler road.

docs.title: Earth Engine in a batch job
docs.text: A job has no terminal to authenticate in: zeit says so instead of waiting for an answer. Authenticate once on the login node with earthengine authenticate (the credentials go to ~/.config/earthengine, which the compute nodes see), or use a service account: export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/home/ana/keys/zeit-sa.json. A node without internet access cannot reach Earth Engine at all: build the tiles of gee_tiles beforehand with zeit.fetch_tiles.

docs.title: A task was killed for memory
docs.text: sacct -j <job>_<task> --format=JobID,State,MaxRSS says OUT_OF_MEMORY. Raise --mem, or lower --chunk-size (each task holds one row of blocks of --chunk-size × --chunk-size pixels at a time, the whole history of each), and resubmit the tasks zeit tiles status lists.

docs.title: A cube larger than a node
docs.text: A job array splits work that comes in tiles. One cube larger than a node's memory, computed by many nodes together, needs a Dask cluster across them (dask-jobqueue); zeit's functions take Dask-backed cubes (see Parallel & Cloud Processing), but a guide for Dask on Slurm is still to come. Cutting the cube into tiles first (gdal_retile.py, or windows of rioxarray) and using a job array is usually simpler.

docs.title: LandTrendr
docs.text:
Map when forests were cleared, burned or degraded, how severe each event was, and whether they recovered, from one satellite image per year.

AnswersWhen did this pixel change, by how much, and how fast? InputOne spectral index, one value per year: (time, rows, cols) OutputFitted vertices per pixel, then maps of year, magnitude and duration ReferenceKennedy et al. (2010), ported from the original IDL

Result of this tutorial. 40 years of annual Landsat NDVI over a 50 km area of Rondônia, Brazil. Left and middle: the landscape before and after. Right: the first year of the largest abrupt vegetation loss in each pixel, as found by LandTrendr and filtered as in steps 3 and 4. Only one event is shown per pixel, and gray does not always mean intact forest. Clearings where NDVI fell slowly, or stayed high as pasture, often have no event that passes the filters: here only about a third of the pixels that went from forest to open land are colored. The whole area, 2.8 million pixels, was segmented in about 5 seconds. Data: annual Landsat NDVI composites exported from LT-GEE on Google Earth Engine.

docs.title: How LandTrendr works
docs.text:
A yearly satellite series is noisy. Clouds, haze, sun angle and a dry year all make the values wobble. LandTrendr looks past that noise by approximating each pixel's history with a few straight line segments. The corners between segments are called vertices, and each segment has a clear meaning:

  • a flat segment is a stable period;
  • a steep drop is an abrupt disturbance (clear-cut, fire);
  • a slow decline is degradation (drought, disease, selective logging);
  • a rise is recovery or regrowth.

Three real pixels from the map above. Grey dots are the yearly NDVI values. Blue lines are LandTrendr's segments, and blue dots are the vertices. The same algorithm tells a permanent conversion, a clearing that regrew, and stable forest apart.

For each pixel the algorithm removes one-year spikes, proposes candidate vertices where the series bends most, and fits models with fewer and fewer segments. It keeps the simplest model that still fits the data well (judged by an F-test p-value). You control how many segments are allowed and how strict the test is.

docs.title: 1. Prepare an annual index stack
docs.text:
LandTrendr needs one value per pixel per year, usually a cloud-free composite of the growing season. Good choices:

  • NBR (Normalized Burn Ratio): the most sensitive to canopy loss and fire. The standard for forests.
  • NDVI: easy to interpret, good for agriculture and savanna, less sensitive to structural forest change.
  • Tasseled Cap Wetness: robust for forest structure.

Store it as a GeoTIFF with one band per year. Google Earth Engine (composite_type="annual") and STAC catalogs with build_annual_composites both produce this. So does LT-GEE: the stack used on this page is an NDVI composite collection exported from LT-GEE, so an existing LT-GEE workflow can move to local processing with Zeit unchanged.

import numpy as np
import zeit

ndvi = zeit.load_raster("LT_Stack_NDVI_Rondonia.tif", validate="landtrendr")
years = ndvi.time.dt.year.values      # 1985 ... 2024, from the band names yr1985 ... yr2024

print(ndvi.dims, ndvi.shape)          # ('time', 'y', 'x') (40, 1671, 1686)

load_raster returns a georeferenced cube with the year of each band in its time coordinate, so the steps below need neither the years nor the CRS again. validate="landtrendr" warns you if the stack looks wrong, for example too few years. A stack whose bands are not named by year is read with start_year=1985.

docs.title: 2. Segment every pixel
docs.text:
lt = zeit.landtrendr(
    ndvi,
    direction="loss",    # we are looking for DROPS in NDVI (the default)
    max_segments=6,      # at most 6 segments, 7 vertices
)

Set direction to match your index

LandTrendr's rules are asymmetric: it treats sudden changes in one direction as disturbance and in the other as recovery. Use direction="loss" (the default) when disturbance makes your index fall (NDVI, NBR, EVI, wetness) and direction="gain" when it makes the index rise (SWIR bands, brightness). With the wrong orientation, about three quarters of the pixels in this tutorial's Rondônia data get different vertex years. Either way, the results stay in the original scale of your data: there is no need to flip the index, as LT-GEE does.

Years without an observation are left out of each pixel's fit: NaN, the raster's NoData value and, for integer stacks without one such as this Int16 NDVI, 0, which is how Earth Engine exports masked pixels (see nodata below).

The result lt is an xarray.Dataset on the same grid and CRS as ndvi. With max_segments=6 each pixel has up to 7 vertices:

  • vertex_year (vertex, y, x): the vertex years (0 past the pixel's last vertex);
  • vertex_value (vertex, y, x): the fitted values at those years (NaN past the last vertex);
  • n_vertices (y, x): the number of vertices;
  • rmse (y, x): how well each fit follows its data. It is used below to separate real events from noise.

docs.title: 3. Extract disturbance maps
docs.text:
extract_events reads the vertices and returns one event per pixel as a set of maps:

loss = zeit.extract_events(
    lt,                     # event_type defaults to the direction LandTrendr ran with: "loss"
    sort_by="greatest",     # which event to keep if there are several
    min_magnitude=2000,     # ignore drops smaller than 0.2 NDVI (data is x10000)
    min_duration=1,
)

list(loss.data_vars)
# ['yod', 'date', 'magnitude', 'duration', 'pre_val', 'post_val', 'rate', 'dsnr']

loss is an xarray.Dataset of (y, x) maps, georeferenced like ndvi:

Map Meaning yod Year of the vertex where the loss begins, i.e. the last year before the drop (0 = no event). The first year in which the loss is visible is yod + 1. date That first year with the loss, as a date (January 1 of yod + 1; NaT = no event). The same variable on events of CCDC and BFAST holds the exact date of the break. magnitude Size of the drop, in the units of your data. duration Years the drop took. 1 is abrupt, larger values are gradual. pre_val, post_val Fitted value before and after. rate magnitude / duration. dsnr Magnitude divided by the fit's RMSE: a signal-to-noise ratio. Values above 2–3 are rarely noise.

sort_by chooses among several losses in the same pixel: "greatest" (largest magnitude), "newest", "fastest", "longest", or "dsnr". Regrowth comes from the same fit with event_type="gain".

docs.title: 4. Clean up and save
docs.text:
Keep confident events, then write GeoTIFFs. The maps carry their georeferencing, so save_raster needs nothing else:

# yod == years[0] means the loss segment starts at the first year. On noisy
# NDVI that is usually a slow decline over the whole record, not a dated event.
confident = (loss.yod > years[0]) & (loss.dsnr >= 3)
first_year = (loss.yod + 1).where(confident, 0).astype("uint16")

zeit.save_raster(first_year, "results/loss_year.tif", nodata=0)
zeit.save_raster(loss.magnitude.where(confident, 0), "results/loss_magnitude.tif", nodata=0)

To write every map as it is, one GeoTIFF each (yod.tif, magnitude.tif, …), pass the whole Dataset: zeit.save_raster(loss, "results/loss").

Isolated single pixels are usually noise. A minimum mapping unit filter removes patches smaller than a given size:

yod = zeit.apply_mmu_filter(loss.yod, mmu_pixels=11)          # patches under 11 pixels become NoData
zeit.save_raster(yod, "results/loss_year_mmu.tif")

The map at the top of this page uses exactly these steps: no event starting in the first year, dsnr >= 3 and an 11-pixel minimum mapping unit.

docs.title: 5. Inspect individual pixels
docs.text:
Plotting a few pixels is the best way to check your parameters. zeit.landtrendr also takes a single pixel's series, and fitted=True adds the fitted trajectory (the series rebuilt from the vertices):

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

row, col = 1471, 819   # the "clear-cut, then pasture" pixel shown above
pixel = ndvi[:, row, col]                      # one series, with its dates
fit = zeit.landtrendr(pixel, fitted=True)
n = int(fit.n_vertices)

plt.scatter(years, pixel, color="grey", label="Observed")
plt.plot(years, fit.fitted, label="LandTrendr fit")
plt.plot(fit.vertex_year[:n], fit.vertex_value[:n], "o", label="Vertices")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

A single pixel's result has the same variables, without the y/x dims:

fit.vertex_year.values
# array([1985, 2002, 2003, 2007, 2008, 2019, 2024], dtype=int16)
fit.vertex_value.values.round()
# array([7972., 8018., 3333., 3734., 4670., 2903., 4230.], dtype=float32)

Any series works the same way: a list or 1-D array with years= (zeit.landtrendr(values, years=years)), or a pandas.Series indexed by dates or years. The same vertices are also in the full result, lt.isel(y=row, x=col), and zeit.landtrendr(ndvi, fitted=True) adds the fitted trajectory of every pixel as fitted (time, y, x).

docs.title: 6. Fit other bands to the same vertices
docs.text:
A classic LandTrendr trick is to segment on one index (say NBR) and then describe the same periods with other bands. This is known as fitting to vertices (FTV), LT-GEE's ftv bands. With every band in one (time, band, y, x) cube (or a Dataset), name the index to segment and the bands to fit:

stack = zeit.load_raster("landsat_indices.tif")      # bands nbr, ndvi, tcw, swir1 per year
lt = zeit.landtrendr(stack, band="nbr", ftv=["ndvi", "swir1"])

lt.ftv_swir1                 # (time, y, x): SWIR1 fitted through the NBR vertices
lt.vertex_value_ndvi         # (vertex, y, x): NDVI at each vertex year

Each band is fitted as the original LandTrendr does (ftv_v1): desawtoothed, then segment by segment through the vertex years, in its own scale. If the bands come from different sources, put them on one grid first with load_raster(..., like=).

docs.title: Tuning the parameters
docs.text:
The defaults follow the original LandTrendr and work well for 25–40 years of Landsat data.

Parameter Default Effect max_segments 6 Maximum segments per pixel. Lower it for short series (about n_years / 5). Too high a value lets noise become "events". spike_threshold 0.9 Dampens one-year spikes before fitting. 1.0 disables it. Lower values remove spikes more aggressively. recovery_threshold 0.25 Rejects recoveries faster than 1/value years (0.25 = at least 4 years to recover fully). Stops a cloudy year from looking like disturbance and instant recovery. pval_threshold 0.05 A model must be at least this significant. Lower values give simpler fits. best_model_proportion 0.75 Prefers models with more vertices whose p-value is at most (2 - best_model_proportion) times the best one, so 0.75 means within 1.25×. min_observations_needed 6 Pixels with fewer valid years are left unsegmented. nodata "auto" Value marking a missing year. "auto": the raster's NoData, or 0 for integer data without one. None: only NaN, which is always missing.

docs.title: Processing large areas
docs.text:
Rasters larger than memory. Pass the file with chunks="auto": nothing is read until the results are written, and then the raster is read, segmented and written block by block:

lt = zeit.landtrendr("LT_Stack_NDVI_Rondonia.tif", chunks="auto")   # lazy
loss = zeit.extract_events(lt, min_magnitude=2000)                    # still lazy
zeit.save_raster(loss, "results/")
# results/yod.tif, magnitude.tif, duration.tif, ...

The same is available from the shell as zeit landtrendr.

Dask cubes and clusters. Lazy xarray cubes (for example from STAC or Zarr) go straight in, and stay lazy. Keep the time axis in one chunk:

annual = annual_ndvi.chunk({"time": -1, "y": 512, "x": 512})   # (time, y, x), one date per year

lt = zeit.landtrendr(annual, max_segments=6)     # or annual.zeit.landtrendr(max_segments=6)
loss = zeit.extract_events(lt, min_magnitude=0.2)
zeit.save_raster(loss, "results/")               # computed chunk by chunk while written

See Parallel & Cloud Processing to run this on a cluster.

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• Use a stable season. Composite the same months every year, so phenology is not mistaken for change.
  • Mask clouds before compositing. Residual clouds create spikes. spike_threshold removes most of them, but clean input always wins.
  • Validate with a sample, not by eye on the map. Draw a stratified sample of the map, label it with zeit.interpret and estimate accuracy and area with zeit.accuracy (see Accuracy & Area).
  • Compare with the published method. Zeit reproduces the original IDL LandTrendr vertex for vertex, see Algorithm Fidelity.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Kennedy, R. E., Yang, Z., & Cohen, W. B. (2010). Detecting trends in forest disturbance and recovery using yearly Landsat time series: 1. LandTrendr — Temporal segmentation algorithms. Remote Sensing of Environment, 114(12), 2897–2910. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2010.07.008
  • Kennedy, R. E., et al. (2018). Implementation of the LandTrendr algorithm on Google Earth Engine. Remote Sensing, 10(5), 691. doi:10.3390/rs10050691
  • LT-GEE code and guide: github.com/eMapR/LT-GEE

docs.title: LTAE & LightTAE
docs.text:
AnswersClassify pixel time series with temporal attention. Input(batch, time, bands) plus the day of each observation OutputClass logits per pixel ReferenceGarnot & Landrieu (2020); written from the paper and the authors' code

The Lightweight Temporal Attention Encoder (L-TAE) is a compact, fast attention mechanism designed specifically for classifying per-pixel satellite image time series — the kind of long, irregularly-sampled sequence of spectral observations you get from a single pixel's history in a data cube. It was introduced in:

Garnot, V. S. F., & Landrieu, L. (2020). Lightweight Temporal Self-Attention for Classifying Satellite Image Time Series. arXiv:2007.00586.

zeit.ai exposes two related classes:

  • LTAE: the reusable temporal-fusion block itself — takes an encoded (batch, seq_len, in_channels) sequence and fuses it into a single (batch, n_neurons[-1]) embedding via multi-head attention. Useful if you want to plug L-TAE fusion into your own custom architecture (e.g. as the temporal-fusion stage of a spatial-temporal model).
  • LightTAE: the full, ready-to-train pixel time-series classifier — a small per-pixel MLP spatial encoder, followed by LTAE temporal fusion, followed by an MLP decoder to class logits. This is the model you want for standard "classify this pixel's time series into a land-cover class" tasks.

Both are written from the paper and from the authors' code (VSainteuf/lightweight-temporal-attention-pytorch, MIT). Where the two differ, the code is followed. They are no longer a port of R sits, and weights trained in sits do not load into them. The authors encode each date with a pixel-set encoder, which summarizes the pixels of a parcel; Zeit's samples are single pixels, so LightTAE uses a per-date MLP in its place.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The "L" in L-TAE stands for lightweight, and the trick that makes it fast is a learned "master query": unlike standard self-attention, where the query vector is computed from the input at every forward pass, L-TAE's query is a single learned parameter per attention head, shared across every input in the batch. This collapses what would normally be an O(seq_len²) self-attention computation down to O(seq_len) — each timestep only needs to attend to the master query, not to every other timestep.

LightTAE's forward pass has three stages:

  1. Spatial encoder (_PixelSpatialEncoder): a small per-timestep MLP (Linear -> BatchNorm1d -> ReLU, stacked) that independently encodes every (pixel, time) spectral observation from n_bands into a higher-dimensional embedding (default (32, 64, 128)).
  2. Temporal encoder (LTAE): adds a sinusoidal positional encoding keyed on day_offsets (day counts from the first observation, not the raw calendar date — so it doesn't matter which year your series starts in), then fuses the sequence via the master-query multi-head attention described above, producing one embedding per pixel.
  3. Decoder: a small MLP (Linear -> BatchNorm1d -> ReLU, stacked) mapping the fused embedding to n_labels class logits (softmax is applied externally, the loss takes raw logits — use torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy, which expects raw logits, or apply softmax/argmax yourself at inference time).

Because the flatten/positional-encoding buffers are sized at construction time from day_offsets, a given LightTAE (or LTAE) instance is tied to one fixed sequence length and temporal sampling pattern for its lifetime — the same constraint as the authors' code, whose positional encoding is built from the dates. If your pixels have varying numbers of valid observations, interpolate/gap-fill them onto a common day_offsets grid before feeding them in.

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text:
LightTAE TempCNN Best for Per-pixel time series with many, well-sampled observations where temporal ordering/attention genuinely helps Shorter or noisier series, or when you want a simpler, faster-to-train baseline Compute cost Moderate (attention has more parameters than a plain conv stack) Lower Mean accuracy on samples_modis_ndvi (see below) 0.915 0.861

See the TempCNN tutorial for the simpler 1D-CNN alternative, and the UTAE tutorial if you need spatially-aware segmentation (a class per pixel over a whole image patch, not just a single pixel's own time series).

docs.title: From a cube to a map
docs.text:
LightTAE classifies each pixel from its series of bands, (time, band). Its positional encoding takes the days since the first date, which zeit.ai.samples computes from the cube's dates (samples.meta["positions"]):

import zeit
from zeit import ai

cube = zeit.load_raster("s2_16day_2022.tif")                # (time, band, y, x)
samples = ai.samples(cube, "samples.gpkg", label="class")
model = ai.train(ai.LightTAE, samples, epochs=50, loss="focal")
classes = ai.predict(model, cube)

Like the authors' network, a model is built for one timeline (its layer norm and positional encoding are sized by it): the cube to classify needs as many dates. See Deep Learning for the samples, the validation blocks and the normalization.

docs.title: Instantiating the Model
docs.text:
zeit.ai.train builds the model for you from the samples (bands, dates, classes); the arguments below pass through it, e.g. ai.train(ai.LightTAE, samples, n_head=8). To build it yourself:

from zeit.ai import LightTAE

model = LightTAE(
    n_bands=6,              # number of spectral bands per observation
    day_offsets=day_offsets,
    n_labels=10,             # number of land-cover classes
    encoder_mlp=(32, 64, 128),  # per-date MLP widths
    decoder_mlp=(64, 32),       # decoder hidden widths
    n_head=16,                  # attention heads
    d_k=8,                      # key size per head
    n_neurons=(256, 128),       # LTAE internal MLP widths (n_neurons[0] must equal d_model)
    d_model=256,
    dropout=0.2,
)

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model = model.to(device)

docs.title: Using the LTAE block on its own
docs.text:
If you want L-TAE's temporal fusion inside a custom architecture (e.g. after your own spatial feature extractor), instantiate it directly:

from zeit.ai import LTAE

temporal_fusion = LTAE(
    in_channels=128,   # dimensionality of your incoming per-timestep features
    day_offsets=day_offsets,
    n_head=16,
    n_neurons=(256, 128),
    dropout=0.2,
).to(device)

# x: (batch, seq_len, in_channels) -> (batch, n_neurons[-1])
fused = temporal_fusion(x)

docs.title: A loop of your own
docs.text: zeit.ai.train covers the usual case. For anything else (another optimizer, a scheduler, augmentation), the SampleSet is a PyTorch Dataset whose items hold the normalized x, the label y and the date positions; see A loop of your own. A model trained this way can still be classified with zeit.ai.predict after zeit.ai.train(model, samples, epochs=0) records the samples' metadata in it.

docs.title: Accuracy against sits
docs.text:
Measured on samples_modis_ndvi of sits (12 dates, 4 classes), with the same 80/20 split on both sides and 5 seeds, the mean accuracy was:

sits, with its defaults Zeit, the authors' defaults Zeit, the pipeline's defaults (150 epochs) TempCNN 0.879 ± 0.027 0.839 ± 0.031 0.861 ± 0.024 LightTAE 0.902 ± 0.016 0.892 ± 0.020 0.915 ± 0.011

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Garnot, V. S. F., Landrieu, L., Giordano, S., & Chehata, N. (2020). Satellite image time series classification with pixel-set encoders and temporal self-attention. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) (pp. 12322–12331). https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR42600.2020.01234
  • Garnot, V. S. F., & Landrieu, L. (2020). Lightweight Temporal Self-Attention for Classifying Satellite Image Time Series. arXiv:2007.00586. https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00586
  • e-sensing/sits, used for the accuracy comparison above: https://github.com/e-sensing/sits

docs.title: Trend Analysis (Mann-Kendall)
docs.text:
Is this area getting greener or browner, and is the trend real or just noise? The Mann-Kendall test answers the first half without assuming anything about the data's distribution, and the Theil-Sen slope says how fast it is changing. Both are robust to outliers such as residual clouds.

AnswersIs there a significant monotonic trend? How steep? InputOne index, ideally one value per year: (time, rows, cols) OutputTrend direction, p-value, Kendall's tau, Sen's slope, and more ReferenceMann (1945), Kendall (1975), Sen (1968); ported from pymannkendall

Result on real data. 40 years of annual Landsat NDVI over Rondônia, Brazil, tested with the autocorrelation-corrected Hamed-Rao variant. Left: Theil-Sen slope in NDVI per decade. Right: pixels with a significant trend at the 5% level. Browning dominates where forest was converted to pasture. Greening shows where earlier clearings regrew. Data: annual Landsat NDVI composites exported from LT-GEE on Google Earth Engine.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Mann-Kendall compares every pair of observations and counts how often the later one is higher. If "later is higher" happens much more often than chance allows, there is an upward trend (and vice versa). It uses only ranks, so it does not care about skewed distributions or a few extreme values.
  • Theil-Sen estimates the slope as the median of the slopes between all pairs of points, so outliers barely move it.

Why not a linear regression? Ordinary least squares assumes normal, independent residuals. Satellite series violate both: indices are skewed, consecutive years are correlated, and missed clouds produce outliers.

docs.title: 1. Build one value per year
docs.text:
The slope is expressed per time step. With one observation per year, it is directly "change per year":

import zeit

# ndvi: (time, y, x) DataArray from build_time_series, any cadence
annual_max = ndvi.groupby("time.year").max().rename({"year": "time"})   # (years, y, x)
annual_max = annual_max.chunk({"time": -1, "y": 512, "x": 512})

A yearly maximum or growing-season median are common choices.

docs.title: 2. Run the test
docs.text:
result = zeit.mann_kendall(annual_max, method="hamed_rao", alpha=0.05).compute()

slope = result.slope                             # NDVI change per year
significant = result.h == 1                      # significant at alpha
browning = significant & (result.trend == -1)
greening = significant & (result.trend == 1)

The result is an xarray.Dataset with one (y, x) map per metric, on the grid and CRS of the cube. A dask cube gives a lazy result; an in-memory cube an in-memory one.

docs.title: 3. Save the maps
docs.text:
zeit.save_raster(result, "results/mk")                       # slope.tif, p.tif, ... one per metric
zeit.save_raster(browning, "results/browning.tif")           # georeferenced from the cube

docs.title: Which variant should I use?
docs.text:
method Use it when "hamed_rao" Default and recommended for annual composites. Corrects the test for autocorrelation (a wet year tends to follow a wet year), which otherwise produces too many false trends. "yue_wang" An alternative autocorrelation correction. Worth comparing when results are borderline. "original" The classic test, for series you know are independent. "seasonal" Raw sub-annual data (16-day, monthly). Tests each season slot separately and combines them (Hirsch & Slack), so you don't need to aggregate to one value per year. Set period to the number of steps per year. 
# 16-day composites tested directly: 23 observations per year
trend = zeit.mann_kendall(ndvi_16d, method="seasonal", period=23)

Units of the slope

For original, hamed_rao and yue_wang, the slope is per array step. With 16-day data that is per 16 days, not per year. For seasonal, it is per full period (per year when period covers a year).

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
Variable Meaning trend 1 increasing, -1 decreasing, 0 no significant trend. h 1.0 if significant at alpha, else 0.0. p Two-sided p-value. z Standardised test statistic. tau Kendall's tau, from −1 to 1. s, var_s Mann-Kendall score and its (corrected) variance. slope Theil-Sen slope, see the units warning above. intercept Intercept of the robust line.

Pixels with fewer than min_valid (default 4) non-NaN values are all NaN.

docs.title: More ways to call it
docs.text:
zeit.mann_kendall reads what it is given (all inputs):

# A GeoTIFF with one band per year, larger than memory: read and computed block by block
mk = zeit.mann_kendall("LT_Stack_NDVI_Rondonia.tif", chunks="auto")
zeit.save_raster(mk, "results/mk")

# A numpy (time, y, x) array: no dates needed
mk = zeit.mann_kendall(stack)

# One series, for testing: a Dataset of scalars
px = zeit.mann_kendall([0.41, 0.44, 0.39, 0.47, 0.52, 0.49, 0.55, 0.58, 0.61, 0.60])
float(px.slope), float(px.p)

From the shell: zeit mann-kendall.

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• Trend is not timing. Mann-Kendall says a monotonic trend exists over the whole period, not when it started. Pair it with LandTrendr or CCDC to find when and how abruptly.
  • Many pixels, many tests. At alpha=0.05, about 5% of trendless pixels will still test significant. Look at spatial patterns, or tighten alpha, before interpreting isolated pixels. To test whether a whole region or a land-cover class is trending, use PARTS, which accounts for the correlation between neighbouring pixels.
  • Mask what cannot trend. Water and bare ground produce meaningless tests. Mask them first.
Validation

The implementation is a Rust port of pymannkendall and matches it field for field on hundreds of synthetic series, for every variant. See Algorithm Fidelity.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Hussain, M. M., & Mahmud, I. (2019). pyMannKendall: a python package for non parametric Mann Kendall family of trend tests. Journal of Open Source Software, 4(39), 1556. doi:10.21105/joss.01556
  • Mann, H. B. (1945). Nonparametric tests against trend. Econometrica, 13(3), 245–259. doi:10.2307/1907187
  • Kendall, M. G. (1975). Rank Correlation Methods (4th ed.). Griffin.
  • Sen, P. K. (1968). Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall's tau. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 63(324), 1379–1389. doi:10.1080/01621459.1968.10480934
  • Hamed, K. H., & Rao, A. R. (1998). A modified Mann-Kendall trend test for autocorrelated data. Journal of Hydrology, 204(1–4), 182–196. doi:10.1016/S0022-1694(97)00125-X
  • Yue, S., & Wang, C. (2004). The Mann-Kendall test modified by effective sample size to detect trend in serially correlated hydrological series. Water Resources Management, 18(3), 201–218. doi:10.1023/B:WARM.0000043140.61082.60
  • Hirsch, R. M., & Slack, J. R. (1984). A nonparametric trend test for seasonal data with serial dependence. Water Resources Research, 20(6), 727–732. doi:10.1029/WR020i006p00727

docs.title: Parallel & Cloud Processing
docs.text:
The same Zeit code runs on one laptop core, on every core of a workstation, or on several machines. This page explains the levels of parallelism, how to spread a folder of tiles over the computers of a local network with one command on each, how to set up a Dask cluster for a single cube larger than one machine, and how to write results that many machines can produce at once.

Level 1Threads of the compiled core inside one process: n_jobs Many tilesA folder of tiles here and on helpers: --helpers, zeit worker Level 2Dask chunks across processes and machines: the .zeit accessor StorageZarr for parallel writes, GeoTIFF for final products RuleChunk in space, never in time

docs.title: Levels of parallelism
docs.text:
Threads within one machine. Every algorithm's per-pixel loop runs in Rust, on several threads. n_jobs=-1 (the default) uses all cores but one (in a cluster job, all of the job's), and needs nothing else: zeit.landtrendr, zeit.ccdc and friends are already parallel.

Tiles across machines. When the data already comes in tiles, each tile is a job of its own: zeit landtrendr tiles/ out/ --helpers runs them here and on the computers of the local network running zeit worker. See Many tiles on several computers: it is the simplest way to use more machines.

Chunks across processes or machines. For a single cube larger than memory, or one area split over more machines, wrap the data in a Dask-backed xarray cube and pass it to the algorithm (zeit.landtrendr(cube), zeit.mann_kendall(cube), …) or to its .zeit accessor form. Zeit maps the compiled code over spatial chunks, and Dask schedules those chunks on its workers.

import xarray as xr
import zeit   # registers the .zeit accessor

cube = xr.open_zarr("s3://my-bucket/annual_ndvi.zarr")["ndvi"]        # (time, y, x), lazy
cube = cube.chunk({"time": -1, "y": 512, "x": 512})                   # whole history per chunk

trend = cube.zeit.mann_kendall(method="hamed_rao")                    # still lazy: a Dataset of maps
trend.to_zarr("s3://my-bucket/ndvi_trend.zarr", consolidated=True)    # computes, in parallel

Chunk in space, never in time

Every algorithm needs a pixel's complete history, so the time axis must be a single chunk (-1). Chunk only y and x. Typical sizes are 256–1024 pixels, small enough that a chunk's full history fits in a worker's memory.

Leave n_jobs at its default

The blocks that run at once share the compiled core's threads (one pool per process), so n_jobs=-1 in every block does not multiply them, and in a dask.distributed worker it is the worker's --nthreads. Setting n_jobs lower only leaves processors idle. See Threads for the measurements.

docs.title: Many tiles on several computers
docs.text: When the work is a folder of tiles (Landsat tiles for LandTrendr, say), every tile is a job of its own and no cluster is needed. Zeit runs the folder on this computer, and any computer of the local network can lend itself with one command. No scheduler, no ports to choose, no versions to align by hand.

docs.title: Once: bring the computers into a group
docs.text:
On the computer that has the tiles:

zeit helpers invite              # shows a code, e.g. K7QM-2XDP, valid for 10 minutes
zeit helpers firewall            # Windows only: lets the helpers reach this computer (asks for admin rights)

On each computer that will help, with the same zeit version installed:

zeit worker --join K7QM-2XDP     # joins the group, then waits for work

From then on, zeit worker is all a helper needs (in a terminal it can leave open, or at startup). It lends all its cores but one (--cores to lend fewer), only runs zeit's own commands, and keeps the computer from sleeping while it works. Any computer of the group can run tiles with the others' help, and invite more.

docs.title: Running the tiles
docs.text:
zeit landtrendr nbr_tiles/ lt_out/ --helpers --max-segments 6              # here and on the helpers
zeit landtrendr nbr_tiles/ lt_out/ --helpers --no-local --max-segments 6   # only on the helpers

import zeit

result = zeit.run_tiles("landtrendr", "nbr_tiles/", "lt_out/", helpers=True, max_segments=6)
result = zeit.run_tiles("landtrendr", "nbr_tiles/", "lt_out/", helpers=True, local=False)   # only coordinate

Every tile gets its own folder, lt_out/<tile name>/, with what zeit landtrendr writes for one file. With --no-local (local=False) this computer processes nothing: it hands out the tiles and collects the results, and stays free for other work. It must stay on, though: the results come back to it.

The run prints the helpers as they join and one progress line:

landtrendr: 120 tiles to process, 538.2 GB; this computer uses 19 cores; helpers welcome
Helpers join by running `zeit worker` (port 47801).
+ lab-03 (192.168.1.23, 15 cores) joined
+ lab-07 (192.168.1.27, 7 cores) joined
landtrendr: 37/120 tiles | 3 computers | sending 104.3 MB/s | ~1 h 12 min left

What happens underneath:

  • The helpers pull. Each asks for a tile when it has room and fetches the next while it processes the current one, so a fast workstation takes more tiles than a laptop without any setting. The largest tiles go first.
  • No waiting for the slowest. Near the end, an idle computer that would finish a straggler clearly sooner runs it too, and the first result wins. The last tile stays on the main computer when it would finish it before a helper.
  • Nothing is lost. A tile that fails is tried again on another computer (after two failures it is listed at the end). A helper that is switched off gives its tiles back to the queue. Stopping the run (Ctrl+C) keeps the finished tiles, and running the same command again processes only the others.

docs.title: Where the tiles come from
docs.text:
• The main computer's disk. The main computer sends each tile to the helper that gets it, in 16 MB pieces read one at a time, so a hard disk is never asked for several files at once (which is much slower than reading them in turn).
  • A NAS that every computer sees. A helper that sees the same file reads it from the NAS itself, and the main computer sends nothing. Mapped Windows drives travel as their UNC path (\\nas\tiles\...), which Windows helpers read directly; a Linux or macOS helper says where the share is mounted: zeit worker --map "\\nas\tiles=/mnt/tiles". The helper copies the whole tile before processing it, which is much faster than GDAL reading it piece by piece over the network.
  • Again. A helper keeps the tiles it received (20 GB by default, --cache-gb), so a second run with other options does not send them again.
  • The results go back the same way: a helper that sees the output folder too (on a NAS) writes them straight into it, otherwise it sends them to the main computer. They are small next to the tiles.

docs.title: What limits the speed: the network
docs.text:
A full Landsat tile, 54.7 million pixels × 41 years, takes about 98 s of LandTrendr on a 20-thread desktop (see Performance). Sending that tile to a helper over a 1 Gbit/s cable (about 110 MB/s) takes:

Tile Size Sent in Helpers the main computer's cable keeps busy* float32, no compression 9.0 GB ~80 s ~1 float32, as Zeit sends it (lossless ZSTD) ~6.3 GB ~57 s ~1.7 int16 (NBR × 10000), no compression 4.5 GB ~40 s ~2.5 int16 (NBR × 10000), ZSTD compression ~2.9 GB ~26 s ~4 the same over Wi-Fi ~2.9 GB ~60–100 s ~1–2

* As fast as that desktop: the time to process a tile divided by the time to send it. Slower helpers take longer per tile, so more of them fit. The compressed sizes were measured on the NBR of that tile (215/067): ZSTD with the floating-point predictor makes float32 1.43× smaller, int16 with ZSTD is 3.1× smaller than float32. Other data compresses differently.

So the format of the tiles matters more than the number of helpers. An index scaled by 10000 as int16 (as Earth Engine exports NBR) with ZSTD compression is a fraction of a float32 stack; the conversion costs four decimal places, so it is your call, not Zeit's. A NAS changes where the bottleneck is (its own network link and disks) but not the arithmetic. A tile stored without compression is sent as a lossless ZSTD copy (made at ~300 MB/s with two threads, faster than a 1 Gbit/s link carries it; compress_transfers=False turns it off). The run warns when the tiles are float32 without compression, and when the helpers spend more than a quarter of their time waiting for tiles: then more helpers will not make it faster.

docs.title: Tiles each computer downloads for itself
docs.text:
The tiles do not have to exist yet. Given as recipes, each computer downloads or builds the tiles it processes, into its own cache, and nothing passes through the main computer:

zeit.run_tiles("landtrendr", zeit.tile_urls(["https://data.example.org/nbr/215_067.tif", ...]), "lt_out/",
               helpers=True)                                               # files on a web server or a bucket

tiles = zeit.stac_tiles(["21LYG", "21LZG"], index="NBR", bands=["nir08", "swir22"],
                        start_year=1985, end_year=2024)                    # annual composites from STAC
tiles = zeit.gee_tiles(["215/067", "216/067"], start_year=1985, end_year=2024)   # medoids from Earth Engine
zeit.run_tiles("landtrendr", tiles, "lt_out/", helpers=True)

From the terminal, a text file of URLs (one per line) works as the input: zeit landtrendr urls.txt lt_out/ --helpers. The composites are written as int16 (the index × 10000) unless dtype="float32".

This only pays off when the computers have independent internet links (another building, a colleague's home over a VPN, cloud machines near the data). In the same office they share one link: a Landsat tile built from STAC is ~41 GB of scenes, so the link, not the number of computers, sets the pace. Earth Engine limits concurrent requests per project, not per computer. The run warns when a helper is on the main computer's network.

docs.title: When the helpers do not appear
docs.text:
• Windows. Run zeit helpers firewall on the main computer (the helpers need no rule: they only connect out). A network marked Public blocks incoming connections without it.
  • Another subnet or a VPN. Broadcasts do not cross routers. Start the helper with the main computer's address: zeit worker --connect 192.168.2.10.
  • Which helpers are listening. zeit helpers list on any computer of the group shows the helpers waiting for work, with their cores and zeit version.
  • Another zeit version. A helper with another version (or other code, as with a development install) is told which version to install, and the main computer says so too.

docs.title: Setting up a cluster
docs.text: For a single cube that does not fit one machine. A Dask cluster has one scheduler, which hands out work, and any number of workers, which do it.

docs.title: On one machine
docs.text:
from dask.distributed import Client, LocalCluster

client = Client(LocalCluster(n_workers=4, threads_per_worker=1))
print(client.dashboard_link)   # live view of tasks, memory and CPU

docs.title: Across machines on a local network
docs.text:
On the machine that will coordinate:

dask scheduler                 # prints its address, e.g. tcp://192.168.1.10:8786

On every other machine (with Zeit installed in the same Python version):

dask worker tcp://192.168.1.10:8786 --nworkers 4 --nthreads 1 --memory-limit 8GB

Then connect from your script:

from dask.distributed import Client
client = Client("tcp://192.168.1.10:8786")

If a worker cannot connect or crashes, see Troubleshooting below.

docs.title: In the cloud
docs.text:
Dask has launchers for most platforms: dask-kubernetes (Kubernetes), dask-cloudprovider (AWS, GCP, Azure), dask-jobqueue (SLURM, PBS on HPC systems), or managed services such as Coiled.

from dask_kubernetes.operator import KubeCluster
from dask.distributed import Client

cluster = KubeCluster(name="zeit", image="ghcr.io/dask/dask:latest", n_workers=20)
client = Client(cluster)

Workers need Zeit installed: use the Zeit Docker image or add pip install zeit-cdts to the worker image.

docs.title: Writing results: Zarr
docs.text:
When many workers write at once, a single GeoTIFF becomes a bottleneck (or gets corrupted). Zarr stores an array as a folder of independently compressed chunks, so every worker writes its own piece, locally or straight to S3 / Google Cloud Storage.

.zeit.to_zarr_optimized() rechunks the result (512 × 512 by default), writes it and consolidates the metadata so it reads fast from object storage:

result.zeit.to_zarr_optimized("gs://my-bucket/result.zarr")

Don't .compute() a large result

.compute() pulls the whole array into the memory of your client. Write it with to_zarr_optimized (or save_raster for results that fit in memory) and let the workers stream it to storage.

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
LandTrendr over a large annual NDVI cube stored as Zarr, on a cluster:

import xarray as xr
from dask.distributed import Client
import zeit

client = Client("tcp://192.168.1.10:8786")

ndvi = xr.open_zarr("gs://my-bucket/annual_ndvi.zarr")["ndvi"]      # (time, y, x), 1985-2024
ndvi = ndvi.chunk({"time": -1, "y": 512, "x": 512})

# Lazy: the years come from the time coordinate; direction="loss" looks for NDVI drops.
lt = zeit.landtrendr(ndvi, max_segments=6)
lt.to_zarr("gs://my-bucket/landtrendr_vertices.zarr", mode="w")     # computes, in parallel

# Event maps from the saved vertices, again chunk by chunk
lt = xr.open_zarr("gs://my-bucket/landtrendr_vertices.zarr")
loss = zeit.extract_events(lt, min_magnitude=2000)
loss.to_zarr("gs://my-bucket/landtrendr_loss.zarr", mode="w")       # yod, magnitude, duration, ...

zeit.landtrendr and extract_events return lazy xarray.Datasets here: each to_zarr runs the compiled code on every chunk in parallel and streams the result to storage. Saving the vertices first means they are computed once, and other event maps (event_type="gain", another sort_by) come from them without segmenting again. The dashboard (client.dashboard_link, port 8787 by default) shows progress, memory and CPU for every worker.

docs.title: Troubleshooting a Dask cluster
docs.text: Connecting a mixed-OS cluster (e.g. a Windows desktop as scheduler + a macOS laptop as a worker) over a home/office network hits a handful of predictable snags. Here's what to check, roughly in the order you'll hit them.

docs.title: Windows Firewall blocks the remote worker
docs.text:
Windows often marks a home/office network as Public, which blocks unsolicited inbound connections by default — the scheduler will start fine locally, but a worker on another machine will simply never be able to reach it.

Fix it with a firewall rule scoped to your LAN subnet (run in an elevated PowerShell), rather than opening the ports to the world:

New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Dask Scheduler (LAN)" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP `
    -LocalPort 8786,8787 -Action Allow -RemoteAddress 192.168.1.0/24

Replace 192.168.1.0/24 with your actual subnet. 8786 is the scheduler port, 8787 the dashboard.

docs.title: Keep Python, dask and distributed versions aligned on every machine
docs.text:
The scheduler/worker wire protocol assumes matching (or very close) dask/distributed versions; a mismatch triggers a VersionMismatchWarning and can cause hard-to-diagnose failures under load. Before connecting a new worker, check:

python -c "import sys, dask, distributed; print(sys.version, dask.__version__, distributed.__version__)"

...and make sure it's close to what the scheduler machine reports. zeit's published PyPI wheels currently cover Python 3.9–3.12 (Windows, Linux, macOS arm64) — there is no prebuilt 3.13 wheel yet, so standardize on a Python 3.12 environment (venv or conda) on every machine to avoid an accidental from-source build.

docs.title: macOS: a worker crash-loops silently the moment a task touches zeit
docs.text:
Symptom: dask worker starts and registers with the scheduler fine. But as soon as a real task imports zeit (e.g. the first zeit.landtrendr() call), the worker process vanishes and Dask's Nanny silently respawns it with a new port — forever. No Python traceback reaches the scheduler or client; calling client.run(...) against that worker just raises CommClosedError: ... Stream is closed.

Cause: two copies of the OpenMP runtime (libomp/libiomp) in one process. Up to zeit 1.7, torch and Zeit's own compiled C++ extension (zeit._core) each linked one; from 2.0 Zeit's core is Rust and links none, so a second copy can only come from another package of the environment. Loading both inside the same process aborts the whole process (OMP: Error #15: Initializing libomp.dylib, but found libomp.dylib already initialized) instead of raising a catchable Python exception — which is exactly what a Nanny-managed silent restart loop looks like from the outside.

Fix: set these two environment variables before launching the worker on macOS:

KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK=TRUE OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 dask worker tcp://<scheduler-ip>:8786 --nworkers <n> --nthreads 1

If a worker is still crash-looping and you need to see the actual OS-level error, look at the raw terminal where dask worker runs directly — Segmentation fault, Illegal instruction, or the OMP: Error #15 line only ever prints there, never through the Dask protocol.

docs.title: dask worker can't find zeit even though you just installed it
docs.text:
If pip install zeit-cdts (or pip install -e .) reported success but a worker still throws ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'zeit', the dask command on your PATH is almost certainly resolving to a different Python installation (a different conda env, a system Python, a pyenv shim) than the one you installed zeit into.

Force it explicitly — activate the right environment, then launch via python -m dask instead of the bare dask binary, so it always uses the currently active interpreter:

conda activate zeit-worker   # or: source your-venv/bin/activate
python -m dask worker tcp://<scheduler-ip>:8786 --nworkers <n> --nthreads 1

docs.title: Sanity-check every worker before submitting real work
docs.text:
From the client/head node, verify zeit actually imports on every connected worker before kicking off a real job — it's much faster to catch a broken worker this way than to debug a stuck/slow distributed run:

from dask.distributed import Client

client = Client("tcp://<scheduler-ip>:8786")

def check():
    import socket, sys
    try:
        from zeit import landtrendr
        return (socket.gethostname(), sys.executable, "ok")
    except Exception as e:
        return (socket.gethostname(), sys.executable, repr(e))

print(client.run(check, on_error="return"))

A clean "ok" (or a normal, readable Python exception) per worker means you're good to go. A CommClosedError / Stream is closed here is the macOS crash-loop symptom described above ("macOS: a worker crash-loops") — fix that first.

docs.title: Too many local read threads can be slower than reading sequentially
docs.text:
If your input files only exist on the machine that's also acting as the client (the common case when the other machines don't share a network drive), you have to read them locally before handing chunks to the cluster. It's tempting to parallelize that read with a large thread pool, but past a certain point you're not adding throughput — you're adding disk-queue contention.

Measured reading 41 full-resolution GeoTIFFs (~218MB each, ~8.9GB total) from a local NVMe drive:

Threads Time 1 (sequential) 26.6s 2 22.9s 4 22.0s (best) 16 100.7s (4.6x slower than sequential!)

A modest thread pool (3-4) beat both sequential and 16 threads by a wide margin. Benchmark this on your own disk before picking a number — the right count depends on whether it's NVMe, SATA SSD, spinning disk, or a network share, but "more threads" is not a safe default assumption.

docs.title: Gathering a big distributed result can OOM a single worker, even though the cluster computed it fine
docs.text:
If you call .compute() (or client.gather()) directly on a large persisted Dask array, Dask may run a "finalize" (concatenation) task on a single worker to assemble the pieces before handing them to the client — and that worker's own --memory-limit might be far smaller than the assembled result, even though every individual chunk fit in memory just fine:

MemoryError: Task 'finalize-...' has 2.84 GiB worth of input dependencies,
but worker tcp://192.168.2.40:55301 has memory_limit set to 1.60 GiB.

Avoid this by gathering block-by-block instead of triggering one big finalize, and assembling the final array yourself on the client (which usually has far more RAM to spare than a single worker's configured limit):

import numpy as np

n_bands = persisted.shape[0]
y_chunks, x_chunks = persisted.chunks[1], persisted.chunks[2]
y_off = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(y_chunks)])
x_off = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(x_chunks)])

block_futs = {
    (by, bx): client.compute(persisted.blocks[:, by, bx])
    for by in range(len(y_chunks))
    for bx in range(len(x_chunks))
}
gathered = client.gather(block_futs)

result = np.empty((n_bands, H, W), dtype=np.float32)
for (by, bx), arr in gathered.items():
    result[:, y_off[by]:y_off[by + 1], x_off[bx]:x_off[bx + 1]] = arr

This also parallelizes the fetch itself (all blocks are requested up front, not one at a time), so it's usually faster than the naive .compute() in addition to being memory-safe.

docs.title: Phenology
docs.text:
Extract the calendar of the growing season for every pixel and every year: when green-up starts, when it peaks, when it ends, and how long it lasts. Use it to map crop calendars, detect late planting or drought, find double cropping, or follow climate-driven shifts in vegetation.

AnswersWhen does the season start, peak and end? Is this year different? InputA dense vegetation-index series (8- or 16-day), optional QA weights Output19 phenology metrics plus fit quality, per season and pixel ReferenceWritten from the papers listed in the references; R phenofit (Kong et al., 2022) is a useful reference to compare outputs with

What phenology extraction produces. Three years of an 8-day NDVI series with noise and cloud drops. For each season, Zeit finds the start (SOS, 50% of the amplitude), the peak and the end (EOS). The shifts between years, such as the later start in 2020, are exactly what anomaly analyses look for.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Raw index series are noisy and gappy, so metrics are not read from the raw points. The pipeline runs four steps per pixel:

  1. Smooth the series with a Whittaker smoother (or HANTS harmonics) to fill gaps and damp noise. whittaker_lambda sets the stiffness.
  2. Split it into seasons, one per trough-to-trough cycle. Double and triple cropping produce several seasons per year.
  3. Fit a smooth parametric curve to each season with Levenberg-Marquardt least squares. The curve is re-weighted iteratively so that low outliers (clouds) pull it less.
  4. Extract the transition dates from the fitted curve with several methods at once.

Available curves (curve=):

Curve Notes "beck" Double logistic of Beck et al. (2006). The default, and a good general choice. "elmore" Double logistic with a summer green-down term (Elmore et al., 2012). "gu" Gu et al. (2009), flexible asymmetric shape. "klos" Klosterman et al. (2014). "zhang" Piecewise logistic (Zhang et al., 2003). "ag" Asymmetric Gaussian. "dl" Plain double logistic.

docs.title: The 19 metrics
docs.text:
Every method below is computed from the same fitted curve, at no extra cost, whatever method= says. All dates are days of the year (with annual=False, days counted from January 1st of the first year).

Family Metrics Definition Threshold TRS2.sos, TRS2.eos Curve crosses 20% of the seasonal amplitude (rising, falling). TRS5.sos, TRS5.eos Crosses 50%. A robust default for start and end of season. TRS6.sos, TRS6.eos Crosses 60%. Derivative DER.sos, DER.eos Fastest green-up and fastest senescence (extremes of the first derivative). DER.pos Peak of the season (first derivative is zero). Gu UD, SD, DD, RD Upturn, stabilisation, downturn and recession dates, from the second derivative. Zhang Greenup, Maturity, Senescence, Dormancy Extremes of the rate of change of curvature. General LOS Length of season in days. POP Position of the peak.

Two quality metrics, R2 and RMSE of the fitted curve, follow the 19 phenology metrics, so the output xarray.Dataset has 21 variables.

docs.title: Processing a raster
docs.text:
zeit.phenology takes the cube as it is: a raster on disk, a (time, y, x) cube in memory or on Dask, a numpy array with dates=, or a single pixel's series. It computes the day numbering and the years from the dates, and by default (annual=True) maps each season to its calendar year, with dates as days of the year.

import zeit

# 1. The dense time series as a (time, y, x) cube; the dates come from the band
#    descriptions (pass dates= for a stack without them)
evi = zeit.load_raster("MODIS_EVI_Series.tif")

# 2. Smooth, fit and extract the metrics, every pixel in parallel (Rust)
pheno = zeit.phenology(
    evi,
    curve="beck",               # Beck's double logistic
    whittaker_lambda=10.0,      # Whittaker smoothness parameter
    apply_whittaker=True,       # apply Whittaker before fitting
    min_season_length=7,        # a season must last at least 7 days
    min_amplitude=0.0,
    min_pixel_amplitude=0.1,    # skip dead/water pixels entirely
    n_jobs=14,                  # 14 CPU threads
)
# An xarray.Dataset of 21 variables (19 metrics + R2 + RMSE), each (year, y, x)
sos = pheno["TRS5.sos"].sel(year=2010)   # day of year; names with dots need brackets

# 3. One georeferenced GeoTIFF per metric, one band per year (2001, 2002, ...)
zeit.save_raster(pheno, "pheno_out")

For a raster larger than memory, pass chunks="auto": the result is lazy and is computed block by block while save_raster writes it. The accessor form, evi.zeit.phenology(curve="beck", ...), is the same function.

docs.title: Worked example: late planting in soybean fields
docs.text:
This section walks through a complete, realistic problem end-to-end: an analyst wants to know whether soybean fields in a Mato Grosso municipality (Brazil) show anomalously delayed green-up in a candidate drought year, compared to a multi-year baseline — a common early-warning question for agricultural monitoring and drought impact assessment. Late green-up (a positive SOS anomaly, in days) is a classic remote signal of delayed planting caused by late onset of the rainy season.

The workflow chains three zeit building blocks: build_time_series (STAC ingestion) → regularize_time_series (temporal regularization) → zeit.phenology (metric extraction), all lazy until .compute() is called — so it scales from a single tile to a whole state without changing the code.

docs.title: Step 1 — Build a multi-year Sentinel-2 cube for the area of interest
docs.text:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import zeit
from zeit import regularize_time_series

# Multi-year window covering the baseline + the candidate drought year (2021)
cube_raw = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="earth_search",
    collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
    tiles=["21LWH"],              # A Sentinel-2 MGRS tile over Mato Grosso cropland
    start_date="2019-07-01",
    end_date="2022-06-30",        # 3 full crop years: 2019/20, 2020/21, 2021/22
    bands=["red", "nir"],
    apply_cloud_mask=True,        # Drops clouds/shadows using the SCL band automatically
)

docs.title: Step 2 — Compute NDVI and regularize to 16-day composites
docs.text:
Phenology curve-fitting expects a reasonably dense, evenly-spaced time axis — raw STAC revisits are irregular (5–12 days, with cloud gaps). We compute NDVI first (single-band, so method="median" is the right choice — medoid needs a band dimension to compare against) and then regularize:

ndvi_raw = (cube_raw.sel(band="nir") - cube_raw.sel(band="red")) / (
    cube_raw.sel(band="nir") + cube_raw.sel(band="red")
)

ndvi_16d = regularize_time_series(ndvi_raw, freq="16D", method="median")

docs.title: Step 3 — Run the phenology engine across all three crop years at once
docs.text:
# The day numbering and the years (2019 ... 2022) come from the cube's dates.
pheno = zeit.phenology(
    ndvi_16d,
    curve="beck",
    apply_whittaker=True,
    whittaker_lambda=5.0,       # a bit looser than default: S2 NDVI is noisier than MODIS
    min_season_length=45,       # ignore green-ups shorter than ~45 days (noise, not a crop cycle)
    min_amplitude=0.15,
    min_pixel_amplitude=0.15,   # skip forest/water/urban pixels entirely — huge speedup at scale
    n_jobs=-1,                  # annual=True (default): one value per calendar year
).compute()

docs.title: Step 4 — Compute the SOS anomaly for the candidate drought year
docs.text:
We use DER.sos (derivative-based Start of Season — see the 19 metrics) and compare the target year against the mean of the other years in the window:

sos = pheno["DER.sos"]   # dims: (year, y, x), values in day-of-year

target_year = 2021
baseline_years = [y for y in sos.year.values if y != target_year]

baseline_mean_sos = sos.sel(year=baseline_years).mean(dim="year", skipna=True)
target_sos = sos.sel(year=target_year)

# Positive = later green-up than the baseline (a delayed-planting / drought signal)
sos_anomaly_days = target_sos - baseline_mean_sos

docs.title: Step 5 — Visualize and export
docs.text:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
sos_anomaly_days.plot(
    ax=ax, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-30, vmax=30,
    cbar_kwargs={"label": "SOS anomaly (days, + = later green-up)"},
)
ax.set_title(f"Planting Delay Anomaly — {target_year} vs. {baseline_years} baseline")
plt.savefig("sos_anomaly_2021.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

# Export as a GeoTIFF for use in QGIS or further zonal statistics (georeferenced from the cube)
zeit.save_raster(sos_anomaly_days, f"sos_anomaly_{target_year}.tif")

docs.title: Interpreting the result
docs.text:
• Anomaly > +15 days: green-up notably delayed relative to the baseline — worth cross-checking against rainfall onset records for that season; a classic drought/late-planting signal.
  • Anomaly < -15 days: notably earlier green-up — can indicate irrigation, an earlier-maturing cultivar, or a shift toward double-cropping.
  • NaN pixels: no season passed the min_amplitude / min_season_length filters in at least one of the years being compared (e.g., fallow land, pasture, or a rotation year) — xarray's alignment propagates this automatically, no special handling needed.
  • This is a remote-sensing signal, not ground truth — always validate against field records or known planting calendars before drawing operational conclusions.

Because every step here (build_time_series, regularize_time_series, phenology) is Dask-backed, the exact same code scales from one MGRS tile to an entire state or country simply by widening bbox/tiles — only the chunk count (and wall-clock time) changes.

docs.title: Double and triple cropping
docs.text:
In regions with intense agricultural activity (like Mato Grosso, Brazil), a single pixel might feature two or even three distinct crop harvests within a single year (e.g., Soybeans followed by Corn).

To capture these dynamics, ask for one value per detected season instead of one per calendar year, with annual=False and max_seasons: 

seasons = zeit.phenology(evi, annual=False, max_seasons=3)
