docs.title: Sentinel-2 Level 1C to Surface Reflectance
docs.text:
A Sentinel-2 Level 1C scene is reflectance at the top of the atmosphere. zeit.level2 takes a product, a .SAFE directory or just its name, to surface reflectance: the water vapour and the gases, the aerosol estimated from the scene's dark targets, the adjacency effect, the topographic and BRDF corrections, and a cloud, shadow, snow and water mask from Zeit's own Fmask. It is what FORCE's force-l2ps does for one image, in the Zeit core.

AnswersWhat was the surface reflectance of this scene, and which pixels can be trusted? InputA Level 1C .SAFE directory or the name of a product, and a DEM in metres (any grid and CRS) or dem="glo30" OutputA Dataset on the scene's 10 m grid: boa, qai, dst, vzn, hot, aod, wvp ReferenceFORCE 3.11.00 (David Frantz, GPL-3.0-or-later; Frantz 2019, Remote Sensing 11:1124); Fmask 4.7 (Qiu, Zhu and Woodcock 2019, Remote Sensing of Environment 231:111205)

What is, and what is not, equal to FORCE

With FORCE's cloud flags, sun, geography and BRDF factor as inputs, every product of level2 equals that of force-l2ps in 100 % of the pixels. The public function does not take those from FORCE: it computes the cloud mask with Zeit's Fmask, the sun with Zeit's own implementation and the BRDF factor with nbar's c-factor. With them it differs a little from FORCE, as the validation shows. It is for Sentinel-2 only and keeps the products on the scene's 10 m grid. The merge of the 20 m bands (merge=) and the coregistration to a reference (reference=) are optional, off by default, and done on the TOA reflectance before the correction, as FORCE does; the merge is compared with FORCE, the coregistration is not (it is AROSICS', FORCE's is another method).

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The .SAFE directory of a Level 1C product: MTD_MSIL1C.xml and one GRANULE/<name>/ with its IMG_DATA. The 13 band files are read by GDAL (the product's JPEG 2000 files, or GeoTIFFs of the same names).
  • A DEM in metres, on any grid and CRS: Zeit puts it on the scene's 10 m grid (bilinear by default, dem_resampling). topography=True, the default, needs it, and without it the call is a ValueError that says to pass the DEM or use topography=False. The atmosphere uses the elevation and the Fmask uses the DEM when it is given.
  • Optionally, a Global Surface Water Occurrence raster (percent) to help the Fmask find water (gswo).

docs.title: Find and download a scene
docs.text:
The scene and the DEM can come from the network, with no account or credential:

scenes = zeit.find_l1c(tile="23LKC", start="2023-07-01", end="2023-07-31", max_cloud=30)
safe = zeit.download_l1c(scenes.iloc[0])    # the path of the .SAFE; a DataFrame downloads them all
dem = zeit.download_dem(safe)               # one GeoTIFF of Copernicus GLO-30 over the scene
l2 = zeit.level2(safe, dem=dem)

Or in one call, with the name of the product and dem="glo30":

l2 = zeit.level2(scenes["product"][0], dem="glo30")

find_l1c searches the sentinel-2-l1c collection of Earth Search. download_l1c takes the files from Google Cloud's public bucket gcp-public-data-sentinel-2, because that one keeps the original layout of the product: only what level2 reads (the two XML files and the 13 band files, 672 MB in the 2023 scene of the validation), each checked by size and MD5, and an interrupted download resumes. They go to the cache (ZEIT_CACHE_DIR/l1c) unless dest= says otherwise. A product that Earth Search lists and the bucket does not have (some reprocessed ones) is a ValueError that names it.

download_dem mosaics the GLO-30 tiles over the scene in their own geometry. Where there is no tile (the sea) the value is the no-data of level2, an area with no tile at all is a ValueError that suggests topography=False, and a scene across the antimeridian is not handled.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import zeit

l2 = zeit.level2(
    "S2B_MSIL1C_20230728T132239_N0509_R038_T23LKC_20230728T150149.SAFE",
    dem="cop_glo30_23LKC.tif",
)
print(l2)

The result is an xarray.Dataset on the grid of the scene (10 m, the CRS and transform of the bands). attrs tell how the correction went: datetime (UTC), sensor, baseline, aod_green (the optical depth of the scene in B03), aod_map (False when the fallback spectrum was used), water_vapor_cm, n_targets (the valid water, shadow and vegetation dark targets), the summary of the Fmask as fmask_* keys, core_seconds and provenance.

Without a DEM, switch the topographic correction off:

l2 = zeit.level2(safe, brdf=False, topography=False)

docs.title: The products
docs.text:
Variable Dimensions What it is boa (band, y, x), int16 Surface reflectance times 10000, _FillValue -9999. band is BLUE, GREEN, RED, REDEDGE1, REDEDGE2, REDEDGE3, BROADNIR, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2 (BROADNIR is B08, NIR is B8A) qai (y, x), int16 FORCE's quality bits: no data, cloud, shadow, snow, water, and what the correction flagged (below) dst (y, x), int16 Distance to the nearest cloud, shadow or snow, in metres on the 10 m grid (0 on the targets). 32767 in the whole image when the scene has no cloud target vzn (y, x), int16 View zenith angle, in degrees times 100 hot (y, x), int16 Haze optimized transformation, in FORCE's units aod (y, x), int16 Aerosol optical depth of the scene's green band, times 1000 wvp (y, x), int16 Water vapour, in cm times 1000

Reflectance in 0-1 comes from boa, with the fill value left out:

red = l2.boa.sel(band="RED")
red = red.where(red != -9999) / 10000

docs.title: Reading the QAI flags
docs.text:
qai packs several flags in each 16-bit value. The ones to know, by bit position (bit 0 is the least significant):

Bit(s) Flag Values 0 No data (outside the scene) 1 = off 1-2 Cloud state 0 none, 1 less confident (the buffer), 2 confident and opaque, 3 cirrus 3 Cloud shadow 1 = shadow 4 Snow 1 = snow 5 Water 1 = water 6-7 Aerosol 0 good, 1 interpolated, 2 high AOD, 3 fill value of the scene 8 Sub-zero reflectance the surface reflectance was below 0 in a band 9 Saturation the surface reflectance was above 1 in a band 10 Low sun the sun's zenith is above 75 degrees 11-12 Illumination 0 good, 1 moderate, 2 poor, 3 deep shadow 13 Slope the slope is above 2 degrees 14 Water vapour fill the water vapour of the pixel is the scene's average

The cloud buffer of the QAI is 300 m, as in FORCE, and Zeit's Fmask never marks cirrus. A clear-sky mask, then, is a few bit operations:

q = l2.qai
off = (q & 1) != 0
cloud = ((q >> 1) & 3) != 0
shadow = ((q >> 3) & 1) != 0
snow = ((q >> 4) & 1) != 0
clear = ~(off | cloud | shadow | snow)

red = l2.boa.sel(band="RED").where(clear) / 10000
nir = l2.boa.sel(band="BROADNIR").where(clear) / 10000
ndvi = (nir - red) / (nir + red)

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default What it does brdf True Normalises the BRDF to nadir view and the sun at the zenith of the scene (FORCE's DO_BRDF). The factor is nbar's c-factor (Roy et al. 2016, 2017), not FORCE's brdf_factor; it enters the AOD retrieval even with brdf=False topography True The topographic correction of the illumination (DO_TOPO). Needs dem aod True Estimates the aerosol optical depth from the scene's dark targets; False uses the fallback spectrum adjacency True The environmental weighting of the adjacency effect multiple_scattering True False is single scattering erase_cloud False Sets the cloud pixels to no data flags None The cloud, shadow, snow and water bits of the QAI per pixel, int16 (nrows, ncols) on the 10 m grid (only bits 1 to 5 are read). With them the Fmask does not run fmask True Runs Zeit's Fmask when flags is None. False runs no cloud detection: there is no cloud flag, and dst is 32767 in the whole image gswo None Global Surface Water Occurrence (percent) for the Fmask, put on the 20 m grid by nearest neighbour fmask_compat False True reproduces three oddities of the original Fmask 4.7 code; the default corrects them dem_resampling "bilinear" The resampling of the DEM onto the grid of the scene (FORCE's default) n_jobs 8 Threads of the correction, the Fmask and the JPEG 2000 decoder merge None "regression" or "improphe": FORCE's resolution merge (RES_MERGE), the red edge 1-3, B8A, SWIR1 and SWIR2 predicted at 10 m from green, red and the broad NIR, on the TOA reflectance before the correction (see below) reference None A raster path or DataArray to coregister the scene to (AROSICS' global shift, coregister), on the TOA before the merge and the correction coreg_band "BROADNIR" The band of the scene that is matched to the reference coreg_ref_band None The band of reference to match (the first by default)

docs.title: Merge the 20 m bands and coregister
docs.text:
FORCE does both before the atmospheric correction, on the TOA reflectance, and so does level2 (the coregistration first): the aerosol, the vapour and the correction then see the merged and shifted bands, and every product comes out aligned.

l2 = zeit.level2(safe, dem="dem.tif", merge="improphe")                         # 10 m red edge, B8A, SWIR
l2 = zeit.level2(safe, dem="dem.tif", reference="base_nir.tif", coreg_band="BROADNIR", coreg_ref_band=1)
print(l2.attrs["coreg_x_shift_px"], l2.attrs["coreg_y_shift_px"], l2.attrs["coreg_success"])

The merge predicts a pixel only if it is not off and has no cloud and no shadow in the QAI (snow and water are predicted), as FORCE does, and uses the arithmetic of FORCE (force=True of sentinel2_resmerge). The coregistration finds one shift on coreg_band (a 10 m band is best) and moves the 13 bands (cubic) and the QAI (nearest neighbour) by it; the reference may be on another grid, it is put on the scene's. If no shift is found the scene is processed as it is and attrs say it (coreg_success, coreg_reason). The pixels the shift uncovers are off. The shift is AROSICS', not FORCE's: FORCE's coregister is another method, so it is not compared with FORCE.

On tile 23LKC (2023), with FORCE's cloud flags, sun, geography and BRDF factor, the merge gives the same qai, dst, hot, aod, vzn and wvp as force-l2ps with RES_MERGE in every pixel of the 120,560,400, and boa differs in 9 to 70 pixels per band with ImproPhe (by 1 to 3) and in 196 to 271 pixels of each of the six merged bands with the regression (by 2 to 12; compared with a FORCE run on one thread: FORCE's regression is not deterministic with several). The merge alone takes 11.4 s with ImproPhe and 182 s with the regression on this scene (8 threads; the regression of FORCE's arithmetic runs on one). A reference made from the scene's own BROADNIR moved by +2.5 pixels in x and -1.5 in y was found as +2.47 and -1.47 (reliability 95.6).

The merge costs memory: the whole call peaked at 21.6 GiB of RAM without it and at 28.7 GiB with either method (the full 10980 x 10980 tile, 8 threads), and took 146 s without it, 158 s with ImproPhe and 332 s with the regression.

docs.title: Your own cloud mask
docs.text:
Zeit's Fmask runs at 20 m. If you have a mask you trust more, give it as flags: the Fmask does not run, and the QAI carries your bits.

import numpy as np

flags = np.zeros((10980, 10980), dtype=np.int16)    # the scene's 10 m grid: (rows, columns)
flags[my_cloud] |= 2 << 1                           # cloud state 2: confident and opaque
flags[my_shadow] |= 1 << 3                          # shadow
l2 = zeit.level2(safe, dem="dem.tif", flags=flags)

docs.title: Water and the Fmask
docs.text:
l2 = zeit.level2(safe, dem="dem.tif", gswo="gswo_23LKC.tif")
fmask_summary = {k: v for k, v in l2.attrs.items() if k.startswith("fmask_")}

The fmask_* keys of attrs are the Fmask's summary, as plain numbers, booleans and strings, so the Dataset can be written to NetCDF.

docs.title: Save and look
docs.text:
l2.zeit.save("l2_20230728")          # a folder: boa.tif, qai.tif, dst.tif, ...
l2.zeit.save("l2_20230728.tif")      # or one multi-band file
l2.zeit.plot()                       # a selector of the variables

See .zeit.save and .zeit.plot for the options.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
level2 was compared with force-l2ps of FORCE 3.11.00 (8 threads) on tile 23LKC (Brazil, UTM 23S, 10980 x 10980 pixels at 10 m). The scenes and the FORCE outputs are not in the repository. The tables are in Against the Original Implementations.

With FORCE's inputs. Given FORCE's cloud flags, sun, geography and BRDF factor, boa (the 10 bands), qai, aod, wvp, hot, dst and vzn are equal to FORCE's in 100 % of the pixels in three runs: 2023-07-28 without BRDF, 2023-07-28 with BRDF (baseline 05.09) and 2021-07-28 without BRDF (baseline 03.01). In 2023 that is 120,560,400 pixels per band.

With Zeit's own sun. The sun of level2 is a clean-room implementation, up to 0.0105 degrees from FORCE's. With it and FORCE's cloud flags (2023, without BRDF), the pixels equal to FORCE's go from 75.04 % (blue) to 92.45 % (SWIR2), and the mean difference from 0.56 to 0.08 in reflectance times 10000.

With Zeit's Fmask. Its cloud-or-shadow mask marks 19.93 % of the pixels against 19.70 % in FORCE's, agreeing in 98.12 % of them (IoU 0.910). Only the shadow diverges, by construction: FORCE marks shadow also inside the confident cloud and uses another version of the Fmask. Against the Sen2Cor scene classification of ESA (2023), the Fmask of Zeit and FORCE's QAI agree with it in 91.28 % of the pixels (IoU 0.58 in cloud or shadow), and mark about 20 % against its 13 %, with the 300 m ring included.

Against ESA's L2A. The L2A of the same tile and date is another chain, so no equality is expected, and FORCE against the L2A is the control. On the pixels valid in the three products, clear in both masks and classified by the SCL as vegetation or bare soil (23,405,935 pixels in 2023), the bias in reflectance times 10000 is:

Band (2023-07-28, baseline 05.09) Zeit minus L2A FORCE minus L2A BLUE -24.58 -25.13 RED 6.16 6.05 NIR 34.94 34.92 SWIR1 -174.71 -174.70 SWIR2 -242.22 -242.22

Zeit and FORCE are at nearly the same distance from the L2A in every band. The L2A is 165 to 242 above both in the two SWIR bands; that bias was not checked against the literature, so it is not known which chain is closer to the truth.

Speed. The whole chain with Zeit's Fmask took 141 to 147 s (113 to 119 s in the core) against 197 s for force-l2ps, both with 8 threads, on a machine that was not dedicated: these times are not a clean benchmark.

Not compared. A scene without any cloud target gives dst 32767 in every pixel; that case was not compared with FORCE.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It is for Sentinel-2 only.
  • It keeps the products on the 10 m grid of the scene. FORCE's reprojection to its datacube is not done.
  • It merges the 20 m bands and coregisters only when asked (merge=, reference=), and only the global shift of coregister; the local warp of coregister_local, the merge of a time series and the other uses of sentinel2_resmerge are steps of their own: Preparing images.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text: level2 is the atmospheric correction of FORCE 3.11.00 (David Frantz, GPL-3.0-or-later; Frantz 2019, Remote Sensing 11:1124) in the Zeit core. The cloud, shadow, snow and water mask is Zeit's port of Fmask 4.7 (Qiu, Zhu and Woodcock 2019, Remote Sensing of Environment 231:111205). The distance to cloud (dst) is rewritten in a clean room from FORCE's public documentation and the outputs of its DST product, and the sun is Zeit's own clean-room implementation. The full signature and every parameter are in the API reference.

docs.title: Siamese Change Detector
docs.text:
AnswersWhere did this area change between two dates? InputTwo co-registered images (batch, bands, H, W) OutputA per-pixel change map ReferenceFC-Siam-diff, Daudt et al. (2018); same outputs as the authors' code

The Siamese Change Detector is a bi-temporal architecture: given two co-registered images of the same area at two different dates, it outputs a per-pixel change probability map. It is the FC-Siam-diff network of:

Daudt, R. C., Le Saux, B., & Boulch, A. (2018). Fully convolutional siamese networks for change detection. 2018 25th IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP) (pp. 4063–4067). https://doi.org/10.1109/ICIP.2018.8451652

zeit.ai.SiameseChangeDetector is written from the paper, not copied from the authors' code (which publishes no license), and it is the same network: with the weights of the authors' SiamUnet_diff (rcdaudt/fully_convolutional_change_detection) it gives the same log-probabilities, to 1e-15 in double precision, for any image size. Trained the same way, the two reach the same accuracy, and zeit's predicts faster (it runs both dates through the encoder in one pass); see Benchmarks.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The core idea of a Siamese network is weight sharing: the same encoder is applied to both images, so that their features live in the same representation space and a difference between them reflects a difference in content, not in how the two images were processed. FC-Siam-diff is a U-Net built on that idea:

  1. Shared encoder (forward_once): four stages of 3×3 convolutions, each followed by batch normalization, ReLU and dropout (16, 16 | 32, 32 | 64, 64, 64 | 128, 128, 128 channels), with a 2×2 max-pooling between stages. Both images, x_t0 ("before") and x_t1 ("after"), go through it with the same weights.
  2. Differences at every scale: at the end of each stage, the absolute difference of the two dates' features, |f₀ − f₁|, is passed to the decoder (the skip connections of the U-Net). The fine scales keep the edges of a clearing or a one-pixel road; the coarse ones bring the context that tells a real change from a change of illumination.
  3. Decoder: from the bottleneck (as in the authors' code, that of the second date), each stage upsamples by 2 (a transposed convolution), concatenates the difference of that scale, and applies the encoder's convolutions in reverse; the last convolution gives the per-pixel logits of num_classes classes (by default 2: "no change" and "change").

The image halves four times, so the windows are 16 pixels or more; any size works (an odd size is padded back in the decoder, as in the authors' code). Both dates go through the encoder in one pass (the authors' code runs it once per date). In prediction the result is the same; in training, batch normalization then takes the statistics of both dates together, which trains as well as the authors' code (F1 0.969 against 0.970 over six seeds) and faster.

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text: Use the Siamese Change Detector for classic bi-temporal change detection: you have exactly two dates (before/after an event — a wildfire, deforestation, a flood, construction) and want a change map between them. If you have a longer time series and want to classify or segment based on the whole trajectory rather than just two snapshots, use LightTAE (per-pixel) or UTAE (whole-patch segmentation) instead.

docs.title: From a cube to a map
docs.text:
The data is a pair of images, (before, after), each a map or a stack of bands on the same grid, and the classes say what changed (e.g. change and same; any number of classes):

import zeit
from zeit import ai

before = zeit.load_raster("s2_2021_08.tif")                           # (band, y, x)
after = zeit.load_raster("s2_2023_08.tif", like="s2_2021_08.tif")    # on the same grid
samples = ai.samples((before, after), "change.gpkg", label="class", patch=64)
model = ai.train(ai.SiameseChangeDetector, samples, epochs=100)
change = ai.predict(model, (before, after), probability=True)

The encoder halves the window four times, so patch is 16 or more (64 or more gives the deepest stage some context). Label both what changed and what did not around it: polygons covering the unchanged land teach the model as much as the changed ones. See Deep Learning.

docs.title: Instantiating the Model
docs.text:
zeit.ai.train builds the model for you from the samples (bands, dates, classes); the arguments below pass through it, e.g. ai.train(ai.SiameseChangeDetector, samples, num_classes=2). To build it yourself:

from zeit.ai import SiameseChangeDetector

model = SiameseChangeDetector(
    in_channels=6,     # spectral bands per image
    num_classes=2,     # 2 for binary change/no-change; more for multi-class change type
    dropout=0.2,       # after every convolution, as in the paper
)

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model = model.to(device)

docs.title: Loss Functions
docs.text:
Two natural options from zeit.ai.losses, depending on how you want to train:

  • FocalLoss / TverskyLoss: apply directly to the classifier's (B, num_classes, H, W) output logits vs. the (B, H, W) label map — the standard approach if you're training the full pipeline (encoders + decoder + classifier) end-to-end as a segmentation problem. Both handle the severe class imbalance typical of change detection (changed pixels are usually a small minority).
  • ContrastiveSiameseLoss: operates directly on the two encoder feature maps rather than the final classifier output (forward_once(x) gives the features of one image at each scale; the first, forward_once(x)[0], is at the full resolution of the label map) — it pulls feature vectors together for unchanged pixels and pushes them apart (up to a margin) for changed pixels. Use this if you want to train the twin encoder as a metric-learning problem (e.g. for downstream thresholding or few-shot change detection), separately from or in addition to the classifier head.
from zeit.ai.losses import FocalLoss, ContrastiveSiameseLoss

criterion = FocalLoss(alpha=0.25, gamma=2.0)
# or, to also supervise the encoder features directly:
contrastive_criterion = ContrastiveSiameseLoss(margin=2.0)

docs.title: A loop of your own
docs.text: zeit.ai.train covers the usual case. For anything else (another optimizer, a scheduler, augmentation), the SampleSet is a PyTorch Dataset whose items hold the normalized x, the label y and the date positions; see A loop of your own. A model trained this way can still be classified with zeit.ai.predict after zeit.ai.train(model, samples, epochs=0) records the samples' metadata in it.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • Daudt, R. C., Le Saux, B., & Boulch, A. (2018). Fully convolutional siamese networks for change detection. In 2018 25th IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP) (pp. 4063–4067). https://doi.org/10.1109/ICIP.2018.8451652

docs.title: Segmentation (SNIC)
docs.text:
Group neighbouring pixels with similar histories into compact regions called superpixels, then work with regions instead of pixels. Classifying one mean time series per field removes salt-and-pepper noise and cuts the number of samples by orders of magnitude.

AnswersWhich pixels belong together as one object (field, patch, stand)? InputAn image or a whole cube: (y, x), (feature, y, x) or (time, band, y, x) OutputA label map, each segment's mean trajectory, centroids and sizes ReferenceAchanta & Süsstrunk (2017); the workflow of R sits

Result on real data. A 320 × 320 pixel area of Rondônia segmented on its full 40-year NDVI history (40 features per pixel). Left: one of the 40 layers. Middle: segment boundaries. Right: each segment filled with its mean. Segments follow field edges and the river because they group pixels with similar trajectories, not just similar values on one date. Data: annual Landsat NDVI composites exported from LT-GEE on Google Earth Engine.

docs.title: Why segment a time series?
docs.text:
zeit.snic works on a single image and on a whole time-series cube: every (time, band) pair becomes one feature, so two pixels are close when their trajectories are close. Two fields with the same average NDVI but opposite seasons fall into different segments. This is the object-based workflow of sits_segment(seg_fn = sits_snic()) in R's sits.

Given the same seeds, Zeit produces the same labels as the authors' reference implementation (github.com/achanta/SNIC), pixel for pixel.

docs.title: How SNIC works
docs.text:
1. Seeds are placed on a grid. Each seed starts a cluster.
  2. A single priority queue holds candidate (pixel, cluster, distance) entries; it starts with every seed at distance 0.
  3. The closest entry is popped. If its pixel is still free, it joins that cluster, the cluster's running means are updated, and the pixel's free 4-neighbours are pushed with their distance to the updated cluster.
  4. Repeat until every pixel is labelled — one pass, no iterations (unlike SLIC's k-means).

The distance combines feature and image space:

\[ d = \lVert \mathbf{c}_i - \mathbf{c}_k \rVert^2 + \left(\frac{M}{S}\right)^2 \lVert \mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{p}_k \rVert^2, \qquad S = \sqrt{N / K} \]

where \(\mathbf{c}\) are the features (all bands at all dates), \(\mathbf{p}\) the row/column position, \(N\) the number of valid pixels, \(K\) the number of seeds and \(M\) the compactness.

Choosing compactness

The feature term is in data units, so \(M\) must follow the scale of your data. Small \(M\) follows the data closely (irregular segments); large \(M\) approaches a regular grid. 0.5 is the sits default for reflectance-scaled cubes; the reference implementation's 10 suits 0-255 CIELAB images. If bands have very different ranges, standardise them first — every feature counts equally in the distance.

docs.title: 1. Segment a cube
docs.text:
import zeit

cube = zeit.load_raster("ndvi_evi_2022.tif")      # (time, band, y, x), e.g. 23 dates x (NDVI, EVI)
seg = zeit.snic(cube, spacing=10, compactness=0.5, grid="hexagonal")

seg.labels       # (y, x) segment ids, -1 = unlabelled (missing pixels), georeferenced
seg.means        # (segment, time, band): the mean trajectory of every segment
seg.n_pixels     # (segment,) pixel counts
seg.centroid_x   # (segment,) centre of mass, in map coordinates (also centroid_y)

Seeds come from one of two places:

Argument Seeds spacing= (+ grid, padding) the grids of the R snic package used by sits_snic() (snic_grid): "rectangular" (default), "diamond", "hexagonal", "random"; default spacing=10, padding=spacing/2 seeds= your own (n, 2) (row, col) pixel positions (takes precedence)

The same works on a single map (y, x), a stack (band, y, x) or a raster path, and as cube.zeit.snic(...).

docs.title: 2. Export polygons
docs.text:
gdf = zeit.snic_to_polygons(seg, include_means=True)
# columns: supercells, x, y (centroid), n_pixels, one column per feature (2022-01-01_ndvi, ...), geometry
zeit.save_raster(seg, "results/snic")              # labels.tif

The segment means can go straight to any classifier (TempCNN, LTAE, TWDTW, random forest…) as one sample per segment.

docs.title: Large images: tiles and parallelism
docs.text:
SNIC is inherently sequential — each step depends on the previous pop — so a single image is segmented on one core. The compiled core was already 1.5–4× faster than the reference C code on one thread in C++ (more so with more features: pixel-major feature layout for contiguous, vectorised distance computations; float32 input used without a float64 copy), and the Rust core of 2.0 takes 0.7–0.9 of that time; the data reordering runs on several threads.

For large scenes, use tile_size: the image is split into tiles that are segmented independently and in parallel, each seed belonging to the tile that contains it — the same block-wise strategy sits_segment() uses. Segments never cross tile edges, and labels remain the global seed index, so the output is identical for any n_jobs.

seg = zeit.snic(cube, spacing=10, compactness=0.5, tile_size=512, n_jobs=-1)

Memory: the core keeps one pixel-major copy of each tile being processed (rows × cols × features values of the input dtype) plus the priority queue.

Fidelity to the reference implementation

From the same seeds, the labels match those of snic.c (Achanta, EPFL). That includes how ties are broken: when two clusters reach a pixel at exactly the same cost, the heap's order decides the winner the same way. The test suite gives Zeit the seeds the original placed and compares labels on RGB-like, noisy, piecewise-constant (many ties) and time-series inputs, in float32 and float64. The original's code is not included in Zeit.

Differences from the original:

  • Seed grid: seeds come from the sits grids (spacing) or your own list, not from the original's FindSeeds. To compare with the original, pass its seeds explicitly, as the test suite does.
  • NaN handling (as in the R snic package used by sits): pixels with a NaN in any feature are left unlabelled (-1), and \(N\) counts valid pixels only. A seed on a NaN pixel gives an empty segment. Gap-fill the cube first (regularize_time_series, apply_whittaker_filter) if you want every pixel labelled.
  • Heap bug fix: the reference pop() never removes the heap's last node. With a single seed it reads an uninitialised pixel index and crashes; on tiny images it can return a label that does not exist. Here the heap drains normally.
  • No RGB→CIELAB conversion: the reference's optional doRGBtoLAB is specific to 8-bit RGB photos; convert beforehand if you need it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Achanta, R., & Süsstrunk, S. (2017). Superpixels and Polygons Using Simple Non-Iterative Clustering. CVPR 2017, 4651–4660.
  • Simoes, R., et al. snic: Superpixel Segmentation with the Simple Non-Iterative Clustering Algorithm (R package), used by sits_snic().
  • Simoes, R., Camara, G., et al. (2021). Satellite Image Time Series Analysis for Big Earth Observation Data. Remote Sensing, 13(13), 2428.

docs.title: Clustering (SOM)
docs.text:
Find the main types of behaviour in a landscape without any labels. A self-organizing map groups millions of pixel trajectories into a small grid of prototypes, each one a typical time series, arranged so that similar prototypes sit next to each other.

AnswersWhich typical trajectories exist here, and where? InputA cube, a stack or a Dataset of maps: every value of a pixel is a feature OutputA cluster map, the prototype trajectory of each cluster and each pixel's distance to it ReferenceKohonen (1990, 2013); bit-exact port of minisom

Result on real data. 40-year NDVI trajectories of 490,000 pixels in Rondônia, clustered by a 2 × 2 batch SOM trained on a sample of 30,000. The prototypes separate a gradient from intact forest (cluster 1) to the land cleared earliest (cluster 4). No labels were used. Data: annual Landsat NDVI composites exported from LT-GEE on Google Earth Engine.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A SOM is a grid of neurons, each holding a prototype vector with as many values as your features. Training repeatedly finds, for each sample, its closest neuron (its best-matching unit, BMU) and moves that neuron and its grid neighbours toward the sample. The neighbourhood and the learning rate shrink as training goes on. The result is a set of prototypes that covers the data and is topologically ordered: neighbours on the grid are similar.

Zeit implements both forms of the algorithm in Rust:

  • Online SOM (Kohonen, 1990): one sample at a time, sequential by definition.
  • Batch SOM (Kohonen, 2013): every prototype is updated from all samples at once in each pass, on several threads. It is much faster on large satellite data sets.

Its engine, zeit.ai.SOM, is an operation-by-operation port of Python minisom. Given the same seed and arguments it draws the same initial weights and sample order and applies the same arithmetic, so the trained codebook is bit-for-bit identical to MiniSom, 30–190 times faster. See Algorithm Fidelity.

docs.title: 1. Cluster a cube
docs.text:
zeit.som takes the cube as it is. Every value a pixel holds off y/x is a feature: each date of an index, each band of each date, or each map of a Dataset (phenology metrics, LandTrendr's event maps...).

import zeit

ndvi = zeit.load_raster("LT_Stack_NDVI_Rondonia.tif")      # (time, y, x), 40 years
clusters = zeit.som(ndvi, x=2, y=2, sample=30_000)

The SOM is trained on a random sample of pixels (sample, reproducible by seed), which is usually enough. Then every pixel goes to its best-matching neuron, block by block if the cube is lazy. Pixels with a missing value (NaN, or the raster's NoData) get no neuron.

sigma is the initial neighbourhood radius in grid units. Small grids (2 × 2, 3 × 3) work as a clustering method. Larger grids (10 × 10 and up) are used to explore the data, or as a first step before grouping neurons.

docs.title: 2. Read the result
docs.text:
clusters.label                       # (y, x): the neuron of each pixel, 1 to x * y (0: no data)
clusters.distance                    # (y, x): distance to the neuron's prototype
clusters.prototypes                  # (neuron, time): one typical trajectory per neuron
clusters.n_pixels                    # (neuron): pixels in each cluster
clusters.attrs["quantization_error"] # mean distance of the sample to its prototypes

clusters.prototypes.sel(neuron=1).plot()
zeit.save_raster(clusters, "results/som")      # label.tif and distance.tif

The prototypes keep the cube's dims and coordinates, so a (time, band, y, x) cube gives prototypes (neuron, time, band). The grid position of each neuron is in the i and j coordinates (minisom's winner). A large distance marks the pixels the map represents poorly, which are often the interesting ones.

docs.title: 3. Look at it
docs.text:
clusters.label.zeit.plot()           # the cluster map, one colour per neuron
zeit.plot(ndvi, fit=clusters)        # click a pixel: its series, with its neuron's prototype

docs.title: 4. Clean labelled samples (optional)
docs.text:
SOMs are also used to check the training data of a supervised classifier: a sample whose class disagrees with the majority class of its neuron is suspicious. zeit.clean_samples trains a SOM on the samples' features and marks each one:

checked = zeit.clean_samples(stack, "samples.gpkg", label="class")
checked[["class", "neuron", "neuron_class", "purity", "keep"]]
rf = zeit.train_classifier(stack, checked[checked.keep], label="class")

purity is the share of the neuron's samples in its majority class: a neuron where two classes mix is a sign that the features cannot tell them apart. This is the idea behind sits_som_clean_samples() in R sits.

docs.title: Online or batch?
docs.text:
algorithm Same as minisom Meaning of num_iters Parallel "online" (default) MiniSom.train(data, num_iters) Number of single-sample updates (default: 20 passes over the sample) No (sequential by definition) "batch" MiniSom.train_batch_offline(data, num_iters) Number of full passes over the data (default 20) Yes (n_jobs)

zeit.som trains online by default. On small grids the batch update can leave neurons empty: a neuron that wins no sample is pulled onto its neighbour's mean and stays there, so two neurons end up identical. The online update does not do this, and on a sample of 50,000 it takes about as long. Batch pays off on large grids and samples, where it runs in parallel.

docs.title: The engine
docs.text:
zeit.som runs on zeit.ai.SOM, the engine, which you can also use directly on samples you arrange yourself, (samples, features):

from zeit.ai import SOM

som = SOM(x=2, y=2, input_len=X.shape[1], sigma=0.8, learning_rate=0.5, random_seed=0)
som.random_weights_init(X)               # or som.pca_weights_init(X)
som.train(X, num_iters=20, algorithm="batch")
prototypes = som.get_weights().reshape(-1, X.shape[1])
bmu = som.predict(X)                     # flat neuron index i * y + j, from 0 to x*y - 1
keep = som.filter_noisy_samples(X, labels)

train continues from the current weights, like minisom, and batch results are identical for any n_jobs. With sample=None and the same arguments (note that zeit.som lets the learning rate fall to 0, decay_function="linear_decay_to_zero", where the engine and minisom default to "asymptotic_decay"), zeit.som gives exactly the engine's prototypes, and label is som.predict + 1. All the methods are listed in the API reference.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Effect x, y 3, 3 Grid size. x * y is the number of prototypes. sample 50000 Pixels to train on (None: all). algorithm "online" "online" or "batch". num_iters None Updates (online) or passes (batch); default 20 passes. sigma 1.0 Initial spread of the neighbourhood function. learning_rate 0.5 Initial learning rate. decay "linear_decay_to_zero" Online: the learning rate falls to 0, so the prototypes settle (minisom's "asymptotic_decay" ends at a third of it). neighborhood "gaussian" "gaussian", "mexican_hat", "bubble" or "triangle". topology "rectangular" "rectangular" or "hexagonal" grid. init "random" "random" (sample pixels), "pca" (first two principal components) or None. seed 42 Seed of the sample, the initialisation and the sample order.

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• Scale features consistently. The distance treats every feature equally. If you mix bands with different ranges, standardise them first.
  • Fill gaps, or accept that gappy pixels get no neuron. Pixels with a missing value are left out. zeit.smooth fills them.
  • Interpret prototypes, not colours. Plot clusters.prototypes to understand what each cluster means, as in the figure above.
  • Reproducibility. Results depend on seed, the sample and the initialisation. Fix them, and you get the same result every run, and the same codebook as minisom with the same settings.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Kohonen, T. (1990). The self-organizing map. Proceedings of the IEEE, 78(9), 1464–1480. doi:10.1109/5.58325
  • Kohonen, T. (2013). Essentials of the self-organizing map. Neural Networks, 37, 52–65. doi:10.1016/j.neunet.2012.09.018
  • Vettigli, G. (2018). MiniSom: minimalistic and NumPy-based implementation of the Self Organizing Map. github.com/JustGlowing/minisom
  • R package sits: sits_som_map() and sits_som_clean_samples().

docs.title: STAC Data Cubes
docs.text:
Build an analysis-ready data cube straight from a cloud catalog. You give an area, dates and bands, and get back a lazy xarray cube: nothing is downloaded until you compute, and then only the pixels you need are read.

DoesSearch a STAC catalog, mask clouds, and stack the images into a cube SourcesEarth Search (AWS), Planetary Computer, Brazil Data Cube, any STAC API OutputA Dask-backed xarray.DataArray shaped (time, band, y, x) NextComposite, smooth, and feed any algorithm

STAC (SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog) is the standard way cloud providers publish satellite imagery. Zeit searches a catalog, keeps the images that match your query, and assembles them with stackstac into one aligned cube.

docs.title: 1. Query a catalog
docs.text:
Select the area with a bounding box, a vector file (vector_path), or tile IDs: MGRS for Sentinel-2, WRS-2 path/row for Landsat.

import zeit

# Option A: Bounding Box
cube = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="earth_search",
    collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
    bbox=[-48.5, -22.5, -48.0, -22.0],
    start_date="2022-01-01",
    end_date="2022-12-31",
    bands=["red", "green", "blue", "nir"]
)

# Option B: MGRS Tiles (Sentinel-2)
cube_tiles_s2 = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="earth_search",
    collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
    tiles=["22JFQ", "22JGQ"], # Fetch specific Sentinel-2 MGRS tiles
    start_date="2022-01-01",
    end_date="2022-12-31",
    bands=["red", "green", "blue", "nir"]
)

# Option C: WRS-2 Path/Row Tiles (Landsat)
cube_tiles_l8 = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="earth_search",
    collection="landsat-c2-l2",
    tiles=["215065"], # 6-digit Path/Row string (Path 215, Row 065)
    start_date="2022-01-01",
    end_date="2022-12-31",
    bands=["red", "green", "blue", "nir"]
)

docs.title: 2. Mask clouds
docs.text:
Zeit can automatically identify the satellite platform (Sentinel-2, Landsat) and apply semantic cloud masking natively before returning the cube. Just pass apply_cloud_mask=True. This will automatically download the respective Quality Assurance (QA) band (like scl for Sentinel) and mask out clouds, shadows, and cirrus.

cube_clean = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="earth_search",
    collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
    tiles=["22JFQ"],
    start_date="2022-01-01",
    end_date="2022-12-31",
    bands=["red", "green", "blue", "nir"],
    apply_cloud_mask=True # Clouds are masked out!
)

docs.title: 3. Other sensors (MODIS and Sentinel-1)
docs.text:
build_time_series is not hardcoded to Sentinel-2/Landsat — it talks to any STAC API, so switching source/collection/bands is enough to pull other sensors from a catalog that hosts them. Microsoft Planetary Computer is the most complete public option for MODIS and Sentinel-1.

Caveat: apply_cloud_mask=True only knows how to decode Sentinel-2's scl and Landsat's qa_pixel bands (see zeit/cube.py). For MODIS and Sentinel-1, leave apply_cloud_mask=False and handle QA/no cloud-masking as shown below.

MODIS (vegetation indices, 250m/16-day)

import zeit
from zeit.qc import qc_modis_summary

cube_modis = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="planetary_computer",
    collection="modis-13Q1-061",  # NDVI/EVI 250m, 16-day composites (modis-09A1-061 for 500m/8-day surface reflectance)
    bbox=[-52.10, -12.55, -51.95, -12.40],
    start_date="2010-01-01",
    end_date="2023-12-31",
    bands=["250m_16_days_NDVI", "250m_16_days_pixel_reliability"],
    apply_cloud_mask=False,  # not recognized for MODIS - masked manually below
)

ndvi = cube_modis.sel(band="250m_16_days_NDVI") * 0.0001  # apply the collection's scale factor
qa = cube_modis.sel(band="250m_16_days_pixel_reliability")

# 0=good, 1=marginal, 2=snow/ice, 3=cloudy -> [1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.2]
weights = qc_modis_summary(qa)

For 500m 8-day surface reflectance (modis-09A1-061), decode the sur_refl_state_500m QA band with zeit.qc.qc_modis_state instead.

Sentinel-1 SAR (radar, no clouds)

cube_s1 = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="planetary_computer",
    collection="sentinel-1-rtc",  # radiometrically terrain-corrected, analysis-ready (prefer this over the raw "sentinel-1-grd" unless you plan to do RTC yourself)
    bbox=[-52.10, -12.55, -51.95, -12.40],
    start_date="2020-01-01",
    end_date="2023-12-31",
    bands=["vv", "vh"],
    resolution=10,
    apply_cloud_mask=False,  # SAR is unaffected by clouds - never pass apply_cloud_mask=True here
)

Radar backscatter is dense (Sentinel-1 revisits every 6-12 days regardless of cloud cover), which makes it a strong complement to optical CCDC/LandTrendr/Mann-Kendall runs in persistently cloudy regions. Check the actual pixel value range before feeding it downstream — RTC gamma-naught can come back as either dB or linear power depending on the processing pipeline, and that changes how you interpret slope/magnitude.

Neither earth_search nor brazil_data_cube currently expose MODIS or Sentinel-1 collections, so planetary_computer is the practical default for both. source also accepts any custom STAC API URL (e.g. a national or provider-specific SAR catalog) if you need one outside the three built-in aliases.

Landsat and Sentinel-2 in one series

HLS (Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2) has both sensors processed alike, on one 30 m grid, with Sentinel-2 adjusted to Landsat 8's bands. Planetary Computer serves its two products; asking for both, with the bands named by role, gives one series sorted by time, each band read from its own product's asset (the NIR is L30's B05 and S30's B8A) and the Fmask band masking clouds and shadows:

hls = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="planetary_computer",
    collection=["hls2-l30", "hls2-s30"],
    bbox=[-52.10, -12.55, -51.95, -12.40],
    start_date="2019-01-01",
    end_date="2024-12-31",
    bands=["blue", "green", "red", "nir", "swir1", "swir2"],
    apply_cloud_mask=True,
    resolution=30,
    epsg=32722,
)   # (time, band, y, x): the six bands, and Fmask

For dates or bands HLS does not have (before 2013, Sentinel-2's 10 m bands), zeit.bandpass_adjust applies HLS's bandpass step to Sentinel-2 L2A and joins it with Landsat Collection 2. It removes only part of the step between the sensors; the reference compares the two on a stable site.

docs.title: 4. Composite to a regular time step
docs.text:
Raw STAC data usually comes in irregular time steps (e.g., passing every 5, 8, or 12 days). For advanced Machine Learning and TWDTW, you must regularize the cube to fixed temporal steps.

You can use zeit.regularize_time_series to composite these observations into regular windows (e.g., 16-day composites) using multi-dimensional medoid or median strategies. Because it uses xarray, this computation remains fully lazy!

from zeit import regularize_time_series

# Create a 16-day Medoid composite
cube_16d = regularize_time_series(cube_clean, freq="16D", method="medoid")

# The output has regular 16-day steps on the 'time' dimension
print(cube_16d.time)

docs.title: Annual composites for LandTrendr
docs.text:
LandTrendr needs one cloud-free value per pixel per year. zeit.build_annual_composites builds that stack directly: one masked median (or medoid) of a seasonal window per year, as reflectance, with the years without scenes left as NaN so the time axis has no gaps.

comp = zeit.build_annual_composites(
    source="planetary_computer",
    collection="landsat-c2-l2",
    bbox=[9.63, 50.92, 12.06, 52.43],   # one 150 km tile
    start_year=1985,
    end_year=2024,
    season=("06-01", "09-30"),
    bands=["nir08", "swir22"],          # only what NBR needs
    epsg=3035,
)
nbr = (comp.sel(band="nir08") - comp.sel(band="swir22")) / (comp.sel(band="nir08") + comp.sel(band="swir22"))
zeit.save_raster(nbr, "nbr_1985_2024.tif")

It reads the scenes as raw integers and reduces each spatial chunk as soon as all of its scenes have arrived, so memory stays bounded however many scenes a year has (in our test, a lazy cube.median("time") over a 150 km tile with 100 scenes exhausted 68 GB of RAM). See STAC download throughput for timings.

Download speed

  • Read only what you need. Download time grows with scenes × bands: each extra band adds about a third for an NBR stack (2 bands + QA).
  • Pick the provider close to you. The same Landsat Collection 2 files are on Planetary Computer (Azure West Europe, free) and on Earth Search (AWS us-west-2, requester-pays bucket: needs AWS credentials and the requester pays about US$ 0.09/GB leaving AWS). Latency matters as much as bandwidth for COG range reads.
  • Run next to the data for many tiles. From a VM in the provider's region, transfer is free and bandwidth is 10–100× a typical office link.
  • Don't push the thread count. The defaults (2048 px chunks, Dask's default threads) are already close to a 200 Mbit/s link's limit. Well beyond about 64 threads in one process, GDAL can deadlock inside its HTTP layer.

docs.title: 5. Compute spectral indices
docs.text:
STAC catalogs serve files, not computations, so the bands an index needs always travel over the network: NDVI needs red and nir. What zeit avoids is storing them. The cube is lazy, so the index is computed chunk by chunk as the bands arrive, and only the index is written to disk.

The index is pre-calculated by the provider. Some catalogs (such as Brazil Data Cube) serve an ndvi asset, or MODIS vegetation indices (modis-13Q1-061 on Planetary Computer). Load it like any band: 

cube_ndvi = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="brazil_data_cube",
    collection="CBERS4A_WFI_L4_SR",
    tiles=["022024"],
    bands=["ndvi"],
)

Compute it from reflectance. zeit.compute_indices finds each band role by its usual asset names (red / B04, nir08 / nir / B08...), so the same call works for Landsat and Sentinel-2 on every built-in catalog. Available: NDVI, EVI, SAVI, kNDVI, NBR, NDMI, NDWI, MNDWI, and NDFI (Landsat: it unmixes the six reflective bands). 

cube_raw = zeit.build_time_series(
    source="planetary_computer",
    collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
    tiles=["22JFQ"],
    bands=["B02", "B04", "B08", "B12"],   # only what the indices need
    apply_cloud_mask=True,
)
idx = zeit.compute_indices(cube_raw, ["NDVI", "EVI", "NBR"])   # (time, 3, y, x), still lazy

docs.title: Spectral temporal metrics
docs.text:
Spectral temporal metrics (STMs) summarize a season per pixel: the median, percentiles and spread of each index over every clear observation. They are a compact, gap-free input for land cover classification. zeit.build_spectral_temporal_metrics builds them per year without ever holding the observations: each spatial chunk is read once as raw integers, masked, turned into indices observation by observation, and reduced to the metrics.

stm = zeit.build_spectral_temporal_metrics(
    source="planetary_computer",
    collection="landsat-c2-l2",
    bbox=[-47.95, -15.85, -47.90, -15.80],
    start_year=2015,
    end_year=2024,
    season=("05-01", "09-30"),                # dry season
    indices=["NDVI", "NBR", "swir1"],          # indices, band roles or asset names
    metrics=["median", "p10", "p90", "iqr", "count"],
    epsg=32723,
)
# (time=10, band=15, y, x): NDVI_median, NDVI_p10, ..., swir1_count
zeit.save_raster(stm.sel(year=2024), "stm_2024.tif")

The index is computed on every observation before the statistics, so NDVI_median is the median NDVI, not the NDVI of the median bands. Band names and order match the Earth Engine version (download_gee_timeseries(composite_type="stm")).

docs.title: 6. Smooth noisy series
docs.text:
Even after masking and compositing, some cloud-affected values remain. zeit.smooth smooths a cube along time, keeping its dates and georeferencing:

Savitzky-Golay follows the cloud drops because it treats every point equally. The Whittaker smoother, given weights of 0 for the cloudy observations, ignores them and recovers the seasonal curve. 
smooth_sg = zeit.smooth(ndvi, method="savgol", window=7, polyorder=2)

weights = clear.astype(float)             # 1 = clear, 0 = cloudy, or QA weights from zeit.qc
smooth_wh = zeit.smooth(ndvi, lmbda=10, weights=weights)

lmbda sets the smoothness of the Whittaker smoother: larger values give a stiffer curve. It takes unevenly spaced dates as they are, and observations that are NaN (masked clouds) weigh 0, so the curve fills them. For per-observation weights from a QA band, see zeit.qc (qc_sentinel2_scl, qc_modis_summary, qc_modis_state). zeit.plot(ndvi, fit=smooth_wh) draws the curve over any pixel you click.

docs.title: Local GeoTIFFs instead of a catalog
docs.text:
Already have the files on disk? load_raster builds the same kind of lazy cube from a folder, parsing dates and bands from the file names.

import zeit

# Files like "SENTINEL_20220101_B02.tif": the regex captures (?P<date>...) and (?P<band>...)
cube_local = zeit.load_raster(
    "/path/to/my/tiffs",
    pattern=r"_(?P<date>\d{8})_(?P<band>B\d{2})\.tif$",
    date_format="%Y%m%d",
    recursive=True,
    chunks="auto",
)   # (time, band, y, x), lazy

# Scenes on different grids (two UTM zones, two orbits): put them on one as they are read
cube_local = zeit.load_raster("/path/to/my/tiffs", pattern=..., like="reference.tif", chunks="auto")

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
The cube is ready for any analysis. Common next steps:

  • one value per year for LandTrendr or Mann-Kendall: build_annual_composites;
  • regular 16-day composites for BFAST, phenology and TWDTW;
  • every clear image, multi-band, for CCDC.

docs.title: TempCNN
docs.text:
AnswersClassify each pixel's time series into land-cover classes, fast. Input(batch, bands, time) tensors with a fixed length OutputClass logits per pixel ReferencePelletier et al. (2019); written from the paper and the authors' code A complete training run. 1,000 noisy NDVI series (23 dates, 12% cloud-contaminated observations) of four classes, split 70/30. After 30 epochs the held-out accuracy is 96%. The only confusion is between single and double cropping, whose second season is weak in many samples. It uses the same model and a training loop like the one below; the full script is in docs/scripts/make_figures.py.

TempCNN is a 1D convolutional neural network designed for classifying per-pixel satellite image time series. It's a simpler, faster-to-train alternative to attention-based models like LightTAE, and a strong baseline for most pixel time-series classification tasks. It was introduced in:

Pelletier, C., Webb, G. I., & Petitjean, F. (2019). Temporal convolutional neural network for the classification of satellite image time series. Remote Sensing, 11(5), 523. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs11050523

zeit.ai.TempCNN is written from the paper and from the authors' code (charlotte-pel/temporalCNN), with their defaults: kernel 5, 64 filters, dropout 0.5 and a dense layer of 256 units. It is no longer a port of R sits, and weights trained in sits do not load into it.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
TempCNN treats the time axis of a pixel's spectral history like the spatial axis of a 1D signal, and applies a stack of 1D convolutions along it:

  1. Three convolutional blocks (Conv1d -> BatchNorm1d -> ReLU -> Dropout, 64 filters and kernel size 5 by default), each convolving over the time axis while keeping every spectral band as a separate input channel.
  2. Flatten: the full (hidden_dim, n_times) feature map is flattened into a single vector — not global-average-pooled. This is a deliberate architectural choice as in the authors' implementation: it means the dense layer's input size is tied to n_times, so a given TempCNN instance is fixed to one sequence length for its lifetime (unlike LightTAE, whose attention mechanism can be more flexible about padding, though day_offsets is still fixed per-instance too).
  3. Dense block (Linear -> BatchNorm1d -> ReLU -> Dropout, default 256 nodes) followed by a final linear classifier producing num_classes logits (softmax applied externally, e.g. via torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy or manually at inference time).

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text:
TempCNN LightTAE Best for Fast baselines, shorter/noisier series, limited training data Longer, well-sampled series where attention over specific timesteps helps Compute cost Lower (no attention, no positional encoding) Moderate Mean accuracy on samples_modis_ndvi (see below) 0.861 0.915

See the LTAE & LightTAE tutorial for the attention-based alternative, and the UTAE tutorial if you need whole-patch spatial segmentation rather than per-pixel classification.

docs.title: From a cube to a map
docs.text:
TempCNN classifies each pixel from its series of bands, (time, band). From a cube and labelled points or polygons:

import zeit
from zeit import ai

cube = zeit.load_raster("s2_ndvi_evi_2022.tif")            # (time, band, y, x)
samples = ai.samples(cube, "samples.gpkg", label="class")   # one sample per pixel
model = ai.train(ai.TempCNN, samples, epochs=50)
classes = ai.predict(model, cube)                           # label (y, x), georeferenced

The flatten before the dense layer ties a model to the number of dates it was built for (as in the authors' network): the cube to classify needs as many, e.g. the same composites of another year. See Deep Learning for the samples, the validation blocks and the normalization.

docs.title: Instantiating the Model
docs.text:
zeit.ai.train builds the model for you from the samples (bands, dates, classes); the arguments below pass through it, e.g. ai.train(ai.TempCNN, samples, dropout_rate=0.3). To build it yourself:

from zeit.ai import TempCNN

model = TempCNN(
    in_channels=n_bands,
    n_times=n_times,               # fixed sequence length this instance is built for
    num_classes=10,
    filters=64,                     # filters of each convolution
    kernel_size=5,
    n_conv=3,                       # convolution blocks
    dense_units=256,
    dropout_rate=0.5,
)

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model = model.to(device)

docs.title: A loop of your own
docs.text: zeit.ai.train covers the usual case. For anything else (another optimizer, a scheduler, augmentation), the SampleSet is a PyTorch Dataset whose items hold the normalized x, the label y and the date positions; see A loop of your own. A model trained this way can still be classified with zeit.ai.predict after zeit.ai.train(model, samples, epochs=0) records the samples' metadata in it.

docs.title: Accuracy against sits
docs.text:
Measured on samples_modis_ndvi of sits (12 dates, 4 classes), with the same 80/20 split on both sides and 5 seeds, the mean accuracy was:

sits, with its defaults Zeit, the authors' defaults Zeit, the pipeline's defaults (150 epochs) TempCNN 0.879 ± 0.027 0.839 ± 0.031 0.861 ± 0.024 LightTAE 0.902 ± 0.016 0.892 ± 0.020 0.915 ± 0.011

The authors' training settings for TempCNN (20 epochs, patience 0, 5% of the samples for validation) stop early on a set as small as this one.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Pelletier, C., Webb, G. I., & Petitjean, F. (2019). Temporal convolutional neural network for the classification of satellite image time series. Remote Sensing, 11(5), 523. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs11050523
  • charlotte-pel/temporalCNN, the authors' code: https://github.com/charlotte-pel/temporalCNN
  • e-sensing/sits, used for the accuracy comparison above: https://github.com/e-sensing/sits

docs.title: Cloud Masking with Tmask
docs.text:
Single-image cloud masks miss thin clouds and small shadows, and every missed cloud looks like a land change to the algorithms downstream. Tmask uses the time dimension instead: it learns each pixel's normal seasonal behaviour and flags observations that are far too bright (cloud) or far too dark (shadow) for that time of year.

AnswersWhich observations are clouds or shadows that the QA band missed? InputGreen and SWIR1 reflectance stacks (× 10,000) and their dates OutputA boolean clear mask, same shape as the input ReferenceZhu & Woodcock (2014)

What Tmask does. Four years of a synthetic 16-day series with 7 clouds (too bright in Green) and 5 shadows (too dark in SWIR1) injected. Tmask fits a robust seasonal model to each band and flags the observations that depart from it too much (orange): all 12 contaminated ones, and nothing else.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
For each pixel, Tmask fits a robust harmonic regression, \(a_0 + c_1 t + a_1 \cos(\omega t) + b_1 \sin(\omega t)\) (iteratively reweighted with Tukey's bisquare, as MATLAB's robustfit in the original and in CCDC's own Tmask, so the outliers barely affect it), to two bands:

  • Green, where clouds are much brighter than the land below them;
  • SWIR1, where shadows are much darker than expected.

An observation is flagged as cloud when its Green value is more than 0.04 (reflectance) above the seasonal model, and as shadow when its SWIR1 value is more than 0.04 below it. Everything else is kept as clear. The fits run in Rust, every pixel in parallel: about 60 µs per pixel (measured with the C++ core of zeit 1.7; the Rust one takes 0.75–0.98 of that time, depending on the system) of 140 dates on one core, some 190 times faster than the scikit-learn Huber fit used before 0.43 (11 ms per pixel).

docs.title: 1. Load Green and SWIR1
docs.text:
Any (time, band, y, x) cube with green and SWIR1 bands, with its dates:

import zeit

cube = zeit.load_raster("landsat/", pattern=r"_(?P<date>\d{8})_(?P<band>\w+)\.tif$")   # reflectance x 10000
cube.band.values      # array(['blue', 'green', 'red', 'nir', 'swir1', 'swir2'], ...)

docs.title: 2. Run Tmask
docs.text:
clear = zeit.tmask(cube, green="green", swir="swir1")
print(clear.dtype, clear.dims)   # bool ('time', 'y', 'x'); True = clear
print(f"{1 - float(clear.mean()):.1%} of observations flagged")

If your reflectance is already in 0–1, pass scale=1.0. Observations without data (NoData, NaN) are not clear. Pixels with 5 or fewer valid observations are not screened, since there is too little data to model the season. A lazy cube (chunks="auto") stays lazy.

docs.title: 3. Use the mask
docs.text:
For CCDC, convert to its QA codes (0 clear, 4 cloud), and combine with the QA band you already have:

import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

tmask_qa = xr.where(clear, 0, 4).astype(np.uint8)
qa = np.maximum(qa_from_qa_pixel, tmask_qa)     # keep the worst of the two

Do not use (~clear).astype(np.uint8) for CCDC

That produces 1 for clouds, and in CCDC's convention 1 means water, which counts as a valid observation. The clouds would be kept.

For everything else, set the flagged observations to NaN before compositing or smoothing:

ndvi_clean = ndvi.where(clear)

To save it, one band per date:

zeit.save_raster(clear.astype(np.uint8), "results/tmask_clear.tif")

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• Use Tmask as a second pass. Apply the sensor's own QA mask first (Landsat QA_PIXEL, Sentinel-2 SCL, or apply_cloud_mask=True in build_time_series) to remove the obvious clouds, then Tmask to catch what it missed.
  • CCDC already includes it. zeit.ccdc runs the original's Tmask screen internally. Running it beforehand is only needed for other algorithms.
  • Large areas. Keep the cube lazy (chunks=): zeit.tmask then works block by block, every pixel of a block in parallel.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • Zhu, Z., & Woodcock, C. E. (2014). Automated cloud, cloud shadow, and snow detection in multitemporal Landsat data: An algorithm designed specifically for monitoring land cover change. Remote Sensing of Environment, 152, 217–234. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2014.06.012

docs.title: Pattern Matching (TWDTW)
docs.text:
Classify pixels by comparing their time series with a few reference patterns, one per class. Time-Weighted Dynamic Time Warping lets a pattern stretch and shift to match a pixel (a crop planted three weeks late is still that crop) while penalising shifts that would be implausible.

AnswersWhich known temporal pattern does this pixel look like? InputA cube (or a pixel's series) and one reference series per class, with dates OutputA class map and a distance (match quality) map ReferenceMaus et al. (2016)

What TWDTW does. Left: reference NDVI patterns for three classes. Middle: a soybean field planted about three weeks later than the reference; the grey lines show how TWDTW aligns each observation to the pattern despite the shift. Right: distances to each class. The pixel is correctly labelled soybean (lowest distance).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Plain distances compare observation 1 with observation 1, 2 with 2, and so on, so a small shift in timing looks like a big difference. Dynamic Time Warping finds the best alignment between two series instead, allowing one to be locally stretched or compressed. The time-weighted version (TWDTW) adds a cost that grows with the time \(\Delta t\) (in days) between matched observations, following a logistic curve:

\[ w(\Delta t) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\text{steepness}\,(\Delta t - \text{midpoint})}} \]

Small seasonal shifts are cheap; implausible ones (matching a January peak to a July peak) cost up to one unit more per pair. With cycle="year" (the default) \(\Delta t\) is measured between days of the year, around the year, so a pattern built from one year matches the same season of any other year, and 31 December is a day away from 1 January. Each pattern may match any stretch of a pixel's series, which can be longer than the pattern (several seasons, several years).

zeit.twdtw computes the distance of the R package twdtw (Maus et al.), checked against it to 1e-12, in Rust, every pixel in parallel, and a two-row dynamic program that stays in the CPU cache. Dates a pixel has no value for (clouds, NoData) are left out of its series.

docs.title: 1. Define reference patterns
docs.text:
A pattern is a typical series of a class: a pandas.Series indexed by dates (or a DataFrame with one column per band). Patterns usually come from the average of a few labelled samples per class.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import zeit

dates = pd.date_range("2021-01-01", "2021-12-31", freq="16D")   # a 16-day series over one year
t = (dates.dayofyear.to_numpy() - 1) / 365

patterns = {
    "Soybean": pd.Series(0.25 + 0.60 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((t - 0.12) / 0.08) ** 2), dates),
    "Pasture": pd.Series(0.50 + 0.08 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * t) + 0.10 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t), dates),
    "Forest":  pd.Series(0.82 + 0.02 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * t) + 0.03 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t), dates),
}

docs.title: 2. Compare one pixel
docs.text:
pixel = ...   # a pandas Series of NDVI indexed by dates
result = zeit.twdtw(pixel, patterns)
dict(zip(result.pattern.values, result.distances.values.round(2)))
# {'Soybean': 1.31, 'Pasture': 3.81, 'Forest': 9.69}
result.label.item()     # 1: Soybean, the first pattern

These are the distances in the figure above (a soybean field planted about three weeks later than the pattern).

docs.title: 3. Classify a whole cube
docs.text:
The same call on a cube (time, y, x) matches every pattern against every pixel in parallel:

ndvi = zeit.load_raster("S2_ndvi_2021.tif")          # (time, y, x), dates from the file
classes = zeit.twdtw(ndvi, patterns)

classes.label            # (y, x): 1 Soybean, 2 Pasture, 3 Forest (0: no observation)
classes.distance         # (y, x): distance to the winning pattern
classes.distances        # (pattern, y, x): distance to every pattern
classes.label.zeit.plot(basemap="satellite")          # the legend names the classes
zeit.save_raster(classes, "twdtw")                    # label.tif, distance.tif, distances.tif

distance is the TWDTW distance to the winning class. High values mean no pattern fits well, which usually deserves a separate "unknown" label:

known = classes.label.where(classes.distance <= classes.distance.quantile(0.95), 0)

To see why a pixel got its class, plot the cube with the result: clicking a pixel draws its series with the winning pattern aligned over it.

zeit.plot(ndvi, fit=classes)

A raster larger than memory stays lazy with zeit.twdtw("ndvi.tif", patterns, chunks="auto"), computed block by block while save_raster writes it.

docs.title: Several bands at once
docs.text:
Give the patterns one column per band, named as the cube's bands; the cube (time, band, y, x) is matched on those bands together (Euclidean distance across bands):

patterns = {"Soybean": pd.DataFrame({"ndvi": soy_ndvi, "swir1": soy_swir1}), ...}
classes = zeit.twdtw(cube, patterns)                  # uses cube.sel(band=["ndvi", "swir1"])

With one-band patterns and a multi-band cube, choose the band: zeit.twdtw(cube, patterns, band="ndvi").

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect steepness 0.1 Steepness of the logistic time weight, per day. Higher values make the cost jump more sharply around midpoint. midpoint 50 Days apart at which a matched pair costs half a unit more. Shifts much shorter than this are nearly free. cycle "year" "year": days of the year, around the year. None: the dates themselves (patterns and pixels from the same season). max_elapsed None Pairs farther apart than this many days are never matched.

Tune midpoint (and steepness, for how much timing matters against the index values) on a few labelled pixels before classifying a whole area. The defaults are R twdtw's time_weight = c(0.1, 50).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Maus, V., Câmara, G., Cartaxo, R., Sanchez, A., Ramos, F. M., & de Queiroz, G. R. (2016). A time-weighted dynamic time warping method for land-use and land-cover mapping. IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing, 9(8), 3729–3739. doi:10.1109/JSTARS.2016.2517118
  • Maus, V., Câmara, G., Appel, M., & Pebesma, E. (2019). dtwSat: Time-Weighted Dynamic Time Warping for Satellite Image Time Series Analysis in R. Journal of Statistical Software, 88(5), 1–31. doi:10.18637/jss.v088.i05

docs.title: Spectral Unmixing
docs.text:
A 30 m pixel is rarely one material. A field can be half crop and half bare soil; a pixel of forest after selective logging is part canopy, part dead wood and part soil. Unmixing estimates the fraction of each material in every pixel from its spectrum, given the spectrum of each pure material (the endmembers). It works on one image or a time series, with a few bands or hundreds.

AnswersWhat fraction of each pixel is vegetation, soil, water…? InputReflectance with a band dimension: (band, y, x) or (time, band, y, x); one spectrum per material OutputA fraction map per material, and the RMSE of the spectrum rebuilt from the fractions ReferenceAdams et al. (1986); Heinz & Chang (2001), fully constrained least squares; Souza et al. (2005)

Result of this tutorial. A 10.5 km window of an EnMAP hyperspectral image (210 bands from 444 to 2446 nm, 30 m) over farmland on the coast north of Groningen, the Netherlands, on 10 August 2022. Top left: the image in near infrared, shortwave infrared and red; crops are orange and red, harvested and bare fields cyan, the Wadden Sea black. The numbered squares are the pure pixels whose spectra are the endmembers. The other panels are the fraction of each endmember and the RMSE of the rebuilt spectrum. The 122,500 pixels of 210 bands were unmixed in 0.33 s. Data: contains modified EnMAP data © DLR 2022.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Linear mixing. The spectrum of a pixel is taken as the sum of the endmember spectra, each weighted by its fraction of the pixel's area, plus an error. A pixel that is 60% crop and 40% soil reflects like 0.6 × the crop's spectrum + 0.4 × the soil's.
  2. The fractions that fit best. For each pixel, zeit.unmix finds the fractions that rebuild its spectrum with the smallest squared error. By default they must be non-negative and add up to one (fully constrained least squares; Heinz & Chang 2001). Each pixel is solved exactly with an active set, in Rust, all pixels and dates in parallel.
  3. The RMSE. The difference between the observed spectrum and the rebuilt one, per band, as a root mean square. It is large where the pixel contains a material that no endmember describes, or where an endmember does not match the material in the image.
  4. Dark endmembers. A material that is almost black (water beyond 700 nm, or a "shade" endmember of zeros) takes up differences in brightness. A field slightly darker than its endmember gets a small fraction of the dark one.
Left: the endmembers, the median spectrum of 3 × 3 pure pixels each. Green vegetation is dark in the red and bright in the near infrared. Dry vegetation (straw and stubble) is bright in the shortwave infrared and has the cellulose absorption near 2100 nm. Soil rises smoothly; water is almost black. The gaps are bands left out (water vapour absorption, noise). Right: a mixed pixel and its spectrum rebuilt from 31% green vegetation, 65% soil and 4% water.

docs.title: 1. Read the image and keep the good bands
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
import zeit

cube = zeit.load_raster("EnMAP_L2A_Groningen_20220810.tif", chunks="auto")
cube = cube.isel(y=slice(560, 910), x=slice(740, 1090)).load()   # (band, y, x): 224 x 350 x 350
refl = cube.where(cube != -32768) / 10000                          # reflectance 0-1, NaN = no data

A pixel with a missing value in any band gets no fractions, so bands without data must go. EnMAP's L2A leaves the bands at 1331–1391 nm empty (they are in a water vapour absorption), and a few bands below 440 nm and near 1950 nm are noisy, with negative reflectance:

empty = refl.isnull().all(["y", "x"])
noisy = (refl < 0).mean(["y", "x"]) > 0.001                        # negative in more than 0.1% of pixels
spectra = refl.sel(band=~(empty | noisy))                          # 210 of the 224 bands

The bands are named like 'Band 45 (647.214 nm)'. Naming them by their wavelength instead is shorter, and endmember tables from a spectral library usually use wavelengths too:

wavelength = [float(b.split("(")[1].split()[0]) for b in spectra.band.values]
spectra = spectra.assign_coords(band=wavelength)                   # 444.5, 449.3, ... 2445.5 (nm)

docs.title: 2. Take the endmembers from the image
docs.text:
Endmembers can come from a spectral library or from the image itself. The image's own pure pixels have the same sensor, atmosphere and date as the pixels to unmix. Here each is the median spectrum of the 3 × 3 pixels around a point chosen in the image: the middle of a green crop, of a harvested field, of a ploughed field, and the open sea.

def spectrum(x, y):
    """The median spectrum of the 3 x 3 pixels around a point (UTM 32N, metres)."""
    return spectra.sel(x=slice(x - 45, x + 45), y=slice(y + 45, y - 45)).median(["x", "y"]).to_series()

endmembers = pd.DataFrame({
    "green vegetation": spectrum(343860, 5918790),     # a green crop
    "dry vegetation": spectrum(344730, 5924490),       # a harvested field: stubble and straw
    "soil": spectrum(345570, 5918190),                 # a ploughed field
    "water": spectrum(338640, 5924250),                # the Wadden Sea
}).T                                                    # rows: endmembers; columns: wavelengths

The table's columns must be bands of the cube: names, or numbers such as wavelengths. A table in reflectance × 10000 is read as such, like the data (scale="auto").

docs.title: 3. Unmix
docs.text:
fractions = zeit.unmix(spectra, endmembers)
list(fractions.data_vars)
# ['green vegetation', 'dry vegetation', 'soil', 'water', 'rmse']

zeit.save_raster(fractions, "results/fractions")      # one GeoTIFF per variable

The result is an xarray.Dataset with one (y, x) map per endmember and the RMSE, on the grid and CRS of the image. On a (time, band, y, x) cube each map is (time, y, x), and a dask cube gives a lazy result.

docs.title: 4. Read the fractions and the RMSE
docs.text:
Over the window, the mean fractions are 0.38 green vegetation, 0.23 dry vegetation, 0.14 soil and 0.24 water. The sea is close to 1 water. On land, water is 0.1 to 0.3: it is playing the part of shade, taking up the difference between darker fields and their brighter endmembers. Read it on land as darkness, not as water.

The median RMSE is 0.015 in reflectance (0.031 at the 95th percentile). The darkest fields in the RMSE map are crops and soils that none of the four spectra describes well. Leaving one material out shows what the RMSE is for. Without the dry vegetation endmember, the median RMSE rises to 0.019 and the 95th percentile to 0.070, and the harvested fields light up in the RMSE map: where dry vegetation is more than 40% of the pixel, the median RMSE goes from 0.020 to 0.049. When a type of surface stands out in the RMSE, add an endmember for it.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
sum_to_one nonneg Median RMSE Sum of the fractions (5th–95th percentile) Smallest fraction True True 0.0149 1 0 False True 0.0133 0.62 to 2.63 0 False False 0.0103 −2.37 to 3.45 −22.5

Fewer constraints always fit the spectrum better, and the fractions mean less. Without them, a near-black endmember like water can take any value: multiplying it by 20 changes the rebuilt spectrum very little. Keep the default unless you have a reason. Non-negative fractions free to sum to anything are what RStoolbox's mesma solves (its sum_to_one only rescales them afterwards). They can be useful when brightness varies a lot and there is no dark endmember.

zeit.unmix(spectra, endmembers, sum_to_one=False)                 # non-negative only
zeit.unmix(spectra, endmembers, sum_to_one=False, nonneg=False)   # ordinary least squares

docs.title: On a multispectral time series
docs.text:
The same call unmixes every date of a (time, band, y, x) cube. With Landsat or Sentinel-2, the endmembers are a table (or a dict) with the cube's band names as columns; bands= maps them when the names differ:

endmembers = {
    "vegetation": {"blue": 0.03, "green": 0.06, "red": 0.04, "nir": 0.40, "swir1": 0.20, "swir2": 0.09},
    "soil":       {"blue": 0.10, "green": 0.14, "red": 0.18, "nir": 0.26, "swir1": 0.34, "swir2": 0.30},
    "water":      {"blue": 0.06, "green": 0.05, "red": 0.03, "nir": 0.02, "swir1": 0.01, "swir2": 0.005},
}
fractions = zeit.unmix(landsat, endmembers)                        # (time, y, x) per endmember

fractions = zeit.unmix(landsat)    # endmembers="souza2005": gv, npv, soil, shade, cloud, and the NDFI

The built-in "souza2005" endmembers (green vegetation, non-photosynthetic vegetation, soil, shade and cloud for Landsat surface reflectance) are the ones CODED uses to map forest degradation in the Amazon. With them, unmix also returns the NDFI, and cloud_threshold masks the observations with clouds that the QA band missed.

Do you need hyperspectral data? The same image reduced to Landsat 8's six bands, with the same pure pixels as endmembers, gives the same green vegetation: the median difference from the 210-band fractions is 0.013, and 0.035 at the 90th percentile. Dry vegetation and soil differ much more, by 0.19 and 0.25 at the 90th percentile. Their spectra differ mainly in narrow features, like the cellulose absorption near 2100 nm, which Landsat's SWIR2 band averages away. With six bands, two endmembers this similar trade fractions between them.

The example 26 builds a synthetic Landsat series from known fractions (a pasture ploughed in 2021, a reservoir filling from 2022), unmixes it with endmembers of its own, compares the fractions with the truth, and tries the three sets of constraints and the Souza endmembers.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Effect endmembers "souza2005" A DataFrame (rows endmembers, columns bands of the cube), a dict, or "souza2005". bands None The cube's band for each column of the endmembers, when the names differ. sum_to_one True Fractions add up to one. nonneg True Fractions are non-negative. scale "auto" What the data's reflectance is multiplied by: 10000 for integers or values above 2, else 1. ndfi True Also the NDFI, when the endmembers are named gv, npv, soil and shade. cloud_threshold None Mask observations whose cloud fraction is above this.

All parameters are in the API reference.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: On 1000 × 1000 pixels of 6 bands and 4 endmembers, RStoolbox's mesma (R) takes 22 s. Zeit takes 1.2 s on one thread and 0.13 s on 19, solving the same non-negative problem. mesma's NNLS stops at a tolerance, while Zeit solves each pixel exactly, so Zeit's residual is never larger. See Benchmarks against the originals. The EnMAP window above, 122,500 pixels of 210 bands, takes 0.33 s on all cores and 1.9 s on one.

docs.title: Good practice
docs.text:
• One spectrum per material, as few materials as the scene needs. Two similar endmembers make their fractions unstable. A material that is present but missing from the endmembers shows up in the RMSE.
  • Endmembers in the same units and conditions as the data. Pure pixels of the image itself are the simplest way. With a library, use spectra resampled to your sensor's bands, and surface reflectance on both sides.
  • The same endmembers for every date of a time series, so that a change of fraction is a change on the ground.
  • Check the RMSE map before reading the fractions.
  • Drop the bands with no data: a missing value in any band leaves the pixel without fractions.
