docs.title: UTAE (U-Net with Temporal Attention Encoder)
docs.text:
AnswersProduce a class map for a whole image patch from its full history. Input(batch, time, bands, H, W) plus dates OutputA class map per patch, and attention maps ReferenceGarnot & Landrieu (2021); bit-exact with the official code

UTAE combines a U-Net with a temporal attention mechanism to perform spatio-temporal segmentation of satellite image time series — producing a full class map over a whole image patch (e.g. 256x256) using its entire observation history, not just a per-pixel classification. It was introduced in:

Garnot, V. S. F., & Landrieu, L. (2021). Panoptic segmentation of satellite image time series with convolutional temporal attention networks. ICCV 2021. doi:10.1109/ICCV48922.2021.00483

zeit.ai.UTAE was ported layer-for-layer from the official reference implementation (VSainteuf/utae-paps, MIT License). This is the most rigorously validated model in zeit.ai: building both implementations with identical weights (loaded via load_state_dict(), with state_dict() key names matching directly, no translation table) and feeding them the same input reproduces the reference implementation's output bit-for-bit exactly (max abs diff = 0.0), including the padded-sequence (irregular temporal sampling) code path.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
UTAE is a multi-scale U-Net where every stage is applied independently to each timestep (weights shared across time — see _TemporallySharedBlock), and temporal fusion happens once, at the bottleneck, via an image-aware L-TAE variant (_LTAE2d). The architecture has four parts:

  1. Encoder: a standard convolutional U-Net encoder (in_conv + a stack of _DownConvBlocks), applied frame-by-frame with shared weights, producing a pyramid of per-timestep feature maps at decreasing spatial resolution.
  2. Temporal bottleneck (_LTAE2d): applies a per-pixel L-TAE (the same "learned master query" multi-head attention mechanism as LTAE, but computed independently at every spatial position of the deepest feature map) to fuse the time dimension into a single feature map, plus per-head, per-timestep attention maps.
  3. Temporal aggregator (_TemporalAggregator): this is UTAE's key idea — the attention maps from step 2 are resampled to each decoder scale and used to weight the temporal aggregation of every skip connection, not just the bottleneck. This propagates the learned "when does this pixel matter" signal to every resolution of the decoder.
  4. Decoder: a standard U-Net decoder (_UpConvBlock stack) that upsamples the fused bottleneck feature, concatenating each attention-weighted skip connection along the way, ending in a final out_conv producing per-pixel class logits over the whole patch.

UTAE supports irregular temporal sampling: pass a pad_value (default 0) and pad shorter sequences in a batch up to a common length with that value — the model automatically builds a pad_mask and skips (or masks out) padded frames in both the shared-weight per-timestep convolutions and the attention mechanism, so you don't need every sample in a batch to have the exact same number of valid observations.

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text: Use UTAE when you need a class map over a spatial patch informed by its full time series — e.g. crop-type mapping, burned-area segmentation, or any task where spatial context (not just a single pixel's own spectral history) matters. If you only need a classification of individual pixels' own time series (no spatial context needed), LightTAE or TempCNN are lighter-weight and faster to train.

docs.title: From a cube to a map
docs.text:
UTAE segments windows of the cube, (time, band, patch, patch), so it trains on patches; polygons give it dense labels:

import zeit
from zeit import ai

cube = zeit.load_raster("s2_2022.tif")                                   # (time, band, y, x)
samples = ai.samples(cube, "fields.gpkg", label="crop", patch=32)        # windows of 32 x 32
model = ai.train(ai.UTAE, samples, epochs=100)
crops = ai.predict(model, cube, overlap=0.5)

The default U-Net halves the window three times, so patch is a multiple of 8. predict slides windows of the same size over the cube, overlapping by overlap, and averages each pixel's probabilities over them, weighted down towards the windows' edges, so the map has no seams; a lazy cube gives the same map, block by block. The dates' positions (days since the first date) are passed at every call, so a model classifies cubes with other dates too. See Deep Learning.

docs.title: Instantiating the Model
docs.text:
zeit.ai.train builds the model for you from the samples (bands, dates, classes); the arguments below pass through it, e.g. ai.train(ai.UTAE, samples, encoder_widths=[32, 32, 64, 64], decoder_widths=[16, 16, 32, 64]). To build it yourself:

from zeit.ai import UTAE

model = UTAE(
    input_dim=6,                    # number of spectral bands
    encoder_widths=(64, 64, 64, 128),
    decoder_widths=(32, 32, 64, 128),
    out_conv=[32, 10],              # final conv stack -> 10 output classes
    str_conv_k=4, str_conv_s=2, str_conv_p=1,  # strided-conv down/up-sampling geometry
    agg_mode="att_group",           # temporal aggregation mode for skip connections
    encoder_norm="group",
    n_head=16,
    d_model=256,
    d_k=4,
    pad_value=0,                    # value used for padded (missing) timesteps
)

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model = model.to(device)

out_conv's last entry sets the number of output classes; encoder_widths/decoder_widths must have matching lengths and equal final entries (assertions enforce this at construction time).

docs.title: A loop of your own
docs.text: zeit.ai.train covers the usual case. For anything else (another optimizer, a scheduler, augmentation), the SampleSet is a PyTorch Dataset whose items hold the normalized x, the label y and the date positions; see A loop of your own. A model trained this way can still be classified with zeit.ai.predict after zeit.ai.train(model, samples, epochs=0) records the samples' metadata in it.

docs.title: Validation Against the Official Reference
docs.text: UTAE (and its internal LTAE2d, _TemporalAggregator, etc.) is a line-for-line port of VSainteuf/utae-paps. Validation methodology: the official repo was cloned locally, both implementations were instantiated with the same hyperparameters and the same random weights (copied via load_state_dict() — the state_dict() key names match with no translation needed), and run forward on identical random input. The outputs were bit-for-bit identical (max abs diff = 0.0), across both the regular (unpadded) code path and the padded-sequence (pad_value/pad_mask) code path used for irregular temporal sampling. This cross-check is not part of the pytest suite, since it requires the reference repo cloned locally rather than a pip dependency — see the source docstring in zeit/ai/utae.py for details.

docs.title: References
docs.text:

  • Garnot, V. S. F., & Landrieu, L. (2020). Lightweight Temporal Self-Attention for Classifying Satellite Image Time Series. arXiv:2007.00586. https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00586
  • Reference implementation: VSainteuf/utae-paps (MIT License)

docs.title: Regional Trends (PARTS)
docs.text:
Is this region getting greener? Do forests and pastures trend differently? Counting the pixels with a significant trend cannot answer these questions. PARTS can: it tests the trend of a whole region, or of classes, with p-values that take into account that neighbouring pixels move together.

AnswersDoes the mean trend of a region differ from 0? Do classes differ? Does a covariate matter? InputA (time, y, x) cube in a projected CRS; optionally a classes layer or covariates OutputEach pixel's AR(1) trend (zeit.ar_trend) and a regional test (zeit.parts) ReferenceIves et al. (2021), Remote Sensing of Environment 266, 112678; the R package remotePARTS

The problem in one figure. A simulated map of 10,000 pixels with no trend at all, only year-to-year noise that neighbouring pixels share. Each pixel's own test still finds 6.6% of them "significant", in patches. A t-test of the 10,000 slopes as if they were independent gives p = 1.5 × 10⁻²¹³, a confident and wrong "yes". PARTS gives p = 0.26: no evidence of a trend, which is the right answer. Made by docs/scripts/make_parts_figures.py.

docs.title: Why counting pixels is wrong
docs.text:
Most trend studies run a test on every pixel and report the share of pixels with a significant trend, or average the slopes of a region and run an ordinary regression or t-test on them. There are two problems with that.

  1. Thousands of tests. At a 5% level, 5% of the pixels of a region with no trend at all come out "significant". So "8% of the pixels are significant" can be noise. You cannot tell how much of it is noise without more work.
  2. Neighbours are not independent. A drought or a wet year affects a whole landscape at once, so nearby pixels go up and down together. 10,000 pixels then carry far less information than 10,000 independent measurements. A t-test or OLS over all pixels treats them as independent, so its standard error is far too small and its p-value far too small. In the figure above it is off by more than 200 orders of magnitude.

The second problem also inflates the first one. Correlated noise makes the significant pixels come in patches, and the share of significant pixels varies a lot from one map to the next. Over 300 simulated maps with no trend, it was 7.5% on average, and above 16% on one map in twenty (details).

PARTS (Partitioned Autoregressive Time Series, Ives et al. 2021) handles both problems. It asks one question of the whole region, so it runs one test instead of thousands. It also measures how strongly pixels are correlated at each distance and builds that into the test.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Your question Use Where are the pixels with a trend, and how steep is it? A per-pixel test: ar_trend or Mann-Kendall Is this region (a park, a municipality, a basin) greening or browning overall? PARTS (zeit.parts(cube, mask=region)) Do forest, pasture and cropland trend differently? Is each one's trend different from 0? PARTS with classes= Does the trend depend on distance to a road, rainfall, elevation? PARTS with covariates= When did the pixels change, and how abruptly? LandTrendr, BFAST, CCDC

Per-pixel maps and PARTS go together: the maps show where the trends are, and PARTS says whether a regional statement is supported by the data.

Mann-Kendall or the AR(1) trend for pixels?

Both test one pixel's series. Mann-Kendall with Sen's slope is non-parametric and robust to outliers. ar_trend fits a straight line whose errors follow an AR(1) process (this year's error carries over into the next). It is the per-pixel step of PARTS, and its residuals are what PARTS uses to measure the spatial correlation. To test a region, use PARTS, whichever per-pixel map you show.

docs.title: Quick start (5 minutes)
docs.text:
The example builds two small cubes of 30 annual images. One has no trend, the other a trend of +0.002 per year. Both have year-to-year noise that neighbouring pixels share. It needs only zeit and its dependencies, and runs in under 10 seconds.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
import rioxarray  # noqa: F401  (adds .rio to xarray)
import zeit


def correlated_noise(rng, n, range_px):
    """An n x n Gaussian field whose correlation decays as exp(-distance / range_px)."""
    m = 2 * n
    i = np.minimum(np.arange(m), m - np.arange(m))
    cov = np.exp(-np.hypot(i[:, None], i[None, :]) / range_px)
    amplitude = np.sqrt(np.clip(np.fft.fft2(cov).real, 0, None) / m**2)
    z = rng.standard_normal((m, m)) + 1j * rng.standard_normal((m, m))
    return np.fft.fft2(amplitude * z).real[:n, :n]


def make_cube(slope, seed=0, years=30, n=80):
    """`years` annual images of n x n pixels of 30 m: a trend of `slope` per year
    everywhere, plus year-to-year noise that neighbouring pixels share."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    noise = np.stack([np.sqrt(0.8) * correlated_noise(rng, n, range_px=10)   # shared by neighbours
                      + np.sqrt(0.2) * rng.standard_normal((n, n))            # each pixel's own
                      for _ in range(years)])
    values = 0.5 + slope * np.arange(years)[:, None, None] + 0.03 * noise
    cube = xr.DataArray(
        values, dims=("time", "y", "x"),
        coords={"time": pd.date_range("1995-01-01", periods=years, freq="YS"),
                "y": 9_000_000.0 - 30.0 * np.arange(n),
                "x": 500_000.0 + 30.0 * np.arange(n)})
    return cube.rio.write_crs("EPSG:32724")   # a projected CRS: distances in metres


flat = make_cube(slope=0.0)          # no trend anywhere
trend = zeit.ar_trend(flat)          # step 1: each pixel's trend and its p-value
share = float((trend.slope_p < 0.05).mean())
print(f"{share:.1%} of the pixels have p < 0.05")

res = zeit.parts(flat, trend=trend, partsize=1000)   # step 2: the region's test
print(res)

7.5% of the pixels have p < 0.05
PARTS: 6400 pixels, 6 partitions of 1000
spatial correlation: {'function': 'exponential', 'range': 278.47413345311355}
nugget (mean of the partitions): 0.1753

                estimate          se         t        p
coefficient
mean        -8.66074e-05 0.000134584 -0.643521 0.519911

7.5% of the pixels are "significant" although nothing is trending. PARTS reads the cube's correlation (it decays over about 280 m, and 17.5% of the variation is each pixel's own) and finds no evidence of a regional trend: p = 0.52. Now the cube with a real trend:

greening = make_cube(slope=0.002)    # +0.002 per year everywhere
res = zeit.parts(greening, partsize=1000)
print(res.table)

             estimate        se          t             p
coefficient
mean         0.001913  0.000135  14.217136  3.854575e-45

The estimate (0.0019 ± 0.00014 per year) contains the true 0.002, and the test is clearly significant. Without trend=, parts fits each pixel's AR(1) trend itself.

res.table is a DataFrame with one row per coefficient (here only the regional mean) and columns estimate, se, t and p.

docs.title: The guide
docs.text:
• How it works: the four steps with figures. Each pixel's AR(1) trend, the spatial correlation, GLS on random partitions, and the combined tests. Every parameter, with its default. How well it is calibrated.
  • Worked example: 41 years of Landsat over north-eastern Brazil. A window where 26% of the pixels are "significant" but the regional trend is not, then a whole scene with zones by distance to the sea and a covariate.
  • Advanced topics: classes and covariates, large rasters, time and memory, CRS, seeds, sensitivity checks, sub-annual data, and parity with remotePARTS.
  • Interpreting, FAQ and pitfalls: reading the output, a template for reporting, common mistakes, and references.

No code?

Janus, the desktop viewer built on Zeit, runs the same test on an ROI, the visible area, or the classes of a layer, from View → Analysis → Trend test.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: Ives, A. R., Zhu, L., Wang, F., Zhu, J., Morrow, C. J., & Radeloff, V. C. (2021). Statistical inference for trends in spatiotemporal data. Remote Sensing of Environment, 266, 112678. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2021.112678

docs.title: Advanced topics
docs.text:
Classes and covariates, large rasters, time and memory, coordinate systems, seeds, sensitivity checks, sub-annual data, and how Zeit compares with the R package remotePARTS.

The snippets on this page run on the quick start's simulated cube (make_cube from the quick start), here with a trend of 0.001 per year (cube = make_cube(slope=0.001, seed=3)). The outputs shown are from those runs. landcover is a layer of three vertical bands (classes 1, 2, 3) with a 10 × 10 hole of NaN. elevation rises from 0 to 500 from west to east.

trend = zeit.ar_trend(cube)       # fit once, test many times

Fitting the per-pixel trends is often the slow part. Fit them once and pass them with trend= to every parts call.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
classes= takes a (y, x) layer on the cube's grid: integers, floats or strings. Each class gets its own mean trend, tested against 0, and the chi-square test says whether the classes' trends differ:

res = zeit.parts(cube, trend=trend, classes=landcover, partsize=1000)
print(res)

PARTS: 6300 pixels, 6 partitions of 1000
spatial correlation: {'function': 'exponential', 'range': 233.61755655314306}
nugget (mean of the partitions): 0.1945

               estimate          se       t           p
coefficient
class 1.0   0.000937162 0.000124039 7.55537  4.8037e-14
class 2.0   0.000903458  0.00011821 7.64285  2.4595e-14
class 3.0   0.000815076 0.000126075 6.46499 1.09311e-10

chi-square test against a single mean: F = 0.6217, df = (2, 998), p = 0.7148

All three classes trend up (the cube has the same +0.001 everywhere), and they do not differ (p = 0.71), which is the right answer for this cube.

  • Pixels without a class (NaN, None) are left out of the test, like pixels without a trend.

  • Row names are class <value>: class 1.0 for a float layer, class 1 for an integer layer. A layer of names gives readable rows:

    names = {1: "forest", 2: "pasture", 3: "crops"}
named = xr.DataArray(np.vectorize(names.get, otypes=[object])(landcover.fillna(0).astype(int).values),
                     dims=("y", "x"), coords=landcover.coords)
zeit.parts(cube, trend=trend, classes=named, partsize=1000).table

                   estimate        se         t             p
coefficient
class crops    0.000815  0.000126  6.464987  1.093110e-10
class forest   0.000937  0.000124  7.555374  4.803704e-14
class pasture  0.000903  0.000118  7.642851  2.459501e-14

  • Comparing two classes. The chi-square test compares all the classes at once. To test one pair, keep only those two:

    two = landcover.where(landcover.isin([1, 2]))
zeit.parts(cube, trend=trend, classes=two, partsize=1000).p_chisqr      # 0.458

    Several pairwise tests are several tests: correct for multiple comparisons (for example, Bonferroni) or plan the comparisons before looking at the results.

  • Small classes. A class contributes to each partition in proportion to its area. A class with only a few pixels in each partition gets an unstable GLS estimate. Janus leaves out the classes with fewer than 10 pixels per partition on average (n_class < 10 × n / partsize). That is a sensible rule here too: merge or drop such classes.

  • Do classes differ even when none trends? This is common on real data, because the regional signal cancels in the comparison (worked example).

docs.title: Covariates
docs.text:
covariates= takes a dict of (y, x) layers. The design is then an intercept plus one column per covariate, and the chi-square test asks whether the covariates, together, explain the trends:

res = zeit.parts(cube, trend=trend, covariates={"elevation": elevation}, partsize=1000)
print(res)

PARTS: 6400 pixels, 6 partitions of 1000
spatial correlation: {'function': 'exponential', 'range': 233.71829816142463}
nugget (mean of the partitions): 0.2019

               estimate          se        t         p
coefficient
intercept    0.00112549 0.000181167  6.21248 5.566e-10
elevation   -9.9908e-07 5.87339e-07 -1.70103 0.0889893

chi-square test against a single mean: F = 2.836, df = (1, 999), p = 0.08649
  • The elevation coefficient is the change in trend per unit of the covariate (per metre here). The intercept is the trend where the covariate is 0. Centre the covariate (subtract its mean) if you want the intercept to be the trend of an average pixel.
  • Pixels where a covariate is NaN are left out.
  • classes= and covariates= can be combined: one mean per class plus the covariates' slopes. Avoid covariates that nearly repeat the classes. In this cube, the classes are bands from west to east and elevation also grows from west to east, and the run reported rank-deficient covariance, replaced as remotePARTS does next to its chi-square p-value: a sign that the design is nearly collinear.
  • A covariate tests a linear effect. In the worked example, zones by distance to the sea differed (p = 0.028) while distance as a covariate had no linear effect (p = 0.46). Try both forms when the shape of the effect is unknown.

docs.title: A region of interest
docs.text:
mask= restricts the test to a region, for example a protected area, a basin, or the land without water:

roi = elevation < 250                      # any (y, x) boolean layer on the cube's grid
zeit.parts(cube, trend=trend, mask=roi, partsize=1000)

To use a polygon, rasterise it on the cube's grid first (rasterio.features.geometry_mask, or regionmask). Combined with classes=, the mask keeps only the classes' pixels inside the region.

docs.title: Large rasters
docs.text:
zeit.parts loads the cube into memory, fits every pixel's trend, then uses npart × partsize pixels. On a large image:

  • Aggregate first. A trend over decades rarely needs 30 m pixels to be tested regionally. The worked example reads a whole Landsat scene (55 million pixels) at 300 m with resampling="average", about half a million pixels. It reads in under a minute and tests in about 10 seconds per question.
  • Or subsample. npart partitions of partsize pixels only ever use npart × partsize pixels (150,000 with 100 partitions of 1500). Testing a regular subsample (cube[:, ::k, ::k]) gives nearly the same answer for less work. On the real window, the full grid gave p = 0.367 (range 23.0 km), one pixel in 2 × 2 gave 0.361 (23.5 km), and one in 3 × 3 gave 0.352 (23.3 km). Janus reads at most 500,000 pixels, one in k × k beyond that.
  • Fit the trends lazily. zeit.ar_trend(path, chunks="auto") computes block by block for cubes larger than memory, and the per-pixel maps can then be saved with zeit.save_raster. The regional test then runs on a coarser or sampled cube with trend= from the same grid.

docs.title: Time and memory
docs.text:
All the timings below are from the real window of the worked example (482,234 pixels) on a 20-thread CPU.

Tuning. Top left: from 4 to 256 partitions of 1500, the SE barely moves (0.00179 to 0.00171), while the time grows from 0.8 s to 22 s. Top right: 40 partitions take 0.2 s at 500 pixels each, 4.0 s at 1500 and 27.5 s at 3000 (time grows as size³). Bottom left: the SE as the partition size changes. On a simulated map with an exponential correlation it is flat. On the real window, where the correlation is not exponential, it grows with the size. Bottom right: ten seeds give p between 0.35 and 0.37.
  • Time grows linearly with npart and as the cube of partsize: each partition needs a Cholesky factorisation of a partsize × partsize matrix.
  • Memory: each thread holds two partsize × partsize matrices of 8-byte floats: 36 MB per thread at 1500 and 144 MB at 3000. With 20 threads at partsize=3000, that is close to 3 GB, on top of the cube. Lower n_jobs if memory is short.

docs.title: How many partitions?
docs.text: Few. The SE combines the partitions' errors with the correlation between them (step 4). When that correlation is high, as on most real maps, more partitions do not reduce the SE: 4 partitions gave 0.00179 and 256 gave 0.00171. A few dozen partitions are enough to estimate the mean and the cross-partition correlation stably. 100 (Janus's cap) is a comfortable default, and npart=None (all the pixels) mostly costs time.

docs.title: Partition size
docs.text:
On a map whose correlation the model describes well, the partition size does not change the answer (the simulated map in the figure: SE within 2% from 300 to 2000 pixels). On the real window, it did: p = 0.13, 0.27, 0.36, 0.43 and 0.54 at 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 3000 pixels. A correlation that stays high at every distance (a regional signal) is poorly described by an exponential, and larger partitions, which span longer distances, see more of it. Take a size dependence like this as a warning about the model, not as a choice to tune:

  • keep the default 1500 (remotePARTS's authors use 1500 to 3000) rather than picking the size that gives the p you like;
  • report the range of p over a few sizes, as in the worked example;

docs.title: Coordinate systems
docs.text:
• Zeit needs a projected CRS. Distances are taken in the cube's units, and a cube in a geographic CRS is refused:

    ValueError: zeit.parts measures distances in the cube's units: reproject a cube in geographic coordinates first (e.g. zeit.load_raster(..., crs='EPSG:...'))

    Use the UTM zone of the region, or an equal-area projection for a large region. range (given or fitted) is then in metres. A cube without a CRS is taken as it is (distances in its coordinates' units, or in pixels without coordinates). - scaled=True divides each partition's distances by the largest of them, as remotePARTS's default distm_scaled does. The range is then a fraction of that largest distance (0.07 on the example cube), not metres. Use it only to match an R analysis. - Janus accepts a geographic CRS: it projects the coordinates equirectangularly at the region's mean latitude and measures distances in km. Over a region of a few hundred km at low or middle latitudes, its distances are within a few percent of a proper projection's. Its ranges are therefore in km, and Zeit's in the CRS units.

docs.title: Seeds and reproducibility
docs.text:
seed= (default 0) draws both the pixels sampled to fit the correlation and the partitions. The same seed and inputs give identical results, on any number of threads. Another seed gives another draw, and so a slightly different answer: on the real window, seeds 0 to 9 gave p from 0.35 to 0.37 and ranges from 22.5 to 23.7 km. A conclusion that changes with the seed is a borderline one. Report the seed you used, or the range of p over a few seeds.

Zeit's partitions are drawn by its own generator (xoshiro256**), not by R's, so the same seed does not give the same partitions as remotePARTS. Janus uses seed=1.

docs.title: Sensitivity checks
docs.text:
The p-value of PARTS depends on the fitted correlation, so check how much it moves when that correlation changes. On the example cube:

fitted = res.correlation["range"]             # 234 m on this cube
for r in (fitted, 2 * fitted, 4 * fitted):
    print(round(r), zeit.parts(cube, trend=trend, range=r, partsize=1000).table.loc["mean", "p"])

234 2.9916553357856155e-16
467 0.00021874609782779472
935 0.09345842713018826

A longer range means more correlated pixels, so less information, a larger SE and a larger p. Since the fitted range tends to be too short (Is it calibrated?), a result that survives a range 1.5 to 2 times the fitted one is a robust one. Other checks:

Check Call Another shape of correlation correlation="exponential_power" (fits range and shape; res.correlation shows them) A known range (another study, a variogram) range=... in the cube's units A fixed nugget nugget=0.2 (a number instead of "ml") Another partition size partsize=1000, 3000 Other draws seed=1, 2, ... The correlation plot below

docs.title: The correlation plot
docs.text:
The most useful single diagnostic is the one in step 2: the correlation of the pixels' residual series against distance, with the fitted curve. This function draws it from the public API (for time="step" and no harmonics; the residuals are the series minus the fitted line):

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def correlation_check(cube, trend, res, n=600, seed=0):
    """Mean correlation of the pixels' residual series against distance, with the fitted curve."""
    t = np.arange(1, cube.sizes["time"] + 1)                     # time="step"
    fitted = trend.intercept.values + trend.slope.values * t[:, None, None]
    resid = (cube.values - fitted).reshape(cube.sizes["time"], -1)
    xs, ys = np.meshgrid(cube.x.values, cube.y.values)
    ok = np.flatnonzero(np.isfinite(resid).all(axis=0))
    pick = np.random.default_rng(seed).choice(ok, size=min(n, ok.size), replace=False)
    r = np.corrcoef(resid[:, pick].T)
    x, y = xs.ravel()[pick], ys.ravel()[pick]
    d = np.hypot(x[:, None] - x, y[:, None] - y)
    iu = np.triu_indices(pick.size, 1)
    d, r = d[iu], r[iu]
    edges = np.linspace(0, d.max(), 30)
    which = np.digitize(d, edges)
    mid = [d[which == i].mean() for i in range(1, edges.size) if (which == i).sum() > 20]
    mean = [r[which == i].mean() for i in range(1, edges.size) if (which == i).sum() > 20]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
    ax.plot(mid, mean, "o", label="mean correlation of the pairs")
    dd = np.linspace(0, d.max(), 200)
    ax.plot(dd, np.exp(-dd / res.correlation["range"]), label="fitted exp(-d / range)")
    ax.axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("distance (CRS units)")
    ax.set_ylabel("correlation of the residuals")
    ax.legend()
    return fig


correlation_check(cube, trend, res).savefig("correlation_check.png")

What to look for:

  • Dots that fall to 0 along the curve, as in the simulated panel of step 2: the model fits, and PARTS is close to calibrated.
  • Dots below the curve near 0, then on it: a nugget. Expected, and handled in step 3.
  • Dots that stay high at every distance (the real panel): a shared regional signal. Expect the answer to depend on the partition size, and run the sensitivity checks.
  • Dots that stay flat near 0, then drop quickly: a smooth, Gaussian-like correlation, which the exponential describes badly. In a simulated check of this kind, 4 of 10 maps with no trend gave p < 0.01. Try correlation="exponential_power", and be cautious with the result.

docs.title: Sub-annual data
docs.text:
With several observations a year, add harmonics for the seasons and give the slope per year:

mt = zeit.ar_trend(monthly, time="year", harmonics=2)     # slope per year; cos1, sin1, cos2, sin2
res = zeit.parts(monthly, trend=mt, time="year", harmonics=2, partsize=500)   # a small test cube

On a simulated monthly cube (10 years, a trend of 0.003 per year and a seasonal cycle), the mean slope was 0.0031 per year and PARTS found 0.0032 ± 0.0003.

  • Pass the same time, harmonics and period to parts as to ar_trend. parts uses them to compute the residual series for step 2, and with different harmonics the residuals would keep the seasons, which inflates the correlation.
  • The AR(1) model describes month-to-month persistence. Strong seasonality of the noise (more variable in the wet season) is not modelled. For long series, annual composites (a yearly mean, median or maximum) are often the more robust input.

docs.title: Missing observations
docs.text:
• gaps="exact" (the default): a missing year counts, so two observations two years apart are correlated by \(\rho^2\). gaps="ignore": the valid observations are taken as consecutive, as remotePARTS does. With few gaps, the two give nearly the same answer (on the example cube with 30% of the values removed at random: 0.000875 against 0.000869).

  • min_valid: ar_trend leaves a pixel NaN when it has fewer valid observations (at least the design's columns + 2). parts has no min_valid of its own, so fit the trends with it and pass them:

    trend = zeit.ar_trend(cube, min_valid=20)
res = zeit.parts(cube, trend=trend)

    Pixels without a trend (NaN) are left out of the test. - No data values: nodata="auto" reads the files' nodata value. When the files have none and use a fill value (0 over the sea, as in the worked example), mask it (cube.where(cube != 0)) or give nodata=0.

docs.title: Parity with remotePARTS
docs.text:
Zeit implements the methods of the R package remotePARTS (Ives et al. 2021) in Rust, and its test suite compares it with results of remotePARTS 1.0.4 (rust/zeit-core/tests/remoteparts.rs). The GLS, each partition's fit and nugget, and the combined coefficients match to 1e-8. The AR(1) fits match fitAR to about 1e-6. The correlation's range matches fitCor to 1e-5, and the chi-square p-value matches to 1e-6 (the accuracy of the Imhof integration).

remotePARTS (R) Zeit (Python) fitAR, fitAR_map zeit.ar_trend fitCor inside zeit.parts (range=None, fit_n, correlation) covar_exp, covar_exppow correlation="exponential", "exponential_power" distm_scaled scaled=True (False, distances in the CRS units, by default) sample_partitions inside zeit.parts (partsize, npart, seed) fitGLS_partition zeit.parts nugget = NA (ML) nugget="ml" ncross ncross part_ttest, part_chisqr results res.table, res.p_chisqr

The known differences:

  • The random draws. Zeit draws the partitions and the correlation sample with its own generator, so its partitions differ from R's even for the same seed. Expect differences of the size of another seed (above).
  • The nugget of crossed partitions. remotePARTS 1.0.4 computes the correlation between partitions after the first without their nugget. Zeit uses each partition's own nugget. With nugget= fixed, the two agree.
  • Defaults. Zeit's scaled=False (remotePARTS: scaled distances) and gaps="exact" (remotePARTS: gaps ignored). For a like-for-like comparison, use scaled=True, gaps="ignore", time="step".
  • The p floor. As in remotePARTS, the chi-square p-value is reported as at least 1e-6.

docs.title: Interpreting, FAQ and pitfalls
docs.text: How to read the output of zeit.parts, how far to trust it, how to report it, and the mistakes that come up most often.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
PARTS: 482234 pixels, 100 partitions of 1500                       ← (1)
spatial correlation: {'function': 'exponential', 'range': 23039.803728581348}  ← (2)
nugget (mean of the partitions): 0.08176                            ← (3)

              estimate         se        t        p
coefficient
mean        0.00151307 0.00170745 0.886154 0.375536                 ← (4)
  1. Pixels, partitions. The pixels with a trend (and a class, a covariate, inside the mask) and how many of them were used (npart × partsize).
  2. Range, in the CRS units. How far the residuals stay correlated: about 0.37 at one range, 0.05 at three. Compare it with the size of the region. A range close to or beyond the region's size means the region shares one signal, and a regional test then has little power.
  3. Nugget, from 0 to 1. The share of a pixel's variation that is its own. Close to 0: neighbours move as one. Close to 1: the pixels are nearly independent.
  4. Each coefficient: the GLS estimate, its standard error, t = estimate / se, and the two-sided p-value of "this coefficient is 0". For mean, it is the regional mean trend, in the units of the slope (per year with annual data or time="year").

With classes or covariates, the last line is the chi-square test: whether the classes differ, or whether the covariates have an effect, with its mean F and degrees of freedom.

docs.title: What the result means, and what it does not
docs.text:
Result Means Does not mean mean: p < 0.05 The region's mean trend differs from 0. The sign of the estimate says which way it goes. That every pixel, or most pixels, trend that way. mean: p ≥ 0.05 No evidence of a regional mean trend at this level. That there is no trend anywhere. Local trends can be real (a city, a reservoir) and average out, or the shared noise can be too large. a class: p < 0.05 That class's mean trend differs from 0. That it differs from the other classes (that is the chi-square test). chi-square p < 0.05 The classes' mean trends are not all equal, or the covariates have an effect. Which classes differ: look at the estimates, or test pairs (Advanced). per-pixel map: 26% significant 26% of the pixels' own tests have p < 0.05. That 26% of the area is changing, or that the region is.

Statistical significance is not ecological importance. A trend of 0.0005 per year over 40 years is a change of 0.02 in the index. Report the estimate with its interval (estimate ± 1.96 SE), not the p-value alone.

docs.title: How much to trust a p-value
docs.text:
PARTS is far better calibrated than the alternatives, but not perfectly (Is it calibrated?). In simulations with an exponential correlation, it gave p < 0.05 on 14% of the maps with no trend, because the fitted range tends to be too short. With the true range given, it gave 6.3%. In practice:

  • Look at the correlation plot (how). If the curve misses the dots badly, the p-value is approximate.
  • Treat p between 0.01 and 0.05 as weak evidence. It is borderline under the method's own small bias. A p of 0.001 is not.
  • Run the sensitivity checks: a range 1.5 to 2 times the fitted one, two or three partition sizes, two or three seeds (Advanced). A conclusion that holds in all of them is solid.
  • Give range= when an independent estimate exists, for example from a variogram of a longer record or a previous study of the region.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
A template for the methods section:

Per-pixel trends of [index] over [years] were estimated by REML assuming AR(1) temporal autocorrelation. The [mean trend of the region / differences in trends among the N classes / effect of covariate] were tested with PARTS (Ives et al. 2021) as implemented in Zeit [version], with an [exponential] spatial correlation function fitted to the residuals of [1000] randomly sampled pixels (range [r] km), [npart] random partitions of [partsize] pixels, a maximum-likelihood nugget per partition, and [seed]. [The sensitivity of the result to the range, the partition size and the seed was checked.]

And for the results, give the estimate, its SE (or 95% interval), t, df and p, and the share of significant pixels only as a description of the map:

The mean trend was +0.00068 ± 0.00074 yr⁻¹ (t = 0.92, p = 0.36). Trends differed among zones (χ² test, F = 2.00, df = 2, 1498, p = 0.028). Individually, 12% of the pixels had a significant trend (p < 0.05), a figure that does not account for multiple testing or spatial correlation.

The worked example ends with a filled-in version.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Why not just count the significant pixels and compare the share with 5%? Because the share varies a lot from map to map when pixels are correlated. In 300 simulated maps with no trend, it averaged 7.5% and exceeded 16% in one map in twenty. No fixed threshold separates "noise" from "trend" without modelling the correlation, and that is what PARTS does.

Why not run a t-test or OLS on all the pixels' slopes? It treats the pixels as independent and gives p-values that are far too small. On the simulated map on the overview page, it gave p = 10⁻²¹³ with no trend at all. In 300 similar, smaller maps, it gave p < 0.05 in 94% of them.

Why not average the region into one series and test that? That is a valid test, and a good check: on the worked example's window it gave p = 0.094 against PARTS's 0.38. It can only answer "is the region's mean trending?", not compare classes or test covariates. It also throws away power when the correlation is short compared with the region, because it averages away the many independent parts of a large region.

Mann-Kendall or AR(1) for the per-pixel step? PARTS uses the AR(1) trend: its residuals feed step 2, and its slope is the response. For maps of pixels, either is fine. Mann-Kendall with Hamed-Rao is robust to outliers, and the AR(1) trend gives a slope with a standard error.

My region has 10,000 pixels. Is that enough? Yes: 6 partitions of 1500, or more partitions of 1000. With fewer than about 3000 pixels, lower partsize so that there are at least two partitions (parts raises an error otherwise). Very small regions have very little independent information when the range is long.

What partsize should I use? Keep the default 1500 (remotePARTS's authors use 1500 to 3000). If the answer depends strongly on it, the correlation model is the problem, not the size (Advanced).

How many partitions? A few dozen to a hundred. More rarely changes the SE (Advanced).

Can I use it on a geographic (lon/lat) raster? Reproject to a projected CRS first; zeit.parts refuses lon/lat (Advanced).

Can I use 16-day or monthly data? Yes, with time="year", harmonics=2 in both ar_trend and parts (Advanced).

Why does another seed give another p? The partitions and the pixel sample are random. Differences of a few hundredths are normal (Advanced).

Does PARTS find where the trends are? No. It tests statements about the whole region, its classes or its covariates. Maps of the per-pixel trends show where. Read them as a description, not as thousands of verdicts.

Is the result the same as remotePARTS in R? The same method, to numerical precision for the same partitions. The partitions themselves differ (another random generator), so expect differences of the size of another seed (Advanced).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Reporting the share of significant pixels as evidence of a regional trend. The share is a description of the map. Use PARTS for the regional claim.
  • Fill values taken as data. Zeros over the sea or outside the scene, with no nodata declared, are read as observations: a pixel that is 0 in some years and land in others gets a meaningless trend, and the sea enters the test. Mask them (cube.where(cube != 0)) or give nodata=.
  • Pixels with too few observations. parts has no min_valid. Fit the trends with zeit.ar_trend(cube, min_valid=...) and pass them with trend=.
  • Different time or harmonics in ar_trend and parts. parts recomputes the residuals for the correlation with its own arguments. Pass the same ones to both.
  • Mixed slope units. With time="step" (the default), the slope is per time step: per year for annual data, per 16 days for 16-day data. Use time="year" for sub-annual series.
  • Water, urban and bare land in a vegetation trend. They trend for other reasons (reservoirs filling, cities growing). Mask them, or make them classes of their own.
  • A smooth (Gaussian-like) correlation. The exponential misfits it and PARTS can be badly anti-conservative. Check the correlation plot and try correlation="exponential_power".
  • Tuning until significant. Choosing the partition size, the seed or the range that gives p < 0.05 invalidates the test. Fix the settings first, then report the sensitivity.
  • Too many class comparisons. Every pairwise test adds a chance of a false positive. Use the chi-square test first, then a few planned pairs.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Ives, A. R., Zhu, L., Wang, F., Zhu, J., Morrow, C. J., & Radeloff, V. C. (2021). Statistical inference for trends in spatiotemporal data. Remote Sensing of Environment, 266, 112678. doi:10.1016/j.rse.2021.112678
  • Morrow, C. J., & Ives, A. R. remotePARTS: Spatiotemporal Autoregression Analyses for Large Data Sets. R package, version 1.0.4. CRAN
  • Imhof, J. P. (1961). Computing the distribution of quadratic forms in normal variables. Biometrika, 48(3/4), 419–426. doi:10.2307/2332763
  • Wilks, D. S. (2016). "The stippling shows statistically significant grid points": How research results are routinely overstated and overinterpreted, and what to do about it. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 97(12), 2263–2273. doi:10.1175/BAMS-D-15-00267.1

docs.title: How PARTS works
docs.text:
PARTS takes four steps. It fits each pixel's trend, measures how the pixels' noise is correlated at each distance, fits a regression of the trends that knows about that correlation in random partitions of the pixels, and combines the partitions into one test. This page goes through each step with figures from real runs and names the parameter that controls each choice.

flowchart LR
    A["(time, y, x) cube"] --> B["1 · each pixel:<br/>AR(1) trend<br/><code>ar_trend</code>"]
    B --> C["2 · residuals of a sample:<br/>correlation vs distance<br/><code>range</code>"]
    B --> D["3 · random partitions:<br/>GLS of the trends<br/><code>partsize, npart, nugget</code>"]
    C --> D
    D --> E["4 · combine:<br/>t-test per coefficient,<br/>chi-square of the design"]

The figures on this page come from docs/scripts/make_parts_figures.py. It runs zeit.ar_trend and zeit.parts on simulated maps whose true correlation is known, and on 41 annual Landsat composites (1985–2025) of north-eastern Brazil (see the worked example).

docs.title: Step 1: each pixel's trend, with AR(1) errors
docs.text:
For each pixel, zeit.ar_trend fits a straight line through the series. Unlike ordinary least squares (OLS), it does not assume that the errors of successive years are independent:

\[ y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \rho\, \varepsilon_{t-1} + \delta_t \]

\(\beta_1\) is the trend (the slope). \(\rho\) is the AR(1) coefficient: how much of one year's departure from the line carries over to the next year. \(\delta_t\) is new, independent noise. \(\rho\) is estimated together with the line by REML (restricted maximum likelihood), and the t-test of the slope uses it. Successive years that resemble each other carry less information than independent years, so the slope's standard error grows with \(\rho\).

Same slope, different certainty. A real pixel, 41 annual values. OLS and the AR(1) fit give nearly the same slope (−0.0035 and −0.0033 per year). The residuals, however, come in runs of years above and below the line (ρ = 0.59). OLS ignores that and reports p = 0.00023. The AR(1) fit doubles the standard error (0.0016 against 0.0009) and reports p = 0.05.

On a whole image, ar_trend gives a map of every coefficient with its standard error, t and p, plus rho:

A 21 × 21 km window at 30 m. Left: the slope of 481,547 pixels. Middle: the 26% with a significant positive slope and the 0.4% with a significant negative slope at p < 0.05. Right: ρ, the autocorrelation of the residuals (median 0.12; highest along the river and the reservoir).

The middle map is where most studies stop. The rest of PARTS asks whether those 26% add up to a regional trend.

Parameter of ar_trend / parts Default What it does time "step" "step": \(t = 1, 2, \dots\) (remotePARTS's choice), so the slope is per time step, which is per year for annual data. "year": decimal years of the dates, so the slope is per year whatever the cadence. harmonics 0 Pairs of seasonal harmonics (cos, sin) added to the line, for sub-annual data. period None Observations per seasonal cycle when time="step" (taken from the dates when not given). gaps "exact" "exact": two observations \(k\) dates apart are correlated by \(\rho^k\), so a missing year counts. "ignore": the valid observations are taken as consecutive, as remotePARTS does. min_valid (ar_trend only) 0 Pixels with fewer valid observations get NaN. At least the design's columns + 2 are always required.

docs.title: Step 2: how correlated are the pixels?
docs.text:
A drought lowers the index of a whole landscape in the same year. A pixel's departures from its own trend (its residuals) are therefore correlated with those of its neighbours, more strongly the closer they are. PARTS measures that correlation:

  1. It draws fit_n pixels (1000 by default) and takes the residual series of each (observed minus fitted line).
  2. For every pair of them, it computes the correlation of their two residual series and the distance between them.
  3. It fits a curve of correlation against distance through all those pairs. By default the curve is the exponential
\[ c(d) = e^{-d / r} \]

where \(r\) is the range. At a distance of one range, the correlation has fallen to 0.37. At three ranges, it has fallen to 0.05.

Correlation against distance. The grey cloud is every pair of 1000 sampled pixels; the dots are the mean correlation at each distance. Left: a simulated map whose true correlation is 0.8 e−d/450 m (the dashed line). The fitted curve (blue, range 366 m) follows the dots closely. Right: the real window. The correlation drops from 1 to about 0.75 between neighbours, then stays near 0.6 at every distance up to 28 km. The whole window shares one interannual signal (wet and dry years), and no exponential curve fits it well.

Pixel-to-pixel correlation is rarely 1, even between neighbours. Part of each pixel's noise is its own: sensor noise, residual clouds, a field ploughed one year. That part, the nugget (\(\nu\)), is not correlated with anything. PARTS estimates the nugget in step 3, not here. As a consequence, a large nugget pulls the fitted curve down near zero distance, so the fitted range tends to be too short: 366 m instead of the true 450 m in the left panel. Is it calibrated? below shows what this does to the p-values.

Parameter of parts Default What it does correlation "exponential" The curve: "exponential", \(e^{-d/r}\), or "exponential_power", \(e^{-(d/r)^s}\), which also fits a shape \(s\) (1 is exponential, 2 is Gaussian-like, smoother). range None The range, in the cube's CRS units (metres for UTM), when you know it. None fits it to the sample. shape None The shape \(s\) of "exponential_power", when known. fit_n 1000 Pixels sampled to fit the curve (1000 pixels make about 500,000 pairs). scaled False True divides the distances by the largest one in each matrix, as remotePARTS's default distm_scaled does. range is then a fraction of that largest distance, not metres.

docs.title: Step 3: a regression of the trends, in partitions
docs.text:
With the correlation known, the right tool for "what is the mean of these slopes?" is a GLS (generalised least squares) regression. GLS weights the pixels by how much independent information they carry: ten pixels in a tight cluster count for much less than ten pixels far apart. For the slopes \(y\) of \(n\) pixels, the covariance assumed is

\[ \Sigma = \sigma^2 \left[ (1 - u)\, V + u\, I ight], \qquad V_{ij} = c(d_{ij}) \]

where \( u\) is the nugget. The estimate is \(\hat eta = (X^ op \Sigma^{-1} X)^{-1} X^ op \Sigma^{-1} y\). \(X\) is the design: a single column of ones for the regional mean, one column per class with classes=, or a column per covariate.

GLS on a whole image is impossible. For 500,000 pixels, \(\Sigma\) has 2.5 × 10¹¹ entries (2 TB) and inverting it takes on the order of \(n^3\) operations. PARTS therefore draws the pixels into random, non-overlapping partitions of partsize pixels (1500 by default) and fits a GLS in each. A matrix of 1500 × 1500 takes 18 MB and inverts in milliseconds. Each partition also gets its own maximum-likelihood nugget (nugget="ml"), searched between 0.001 and 0.999.

Partitions. Left: three of six random partitions of a simulated 60 × 60 map. Each one is spread over the whole map. Right: the GLS estimate of the mean trend in each of 100 partitions of 1500 pixels of the real window (dots), their mean (blue line), and two 95% intervals. Treating the partitions as independent gives a very narrow interval (SE 0.00002, orange). PARTS gives a much wider one (SE 0.0017, light blue), because the partitions are themselves correlated. Parameter of parts Default What it does partsize 1500 Pixels per partition. remotePARTS's authors use 1500 to 3000. Time grows as partsize³ and memory as partsize² (see Advanced). npart None How many partitions. None uses all the pixels (n // partsize partitions). A few dozen to a few hundred are usually enough (see below). At least 2. nugget "ml" "ml": each partition's maximum-likelihood nugget. A number fixes it for every partition. seed 0 Seed of the pixel sample of step 2 and of the partitions. mask None A (y, x) boolean layer: only these pixels are tested (an ROI, a land mask).

docs.title: Step 4: combining the partitions
docs.text:
The partitions are random samples of the same correlated map, so they are not independent: a pixel in partition 1 has neighbours in partition 2. PARTS therefore cannot treat 100 partition estimates as 100 independent measurements. It combines them in three steps.

  • The estimate of each coefficient is the mean of its partition estimates, \(\bar\beta = \frac1P \sum_p \hat\beta_p\).
  • The correlation between partitions, \(\bar r\), is computed from the fitted covariance (not from the data) for every pair among the first ncross partitions (6 by default, so 15 pairs) and averaged.
  • The standard error combines the partitions' own standard errors \(s_p\) with that correlation:
\[ \mathrm{SE}(\bar\beta) = \frac{1}{P} \sqrt{(1 - \bar r) \sum_p s_p^2 + \bar r \Big( \sum_p s_p \Big)^2 } \]

With \(\bar r = 0\), this is the usual standard error of a mean of independent estimates, which shrinks as \(1/\sqrt{P}\). With \(\bar r\) close to 1, it stays close to a single partition's standard error however many partitions are added. Real maps fall in between, usually closer to 1. That is why more partitions barely change the answer (Advanced).

t = estimate / SE is then compared with a t distribution, giving the t-test of each coefficient: is the regional mean, or this class's mean, different from 0?

With classes or covariates there is a second test, the chi-square test of the design: does the design explain the trends better than a single mean? With classes, that means "do the classes' trends differ?". With covariates, it means "do the covariates have an effect?". Each partition gives an F statistic of its GLS against a single mean. The mean F over the partitions, times npart × df1, is compared with a sum of correlated chi-squares (Imhof's method) whose correlation comes from the same cross-partition step. Like remotePARTS, Zeit reports p-values below 10⁻⁶ as 10⁻⁶.

Parameter / output Default What it does ncross 6 Partitions crossed to estimate \(\bar r\) (all pairs among them). res.table estimate, se, t, p per coefficient (mean, class …, or intercept and each covariate). res.p_chisqr, res.f, res.df1, res.df2 The chi-square test of the design (None without classes or covariates), the mean F, and its degrees of freedom. res.correlation, res.nuggets The function and range used, and each partition's nugget. res.partitions Each partition's coefficients and nugget, one row per partition. res.npart, res.partsize, res.n_pixels What was actually run.

docs.title: Is it calibrated?
docs.text:
A test is calibrated if, when there is no trend, it gives p < 0.05 in 5% of the cases. To check this, the figure script simulated 300 maps of 60 × 60 pixels and 30 years with no trend: a noise correlated over 450 m (range), a nugget of 0.2 and an AR(1) of 0.3 in time. It ran both tests on each map, then repeated with real trends of increasing size.

300 maps with no trend, then 100 maps per trend. Left: the t-test of the pixels' slopes as if independent gives p < 0.05 on 94% of the maps. PARTS gives p < 0.05 on 14% of the maps (6.3% at p < 0.01), and on 6.3% when the true range is given instead of fitted (black outline). Middle: the share of significant pixels on maps with no trend averages 7.5%, exceeds 16% on 5% of the maps and reaches 21.5%. Right: how often each test detects a real trend. The naive test is "significant" whatever the trend; PARTS detects 57% of trends of 0.0005 per year and 90% of trends of 0.0008 per year (the noise SD is 0.03).

What this means in practice:

  • PARTS fixes most of the problem. The naive test rejected a true null on 94% of these maps. PARTS rejected it on 14%.
  • With a fitted range, PARTS is somewhat anti-conservative. Its p-values are a little too small. The cause is the short range of step 2: the median fitted range was 365 m against the true 450 m. With the true range given, the false-alarm rate fell to 6.3%. The fit of the correlation is the same as in remotePARTS (Zeit matches its fitCor), so this is a property of the method, not of this implementation.
  • The model of the correlation matters. When the correlation is not exponential, PARTS can be far off. In a check with noise smoothed by a Gaussian filter (a correlation that is flat near zero, then falls fast), 4 of 10 null maps gave p < 0.01. correlation="exponential_power" found a shape near 2, but it did not fully repair the test. Always look at the correlation plot (step 2) before trusting a p-value.

The practical recommendations that follow (a stricter level, sensitivity checks, giving range= when it is known) are in Interpreting, FAQ and pitfalls.

docs.title: Worked example: 41 years of Landsat
docs.text: A full analysis on real data, from loading the rasters to a sentence you could put in a paper. In a 21 km window of north-eastern Brazil, a quarter of the pixels have a significant greening trend, yet the region as a whole does not. Over the whole scene, zones at different distances from the sea differ in their trends, although none of them differs from 0. Every number below is the output of the code shown.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
41 annual Landsat medoid composites of a vegetation index, 1985 to 2025, over the Sergipe and Alagoas coast (Landsat path/row 215/067, around the lower São Francisco river). One GeoTIFF per year (landsat_medoid_1985.tif … landsat_medoid_2025.tif), in EPSG:4326 (longitude/latitude) at about 30 m, 7478 × 7319 pixels. The sea and the area outside the scene are 0, with no nodata value declared.

To follow along with your own data, you need a folder of annual rasters of one index. Every step below applies unchanged.

docs.title: 1. Load a window, in a projected CRS
docs.text:
PARTS measures distances between pixels, so it needs a projected CRS. In degrees, a step east and a step north are different distances. zeit.parts refuses a cube in a geographic CRS. Read the window in the files' own CRS first, then reproject it to UTM zone 24S (SIRGAS 2000, EPSG:31984) at 30 m:

import numpy as np
import xarray as xr
import zeit

folder = "215_067"                       # the 41 annual GeoTIFFs
west, south, east, north = -38.147498, -9.460877, -37.958851, -9.272231

geo = zeit.load_raster(folder, clip=(west, south, east, north))   # lon/lat, as stored
win = zeit.load_raster(geo, crs="EPSG:31984", res=30)            # SIRGAS 2000 / UTM 24S, 30 m
print(dict(win.sizes))

{'time': 41, 'y': 698, 'x': 694}

Clip first, then reproject

zeit.load_raster(folder, clip=..., crs=...) applies the clip after reprojecting, so the bounds must then be in the target CRS. Giving lon/lat bounds together with crs= fails with "no data in bounds". The two calls above avoid the question.

docs.title: 2. Each pixel's trend
docs.text:
ar = zeit.ar_trend(win)                  # annual data: the slope is per year
valid = ar.slope.notnull()
sig = ar.slope_p < 0.05
print(f"pixels with a trend: {int(valid.sum())}")
print(f"significant up:   {float((sig & (ar.slope > 0)).sum() / valid.sum()):.1%}")
print(f"significant down: {float((sig & (ar.slope < 0)).sum() / valid.sum()):.1%}")
print(f"mean slope: {float(ar.slope.mean()):.5f} per year, median rho: {float(ar.rho.median()):.2f}")

pixels with a trend: 482234
significant up:   25.9%
significant down: 0.4%
mean slope: 0.00128 per year, median rho: 0.12
The maps of ar.slope, of ar.slope_p < 0.05 by sign, and of ar.rho. The figures on these pages were made by docs/scripts/make_parts_figures.py on the window's exact pixel bounds, one column narrower than the rounded bounds above (481,547 pixels), so their numbers can differ from those printed here in the third digit.

A quarter of the pixels are significantly greening. The usual next sentence would be "the region is greening". PARTS tests whether the data support that sentence.

docs.title: One pixel, up close
docs.text:
Why use an AR(1) trend rather than plain OLS? Take a single pixel:

from scipy import stats

series = win.sel(x=606198.55, y=8954073.29, method="nearest").values
ols = stats.linregress(np.arange(series.size), series)
print(f"OLS:   {ols.slope:.5f} +/- {ols.stderr:.5f}, p = {ols.pvalue:.2g}")
one = zeit.ar_trend(series)
print(f"AR(1): {float(one.slope):.5f} +/- {float(one.slope_se):.5f}, p = {float(one.slope_p):.3f}, "
      f"rho = {float(one.rho):.2f}")

OLS:   -0.00350 +/- 0.00086, p = 0.00023
AR(1): -0.00326 +/- 0.00163, p = 0.053, rho = 0.59

The two slopes are nearly the same. With ρ = 0.59, however, the 41 years carry much less independent information than OLS assumes, and the AR(1) standard error is twice as large. zeit.ar_trend also accepts a single series (a list, an array, a pd.Series) and returns a Dataset of scalars.

docs.title: 3. The regional test
docs.text:
res = zeit.parts(win, trend=ar, npart=100)
print(res)

PARTS: 482234 pixels, 100 partitions of 1500
spatial correlation: {'function': 'exponential', 'range': 23039.803728581348}
nugget (mean of the partitions): 0.08176

              estimate         se        t        p
coefficient
mean        0.00151307 0.00170745 0.886154 0.375536

It took 9 seconds on a 20-thread CPU. Reading the output line by line:

  • 482,234 pixels, 100 partitions of 1500. 150,000 pixels were used. The region holds enough for 321 partitions, but 100 give the same answer (Advanced).
  • Range 23 km. The residuals are correlated over distances comparable to the window itself (21 km across).
  • Nugget 0.08. Only 8% of a pixel's year-to-year variation is its own. The rest is shared with its neighbours.
  • mean: 0.0015 ± 0.0017 per year, p = 0.38. The regional mean trend is positive, but its standard error is as large as the estimate. There is no evidence of a regional trend.

How can 26% of the pixels be significant while the region is not? Because the pixels are not 482,234 independent witnesses. The whole window rises and falls together with wet and dry years, so it behaves almost like one very long-lived pixel observed 41 times. A rising mean over 41 years with large shared interannual swings is not strong evidence of a trend.

docs.title: 4. Check the answer
docs.text:
A p-value is only as good as the model behind it. Three checks take a minute.

The spread of the partitions. If the estimate varies a lot from one partition to the next, the regional mean is not well defined:

print(f"spread of the partitions' estimates: {res.partitions['mean'].std():.5f}")

spread of the partitions' estimates: 0.00014

The partition estimates agree with each other (0.00014). The large SE (0.0017) does not come from disagreement between partitions. It comes from what every partition shares: the correlated signal.

The mean series. A simple sanity check is to average the window into one series and test that series' trend. The pixels' correlation then plays no role at all:

mean_series = win.mean(("y", "x")).values
m = zeit.ar_trend(mean_series)
print(f"mean series: {float(m.slope):.5f} +/- {float(m.slope_se):.5f}, p = {float(m.slope_p):.3f}, "
      f"rho = {float(m.rho):.2f}")

mean series: 0.00129 +/- 0.00075, p = 0.094, rho = 0.15

It agrees with PARTS: the same positive trend, not significant. When the whole region shares one signal, as here, this check is close to what PARTS does. When the correlation is short compared with the region, PARTS has much more power than the mean series.

The correlation plot, and sensitivity to the partition size. The correlation plot of this window shows a correlation near 0.6 at every distance, which no exponential curve fits well. When the model misfits like that, the answer depends on the partition size, because a larger partition spans longer distances and sees more of the shared signal:

for size in (500, 1500, 3000):
    r = zeit.parts(win, trend=ar, partsize=size, npart=40)
    print(size, r.table.loc["mean", ["se", "p"]].round(4).to_dict())

500 {'se': 0.001, 'p': 0.1332}
1500 {'se': 0.0018, 'p': 0.3831}
3000 {'se': 0.0025, 'p': 0.5535}

p goes from 0.13 to 0.55, and every one of these values gives the same conclusion. On a simulated map whose correlation is exponential, the partition size does not matter (Advanced). Report a sensitivity check like this one when your correlation plot looks like this.

docs.title: 5. Save the maps
docs.text: zeit.save_raster(ar[["slope", "slope_p", "rho"]], "results/ar")   # slope.tif, slope_p.tif, rho.tif

docs.title: 6. The whole scene: zones and a covariate
docs.text:
Next, a question that needs classes: do the trends differ with distance to the sea? The whole scene is read at 300 m (an average of 10 × 10 pixels), which keeps it to about half a million pixels:

scene = zeit.load_raster(folder, crs="EPSG:31984", res=300, resampling="average")
scene = scene.where(scene != 0)          # 0 is the sea and outside the scene
print(dict(scene.sizes))

{'time': 41, 'y': 731, 'x': 740}

The zones come from the distance of each land pixel to the sea: coastal (under 40 km), transition (40–100 km) and interior (over 100 km). Building them is ordinary raster work, unrelated to PARTS:

Building the land mask, the zones and the distance to the sea 
from scipy import ndimage

# the source's footprint on the UTM grid (a coarse grid of ones, in lon/lat, reprojected)
lon0, lat0, step, nx, ny = -38.416992, -9.137483, 0.000269494585, 7478, 7319
fp = xr.DataArray(np.ones((ny // 10, nx // 10), "float32"), dims=("y", "x"), coords={
    "y": lat0 - step * ny * (np.arange(ny // 10) + 0.5) / (ny // 10),
    "x": lon0 + step * nx * (np.arange(nx // 10) + 0.5) / (nx // 10)})
fp = fp.rio.write_crs("EPSG:4326").rio.write_nodata(np.nan)
inside = fp.rio.reproject_match(scene.isel(time=0)).notnull().values

# water: dark on average, or mostly missing; the sea is the water body in the south-east corner
water = inside & ((scene.mean("time") < 0.05) | (scene.notnull().sum("time") < 30)).values
labels, _ = ndimage.label(water)
rows, cols = np.nonzero(water)
k = np.argmax(rows + cols)
sea = labels == labels[rows[k], cols[k]]
coast_km = ndimage.distance_transform_edt(~sea, sampling=300.0) / 1000.0
land = inside & ~water

like = dict(dims=("y", "x"), coords={"y": scene.y, "x": scene.x})
zones = xr.DataArray(np.where(land, np.digitize(coast_km, [40, 100]) + 1, np.nan), **like)
land = xr.DataArray(land, **like)
coast_km = xr.DataArray(np.where(land, coast_km, np.nan), **like)

The scene has gaps (clouds, water), so pixels need at least 30 valid years. parts does not take min_valid, so the trends are fitted first and passed with trend=:

ar_s = zeit.ar_trend(scene, min_valid=30)

res_mean = zeit.parts(scene, trend=ar_s, mask=land, npart=100)              # the whole land
res_cls = zeit.parts(scene, trend=ar_s, classes=zones, npart=100)           # the three zones
res_cov = zeit.parts(scene, trend=ar_s, mask=land, covariates={"coast_km": coast_km}, npart=100)
print(res_mean, res_cls, res_cov, sep="\n\n")

PARTS: 493932 pixels, 100 partitions of 1500
spatial correlation: {'function': 'exponential', 'range': 117690.30429186746}
nugget (mean of the partitions): 0.3157

               estimate          se        t        p
coefficient
mean        0.000681751 0.000741318 0.919647 0.357759

PARTS: 493932 pixels, 100 partitions of 1500
spatial correlation: {'function': 'exponential', 'range': 117690.30429186746}
nugget (mean of the partitions): 0.3268

               estimate          se        t        p
coefficient
class 1.0   0.000783492 0.000734098  1.06729 0.285845
class 2.0   0.000522905 0.000728719 0.717568 0.473025
class 3.0     0.0006726 0.000726753 0.925486 0.354714

chi-square test against a single mean: F = 2.002, df = (2, 1498), p = 0.02751

PARTS: 493932 pixels, 100 partitions of 1500
spatial correlation: {'function': 'exponential', 'range': 117690.30429186746}
nugget (mean of the partitions): 0.3194

               estimate         se        t        p
coefficient
intercept   0.000146828 0.00104186 0.140929 0.887926
coast_km    4.34878e-06 5.9285e-06 0.733538 0.463232

chi-square test against a single mean: F = 0.6135, df = (1, 1499), p = 0.4435

The three runs took 30 seconds together.

Zones by distance to the sea. Left: coastal (68,696 pixels of 300 m), transition (151,311) and interior (273,925). Right: each zone's GLS mean trend from PARTS with its 95% interval (blue), next to the plain mean of the pixels' slopes with the interval it would have if the pixels were independent (orange, too narrow to see). The arrows give the share of pixels with a significant positive or negative trend in each zone.

Reading the three results:

  • The land as a whole: +0.00068 ± 0.00074 per year, p = 0.36. No evidence of a regional trend, as in the window. Over the whole scene, the correlation reaches much farther (range 118 km) and a third of the variation is each pixel's own (nugget 0.32).
  • Each zone against 0: none of them differs from 0 (p = 0.29, 0.47 and 0.35).
  • The zones against each other: chi-square p = 0.028. The zones' trends differ. The coast trends up more than the transition zone.

How can the zones differ when none of them differs from 0? The regional signal (droughts, wet years) is shared by all three zones. It makes each zone's mean uncertain, but it cancels when the zones are compared. Differences between classes are often much easier to detect than the classes' own trends.

  • Distance to the sea as a covariate: +4.3 × 10⁻⁶ per year per km, p = 0.46. No evidence of a linear effect. The zones differ, but not along a straight line with distance: the transition zone trends lower than both the coast and the interior. The zones capture a non-linear pattern that a single slope misses.

The plain means of the zones (orange in the figure) are quite different from the GLS means (blue), and one of them is even negative (transition, −0.00026). GLS gives less weight to pixels that are redundant with their neighbours, so where big clusters of similar pixels sit matters less. Report the GLS means.

Class names

The zones layer is a float layer (NaN where there is no class), so the rows are class 1.0, class 2.0, class 3.0. An integer layer gives class 1. A layer of strings gives class forest. Select a row with res_cls.table.loc["class 1.0"].

docs.title: 7. Report it
docs.text:
Trends of the annual vegetation index (1985–2025) were fitted per pixel with an AR(1) model by REML and tested regionally with PARTS (Ives et al. 2021), as implemented in Zeit (zeit.parts: exponential spatial correlation fitted to the residuals of 1000 pixels, range 118 km; 100 random partitions of 1500 pixels; maximum-likelihood nugget). The mean trend of the land area was not significantly different from 0 (+0.00068 ± 0.00074 yr⁻¹, t = 0.92, p = 0.36), although 12% of the pixels had a significant trend individually. Trends differed among the three zones of distance to the sea (correlated chi-square test, F = 2.00, df = 2 and 1498, p = 0.028), with no zone differing from 0 on its own (p ≥ 0.29).

The 12% comes from the per-pixel map:

sig, slope = ar_s.slope_p < 0.05, ar_s.slope
for k, name in [(1, "coastal"), (2, "transition"), (3, "interior")]:
    z = (zones == k) & slope.notnull()
    print(f"{name:10s} up {float((z & sig & (slope > 0)).sum() / z.sum()):.1%}, "
          f"down {float((z & sig & (slope < 0)).sum() / z.sum()):.1%}")
on_land = land & slope.notnull()
print(f"all land   up {float((on_land & sig & (slope > 0)).sum() / on_land.sum()):.1%}, "
      f"down {float((on_land & sig & (slope < 0)).sum() / on_land.sum()):.1%}")

coastal    up 24.4%, down 6.0%
transition up 2.3%, down 3.5%
interior   up 10.3%, down 0.4%
all land   up 9.8%, down 2.1%

Interpreting, FAQ and pitfalls has a general template for reporting.

docs.title: The whole script
docs.text: The code on this page, run top to bottom, took 3 minutes on a 20-thread machine, most of it spent reading the rasters. The figures are made by docs/scripts/make_parts_figures.py in the repository (ZEIT_DOCS_PARTS=<folder> python docs/scripts/make_parts_figures.py).
